Therefore, the gifts named in the verse are fitted rather than accidental. The earth can sustain life because the Creator knew every relation on which life would depend. The heavens hold their order because no detail escaped His decree. Perfect knowledge also returns the reader to the coming account. The One to whom all will return already knows what each person did with life and with the world placed at hand. Today, knowledge of nature can grow while awareness of its Lord grows weak. This ending joins them again. To study a thing is to meet more of what God knows fully; to use it well is to answer the wisdom and mercy with which He created it.

---

## Verse 2:30

> ˹Remember˺ when your Lord said to the angels, “I am going to place a successive ˹human˺ authority on earth.” They asked ˹Allah˺, “Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood while we glorify Your praises and proclaim Your holiness?” Allah responded, “I know what you do not know.”

**THE EARTHLY STORY IS ANNOUNCED IN THE HEAVENLY ASSEMBLY**

The surah now opens the account of Adam with a scene before human life on earth: ***“˹Remember˺ when your Lord said to the angels, “I am going to place a successive ˹human˺ authority on earth.” They asked ˹Allah˺, “Will You place in it someone”***. The command to remember makes this more than a report about a distant beginning. It explains the honour, burden, weakness, and hope carried by Adam’s children. God speaks of the human task before Adam appears in the narrative, which means that humanity is not an accident within the earth made in verse 29. The Lord chose an earthly setting and told the angels what He would place there. Ibn ʿAbbās applies the authority first to Adam, created from the earth. Other early readings stress the successive sense: children follow parents, one age replaces another, and the trust continues through changing lives. Another verse tells humanity, (6:165 — **“He is the One Who has placed you as successors on earth and elevated some of you in rank over others,”**) then calls what they receive a test. Succession therefore joins honour to account. No generation owns the earth without limit. Each receives a place already shaped by God, uses it briefly, and leaves both its good and its damage to those who follow.

**AUTHORITY UNDER GOD IS NOT INDEPENDENCE FROM GOD**

The human role includes rule, cultivation, judgment, and carrying out duties in the world, but it does not make people rivals to their Lord. A successive authority acts within a grant and remains answerable to the One who grants it. God loses no power when He gives a creature real choice or a field in which to act. This is why human worth cannot rest in control alone. A ruler can abuse authority, a worker can ruin what was entrusted, and a whole people can hand a wounded land to their heirs. The title is a charge before it is praise. When David receives authority, the command beside it is, (38:26 — **“˹We instructed him:˺ “O David! We have surely made you an authority in the land, so judge between people with truth.”**). Truth sets the limit of rule. The successive sense adds a second limit: present users did not make the earth and will not remain on it. Their claim is temporary, while God’s ownership is complete. Therefore, care for land, life, law, and future people is not an optional kindness added to the human role. It follows from receiving power as a trust. The verse gives dignity without feeding pride, because the same words that raise humanity keep its authority under “your Lord.”

**THE ANGELS NAME THE DARKEST USE OF HUMAN FREEDOM**

The angels continue with one ***“who will spread corruption there”***. Their question is not disobedience. The Quran describes angels as those (21:27 — **“who do not speak until He has spoken, ˹only˺ acting at His command”**). God had spoken to them, and they sought the wisdom in a creature able to spoil the place entrusted to it. Early reports connect their knowledge with creatures who had lived and caused harm on earth before Adam. Other explanations allow that God informed them, or that they understood such risk from the nature of the announced earthly successor. The verse does not choose among these accounts, so its central lesson should not depend on one. What matters is that the danger they name is real. Corruption can enter worship, law, wealth, family, land, and public trust. It is broader than one crime, but every form turns a gift away from the end God set for it. This is why authority and corruption stand in sharp tension. The hand able to plant can burn; the mind able to order can deceive; and the group able to guard peace can turn power into fear. Human honour is not a claim that every human act is noble. It is the grant of a task in which obedience can become deeply noble and revolt terribly destructive.

**SHED BLOOD STANDS OUT WITHIN THE WIDER HARM**

The angels add ***“and shed blood while we glorify Your praises”*** ***“and proclaim Your holiness?””*** Bloodshed is named after corruption as a grave part singled out from the whole. Unjust killing destroys a life God formed, terrorizes those who remain, and often begins new rounds of revenge. The Quran later sets murder beside the worth of rescue: (5:32 — **“murder or mischief in the land—it will be as if they killed all of humanity; and whoever saves a life,”**). That scale shows why blood cannot be treated as one ordinary cost of rule. The angels contrast this danger with their own ceaseless worship. They glorify God with praise, clearing Him of every defect while thanking Him for every perfection. They proclaim His holiness and keep themselves devoted to His command. Their words do not inform God of something He forgot. Nor do they prove that worship consists only in leaving the complex world untouched. Rather, the contrast sharpens the puzzle: a creation free from such revolt already praises God, while the new creature will be able to obey or destroy. The reason for that choice lies beyond what the angels then know. Their question itself models a clean request for understanding. It names the feared harm without accusing the Lord of injustice and places the question inside praise.

**DIVINE KNOWLEDGE HOLDS GOODS THE QUESTION CANNOT YET SEE**

The answer is brief: ***“Allah responded, “I know what you do not know.””*** God does not deny that corruption and bloodshed will occur. Human history makes the angels’ concern painfully visible. The response says that this truth does not exhaust what the human creation will contain or what divine wisdom will bring through it. Adam will soon be taught names that the angels do not know: (2:31 — **“He taught Adam the names of all things, then He presented them to the angels and said,”**). From Adam’s children will come prophets, truthful servants, people who repent, scholars, just rulers, patient carers, and ordinary believers who choose good when evil is open to them. Their worship has a form different from angelic constancy because it rises through desire, trial, error, learning, and return. The point is not that later good makes one unjust death small. God knows each wrong fully and judges it. The point is that finite knowledge may see a true danger without seeing the whole wisdom. This answer teaches humility whenever a divine decree exceeds present sight. Faith need not call harm good or silence a sincere question. It must refuse to infer that no wise end can exist merely because a grave cost is visible. The Lord knows the hidden capacity, the future history, the justice to come, and the mercy by which flawed human beings may fulfil the trust.

---

## Verse 2:31

> He taught Adam the names of all things, then He presented them to the angels and said, “Tell Me the names of these, if what you say is true?”

**HUMAN HONOUR BEGINS WITH RECEIVED KNOWLEDGE**

The answer to the angels begins with an act of teaching: ***“He taught Adam the names of all things”***. Adam’s distinction is not self-made brilliance set against a less able creation. Adam does not teach himself, so the honour itself teaches dependence. The human being who will act on earth is equipped to recognize, name, remember, and communicate about what lies around him. Naming makes shared thought possible. People can distinguish water from fire, one creature from another, a tool from its use, and a person from a crowd. They can pass such knowledge across distance and from one age to the next. This power fits a creature whose children will succeed one another, since each generation need not begin with an empty store of words and skill. Yet the source remains divine. The Quran joins creation and expression in the words (55:4 — **“˹and˺ taught them speech”**). It also opens the message of reading by naming the One who (96:5 — **“taught humanity what they knew not”**). Therefore, knowledge supports the human trust only when it keeps the humility of a learner. If names are used to lie, hide harm, or make pride sound wise, the gift has been turned against its Giver.

**ALL THE NAMES INCLUDE THE COMMON WORLD OF HUMAN LIFE**

Early readers differed over the full range of the names. Ibn ʿAbbās includes the words people use for human beings, animals, sky, earth, land, sea, and even common vessels. Another report from him applies them to Adam’s descendants, while Mujāhid takes them as the names of all things. Some readers understood the objects named to include angels or other rational beings. These views agree on the breadth of the gift even when they locate its main objects differently. The mention of simple household things is especially useful. Human stewardship does not operate only through lofty ideas. It needs words for food, tools, places, bodies, duties, and the ordinary things through which care or harm occurs. The point is not that Adam mastered every later science in its developed form, or that every human child is born knowing a full vocabulary. Each child still begins in need: (16:78 — **“And Allah brought you out of the wombs of your mothers while you knew nothing, and gave you hearing, sight,”**). The gift shown in Adam includes the created capacity and first divine teaching from which human language and learning unfold. This is why education should not despise the ordinary. A true name for a common thing may guard life, preserve craft, or let one person teach another what neither could manage alone.

**THE THINGS ARE PRESENTED SO KNOWLEDGE BECOMES CLEAR**

After Adam receives the names, the scene continues: ***“then He presented them to the angels”*** ***“and said, “Tell Me the names of these”***. The pronoun can point to the beings or things named, while early explanations also speak of the names themselves being displayed with their objects. In either case, this is not a test by which God discovers an answer. He already knows the angels’ measure and Adam’s gift. The presentation makes the difference manifest to the participants and to every later reader. A claim about fitness for the earthly role is answered with a concrete act of knowledge. This matters because hidden ability cannot guide action until it meets a real object. Adam must not merely possess an unseen store; he will soon speak the names. The angels, for all their purity and praise, cannot supply knowledge not given to them. Their limit is not a flaw in God’s making. It shows that each creature has a place and that one excellence does not contain every other excellence. Human beings should learn the same lesson in smaller settings. Strength in worship, memory, craft, leadership, or study never turns one person into the owner of every gift. The scene breaks the habit of ranking worth by the single ability one happens to possess.

**THE CHALLENGE EXPOSES A LIMIT WITHOUT SHAMING THE LEARNER**

The condition closes the address: ***“if what you say is true?””*** Early explanation links it to the implication that a creature at risk of corruption could not be more suited to the earthly task, or that the angels’ existing knowledge made them more fit. Their concern in verse 30 named a real danger, but it did not contain the whole account. God now brings forward one part they did not know. The reason is not to mock a sincere question. It is to teach that a sound conclusion cannot reach beyond the knowledge on which it rests. Verse 32 will show the angels accepting that lesson at once. Their response becomes a model of scholarship rather than a defeat. No creature grasps divine knowledge except what God grants: (2:255 — **“but no one can grasp any of His knowledge—except what He wills ˹to reveal˺. His Seat encompasses the heavens and the earth,”**). Adam’s knowledge therefore cannot support pride either. The same God who taught him can increase, withhold, or test what he knows. Even the Prophet is told to pray, (20:114 — **““My Lord! Increase me in knowledge.””**). The lasting human dignity in this scene lies not in pretending to know without limit, but in receiving truth, naming it faithfully, and using learned power under the wisdom of the One who teaches.

---

## Verse 2:32

> They replied, “Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. You are truly the All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

**GLORY COMES BEFORE ANY DEFENCE OF THE SELF**

The angels answer the test without bluff or excuse: ***“They replied, “Glory be to You!”*** Their first concern is to declare God free from defect, injustice, and error. They do not protect their earlier question by pretending to know the names. They also do not turn their inability into a charge that the task was unfair. Glory places the Lord’s perfection above the limit just exposed in them. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the response as a return from what they had said, which gives it the shape of repentance as well as praise. The angels had named a true danger in human corruption, but now they see that their knowledge did not hold the whole wisdom. They correct their stance at once. This is why their response is stronger than simple silence. Silence could hide pride, fear, or confusion; glorification openly assigns every defect to the creature’s view and none to the Creator. The scene also completes the proper manner of their question in verse 30. They asked within praise, received an answer, and submitted when the answer revealed their limit. The Quran elsewhere says angels are those (66:6 — **“who never disobey whatever Allah orders—always doing as commanded”**). Here obedience includes the humility to let new knowledge change the conclusion formed from what was known before.

**CREATED KNOWLEDGE NEVER ESCAPES THE GIFT OF TEACHING**

Their confession continues: ***“We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. You are truly the All-Knowing, All-Wise.””*** The first half does not mean that the angels know nothing at all. They had already spoken truly about praise, holiness, corruption, and bloodshed. It means that every true thing they know came within a measure God granted. Their knowledge is real, but it is received. The same is true of Adam even though he now knows names they do not. His distinction came through teaching, not through an independent store beyond God’s reach. Therefore, the test produces no ground for pride on either side. It displays different gifts under one Teacher. Human beings meet this truth from birth, study, correction, memory, and loss. A skilled person can forget; a student can learn; and one field can remain closed to a master of another. The Quran tells humanity that it has (17:85 — **“been given but little knowledge.””**). Calling that share little is not contempt for learning. It is the right measure of creaturely knowledge beside the One whose knowledge has no edge. This is why growth in learning should increase care in speech. The more a person sees of a subject, the more clearly he can see what remains beyond him.

**ADMITTING IGNORANCE IS PART OF TRUSTWORTHY KNOWLEDGE**

The angels do not guess in order to preserve status. Their example turns the admission of ignorance into an act of truth and worship. An answer given without knowledge may impress a hearer for a moment, but it breaks the bond between words and reality. In matters of faith, law, safety, medicine, family, or public duty, such false confidence can also harm others. The Quran rebukes those who move from limited knowledge into baseless argument: (3:66 — **“but why do you now argue about what you have no knowledge of? Allah knows and you do not know”**). The difference is not between speaking and never speaking. It is between reporting what one has been taught and claiming what one has not. A faithful learner can say that evidence supports one conclusion, that another matter remains uncertain, or that someone else knows more. This does not weaken authority. It makes authority safe. The angels lose no honour by refusing a false answer; the next verse will let them learn through Adam. Their knowledge can increase because they first tell the truth about its present limit. Today, easy access to many words can make borrowed facts feel like full mastery. This verse restores a clean boundary: use what has truly been learned, seek more where needed, and do not cover a gap with confident sound.

**THE TWO DIVINE NAMES EXPLAIN THE HUMAN CHOICE**

The two divine names close the reply. The All-Knowing possesses what is open and hidden, past and future, whole and detail. The All-Wise places each creature, gift, command, and result in its right setting. Knowledge without wisdom could identify facts without ordering them to a good end; wisdom without knowledge could not judge every factor. In God the two are perfect and inseparable. This directly answers the concern of verse 30. He knew the blood that would be shed, but He also knew Adam’s teachable nature and every faithful life to come. He understood the cost and the good with a fullness unavailable to the angels at that point. The order of the names also matters to the scene. God knew what they did not, and His choice of an earthly successor rested on wisdom rather than mere power. Elsewhere clear commands are joined to the same pair: (24:18 — **“And Allah makes ˹His˺ commandments clear to you, for Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise”**). The believer may not yet see every reason, but trust does not rest on darkness. It rests on the known perfection of the One who commands. The angels’ answer therefore joins humility with confidence: they deny full knowledge to themselves while affirming that complete knowledge and flawless wisdom are exactly where they must be.

---

## Verse 2:33

> Allah said, “O Adam! Inform them of their names.” Then when Adam did, Allah said, “Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?”

**ADAM’S GIFT BECOMES KNOWLEDGE SHARED WITH OTHERS**

The command turns the hidden gift into a public act: ***“Allah said, “O Adam!”*** ***“Inform them of their names.””*** In verse 31 the angels were asked to tell God, who already knew. Here Adam is told to tell the angels, who do not yet know. The change gives knowledge a social purpose. Adam is not taught merely to possess a private rank; what he received now becomes a means by which another creation learns. This is fitting for the father of a race whose members will depend on teaching. A name can pass from teacher to student, parent to child, witness to judge, and one age to the next. The knowledge may begin as a distinction, but its good appears when it is spoken truthfully for those who need it. Early readers therefore saw Adam placed in the role of a teacher before the angels in this scene. The honour does not make him the source of truth. He can inform them because God first informed him. That order protects both learning and teaching from pride. A teacher gives what was received, and a student may hold another gift the teacher lacks. Knowledge remains a trust moving among creatures, while its first source and final measure belong to God.

**ADAM SHOWS THE GIFT RATHER THAN CLAIMING IT**

The verse continues, ***“Then when Adam did, Allah said, “Did I not tell you”***. Adam names what is presented, and the difference announced in the prior verses becomes plain. This matters because a claim of knowledge and the faithful use of knowledge are not the same. The first may be made by anyone; the second answers the object, moment, and hearer with truth. Adam’s performance shows the capacity God gave him. It also answers the angels without insulting their worship or erasing their own excellence. They lacked these names because they had not been taught them, and they had already confessed that limit. Now they learn. Human beings should not turn this event into a general right to boast over angels, much less over other people. Adam’s honour rests in a gift he obeyed God by using. The same pattern governs later learning. Memory without truth can mislead, speech without duty can manipulate, and skill without obedience can serve corruption. The reason knowledge supports human authority is that it can identify what exists, distinguish duties, guide action, and be passed on. When it is used to blur names and hide reality, it undermines the very trust this scene establishes.

**THE UNSEEN EXCEEDS EVERY CREATED FIELD OF VIEW**

The reminder is ***“that I know the secrets of the heavens”*** ***“and the earth, and I know what you reveal”***. The secrets are the unseen realities hidden from created senses and inference. They include what has not yet occurred, what lies outside a creature’s place, and what no one could know unless God disclosed it. Heaven did not make the unseen open to the angels merely because they dwell in a higher realm, just as life on earth will not make it open to Adam’s children. Each creature sees from a given field; God knows heaven and earth without boundary. Another verse states, (35:38 — **“Indeed, Allah is the Knower of the unseen of the heavens”**) and then joins that knowledge to what hearts hide. This explains how God could answer the angels’ concern with certainty. He knew not only the violence that would occur but every prophet, act of justice, repentance, discovery, prayer, and mercy that no angel had yet seen. The unknown future was not unknown to Him. Therefore, the words do not tell believers to call every mystery solved. They teach where complete knowledge rests. Study can widen a human field, and revelation can disclose what senses cannot reach. Neither turns a limited knower into the Knower of all secrets.

**OPEN SPEECH AND HIDDEN MOTIVE STAND UNDER ONE KNOWLEDGE**

The final words are ***“and what you conceal?””*** God knew the angels’ spoken concern and whatever had not been spoken. Early explanations differ about the concealed matter. Some link it to an inward claim attributed to the angels about their greater knowledge or rank. Others link it to the pride Iblīs kept hidden, which the next verse will expose when he refuses the command concerning Adam. Ibn ʿAbbās also relates the words to what would be shown and withheld in the coming act of obedience. The verse itself leaves the object broad, so one disputed report should not be made its only sense. Its certain claim is wider: disclosure and concealment are equally open to God. The Quran tells every person, (3:29 — **“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Whether you conceal what is in your hearts or reveal it, it is known to Allah.”**). This knowledge reaches beyond polished speech to the motive beneath it. A public act of praise cannot hide pride, and an unseen sincere act cannot be lost. The effect should be both fear and comfort. Hidden sin needs repentance even when reputation remains clean; hidden faith and effort remain known even when no human being thanks them. In this scene, divine knowledge closes the gap between appearance and reality before the command to prostrate makes each inward stance visible through action.

---

## Verse 2:34

> And ˹remember˺ when We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam,” so they all did—but not Iblîs, who refused and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful

**HONOUR GIVEN UNDER A DIVINE COMMAND**

Adam does not demand that the angels bow to him. The order comes from above them both: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We said to the angels,”*** ***““Prostrate before Adam,””***. His knowledge had shown his gift. The angels must now give him the honour God has assigned. Qatādah makes the point clear: they obeyed God and bowed before Adam. Because God Himself commanded it, the act could not mean treating Adam as another god. Worship remained the Creator’s right. They bowed to honour Adam as their Lord had told them to do. The other account shows that none held back: (15:30 — **“So the angels prostrated all together—”**). Their concern about human bloodshed did not make them resist the command. They had owned the limits of what they knew. Now they acted on that truth. This matters because faith must do more than agree that God knows best. It must yield to His will when He gives someone else a higher rank. Adam’s gift and the angels’ act alike come under the rule of one Lord.

That ancient act does not give Muslims permission to prostrate before a ruler, teacher, or saint. Earlier laws allowed a bow of respect, as the story of Joseph shows: (12:100 — **“and they all fell down in prostration to Joseph,”**). That act was allowed then. It is not a right passed down to all later peoples. In the account of Muʿādh’s return from Syria carried by Ibn Mājah, the Prophet forbade him to bow in this way. An act meant to show respect need not be an act of worship. But that does not make every such act lawful. The law now bars this bow to a human being, even as a mark of respect. Its use in Adam’s story was lawful because of the command given there, not because creatures may claim it for themselves. The Quran directs worship to the Maker rather than His signs: (41:37 — **“but prostrate to Allah, Who created them ˹all˺, if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺”**). Adam’s rank was a gift. No later spiritual leader can turn that gift into a demand that followers prostrate before him.

**THE EXCEPTION REVEALS MORE THAN A DIFFERENT ORIGIN**

The angels do not delay: ***“so they all did—but not Iblîs,”***. The link between the order and the act shows their will to obey. Iblīs alone holds back. Being among the angels does not make him one of their kind. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās places him in a group of angels called jinn. The other early reading, held by al-Ḥasan, denies that he was ever an angel. The latter view is followed here because he is plainly identified as one of the jinn: (18:50 — **“who was one of the jinn, but he rebelled against the command of his Lord.”**). He stood with the angels and shared their command, though he was of another kind. In Muslim, ʿĀʾishah reports that the Prophet described angels as made from light and jinn from smokeless fire. He therefore cannot claim that the order did not bind him. God later asks him why he failed to obey when commanded. His place among the angels gave him no right to refuse.

The words ***“who refused”*** describe his choice, and ***“and acted arrogantly,”*** show the pride that drove it. The order was clear, and he had the strength to bow. He considered himself above the one being honoured. His own words make his claim plain: (7:12 — **““I am better than he is: You created me from fire and him from clay.””**). Qatādah connects this pride with envy of Adam’s honour. Fire and clay became an argument only because Iblīs wished his own origin to overrule God’s choice. The fault thus went deeper than a wrong view of fire and clay. He would obey God only if the command agreed with his own sense of rank. The angels had accepted that knowledge might lie beyond them; he treated his limited judgement as final. The contrast is exact. They lost no honour by bowing. His pride cost him the rank he hoped to keep. Learning, worship, or honoured company cannot protect a person who uses those gifts to reject a truth because another person receives its benefit.

**A REFUSAL THAT BECAME REBELLION**

The judgement follows: ***“becoming unfaithful”***. This does not mean that every failure to obey has the same character as Iblīs’s act. The account joins his refusal to arrogance and to a challenge against the command itself. Ibn ʿAbbās explains the end as his becoming a disbeliever through that rejection; another transmitted explanation relates it to what God had already known of him. These readings differ over the time described. Neither means that God learned something new about him when he refused. His act brought his hidden state to light. Because he set himself against the Lord’s judgement, the refusal was an act of unbelief. Adam will also disobey, but his response will be confession and repentance rather than a claim that God’s judgement is wrong. The two acts are not the same. That distinction prevents the warning from turning into despair for every sinner. Past worship is no excuse for refusing a known truth now. God’s reply strips him of the rank he claimed: (7:13 — **“You are truly one of the disgraced.””**).

In Muslim, Abū Hurayrah relates the Prophet’s description of Satan’s tears when a person recites a verse of prostration and bows down. The lament turns on the contrast: the human being obeyed and has Paradise, while Satan refused and has the Fire. The report links that first refusal to an act of worship still performed. It does not ask a believer to recreate the angels’ gesture toward Adam. It points instead to obedience when God calls His servant to bow. Pride seeks to rise above others. In worship, the body that might be used to show strength is brought low before God. The Quran places the angels among those who bow to God: (16:49 — **“as do the angels—who are not too proud ˹to do so˺”**). Their act shows why awe of God must reach beyond a feeling in the heart. It takes the form commanded by God. Two paths stand apart: to receive honour and obey, or to claim it against the Giver’s will.

---

## Verse 2:35

> We cautioned, “O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat as freely as you please, but do not approach this tree, or else you will be wrongdoers.”

**A HOME SHARED BEFORE THE EARTHLY JOURNEY**

A wife and a home follow the honour shown to Adam. God addresses him directly: ***“We cautioned, “O Adam!”*** ***“Live with your wife in Paradise”***. The welcome includes his wife; she is not outside the gift or merely watching him receive it. Both belong in this dwelling. The Quran later recalls humanity’s shared beginning in a single soul, (4:1 — **“and from it He created its mate, and through both He spread countless men and women.”**). Marriage thus enters the account before life on earth begins. It provides companionship and a shared dwelling under God’s care. The address first names Adam, then joins his wife to him. The commands about eating and the tree will address them both. This change matters because each is allowed the food and each is bound by the limit. Nor does being told to live in a place mean owning it without condition. A host may grant a guest the use of a home without giving away the house. Adam receives a dwelling from its Lord, and must live there under that Lord’s word.

Two readings of this dwelling need to be kept distinct. The heavenly-Paradise reading takes it as the Garden later promised to believers. The earthly-garden reading objects that the blessed will never be made to leave Paradise: (15:48 — **“nor will they ever be asked to leave”**). Yet that promise concerns their final reward, not every earlier entry into the Garden. Adam was there under a test, before the earthly life already announced for him. His stay need not carry all the terms of the final reward. The heavenly reading is adopted here. The definite reference to Paradise points to the known Garden, and the account of Adam’s entry and exit fits that sense. In Muslim and al-Nasāʾī, Abū Hurayrah reports that the Prophet named Friday as the day Adam was created, admitted to Paradise, and taken out of it. The report fixes those events without supplying a map of the unseen. The account requires belief in the dwelling God granted, not guesses about a route, an earthly site, or the length of every stage.

**FREE ENJOYMENT DOES NOT REMOVE EVERY LIMIT**

Permission is broad: ***“and eat as freely as you please,”***. Ibn ʿAbbās explains this as ample living, with room to eat where and when they wished. The food is not described as a scarce ration earned through hard work. It is ready for their use and brings no strain. A second account spells out the ease: (20:118 — **“Here it is guaranteed that you will never go hungry or unclothed”**) and (20:119 — **“nor will you ˹ever˺ suffer from thirst or ˹the sun’s˺ heat.””**). Hunger, lack of clothing, thirst, and heat will belong to the burden of earthly life, not to this welcome. The command to eat therefore gives leave; it does not force them to keep eating. The words about their own wish show that freedom plainly. Mujāhid’s gloss of food taken without account also belongs within this broad grant. It cannot cancel the tree’s stated exception. God gives much and withholds one thing. Since the allowed food is so plentiful, need cannot make the forbidden tree their only means of life. The setting makes the test clear: enjoyment of a gift must not be confused with freedom from the Giver’s rule.

The limit is stated before either person crosses it: ***“but do not approach this tree,”***. The warning reaches the approach to the tree, not only the act of eating. This shuts the path by which desire might become an excuse to take what was withheld. The command also points to a known tree. Its identity was clear to the two people addressed, even though its kind is not given to later readers. Reports name wheat, a vine, or a fig tree, but those differing names cannot all settle the question. No detail needed for obedience is missing. Adam and his wife knew what to avoid; later readers know that a clear limit was set. The story does not teach that the tree had an evil power of its own. Its place in the test came from the command concerning it. That is why curiosity about its species cannot replace attention to the warning. The useful knowledge is where God set the boundary and why a servant must not treat wide permission as permission without end.

The consequence is made explicit: ***“or else you will be wrongdoers.””***. The final clause ties wrong to crossing the limit; it is not merely advice about which food tastes best. Ibn ʿAbbās explains the harm as harm done to themselves. They would put their own good at risk by turning from the One who had provided it. Their later confession repeats that judgement: (7:23 — **““Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves.”**). This link keeps the story from being read as a contest between a harsh command and a harmless appetite. The command protected their welfare within a gift already full of ease. It also joined them in responsibility. Both had heard the warning, and both would need to return to God after the lapse. Neither can be excused simply by pointing to the other. The distinction from Iblīs remains important: a fall into wrong need not become a defence of wrong. Here the danger is named in advance so that the two may keep clear of it, not so that mercy may be closed to them forever.

---

## Verse 2:36

> But Satan deceived them—leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in, and We said, “Descend from the heavens ˹to the earth˺ as enemies to each other. You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay.”

**A PROMISE OF SAFETY USED TO BRING ABOUT LOSS**

Satan attacks the trust on which life in the Garden rests: ***“But Satan deceived them”***. The one who refused to honour Adam now seeks to turn him from God’s word. Ibn ʿAbbās explains the act as leading the pair astray. The wording carries the sense of a slip, while another recitation brings out their removal from the Garden. These are linked events: the lapse becomes the means of losing their place. The fuller account shows how the trap worked. Satan offered lasting life and rule: (20:120 — **“Shall I show you the Tree of Immortality and a kingdom that does not fade away?””**). He then hid his hostile purpose under an oath: (7:21 — **“And he swore to them, “I am truly your sincere advisor.””**). The lure was not presented as ruin. It was presented as a way to keep and enlarge the good they already had. That is why the known command mattered more than the voice claiming to help. A pledge of goodwill could not change what God had forbidden. The warning reaches any claim that a clear wrong will secure a person’s future. The promised gain may be the very means by which present good is lost.

The result was ***“leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in”***. What they lost included ease, shelter, and the food freely given to them. The other account adds the shame that followed eating: (7:22 — **“their nakedness was exposed to them, prompting them to cover themselves with leaves from Paradise.”**). The verse attributes the fall to Satan because his deceit brought about their lapse. It does not grant him power to overrule God or to drive people from Paradise on his own. The command to leave comes from God in the next clause. Cause and authority must therefore be kept apart: Satan tempted, the pair ate, and their Lord judged. Nor does naming the tempter remove their own part in what happened. Satan’s later address to those who follow him states the limit of his power: (14:22 — **“I only called you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me; blame yourselves.”**). The parallel concerns his method, not an equal judgement upon Adam and those later followers. Adam will repent. His enemy’s role explains the danger; it does not turn an act done through deception into an act for which no one must seek pardon.

**THE CONFLICT CONTINUES AFTER THE CHANGE OF DWELLING**

The divine order is ***“and We said, “Descend from the heavens ˹to the earth˺”***, followed by ***“as enemies to each other.”***. The address is plural. Its reach is wider than a private quarrel between husband and wife. Mujāhid explains the enmity as that between Adam and his offspring, and Iblīs and his offspring. The warning thus follows the human family into its new life. Another reading extends the address through Adam and his wife to the strife that will arise among their children. These senses can meet: the enemy who seeks human ruin also encourages people to wrong one another. But the sentence is not an order to hate a spouse or a neighbour. It describes a danger to be faced, not a licence to produce more harm. The Quran gives the proper response to the chief enemy: (35:6 — **“Surely Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy.”**). Since Satan has already offered ruin in the dress of sincere advice, treating him as an enemy means refusing his counsel rather than merely speaking against him. The setting changes from Paradise to earth; the need to hold to God’s word does not.

**SUSTENANCE IS GRANTED WITH A TERM ATTACHED**

Even the order to leave contains a gift: ***“You will find in the earth a residence”*** ***“and provision”***. Earth is not described as a place where God will give them nothing. It has room for life, food, clothing, and the means of meeting human needs. Abū al-ʿĀliyah connects the residence with the earth made ready as a resting place. Another transmitted reading, from al-Suddī, includes the graves in which people will lie. The broader meaning can hold both stages. Earth receives human beings in life and in death, but neither state is their final end. The parallel account joins the stages: (7:25 — **““There you will live, there you will die, and from there you will be resurrected.””**). Provision concerns what can be used during that earthly course. It is real good, not an illusion to be despised because it passes away. Yet it is not the ease they have left. Food must be sought, bodies must be sheltered, and life must be lived amid trial. God has prepared the means without promising that the path through them will be free of toil or conflict.

The limit is ***“for your appointed stay.””***. Al-Suddī takes the end of enjoyment as death; Mujāhid relates the term to the Resurrection, when the world’s course ends. One concerns each person’s span, the other the span of earthly life as a whole. Neither makes the earth a lasting home. The fall also does not place an inherited sin upon every child of Adam. The rule of personal responsibility remains: (6:164 — **“No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another.”**). Later people share the setting of toil and temptation, not a guilt charged to them for an act they did not commit. Adam himself is not left beyond mercy. The Quran says, (20:122 — **“Then his Lord chose him ˹for His grace˺, accepted his repentance, and guided him ˹rightly˺”**). His accepted return to God does not cancel the earthly task announced before the lapse. This is why earthly life cannot simply be called proof that its people have been cast off. It is the place of their appointed trial, with provision for the journey and guidance still to come. The finite stay gives urgency to that guidance; it does not make the stay meaningless.

---

## Verse 2:37

> Then Adam was inspired with words ˹of prayer˺ by his Lord, so He accepted his repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful

**THE WAY BACK IS ITSELF A GIFT**

Forgiveness begins here with help given to the one who has fallen: ***“Then Adam was inspired with words”*** ***“˹of prayer˺ by his Lord,”***. Adam does not find a path back by denying the command or defending what he did. His Lord teaches him how to turn. The source of the words is therefore part of their meaning. The Lord who judged the lapse has not ceased to care for the servant. Al-Ḥasan explains the receiving of these words as learning them and acting upon them. They are not sounds placed on the tongue while the heart keeps its former stance. Adam takes them as the truth about himself and his need. Another recitation makes the words the subject, as words coming to meet Adam. The two readings draw attention to both sides of the event: help reaches him, and he receives it. This is why repentance cannot become a ground for self-praise. Even the resolve to return is a mercy. The same order appears in a later account: (9:118 — **“Then He turned to them in mercy so that they might repent.”**). Divine kindness opens the way; the servant must actually walk it. Adam’s shame is thus met with teaching, not with a command to invent a cure beyond his reach.

The prayer identified by Mujāhid and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr gives the words their clearest Quranic form: (7:23 — **““Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be losers.””**). Its parts belong together. The pair address God as their Lord, own the wrong, seek pardon and mercy, and admit what loss would mean without them. They do not offer the serpent, the tempter, or the tree as an excuse that clears their own act. Nor do they claim that their earlier honour puts God under a debt to forgive them. The prayer speaks in the plural, which also prevents the mention of Adam alone here from excluding his wife from repentance. Both had faced the command; both confess their need. The same truthful approach appears in Moses’ plea: (28:16 — **““My Lord! I have definitely wronged my soul, so forgive me.””**). Jonah likewise joins praise of God to an admission of wrong: (21:87 — **“Glory be to You! I have certainly done wrong.””**). The situations differ, but the prayers share a refusal to blame God for the servant’s fault. These are words of worship because they place greatness and need where they belong. Their force lies in a true return of heart and conduct, not in a claim that uttering a formula makes continued wrongdoing safe.

**PARDON FROM THE LORD WHO INVITES RETURN**

The answer is not left uncertain: ***“so He accepted his repentance.”***. God accepted the return that He had enabled. The prayer did not merely bring Adam relief from shame while leaving his standing with God unchanged. It brought pardon. In an account from Ibn ʿAbbās carried by al-Ḥākim, Adam asks whether repenting and putting matters right will lead to his return to Paradise. The answer is yes. That account carries hope within repentance, not a right to go on sinning because a return has been promised. The turn has to be real. Regret for the wrong must lead to leaving it and resolving not to resume it. The Quran links the two: (25:71 — **“And whoever repents and does good has truly turned to Allah properly”**). This also explains why pardon need not erase every worldly effect of an act. Adam’s earthly life will still follow, but it does not mean his prayer was refused. The present verse states the acceptance plainly. The general promise extends beyond the first human being: (4:110 — **“Whoever commits evil or wrongs themselves then seeks Allah’s forgiveness will certainly find Allah All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”**). A past fault need not remain a person’s final state. The door opens through seeking God’s forgiveness, not through declaring the fault harmless or calling despair a form of piety.

The closing names explain the answer: ***“Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance,”***, ***“Most Merciful”***. The Arabic expression behind repentance concerns a return. For the servant it is a turn away from sin toward obedience. When used of God here, it means His gracious turn toward the servant, not repentance from any wrong of His own. The name expresses His repeated acceptance of those who return and the great number of people He pardons. Mercy appears at both ends of Adam’s change: God supplies the words, then accepts the prayer made with them. A later verse joins these truths to His knowledge: (42:25 — **“He is the One Who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons ˹their˺ sins. And He knows whatever you do”**). Since He knows what people do, no outward show can force an acceptance that the heart and conduct deny. Yet His knowledge is not a reason for the sincere sinner to hide. Adam’s fault was already known when the words were given. The right response to that knowledge is the honest confession the verse teaches. No human being owns this pardon or can sell access to it. A teacher may show the prayer and call a person to repent; the Lord alone forgives the sin. His mercy makes return possible without making wrongdoing right.

---

## Verse 2:38

> We said, “Descend all of you! Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows it, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**PARDON DOES NOT CANCEL THE EARTHLY CALLING**

After the acceptance of repentance, the order to leave is heard again: ***“We said, “Descend all of you!”***. Its return does not mean that Adam’s prayer failed. The earlier command described the place of settlement and the hostility he would face. This one sets out the guidance by which life there must be lived. The order is repeated because each statement explains a different side of the descent. There is no need to invent two journeys from two separate gardens to account for the repetition. Earth was already named in the first command. More deeply, the earthly calling preceded the lapse itself: (2:30 — **““I am going to place a successive ˹human˺ authority on earth.””**). Forgiveness restores Adam’s relation to his Lord without removing that calling. The whole account holds these truths together. Sin has consequences, pardon is real, and God’s purpose is not overturned by the tempter’s scheme. Since more than one person is addressed, the promise reaches beyond Adam’s private future. It opens the course of human life in which Adam’s children will need the same Lord’s teaching.

**TEACHING GIVEN FROM GOD REQUIRES A HUMAN RESPONSE**

The promise begins, ***“Then when guidance comes to you from Me,”***. The source matters: the guidance is from God, not a rule Adam’s children devise simply to comfort themselves in exile. Abū al-ʿĀliyah explains it through prophets, messengers, clear signs, and plain teaching. Al-Suddī points to God’s revealed Book. The readings agree because a messenger brings the Book and teaches what the Lord asks of His people. God does not provide earth as a home and then leave its people with no word about their end. The Quran describes the wide reach of this gift: (16:36 — **“We surely sent a messenger to every community, saying, “Worship Allah and shun false gods.””**). The guidance names both the Lord to worship and the false objects to refuse. It is therefore more than skill at finding food or building a house. Those skills sustain earthly life; revelation teaches how that life should answer to its Maker. The work of the messengers also makes the demand clear, (4:165 — **“so humanity should have no excuse before Allah after ˹the coming of˺ the messengers.”**). Receiving such teaching is a mercy that brings responsibility with it.

The condition is ***“whoever follows it,”***. The difference between hearing and following is the response to what has been heard. The guidance must be believed where it tells the truth, obeyed where it commands, and heeded where it warns. Otherwise, its arrival alone would make every hearer safe, and the next verse’s warning to those who reject it would lose its force. Because the promise is tied to following, the arrival of guidance calls for a choice rather than granting safety without one. This does not make guidance a prize earned without God’s help. The preceding verse has already shown that even the way to repent is taught by Him. It means that His gift is received through a real response. The parallel promise states, (20:123 — **“whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray ˹in this life˺ nor suffer ˹in the next˺”**). Ibn ʿAbbās explains that promise as freedom from being led astray in this life and from misery in the Hereafter. The two stages are joined. The path is not merely admired now and then recovered at death; it is followed through the life for which the direction was given.

**SAFETY CONCERNS THE END, NOT A LIFE WITHOUT ALARM**

Those who follow are promised that ***“there will be no fear for them,”***. Fear looks toward a harm still ahead. Ibn Zayd applies the assurance to what lies before a person after death, the great concern at the end of earthly life. The follower of guidance will not be abandoned to the punishment from which the message warned him. This cannot reasonably mean that a believer never feels alarm during the present trial. The Quran says of a prophet, (20:67 — **“So Moses concealed fear within himself”**). That fear did not place Moses outside divine guidance. Nor does fear of God contradict the promise. Reverence moves a person to obey; the promised safety is the outcome of that path, not a ban on every feeling along it. This is why the assurance must not be used against those in grief or danger. Being frightened does not disprove a believer’s faith. The question settled here is where following God’s guidance leads, beyond the threats that earthly life contains.

**THE LOSS LEFT BEHIND WILL NOT RULE THE FINAL HOME**

The promise also reaches backward: ***“nor will they grieve”***. Grief concerns a good lost, a hurt endured, or a hope that was not fulfilled. At the final home, such loss will no longer govern the life of those admitted to God’s mercy. Their own words make that end clear: (35:34 — **““Praise be to Allah, Who has kept away from us all ˹causes of˺ sorrow.”**). This is more than being spared a future threat. It is release from the sorrow carried out of the past. Yet the assurance does not require a cold heart in this world. Jacob could turn his sorrow toward God and remain faithful: (12:86 — **““I complain of my anguish and sorrow only to Allah,”**). The promise gives sorrow an end, not a verdict that every mourner has strayed. Fear and grief thus span the two directions in which distress reaches. God’s guidance leads beyond both. Adam’s descendants begin on earth with a warning about their enemy, but they are not sent without a way home. The closing assurance supplies the hope that makes their earthly duty something more than the management of loss.

---

## Verse 2:39

> But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.”

**REJECTION IS NOT ANOTHER WAY OF FOLLOWING**

The promise of safety has a stated opposite: ***“But those who disbelieve”*** ***“and deny Our signs”***. These words describe a response to the guidance just promised. Ibn ʿAbbās connects the denial with the scripture and the messenger sent with it. The signs are not empty labels for private feelings. They are the evidence, revealed words, and clear teaching by which God makes His message known. To deny them is to reject what they establish. Disbelief can take the form of refusing a command or treating a true message as false. It need not always arise from a lack of information. Pharaoh’s people supply a later example: (27:14 — **“And, although their hearts were convinced the signs were true, they still denied them wrongfully and arrogantly.”**). That passage concerns their own case, but it shows why knowledge and submission cannot be treated as the same thing. Because pride may resist a truth already recognized, the cure is not always another fact. The will to obey also matters. This is why the warning follows guidance rather than replacing it. God shows the way and states the result of rejecting it. The two verses do not offer two equally sound paths with different outward customs.

**THE WARNING MUST BE KEPT WITHIN ITS STATED TERMS**

A person who stumbles and repents is not described by this verse merely because a fault occurred. Adam’s accepted return has just made that distinction plain. The threat is for those who reject the truth, not for every person who has done a wrong. A reader also cannot know each person’s heart or what teaching truly reached him. God sets a rule for His judgement: (17:15 — **“And We would never punish ˹a people˺ until We have sent a messenger ˹to warn them˺”**). Since God judges each case justly, His broad warning grants no right to declare the fate of each person. Its seriousness remains intact without such claims. The threat concerns those who die in unbelief. It does not shut the way back before death. The call to return is clear: (39:53 — **“Do not lose hope in Allah’s mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins.”**). Hope does not cancel the threat, because repentance means turning back rather than insisting that God’s signs are false. The difference between Adam and Iblīs has already shown the two movements. One owns the wrong and receives mercy; the other makes pride a defence of refusal.

**AN ABIDING HOME, NOT A PASSING ENCOUNTER**

Those described ***“will be the residents of the Fire.”***. These are its people, bound to it as their lasting home. The distinction matters because a believer may be punished for a sin without being condemned to stay forever. Muslim carries Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī’s report that the Prophet spoke of two groups: the Fire’s abiding people and others punished for their sins. The latter are reduced to a state like charcoal before leave for intercession is granted. The report therefore does not promise an exit to those whom this verse describes as remaining forever. It distinguishes another group from them. Nor does it make sins harmless for those who believe. Even where a person will at last come out, the pain of the Fire is not a slight matter. The reading must preserve both truths: the warning here has a defined object, and faith is no excuse to treat disobedience lightly. The verse’s description of residence prepares the reader for the final words, which settle how lasting that relation to the Fire will be.

The end is explicit: ***“They will be there forever.””***. Long duration and unending duration are different claims. Here the latter is meant. Another account describes the path of those who persist in disbelief and wrong as leading to Hell, (4:169 — **“to stay there for ever and ever.”**). Nor does death provide release there: (35:36 — **“where they will not be ˹allowed to be˺ finished by death, nor will its torment be lightened for them.”**). Because these verses speak of life under judgement and of a stay without end, they rule out a merely long sentence. The warning names a real outcome, not just the shame of knowing that a wrong choice was made. At the same time, the story has placed this outcome after the teaching of repentance and the promise of guidance. Human life does not begin with a verdict that every descendant of Adam is condemned. It begins with provision, a warning about the enemy, a taught path of return, and a message to follow. The final division turns on the response to that message. The coming account of the Children of Israel will bring that choice into the history of a community already blessed with revelation.

---

## Verse 2:40

> O children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you. Fulfil your covenant and I will fulfil Mine, and stand in awe of Me ˹alone˺

***“O children of Israel!”*** calls the descendants of Jacob by their father’s honoured name. Israel here is Jacob, the son of Isaac and grandson of Abraham. It is a name in the history of the prophets, not a claim that descent alone secures salvation. Ibn ʿAbbās explains the name through the sense of being God’s servant. The appeal therefore recalls an ancestor whose worth lay in serving God. His children are invited to act in keeping with that inheritance. A similar appeal recalls Noah, (17:3 — **“He was indeed a grateful servant.””**). The honour of a forefather should move later people toward his faithfulness, not excuse them from it. In the setting of this chapter, the address comes especially to the Jewish communities of Madinah and its surroundings. Their knowledge of earlier revelation makes the coming reminder close and recognizable. After the account of humanity’s first father, the Quran now addresses a family of nations with its own long record of divine gifts. This narrows the historical setting without changing the rule just stated: guidance must be followed when it comes from God.

**MEMORY THAT CALLS FOR GRATITUDE**

The first demand is ***“Remember My favours upon you.”***. Remembering here must do more than preserve stories about a distinguished past. The favours call for gratitude toward the One who gave them. Mujāhid includes the water brought from rock, the manna and quails, and rescue from Pharaoh’s rule. Abū al-ʿĀliyah draws attention to prophets raised among them and Books revealed for their guidance. Bodily safety and revealed teaching thus belong within the same remembrance. The later generations did not themselves pass through the sea, but their life as a community depended upon that rescue. Because a gift can reach children through their parents, God may remind the children of what He gave their fathers. Moses had made the same appeal: (5:20 — **“Remember Allah’s favours upon you when He raised prophets from among you, made you sovereign,”**). Such memory should humble rather than inflate them. It begins with what God did, not with a claim that their own worth forced His hand. The right answer is to use the inherited good in obedience to its Giver.

**A COMMITMENT WITH DUTIES AND A PROMISED RETURN**

The reminder becomes a demand for faithfulness: ***“Fulfil your covenant”***. The covenant is not an empty title of honour. It binds conduct. Qatādah and Mujāhid connect it with the covenant whose terms include (5:12 — **“If you establish prayer, pay alms-tax, believe in My messengers, support them, and lend to Allah a good loan,”**). Prayer, giving, belief, and support for the messengers form a single duty toward God. A people cannot preserve that duty by accepting earlier messengers while rejecting a later one whom God sends. This is why Ibn ʿAbbās applies the covenant here to belief in Muhammad and obedience to his message. The specific application does not replace the wider covenant; it brings that covenant to bear on the choice now before the hearers. Their own received scripture is not offered as a shelter from further truth. It is part of the evidence that should prepare them to recognize it. To fulfil a pledge is to carry it through when its demand becomes costly, not merely to honour it while it confirms an established position.

God’s reply is ***“and I will fulfil Mine,”***. The two sides are related, but they are not equal powers bargaining over an uncertain result. God sets the terms and freely promises the reward. Human obedience does not place Him under a debt imposed by anyone else. His own promise is the firm ground of hope. Al-Suddī explains the promised fulfilment as admission to Paradise for those who obey. The language of covenant therefore gives hope a clear direction: attend to what has been required and trust the One who has promised. Elsewhere the Quran asks, (9:111 — **“And whose promise is truer than Allah’s?”**). The uncertainty lies in human faithfulness, not in God’s truth. This duty also reaches those who now read the verse as Muslims; it is not a failing safely assigned to another community. A report carried by Muslim describes a flag raised beside each betrayer on the Day of Judgement, its size marking the extent of the betrayal. A broken trust that seemed hidden in worldly life is then made plain. A pledge must be kept; a good name among loyal people cannot replace the deed.

**AWE THAT OUTWEIGHS THE PRESSURE OF PEOPLE**

The closing command guards the covenant: ***“and stand in awe of Me ˹alone˺”***. The wording gives God the sole place in the awe that governs obedience. It does not deny the natural fear of a danger or demand that a person stop taking wise precautions. It refuses to let fear of losing rank, followers, or income become a reason to betray known truth. In the address to the keepers of the Torah, the same demand is stated directly: (5:44 — **“So do not fear the people; fear Me!”**). The relation is close. People entrusted with a Book may know what it requires yet shrink from saying so when their audience resists. Since the covenant is with God, the audience cannot release them from it. The reminder of favours first awakens gratitude; the promise then gives hope; the final command supplies the fear that checks disloyalty. Neither fear alone nor a claim of inherited favour is allowed to govern the response. Jacob’s descendants are called back to the service by which their father was honoured: receiving God’s gifts with thanks and keeping His word above every competing claim.

---

## Verse 2:41

> Believe in My revelations which confirm your Scriptures. Do not be the first to deny them or trade them for a fleeting gain. And be mindful of Me

**HONOURING EARLIER REVELATION BY RECEIVING THE NEW**

The covenant now makes a direct claim on its hearers: ***“Believe in My revelations”*** ***“which confirm your Scriptures.”***. The revelation being received is the Quran. It does not ask them to deny that God sent earlier Books. Rather, its message agrees with the truth He had already taught. Another passage states the relation plainly: (3:3 — **“the Book in truth, confirming what came before it, as He revealed the Torah and the Gospel”**). Abū al-ʿĀliyah also connects the confirmation with the description of Muhammad known from the earlier scriptures. The Quran speaks of the Messenger (7:157 — **“whose description they find in their Torah and the Gospel.”**). Confirmation therefore works in two related ways: the same basic faith is upheld, and the promised messenger has come. A change in a particular law need not make the two messages false to one another. God may prescribe a rule for one time and replace it when He sends a later law. The unity lies in their divine source and truth, not in making every ruling timeless. Nor does this confirmation approve whatever people may add to a Book. Since the command concerns what God revealed, loyalty to that revelation should lead toward the Quran, not become a reason to refuse it.

**A FIRST REFUSAL CAN LEAD OTHERS**

The warning ***“Do not be the first to deny them”*** addresses people whose knowledge should have prepared them to believe. Ibn ʿAbbās stresses that they possessed knowledge others did not have. Their learning thus increased the duty to recognize the message. They were not the first people anywhere to reject Muhammad; opposition in Makkah had already preceded this address. The force is that they should not lead their own community into denial. Others looked to them as people trained in scripture, so their refusal could become an excuse for many further refusals. This is why being first makes the warning sharper. It does not make later denial lawful. The Quran describes the added burden of those who mislead: (16:25 — **“as well as some of the burdens of those they mislead without knowledge.”**). That burden comes from their own act of leading others astray, not from cancelling the responsibility of the followers. Knowledge is therefore a trust with a public effect. It can open the way to faith or place an obstacle before people who assume that their teachers have examined the evidence honestly.

**PAYMENT FOR SERVICE IS NOT A PRICE FOR SILENCE**

The next prohibition is not to ***“or trade them for a fleeting gain.”***. Gain may take the form of money, office, influence, or the approval that keeps a leader in place. The wrong occurs when the truth is withheld or changed to protect that gain. An important teaching then becomes a tool for preserving the teacher’s position. Because worldly benefit ends, even a large return is small beside the good being surrendered. The Quran gives the right comparison: (16:95 — **“What is with Allah is certainly far better for you, if only you knew”**). The warning is not against a poor bargain that could be repaired by asking a higher price. No payment can make false witness about God lawful. It is the exchange itself that is corrupt. In this setting, concealing the Messenger’s description or refusing the Quran for the sake of influence places a passing interest above a known duty. The same wrong remains possible for a Muslim who bends a religious answer to please a patron. The verse’s first audience does not confine its rule to one people.

A teacher’s pay for the time spent teaching the Quran correctly is a separate question. Abū Ḥanīfah’s earlier ruling disallowed such wages because teaching was treated as a duty of worship. Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Aḥmad allowed teaching wages, since pay for sound teaching is not a payment to sell or hide the truth. Its evidence includes the report from Ibn ʿAbbās in al-Bukhārī, in which the Prophet approves payment for Quranic recitation used in healing. The report is about healing prayer, not a class fee. Yet it shows that payment for work with the Quran is not always unlawful. The ruling that allows pay is adopted here. A teacher paid to teach faithfully is not being paid to make revelation say something else. Later Hanafi jurists also allowed teaching wages when public support had failed and teachers needed a livelihood. This did not permit taking bribes or withholding an urgently owed explanation until payment arrived. The distinction protects both sides of the trust: the message must remain true, and those who devote their working time to transmitting it need not be deprived of lawful support.

Al-Dārimī records Abū Ḥāzim telling the ruler Sulaymān that just speech is truth spoken before someone whose power is feared or whose favour is sought. In that same encounter, he refuses to let offered wealth become a price for his counsel. The point is not that every gift to a teacher is forbidden; the preceding distinction would rule out that reading. It is that fear and hope must not decide whether the truth is spoken. A gift tied to a desired answer is no longer merely help for the work. It reaches into the judgement the hearer is entitled to receive. The covenant concerning scripture requires its holders (3:187 — **“to make it known to people and not hide it,”**). An audience may reward concealment more readily than candour. Since the knowledge was entrusted by God, the audience’s preference cannot transfer ownership of it to a ruler, donor, or teacher. Its duty remains disclosure in truth.

**MINDFULNESS THAT GOVERNS THE CHOICE**

The verse closes with ***“And be mindful of Me”***. Being mindful means guarding against God’s punishment by obeying His commands and shunning what He forbids. For Ṭalq ibn Ḥabīb, such obedience rests on knowledge from God and hope for His mercy. Avoiding sin is joined to that knowledge and fear of punishment. Knowledge, hope, and fear belong together in that account. A teacher does not honour God by replacing sound knowledge with alarm, or by invoking mercy to conceal a known command. The warning therefore asks for an inward loyalty that can withstand pressure on the outward answer. The previous verse called for awe; here that awe must govern the choices just named. It requires belief in the message, refusal to lead others into denial, and loyalty that does not trade truth for gain. These are connected duties because each can be defeated by the same desire to preserve one’s place. God’s judgement lasts after a salary, title, or following has passed away. Mindfulness weighs the choice by that lasting account rather than by the size of the immediate reward.

---

## Verse 2:42

> Do not mix truth with falsehood or hide the truth knowingly

**A TRUE PART CAN HIDE A FALSE WHOLE**

The command ***“Do not mix truth with falsehood”*** concerns more than a wholly false statement. Ibn ʿAbbās explains it as mixing facts with lies. The danger is that sound teaching lends credit to what has been added to it. A hearer may recognize one true part and accept the rest without seeing the change. Mixing thus differs from an open refusal of truth: it can preserve the appearance of belief while turning belief away from its proper object. The force of the command is to keep the boundary clear. God’s revealed word must not be blended with an invented claim and then presented as one message from Him. The earlier command to believe in revelation gives this duty its setting. Those who know a Book should help others distinguish what it teaches from what it does not. Because their knowledge gives their words weight, they can make falsehood harder to detect than someone who speaks without such standing. That weight is a reason for care, not a right to recast the truth.

Abū al-ʿĀliyah gives a pointed example: some acknowledged Muhammad as a messenger but claimed that his mission was not to them. The admission retained a true part, while the added restriction denied the reach of his call. The Quran states that reach in his commanded address to humanity: (7:158 — **“I am Allah’s Messenger to you all.”**). The false restriction therefore changes the duty that follows from admitting the truth. It is not a harmless qualification. A person who accepts only a messenger for someone else can appear fair while refusing the message directed to himself. Ibn Zayd also applies the warning to mixing the revealed Torah with what people wrote into it. The examples differ, but both protect the line between a gift from God and a human addition. This is why a correct quotation does not by itself make an explanation correct. A statement placed beside it can narrow, reverse, or hide what the quotation establishes. Faithful teaching must preserve the meaning as well as the words.

**WHAT IS LEFT UNSAID CAN ALSO MISLEAD**

The prohibition continues, ***“or hide the truth”***. Distortion and silence are two different ways to keep people from the same good. The first gives them a mixed account; the second withholds the part they need. Ibn ʿAbbās relates this concealment to knowledge of the Messenger and what he brought, already found in the scriptures held by those addressed. A later verse describes that recognition and then adds, (2:146 — **“Yet a group of them hides the truth knowingly”**). The wording identifies a group; it does not charge every person of a lineage with an identical act. The grammar here can join two separate prohibitions, or describe the combining of distortion with concealment. The broader reading is clearer because each act is itself wrong. The ban does not mean that either practice becomes lawful when carried out without the other. Someone who tells no lie but hides a truth he owes may still mislead. Someone who states that truth and surrounds it with false claims has not discharged the trust merely by mentioning it.

The final word, ***“knowingly”***, makes the charge more serious. The rebuke falls on people who possess the relevant knowledge, not on someone who simply has not learned the answer. Their knowledge should have restrained them from the deed. Instead, they used the advantage it gave them to leave others without clear guidance. This is why learning can increase responsibility rather than offer a defence against it. The Quran repeats the challenge to the People of the Book: (3:71 — **“Why do you mix the truth with falsehood and hide the truth knowingly”**). Its question exposes the clash between knowing and hiding. It also guards against treating a scholar’s status as proof that every statement is true. ʿAlī’s counsel is to recognize truth and then recognize its people, rather than make the rank of people the measure of truth. That counsel does not abolish the need for sound teachers. It denies them the right to overrule what is known to be true. The trust belongs to the knowledge they bear, not to the prestige that gathers around them.

**WISE DISCLOSURE DOES NOT ALLOW A FALSE ANSWER**

The duty to make truth clear is not a demand to say everything to everyone in the same form. In a report carried by al-Bukhārī, ʿAlī urges teaching people what they can understand, lest the way it is presented lead them to deny God and His Messenger. In Muslim’s introduction, Ibn Masʿūd likewise warns that a report beyond a people’s understanding may become a trial for some of them. The point is to help truth reach its hearers, not to keep it from them for private gain. A teacher may choose the order and level of an explanation, or decline to guess at what he does not know. Such care is not the knowing concealment blamed here. Since a needed answer may be clear from a situation itself, duty also need not wait for someone to ask a polished question. Where people are being misled, the need can call for clarification. None of these distinctions allows a false answer to replace a true one. Caution about when to speak cannot make lying a form of faithful teaching.

Repair must address the harm done by the silence or the mixture. A private change of mind may leave the public error in place. The Quran’s promise of pardon in the later passage includes those who (2:160 — **“repent, mend their ways, and let the truth be known,”**). Repentance, reform, and disclosure belong together because the wrong had kept others from guidance. The repair should make clear what was false, restore what was hidden, and stop presenting personal additions as revelation. This does not require filling every lesson with remote disputes that its hearers do not need. It requires a true account of the matter on which they are entitled to guidance. The difference is between serving their understanding and managing it for the speaker’s advantage. The verse began with a mixture and ended with knowledge. Its demand is that knowledge be used to undo confusion rather than to manufacture it. Only then does possession of scripture perform its proper work: making the path of obedience clearer for those who hear it.

---

## Verse 2:43

> Establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and bow down with those who bow down

**KEEPING THE PRAYER IN ITS PROPER FORM**

Belief in the message is to take visible form in worship: ***“Establish prayer,”***. The people addressed must not remain observers who discuss scripture while standing outside its demands. Qatādah identifies prayer and the alms due beside it as two binding duties. Establishing prayer means keeping it faithfully, with its required acts and conditions, rather than merely performing a gesture from time to time. The command does not invent worship for a people who had never known it. Jesus speaks of the duty (19:31 — **“to establish prayer and give alms-tax as long as I live”**). Earlier messengers taught prayer and giving, even where the prescribed forms differed. Here those duties must be fulfilled in obedience to the Messenger whose revelation the preceding verses command them to believe. Because the call to worship follows that call to faith, the two cannot be separated into rival claims. Respect for earlier revelation is not a reason to refuse the worship now required. The response involves time, bodily action, and willing submission to God, not an opinion about the merits of someone else’s religion.

Regular prayer has an appointed place in the day: (4:103 — **“Indeed, performing prayers is a duty on the believers at the appointed times”**). Its timing prevents worship from being postponed whenever another wish seems more pressing. Its form also matters. In the account from Rifāʿah ibn Rāfiʿ carried by al-Nasāʾī, the Prophet sends a man back to repeat a prayer that he has not performed properly. He then teaches him to let the body settle in its positions, including bowing, standing upright, and prostrating. Since each act must be done fully, rushing through the movements does not fulfil the command. The heart’s humility does not excuse carelessness with the body, nor can correct movements excuse deliberate neglect of the heart. Prayer is meant to shape the person who performs it: (29:45 — **“Indeed, ˹genuine˺ prayer should deter ˹one˺ from indecency and wickedness.”**). If wrongdoing persists, the worshipper should therefore examine how prayer is being kept, not claim that God’s promise has failed. The command seeks a sustained act of obedience whose effects reach beyond the moments spent standing and bowing.

**WEALTH HAS A DUE THAT THE OWNER DOES NOT INVENT**

The next duty is ***“pay alms-tax,”***. This is zakāh, the prescribed due from wealth that meets its conditions, not simply a generous feeling or whatever donation the owner finds convenient. Giving it requires delivery to those entitled to receive it. The Quran identifies its recipients, beginning with (9:60 — **“Alms-tax is only for the poor and the needy,”**). Their right is not created by the donor’s wish to be praised. The act also cleanses the giver: (9:103 — **“charity to purify and bless them,”**). What leaves the hand can free the heart from a claim of absolute ownership. Its growth lies in blessing and reward, not in a promise that the sum remaining in a purse instantly increases. Prayer and this due thus make different claims upon the same believer. One requires the body and time; the other requires surrender of a share of wealth. Paying is an act of worship because God has assigned the obligation. It cannot be replaced by admiration for charity while the amount actually owed is kept back.

To work out the amount due, the giver needs the Prophet’s teaching. In al-Bukhārī, Ibn ʿUmar reports that the Prophet set a tenth on crops watered by rain or natural sources, and half that rate on crops watered by irrigation. The difference takes account of the work involved in supplying water. It does not leave the owner free to choose either rate.
