The same collection carries Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī’s report of minimum amounts below which no due is taken from specified kinds of wealth. A person must therefore learn the rule for his wealth, not use the broad command to choose a sum at will. Not every possession falls under one rate or one threshold. The practical issue is the right amount, from the right property, delivered in the right way. This also explains why voluntary giving and the prescribed due are not identical. Generosity may go beyond what is owed, but a larger display of kindness elsewhere does not by itself discharge the amount owed.

**ENTERING THE ROW WITHOUT CLAIMING A PLACE ABOVE IT**

The words ***“and bow down”*** name a bodily act that belongs to prayer. Bowing can express submission in ordinary speech, but the prayer setting gives it its specific ritual sense here. Muqātil understands the address as calling the People of the Book to pray with Muhammad and his Companions. Naming bowing can therefore stand for the whole prayer, because it is one of the prayer’s essential acts. It is not an invitation to offer an isolated bow as a substitute for the rest. The Quran elsewhere joins the movements: (22:77 — **“O believers! Bow down, prostrate yourselves, worship your Lord,”**). Nor is bodily bowing wholly unknown in the worship of earlier servants of God. Mary is told, (3:43 — **“and bow along with those who bow down.””**). The present command is thus best understood through the worship and company required, rather than a sweeping claim that no earlier prophet’s followers ever bowed. The person’s willingness to lower himself before God must take the form God teaches, not a form chosen to protect his own dignity.

The added demand is to do so ***“with those who bow down”***. Those addressed must join the people at prayer, not merely approve of them from a distance. The legal weight of congregational prayer also depends on the Prophet’s teaching. In Aḥmad’s ruling, each man able to attend must do so. In Muslim’s report from Abū Hurayrah, a blind man seeks permission to pray at home because he has no guide; after learning that he hears the call, the Prophet tells him to attend. The strongly urged practice reading instead stresses the report from Ibn ʿUmar in Muslim that prayer together exceeds prayer alone by twenty-seven degrees. That comparison recognizes a prayer performed alone, so the dispute also concerns whether attendance determines validity. This duty for able men without a valid excuse is adopted here, because the instruction to answer the call is direct. This need not make every prayer offered alone invalid. Being bound to attend is one issue; whether a prayer offered alone is valid is another. Neither view makes it a slight matter to keep away from the prayer in the mosque.

Joining the row also changes the place from which a learned person serves. He is no longer outside the practice, advising others to do what he regards as beneath himself. Knowledge is used to guide worship. In al-Bukhārī, Ibn ʿUmar relates that Sālim, the freedman of Abū Ḥudhayfah, led the early emigrants in prayer because he knew more of the Quran. His service shows that birth and rank do not decide who is fit to lead. The congregation needs knowledge of the prayer and faithful conduct, not a claim of social importance. Once an imam leads, those behind him must follow rather than race him. The warning in al-Bukhārī and Muslim against raising the head before the imam makes that discipline serious. The shared act is not a contest to finish first. Thus the closing command answers both pride and isolation. The one who accepts God’s message joins its people in an ordered act of worship, serving through what he knows and submitting alongside those he might once have looked down upon.

---

## Verse 2:44

> Do you preach righteousness and fail to practice it yourselves, although you read the Scripture? Do you not understand

**COUNSEL THAT FAILS TO REACH THE COUNSELLOR**

The call to join the worshippers is followed by a challenge to those who direct others: ***“Do you preach righteousness”***. Righteousness covers obedience to God, not one isolated act of kindness. Ibn ʿAbbās describes teachers in Madinah who told Muslim relatives and close associates to remain firm in following Muhammad, acknowledging that his message was true. Yet they did not follow him themselves. Their advice showed that the difficulty was not simply a lack of knowledge about the message. Another early explanation, from Ibn Jurayj, includes commands to pray and fast that the speakers themselves neglected. These applications belong to the same charge: a person correctly identifies a duty, then behaves as if it belongs only to others. The question therefore does not condemn good counsel. It asks why the counsellor has left himself outside it. Nor is this warning confined to its first audience. Believers hear the corresponding challenge, (61:2 — **“O believers! Why do you say what you do not do”**). Teaching a true rule does not give the teacher an exemption from it; the very reason offered to the hearer also bears upon the speaker.

The contradiction is exposed in ***“and fail to practice it yourselves,”***. The neglect is not an innocent lapse of memory that makes the duty unknown. Their public instruction shows that they retain the knowledge. What is missing is its claim upon their own conduct. Because speaking well can earn respect, a person may begin to live on the credit of an instruction he never follows. The account carried by al-Bukhārī and Muslim from Usāmah ibn Zayd makes the danger plain: the Prophet describes a man punished in the Fire who had commanded good and forbidden evil while doing the opposite. The man circles with his entrails trailing, like a donkey turning a mill. Those who knew his counsel ask how he came to such an end, and he admits the split between his speech and his deeds. The report does not say that his hearers were wrong to follow sound advice. It shows that benefiting them did not excuse his own refusal. A message may guide others while its teacher remains in danger from the very wrong he warned them against.

**LEARNING MUST BIND THE ONE WHO POSSESSES IT**

The added circumstance, ***“although you read the Scripture?”***, removes another excuse. They are not strangers to the written command. Reading includes studying what the Book teaches, as Ibn ʿAbbās explains, and the Scripture in this address is the Torah. Its presence should bring the command closer to them. Instead, the contrast between a well-read tongue and a disobedient life makes their conduct more blameworthy. The Quran states the gravity of that divide: (61:3 — **“How despicable it is in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do”**). Since the speaker already knows what he commends, he cannot treat his instruction as a payment that clears the debt of action. Knowledge is entrusted for obedience, not only for public use. This does not mean that a person with less learning has no duty to learn or act. It means that greater knowledge takes away the claim that the demand was unseen. The warning reaches every teacher who can find the rule for a pupil, neighbour, or family member but refuses to let the same rule govern his own choices.

The closing appeal, ***“Do you not understand”***, asks for judgement that reaches conduct. It is not a claim that those addressed lack the mental ability to read, argue, or remember. Their failure lies in refusing the conclusion their own teaching requires. Understanding should hold a person back from a known harm and direct him toward a known good. The Arabic sense associated with reason includes restraint, as a tether keeps an animal from straying. The image explains what is lacking: the knowledge has not restrained its possessor. Wisdom is a great gift, (2:269 — **“And whoever is granted wisdom is certainly blessed with a great privilege.”**), but possessing information about a good path is not the same as walking it. This is why the rebuke can address learned people without contradiction. Their learning supplies the premises; their conduct rejects the conclusion. Sound judgement would turn the charge inward before using it against someone else. It would ask the teacher to place himself under the command he has already explained, rather than search for a privilege attached to the role of explaining it.

The remedy is neither silence nor a pretence of being faultless. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr warns that if complete freedom from faults were required before anyone urged good, such counsel would cease. Al-Ḥasan likewise rejects a fear that lets the duty of advising others disappear. There are two obligations: to act rightly and to call others toward what is right. Failure in one does not release a person from the other. A man who neglects prayer must correct that neglect; he does not repair it by also refusing to encourage his child to pray. Yet the permission to give counsel is no excuse to remain unchanged. The prophetic model is Shuʿayb’s declaration, (11:88 — **“I do not want to do what I am forbidding you from.”**). His stated aim joins reform of others to faithfulness in himself. The right response to the warning is therefore to keep truthful counsel, confess personal shortcomings without defending them, and work to remove the contradiction. The verse makes learning more demanding precisely because knowledge brings the command within reach.

---

## Verse 2:45

> And seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is a burden except for the humble—

**THE MEANS OF CARRYING OUT A DIFFICULT DUTY**

Rebuke is followed by help for those who must change: ***“And seek help through patience”***. In the immediate setting, they need strength to keep the covenant, tell the truth, and give up gains that stand against faith. Patience is more than waiting for pain to pass. It keeps the person doing right, holds him back from sin, and steadies him when a loss cannot be undone. In each case, the first urge must not decide the response. The command is also addressed directly to believers elsewhere, with the assurance (2:153 — **“Allah is truly with those who are patient”**). Its reach is therefore wider than the first audience’s particular struggle. In Muslim, Abū Hurayrah reports the Prophet’s command, *"Strive for what benefits you, seek God’s help, and do not give up."* Effort and reliance belong together in that instruction. Because God has appointed means of help, using them does not compete with seeking help from Him. Patience is one such means: it keeps a rightful aim from being abandoned simply because its fruit is not immediate.

Fasting makes this restraint visible, which explains Mujāhid’s reading of patience here as fasting. The person leaves food and other desires at God’s command, learning that an appetite need not rule merely because it is present. That reading identifies a strong form of patience rather than exhausting the word’s whole meaning. The surrounding demands also require truthful speech, faithful worship, and resistance to greed. A fast would not excuse failure in those duties. Nor does patience require a bereaved person to feel no sorrow. The heart may hurt without the person turning against God or leaving what he owes undone. The Quran promises, (39:10 — **“Only those who endure patiently will be given their reward without limit.””**). The reward makes sense because restraint may be costly even when no one else sees it. A person who quietly refuses an unlawful gain has exercised patience as truly as one who endures an outward misfortune. The command trains conduct, not a display of being beyond ordinary human feeling.

**TURNING TOWARD GOD WITH THE TROUBLE STILL PRESENT**

Help is sought also through ***“and prayer.”***. This is the prayer already commanded, not only a general wish that matters improve. In Abū Dāwūd and Aḥmad, Ḥudhayfah reports that the Prophet would pray when troubled by a pressing matter. The Prophet did not wait for trouble to pass before turning to God. Prayer was part of seeking help while the trial lasted. Recitation recalls God’s commands and promises, bowing checks pride, and supplication places need before the One who can answer. God’s instruction to Moses joins prayer to its purpose: (20:14 — **“and establish prayer for My remembrance”**). Prayer brings God’s word back before the mind, so that fear need not drive out every other thought. This does not promise that every earthly loss will be reversed immediately. It gives the servant a way to obey, ask, and recover steadiness without pretending the trial is unreal. Patience helps a person keep his duty; prayer renews his bond with the Lord for whose sake he keeps it. The two forms of help strengthen rather than replace one another.

**WHY A SOURCE OF HELP MAY FIRST FEEL HEAVY**

The acknowledgement ***“Indeed, it is a burden”*** prevents an easy misunderstanding. The offered help itself requires effort. Mujāhid takes the reference to be prayer, the nearest named act, and that is the most direct reading here. Another reading includes the whole instruction to seek help through patience and prayer. On either reading, the command is not pretending that change is painless. Prayer interrupts work and desire at appointed times. During it, even ordinary lawful acts such as eating and casual conversation are set aside. The person must leave the freedom to follow each new impulse. That is why prayer may feel heavy to a heart still determined to govern everything by its own wishes. The Quran describes the hypocrites standing for prayer (4:142 — **“they do it half-heartedly only to be seen by people—hardly remembering Allah at all”**). Their outward act lacks the inward purpose that would make it welcome. The contrast concerns the heart’s governing stance, not a rule that every passing struggle with tiredness or distraction proves hypocrisy. The verse directs that struggling heart toward the quality that makes obedience easier.

**HUMILITY IS NOT AN ACT PUT ON FOR ONLOOKERS**

The exception is ***“except for the humble—”***. These are people whose hearts yield to God, taking His promise and warning seriously. Ibn ʿAbbās connects their humility with belief in what God has revealed. Their quietness is not merely an outward style. Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī rejects the idea that rough clothes, coarse food, and a lowered head by themselves make a person humble. He points instead to treating high and low alike where truth is concerned, and submitting to the duties God has laid down. Since that submission reaches the will, prayer is no longer simply an interruption imposed from outside. It becomes a meeting the servant desires. The Quran describes the successful believers as (23:2 — **“those who humble themselves in prayer”**). A composed body can express that inward state, but a staged appearance cannot supply it. Someone may speak clearly and walk with purpose while remaining lowly before God. The measure is not how convincingly he looks subdued to other people, but whether God’s command finds a willing response within him.

The worth of a prayer and the ruling that it is valid are not the same thing. A strict reading, reported from Sufyān al-Thawrī and al-Ḥasan, treats prayer without humility as invalid. The other ruling does not treat a loss of focus like a failure to intend worship or to perform its required acts. This latter ruling is adopted here. A prayer begun with a true intention does not become void merely because the mind wanders, though its spiritual reward and benefit are impaired. That distinction accords with the governing limit (2:286 — **“Allah does not require of any soul more than what it can afford.”**). It does not make carelessness desirable or excuse missing a required act. The person still seeks to pray with his whole heart, not merely to do the least that makes his prayer valid. Hope in mercy and fear of neglect both remain. The verse therefore neither demands a performance of emotion nor releases the heart from worship. Genuine surrender is the aim, and the following verse explains the belief that sustains it: the servant expects to meet his Lord.

---

## Verse 2:46

> those who are certain that they will meet their Lord and to Him they will return

**CONVICTION BEFORE THE APPOINTED DAY ARRIVES**

The humble people of the preceding verse are now described as ***“those who are certain”***. Their prayer is sustained by a conviction about where life leads. In Arabic, the expression used here can carry either firm conviction or supposition; the setting decides the sense. Al-Suddī explains it as certainty. Ibn Zayd adds that the event has not yet been seen, but that this does not make their belief a doubtful guess. They trust the Lord’s account of what is coming. The same use appears in the words of the person who receives his record with joy: (69:20 — **“I surely knew I would face my reckoning.””**). He had lived in expectation of the reckoning before it became visible. This is why the belief changes the weight of present duties. Prayer is not wasted time if the one performing it knows that he will stand before its Lord. Nor is avoiding a forbidden gain a loss with no further account. The future is not yet present to the senses, but it is already part of the believer’s judgement about what matters. Certainty concerns God’s promise, not a boast that the believer has already secured a favourable verdict for himself.

What they know is ***“that they will meet their Lord”***. The meeting includes standing before God to answer for life and deeds. It is not confined to the humble, although they are the people who prepare for it. The Quran addresses humanity as a whole: (84:6 — **“O humanity! Indeed, you are labouring restlessly towards your Lord, and will ˹eventually˺ meet the consequences”**). That common end makes the present contrast serious. A person may deny the reckoning, but denial does not remove him from it. In al-Bukhārī and Muslim, ʿAdiyy ibn Ḥātim reports the Prophet’s teaching that each person will be addressed by his Lord without an interpreter between them. Looking around, the person finds the deeds he has sent ahead; the warning then urges protection from the Fire even through giving half a date. The small gift matters because the future account reaches the acts that may seem too slight for notice now. Neither a spokesman nor public rank can stand in for the person’s own response. The humble therefore learn to place even ordinary choices within that account. They do not wait for the appointed day before treating it as real, and they do not suppose that a respected place among people guarantees a safe place before God.

**HOPE DOES NOT REQUIRE FORGETTING THE ACCOUNT**

Meeting the Lord is not presented only as a terror for the believer. The Quran joins its warning with encouragement: (2:223 — **“Be mindful of Allah, and know that you will meet Him. And give good news to the believers”**). The divine title recalls the One who has nourished and guided His servants, not a judge unaware of their need. In the report from Ibn ʿUmar carried by al-Bukhārī and Muslim, the Prophet describes God shielding a believer while bringing his sins before him. After the believer admits them, God declares that He concealed them in worldly life and now forgives them. That pardon is mercy, not proof that the sins were never wrong. Some early readings also connect the meeting with the honour of seeing God, for the blessed faces are described as (75:23 — **“looking at their Lord”**). That special gift must not be confused with the bare fact that all people return for judgement. The verse’s immediate point is the certainty that shapes worship; the other texts show why hope belongs beside fear. Since the Lord can forgive what no creature can erase, the servant has reason to approach Him rather than avoid His command. Trust does not presume upon pardon, and fear does not make sincere obedience pointless.

The closing assurance is ***“and to Him they will return”***. Abū al-ʿĀliyah understands this as their return on the Day of Resurrection. Death begins the journey out of earthly life, but the return here includes being raised and brought to judgement. The earlier account makes that order plain: (2:28 — **“then He will cause you to die and again bring you to life, and then to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned”**). The second raising cannot be reduced to the first death. All affairs reach God’s judgement, and no power claimed in this world can make that end belong to someone else. The return also explains why the two clauses are joined. They will meet the Lord, and their final disposal is His; the appointment is not one encounter after which they pass beyond His authority. Because that is their settled expectation, worship gains a lasting purpose even when its present cost is felt. A tiring day, a hidden sacrifice, or an unanswered desire does not become the whole story. The humble can endure without claiming to control the outcome. Their Lord knows what they have done and will judge it justly. Thus belief in the return gives prayer both seriousness and hope: the act is offered now to the One before whom the servant will finally stand.

---

## Verse 2:47

> O Children of Israel! Remember ˹all˺ the favours I granted you and how I honoured you above the others

**GRATITUDE IS RECALLED BEFORE JUDGEMENT IS NAMED**

The call comes back to Jacob’s people: ***“O Children of Israel!”***. They have heard it before, but its place here gives it fresh force. The first reminder led to the pledge (2:40 — **“Fulfil your covenant and I will fulfil Mine,”**). This one leads toward the Day when no person can buy his way out or use force to save himself. God calls them to obey from thanks for His gifts and from fear of that Day. Neither reason cancels the other. A gift calls for thanks; it does not give leave to break the Giver’s command. The past rebukes have not made the gifts themselves false. God does not ask them to cast away every good thing in their history. He asks them to act in keeping with what He gave. This is why the summons returns with a reminder of honour, not just another threat. The way to obey is still open. Their people had been taught and helped before, and the word now reaching them comes from the same Lord. Their past should make them more ready to heed it.

The words ***“Remember ˹all˺ the favours I granted you”*** gather many gifts into one reminder. They had been given scripture, taught by messengers, and freed from the rule of those who oppressed them. Abū al-ʿĀliyah includes kingship, messengers, and Books among the good granted to them. Moses had set such gifts before his people: (5:20 — **“Remember Allah’s favours upon you when He raised prophets from among you, made you sovereign,”**). The call to remember is thus about more than wealth. It includes freedom to live and knowledge of how to serve God. Those addressed in Madinah had not stood beside Moses, but they still shared in the good that followed his people’s rescue. A child can live in safety because an earlier generation was saved. The past gift has not ceased to matter simply because the child did not see it given. The same holds for the teaching passed down to him. He receives a duty of thanks with the benefit. That is why a proud tale about the fathers is not enough. The children must use well what has reached them, rather than turn it into a reason to refuse God’s present command.

**A FAVOUR WITH A HISTORICAL SETTING**

God then singles out the honour: ***“and how I honoured you”*** ***“above the others”***. Qatādah takes the comparison to concern the peoples of that time. The other nations among whom they lived had not all been given the same gifts. This gives the praise a clear setting. It does not rank every person born into one people above every person born into another, for all ages to come. Yet the gift was real and came by God’s choice: (44:32 — **“And indeed, We chose the Israelites knowingly above the others”**). The honour is His to give; it is not a worth that the people possessed apart from Him. A wider comparison can also concern one kind of gift, such as the prophets raised among them, without claiming that they excelled in every respect. The sense followed here is the early reading about the peoples of their age. It states the gift without making it a claim that no later people could receive a higher place. The word of God must be read with His other words, including the praise He gives to the community of a later Messenger.

**HONOUR STILL REQUIRES A FAITHFUL RESPONSE**

That later praise is explicit: (3:110 — **“You are the best community ever raised for humanity—you encourage good, forbid evil, and believe in Allah.”**). In al-Tirmidhī, Muʿāwiyah ibn Ḥaydah reports that the Prophet described his community as completing seventy nations and as the best and most honoured of them before God. Al-Tirmidhī graded the report ḥasan, or good. The later gift does not make the earlier one false. It rules out the claim that Israel’s preference must mean supremacy over every future community. The praise given to Muslims also names what their honour involves: faith, urging good, and forbidding evil. Ibn Zayd ties it to those who obey God and keep His commands. A Muslim who reads this warning must therefore accept its force for himself. A community’s name cannot stand in for the conduct required of its members. God links raised rank to faith and knowledge: (58:11 — **“Allah will elevate those of you who are faithful, and ˹raise˺ those gifted with knowledge in rank.”**). The right use of honour is to fulfil the trust that comes with it. This keeps the reminder and the coming warning together. Their fathers’ gifts call for thanks now; the final account will judge their own response, not accept pride in those fathers as its replacement.

---

## Verse 2:48

> Guard yourselves against the Day on which no soul will be of help to another. No intercession will be accepted, no ransom taken, and no help will be given

The reminder of favour now leads to a warning: ***“Guard yourselves against the Day”***. The Day is the Resurrection and the judgement that follows it. No one can guard himself by making that Day fail to arrive. The protection sought is from its punishment, through faith, repentance, and obedience while the chance to act remains. This gives the command a practical force. It does not ask for alarm with no way of responding. It asks the hearers to stop relying on forms of rescue that will not lie in human hands there. The reason is stated elsewhere: (82:19 — **“all authority on that Day belongs to Allah ˹entirely˺”**). God has not lost command in worldly life and regained it only then. On that Day, however, the powers that people mistook for a final refuge will plainly fail them. The warning therefore follows the reminder of honour closely. An honoured ancestry cannot turn the final judgement into a favour owed to every descendant, regardless of his own response to God.

**NO FRIEND CAN TAKE OVER ANOTHER PERSON’S ACCOUNT**

It is the Day ***“on which no soul will be of help to another.”***. Al-Suddī explains this as one person being unable to suffice for another. The broad wording leaves no special right for a close relative or a person of rank. Even the strongest family bond is included: (31:33 — **“no parent will be of any benefit to their child, nor will a child be of any benefit to their parent.”**). Abū Hurayrah’s report in al-Bukhārī and Muslim records the Prophet warning his daughter Fāṭimah that he cannot avail her against God. The warning removes a claim of safety based simply on being his child. It does not deny a prayer or plea that God Himself permits. The point is that the family relation has no power to compel a favourable judgement. Someone who owes obedience cannot appoint another person to have obeyed in his place, as though one account could be settled by borrowing a neighbour’s life. This is why the verse speaks to people who take pride in their fathers. Their fathers’ righteousness is not a payment that makes their own refusal harmless.

The rule does not prevent God from settling wrongs done between people. That is His judgement, not a private arrangement by which a friend buys another friend’s release. In al-Bukhārī, Abū Hurayrah reports the Prophet’s warning to seek release from wrongs done to others before a Day with no gold or silver to pay them. Good deeds are then taken to meet the injured person’s claim; if they run out, the wrongdoer bears a further burden of sins. The transfer follows his own wrongdoing. It is not an innocent person volunteering to erase another’s guilt. The distinction matters because the failure of earthly means does not leave the injured without justice. The creditor’s claim has not vanished merely because money can no longer settle it. A person should therefore put a wrong right while he can restore what he owes and seek pardon. Neither a generous friend nor a noble relative can grant him leave to keep another person’s right unpaid.

**A PLEA HAS NO AUTHORITY APART FROM GOD’S LEAVE**

The next denial is ***“No intercession will be accepted,”***. Intercession is a plea made for someone else, seeking a benefit or removal of harm. Here it cannot serve as a promised escape for one who persists in rejecting God’s message. Ibn ʿAbbās relates the denial to the unbelieving soul. A reading that extends it to every sinful believer would conflict with the permission stated elsewhere: intercession brings no benefit (20:109 — **“except by those granted permission by the Most Compassionate and whose words are agreeable to Him”**). Even the angels (21:28 — **“They do not intercede except for whom He approves,”**). The accepted plea is therefore itself subject to God, not a power set beside Him. The absolute-denial reading is not adopted. Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī carry Anas’s report that the Prophet’s intercession is for people of his community who have committed major sins. That report prevents the warning from being turned into a claim that every such sinner is beyond help forever. It does not promise a sinner control over the outcome or make sin safe. The difference is between a plea that God allows in mercy and an appeal that someone imagines God must accept because of the speaker’s rank. Only the former is affirmed. Both the warning and the permission protect the same truth: the decision belongs to God.

**NO PRICE CAN BUY RELEASE AFTER REJECTION**

Nor will there be ***“no ransom taken,”***. A ransom is something offered in exchange for release. Abū al-ʿĀliyah explains the word in precisely that sense. The problem is not that the offender has brought too little and might succeed with a larger sum. The Quran puts the imagined price beyond ordinary wealth: (3:91 — **“Indeed, if each of those who disbelieve then die as disbelievers were to offer a ransom of enough gold to fill the whole world, it would never be accepted from them.”**). All the world’s gold would fail because the missing thing is not wealth. Money cannot turn a life ended in rejection into a life of faith. The verse is not denying the worth of giving while a person can still obey. A charitable gift made now in obedience and an offer made later to escape judgement are different acts. Nor does it cancel payments that God has lawfully prescribed for particular duties during earthly life. Those payments are accepted on His terms; they are not a right to bargain with Him about the final account. The warning closes a false hope that the rich can purchase what the poor must answer for.

**POWER CANNOT ENFORCE WHAT PLEADING CANNOT OBTAIN**

The last assurance is ***“and no help will be given”***. If no plea or price succeeds, there is no stronger ally waiting to force a release. Protection belongs to God, (23:88 — **“protecting ˹all˺ while none can protect against Him,”**). A group cannot defeat the judgement that each member is unable to escape. The closing breadth thus leaves no refuge in a ruler, a patron, or a power treated as divine. The several denials describe distinct hopes familiar from earthly life: another person may meet a debt, a respected voice may plead, money may ransom, or force may rescue. None is an independent means of escape before God. This is not a ban on helping people in the world where He commands mutual care. It is a warning not to mistake such limited help for power over His verdict. Since rescue cannot be organized against the Judge, the proper preparation is to turn toward Him. The hearers are still being addressed before the Day arrives. The warning takes away false shelters so that faith and repentance, rather than wealth or ancestry, govern their response.

---

## Verse 2:49

> ˹Remember˺ how We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with dreadful torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women. That was a severe test from your Lord

**RESCUE FROM A RULE THAT MADE FAMILY LIFE UNSAFE**

The gifts just recalled now take the form of a particular rescue: ***“˹Remember˺ how We delivered you”*** ***“from the people of Pharaoh,”***. Pharaoh is the title of the Egyptian ruler in the story of Moses. His people here include the followers and agents who upheld his rule, not merely his close family. God brought the Israelites out from the power of that ruler and his servants. The later hearers are addressed through their people’s history: the rescue of their forefathers made their own continued life possible. But the main stress is now on the hand that saved them. The Lord who will judge them is also the Lord who broke a power they could not escape by themselves. His purpose is stated in the fuller account: (28:5 — **“But it was Our Will to favour those who were oppressed in the land,”**). Their enemies’ strength was real, yet it did not give those enemies the last word. To remember this rescue is therefore to remember whose gift freedom was. The following words explain how great the need for that rescue had been.

They were delivered from people ***“who afflicted you with dreadful torment,”***. The description covers sustained ill-treatment, not a single harsh encounter. Al-Suddī includes the degrading labour imposed on the Israelites, together with the killing of their sons. The regime made use of their bodies and skills while denying them safety in their homes. The killing that follows in the verse explains the dreadfulness of the torment; it is not a minor detail added to a vague complaint. The people carrying it out are also named as its agents. Pharaoh’s command does not make their hands disappear from the deed. Because the violence is attributed to those who perform it, service to a ruler is not a way to rename cruelty as innocence. This does not supply every rule by which a court must judge a case of coercion. It fixes the moral fact in the story: a ruler’s policy was carried into the lives of families by people who served him. The rescue ended subjection to that whole power, not merely dislike of one man’s title.

The horror includes ***“slaughtering your sons”***. An account from Ibn ʿAbbās relates that Pharaoh was warned of a boy to be born among the Israelites whose rise would end his rule. The killing was ordered in fear for the throne. That account explains the fear behind the policy; the verse itself lays the deed before the hearer. The sons are understood here as the male children, especially the newborn, rather than only grown men. The danger faced by Moses’ mother supports that reading. She is told, (28:7 — **““Nurse him, but when you fear for him, put him then into the river,”**). Because the threatened child was still nursing, the policy cannot be confined to the killing of adult men. God taught his mother how to preserve him. The effort to secure the throne thus struck at those least able to resist. Yet the child whose life Pharaoh sought to prevent was not beyond God’s protection. This makes the rescue more than escape from forced work. It preserved a people’s future against a policy that reached into the birth of their children.

The paired act is ***“and keeping your women.”***. Keeping them means leaving them alive, and the expression includes the girls who would grow into women as well as the women already living. It does not mean that they were left free or treated kindly. Ibn Jurayj connects their retention with enslavement. That describes the condition imposed upon them, while being kept alive is the immediate sense of the wording. The two sides of the policy served the same power: sons were slain and women were kept under the ruler’s control. When Moses later confronts Pharaoh, the threat is renewed with the stated aim, (7:127 — **““We will kill their sons and keep their women. We will completely dominate them.””**). The two explanations can stand together because both concern Pharaoh’s grip on power. The women’s survival was not a favour that could cancel the killing of the sons. A life preserved for service under terror remains a life in need of rescue. The verse holds the losses and the enforced survival together within the torment God ended.

**AFFLICTION AND RELEASE BOTH TEST THE RESPONSE**

The closing judgement begins, ***“That was a severe test”***. A test can come through pain, but it can also come through a gift. Ibn ʿAbbās explains the trial here as a blessing, directing attention to the rescue with which the verse begins. The nearer account of slaughter also makes the sense of a grievous ordeal plain. Since the verse recalls both their suffering and their rescue, the whole change of condition is treated here as a test. Patient endurance was not the only response required; freedom would also test their willingness to give thanks. The Quran states the principle, (21:35 — **“And We test you ˹O humanity˺ with good and evil as a trial,”**). Pain calls for steadfastness; good calls for thanks. Neither condition places the person outside duty to God. Relief is not simply the end of every test, since it brings a new question about the use of the gift. The story is recalled to people now possessing the fruit of rescue. Their answer must include faithfulness to the Lord who gave it, not only grief for what their forefathers suffered.

The trial is ***“from your Lord”***. God’s rule over the event does not make Pharaoh’s deed good. The fuller narrative gives the ruler a clear verdict: (28:4 — **“He was truly one of the corruptors”**). God can let a tyrant act for a time without granting him the right to act, and He can bring rescue from a danger that the tyrant meant to make final. These are different kinds of agency. The men who killed are responsible for killing; the Lord who tested and delivered His servants is not praised for their cruelty. Nor does the suffering described here prove that the sufferers were worthless before Him. The verse names their trial as severe and their rescue as His gift. The title of Lord thus holds together power and care. Their life was never beyond His reach, even while it lay under Pharaoh’s rule. Remembering the event should turn them toward the One who saved them and away from the habits of pride and domination from which they were saved. The next verse recalls the act that made the rescue complete.

---

## Verse 2:50

> And ˹remember˺ when We parted the sea, rescued you, and drowned Pharaoh’s people before your very eyes

**WHEN THE WAY AHEAD SEEMED CLOSED**

Moses had led his people out by God’s command, but Pharaoh’s pursuit brought them to a place where escape seemed barred. The enemy was behind them and the sea ahead. Their cry was (26:61 — **““We are overtaken for sure.””**). Moses answered, (26:62 — **““Absolutely not! My Lord is certainly with me—He will guide me.””**). The present verse recalls how that trust was vindicated: ***“And ˹remember˺ when”*** ***“We parted the sea,”***. Parting means that the waters were divided to make a way through. The narrative is about an act of God that altered their immediate danger, not merely a change in how frightened people felt. The command to Moses is explicit: (26:63 — **““Strike the sea with your staff,” and the sea was split, each part was like a huge mountain”**). His staff was used in obedience; it did not possess a power over the sea apart from God. Because the act came at the Lord’s command, the event is a sign supporting the messenger who followed that command. The people’s fear describes the danger as they saw it. Moses’ answer rests on a promise beyond what the visible road could offer, and the opened sea supplies the way he trusted God to give.

**A PASSAGE THAT REMOVED TWO DANGERS AT ONCE**

The result is ***“rescued you,”***. The Israelites were saved both from being overtaken and from drowning in the sea they crossed. The fuller instruction promises a dry passage and tells Moses, (20:77 — **“Have no fear of being overtaken, nor be concerned ˹of drowning˺.””**). Water did not merely move aside while leaving them a trap in the seabed. The way was made fit for the people who had to pass through it. Al-Suddī relates that twelve paths opened, one for each tribe. This is a transmitted account of the crossing; the verse’s own brief statement fixes the central fact of rescue. The sea is commonly identified as the Red Sea, but the verse does not name the exact crossing place. Its purpose is to make the gift clear. The trapped people were not asked to defeat the pursuing army before they could be delivered. They followed the path God opened. Their passage shows why trust in God is not the same as refusing to act: Moses obeyed, and the people crossed, while the power that made their action possible belonged to their Lord.

**THE PURSUIT ENDS WITH THE PURSUERS**

The same event has a second outcome: ***“and drowned Pharaoh’s people”***. Pharaoh is not excluded by the mention of his people. Another verse states, (17:103 — **“but We drowned him and all of those with him”**). The followers who carried his power into the pursuit shared the end of their leader. He could not make the path opened for Moses remain a path of safety for his own attack. This is why the rescue and drowning are placed together. The danger was not merely put at a greater distance, leaving the army free to renew the chase. It was ended. There is also a sharp reversal in the place of water in Pharaoh’s claims. He had boasted of Egypt and its streams, (43:51 — **“Am I not sovereign over Egypt as well as ˹all˺ these streams flowing at my feet?”**). The ruler who treated those waters as a sign of his greatness could not make water obey him here. His rank, force, and confidence did not turn the sea into his servant. The event separates God’s power from the ruler’s claim to possess it, while releasing the people whom that claim had helped to enslave.

**SIGHT CONFIRMS THE END OF THE THREAT**

The rescue took place ***“before your very eyes”***. The plain sense is direct sight, not merely knowledge gained later. The people saw the danger overcome at the place where their own escape had seemed impossible. Seeing the enemy’s end added assurance to escape itself. Fear could otherwise leave open the thought that Pharaoh still lived and would return. Qays ibn ʿUbād relates an account of their doubts about his death being answered when his body was cast upon the shore. The Quran separately states the purpose of preserving that body: (10:92 — **“Today We will preserve your corpse so that you may become an example for those who come after you.”**). The sign is not a grant of safety to the drowned ruler. It makes his defeat visible to those who might still fear or admire his power. Because the rescue was witnessed, its remembrance should carry more than a vague belief that life had somehow improved. Their people had seen the sea become a road, and had seen the pursuing power fail. The same sight that brought relief also established a duty to recognize the Lord who had delivered them.

**A FAST OF THANKS KEEPS THE DELIVERANCE IN MEMORY**

The event also belongs to the meaning of the fast of ʿĀshūrāʾ. Ibn ʿAbbās’s account, preserved in al-Bukhārī and Muslim, describes the Prophet finding Jews in Madinah fasting in remembrance of the day God saved Moses and his people. They explained that Moses had fasted in thanks. The Prophet affirmed his own closeness to Moses, fasted, and commanded the fast. The response makes the remembered deliverance an occasion for worship, not a claim that the blessing belongs to a people apart from obedience to its Giver. It also shows the bond between the messengers. Honour for Moses is expressed by following the divine guidance Muhammad brings, rather than by setting one messenger against another. Since the fast recalls rescue, its purpose is gratitude for an act that no human army could have accomplished at that place. The body that receives food by God’s provision willingly leaves it for His sake. The remembrance thus passes into an act of thanks rather than remaining only a tale about another people’s danger.

The history of the fast needs to be kept complete. Muslim and al-Bukhārī transmit ʿĀʾishah’s account that Quraysh and the Prophet had already fasted ʿĀshūrāʾ in Makkah. The encounter in Madinah was therefore not the first occasion on which he observed it. Her report also explains that, after Ramadan was prescribed, a person could keep this fast or leave it; it was no longer an obligation alongside Ramadan. The day is understood here as the tenth of Muḥarram, with the ninth added as a recommended companion day. Al-Tirmidhī’s report from Ibn ʿAbbās names the tenth, while Muslim records the Prophet’s stated intention to fast the ninth if he lived another year. Reading the latter as an addition, rather than a replacement, preserves both instructions. The virtue remains great: Abū Qatādah reports in Muslim that the Prophet hoped its fast would expiate the preceding year. These teachings give the remembrance a defined practice and prevent a claim that gratitude needs an invented rite. The sea was parted by God; the thanks offered afterward must likewise follow His guidance.

---

## Verse 2:51

> And ˹remember˺ when We appointed forty nights for Moses, then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully

**AN APPOINTED TERM FOR GUIDANCE, NOT ABANDONMENT**

Freedom from Pharaoh left the people in need of a revealed rule for their life together. The next reminder concerns its preparation: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We appointed forty nights for Moses”***. Moses went to the appointed place on the mountain, while his people remained under Aaron’s care. The stated term belongs to God’s arrangement, not to a promise the people could shorten when waiting became hard. Its full length is explained elsewhere: (7:142 — **“We appointed for Moses thirty nights then added another ten—completing his Lord’s term of forty nights”**). Abū al-ʿĀliyah relates it to the month of Dhū al-Qaʿdah and the first ten nights of Dhū al-Ḥijjah. Counting by nights includes the days belonging to them; it does not describe forty brief meetings with a return home between each one. The term was set apart for what Moses would receive from his Lord. The transmitted reading of Abū ʿAmr presents God’s promise, while the reading behind the appointment wording also brings out Moses’ willing response. Neither puts God and His servant on the same level. God fixes the call; Moses accepts and obeys. Because the absence served their need for guidance, it should have led the people to wait faithfully. The promise was another gift, not the withdrawal of the care that had brought them through the sea.

That setting gives weight to the next turn: ***“then you worshipped the calf”***. The wrong was not simply the making of an object. The calf was taken as a god, and worship was directed to it. The Quran identifies the material used: (7:148 — **“his people made from their ˹golden˺ jewellery an idol of a calf that made a lowing sound”**). Al-Suddī’s account connects the gathered ornaments with the work of the Sāmirī, who shaped the calf and urged the people to treat it as their deity. The lowing drew their attention, but it could not prove divinity because a created creature can also make a sound. Mujāhid describes a hollow form through which wind passed; al-Ḥasan’s account understands a living calf. The rebuke does not depend on choosing an account of how the sound arose. Even a living creature is not its own creator. The question the Quran presses is whether the object could answer or govern their affairs: (20:89 — **“it did not respond to them, nor could it protect or benefit them”**). Neither its rich material nor its strange appearance supplied the knowledge, power, and guidance that belong to God. The people had received a promise of revelation, yet turned to something made from possessions they had brought with them. They treated an object within their reach as though it were the source of the rescue they had already received.

**A TEMPORARY ABSENCE DOES NOT REMOVE A KNOWN DUTY**

The words ***“in his absence”*** refer to Moses’ departure, not his death. They had reason to expect his return, and another prophet was present to warn them. Aaron told them, (20:90 — **“You are only being tested by this, for indeed your ˹one true˺ Lord is the Most Compassionate”**). He did not authorize the calf’s worship or regard it as another path to the same Lord. Their reply was a refusal to stop: (20:91 — **“We will not cease to worship it until Moses returns to us”**). Since the warning had already been given, waiting for Moses was not an innocent way of suspending judgement. It prolonged a practice they had been told to leave. The contrast also explains why Aaron’s part in the story matters. The people were not deprived of every voice of guidance when Moses went away. Aaron appealed to them, although he feared that a split would tear the people apart. His difficulty in ending their conduct does not turn his warning into approval of it. Because the duty came from God, its force did not depend on Moses remaining visibly present. Moses’ absence changed who was there to address them; it did not change who alone deserved their worship.

The final description is ***“acting wrongfully”***. It judges the act they were committing. Worship belongs to God, so transferring it to the calf placed devotion where it could not rightly belong. The same gravity appears in Luqmân’s warning, (31:13 — **“for associating ˹others with Him˺ is truly the worst of all wrongs”**). This was more than impatience with a timetable or a mistake about when Moses would return. The people had replaced the worship taught by the messenger with worship of a creature. They wronged themselves by that choice, despite the gifts that should have helped them recognize their Lord. The collective address cannot mean every person worshipped the calf, because Aaron’s opposition is explicit. Nor does it give later readers leave to turn a named wrong in this history into inherited guilt for every descendant. The Book distinguishes the acts of successive generations: (2:134 — **“For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned”**). The hearers are made to face their community’s past so that they do not repeat its refusal of guidance. The episode shows why witnessing rescue does not by itself ensure lasting obedience. A gift still calls for a faithful response, and a leader’s absence cannot make a clear wrong right.

---

## Verse 2:52

> Even then We ˹still˺ forgave you so perhaps you would be grateful

**FORGIVENESS FOLLOWS A BREACH THAT STILL MATTERS**

The opening ***“Even then”*** holds the new gift beside the offence just described. The people had worshipped the calf after being delivered from Pharaoh and given clear signs. Abū al-ʿĀliyah relates the pardon to that very breach. God did not forgive because there had been no wrong, nor because the wrong was too slight to matter. Its gravity makes the mercy more striking. The same history is recalled in another passage: (4:153 — **“Still We forgave them for that ˹after their repentance˺”**). Since the crime and the pardon are both named, neither can be used to erase the meaning of the other. The calf did not become worthy of worship when its worshippers were forgiven. Rather, people who had placed themselves in danger were given a way back. This is why pardon belongs among the favours the Israelites are told to remember. Rescue from an enemy had preserved their lives; forgiveness now preserved them from the final ruin toward which their own act had led. Mercy did not leave the history at the point of their betrayal.

The words ***“We ˹still˺ forgave you”*** place the act of pardon with God. The sense includes wiping away an offence and passing over the punishment it has earned. It is not merely the fading of human memory about an event. Ibn ʿAbbās connects the favour with God’s not destroying the people altogether. Their continued life was not proof that the calf had been accepted. Nor is pardon here a promise that repentance can be left out. The account of their return says, (2:54 — **“Then He accepted your repentance”**). That link matters because a gift of forgiveness cannot be turned into permission to persist in the same rejection. The people were brought back under the authority they had defied. Pardon need not mean that nothing painful had occurred during that return; it means that God accepted it and did not leave them to the full outcome of their sin. The next description of their repentance gives its own details. Here the stress is on the mercy that followed a real offence, not on a denial that the offence ever deserved judgement.

**WHY MERCY IS FOLLOWED BY AN EXPECTATION**

The purpose is expressed in ***“so perhaps you would be grateful”***. Gratitude is the fitting response to mercy received, rather than a price already paid to secure it. The wording places a duty before those who have been spared. Its note of expectation does not mean that God is unsure what they will do. The Lord is described as having (2:29 — **“˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things”**). Here the expression directs the people toward the response that pardon should produce. A person looking at such a gift would have reason to expect thanks from its recipient. Yet being given a reason to obey does not remove the person’s capacity to turn away again. This is why the last clause is an appeal, not a claim that every forgiven person has already become grateful. The relation between the clauses is plain: God has dealt with them in mercy so that their conduct may answer that mercy. Gratitude recognizes both the giver and the value of what was given. Forgetting the need for pardon would make the person less able to give that answer.

**THANKS TAKES THE FORM OF OBEDIENCE**

Gratitude reaches the heart, speech, and deeds. It acknowledges the gift, speaks rightly of its giver, and uses what has been received in a way pleasing to Him. Muslim preserves the Prophet’s teaching that the command given to believers agrees with that given to the messengers. The messengers are told, (23:51 — **“Eat from what is good and lawful, and act righteously”**), while believers are told, (2:172 — **“And give thanks to Allah if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺”**). The parallel explains why gratitude cannot be reduced to a polite phrase. Good action gives the acknowledgment a form in life. The family of David receives the direct instruction, (34:13 — **“Work gratefully, O family of David!”**). For the people forgiven after worshipping the calf, the first fitting act was to leave that false worship and remain faithful to God. Because the pardon restored a relation they had violated, thanks must include care for that relation. Praise offered while defending the old offence would contradict its own purpose. The gift is recognized by a changed response, not by claiming that mercy has made obedience unnecessary.

Al-Fuḍayl describes gratitude for a favour as not disobeying God after receiving it. That account does not require pretending to be beyond every future fault. It refuses the use of mercy as an excuse to stop resisting the wrong. Gratitude also makes a person fair toward the human means through which help has reached him. Abū Hurayrah reports in Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī that the Prophet said, *"He who does not thank people does not thank God."* Thanks to people does not make them rivals to God; it acknowledges the help He allowed them to give. In this history, the people owed attention to the prophetic guidance that called them back, not renewed attachment to the object that misled them. Even the ability to repent and give thanks is a gift, so gratitude is not a claim to have repaid God in full. It is a willing use of what He has given. The continued opportunity to obey becomes part of the mercy remembered, and the answer to that mercy is faithful service.

---

## Verse 2:53

> And ˹remember˺ when We gave Moses the Scripture—the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺ that perhaps you would be ˹rightly˺ guided

**THE WRITTEN GIFT THAT CONTINUES THE RESCUE**

God gave the people a rule to live by, not only an escape from danger. The reminder is ***“And ˹remember˺ when We gave Moses the Scripture”***. The Scripture given to Moses is the Torah. It is called a book because its teaching was set down, not left as a passing impression of an event. The account of the Tablets states, (7:145 — **“We wrote for him on the Tablets ˹the fundamentals˺ of everything; commandments and explanations of all things”**). The people could return to what had been given and learn what God required. Moses received it as a messenger, not as the author of a rule drawn from his own wishes. Although he is the named recipient, the gift concerns the people to whom he was sent. The same grant is described as (28:43 — **“an insight for the people, a guide, and mercy”**). This makes its place among the favours clear. Freedom without knowledge of the way to serve God would leave them vulnerable to another false claim, as the calf had shown. Because God gave them teaching as well as rescue, they were not left to build their worship around whatever sight or voice next impressed them.

The Scripture is further described as ***“the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺”***. Mujāhid identifies this standard with the Book itself: it separates truth from falsehood. These are two ways of describing the same gift, rather than proof that two different books were given. One description identifies the written revelation; the other explains what it does. The parallel account gives Moses and Aaron (21:48 — **“the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺—a light and a reminder for the righteous”**). A light makes what lies on the path visible; the standard lets competing claims be judged. It makes known the lawful and the forbidden, right worship and false worship, duties and the acts that violate them. Since the rule comes from God, the people must measure their conduct by it rather than change the rule to suit a preferred conduct. That is the difference between receiving guidance and merely possessing words. A text used only to confirm whatever its readers already desire is not being allowed to do the separating for which it was given.

The underlying sense of separation also explains other early readings. Ibn Zayd connects the standard with the victory that distinguished Moses and his people from Pharaoh’s forces. He draws a parallel with Badr, (8:41 — **“on that decisive day when the two armies met ˹at Badr˺”**). Clear signs can expose a false claim and vindicate a messenger, just as a revealed command distinguishes right action from wrong. This gives the wider reading a real connection to the story, rather than making it a different subject with no ground in the wording. Yet the Book is the nearest gift named here, so the reading adopted is that its teaching itself supplies the standard. The earlier division of the sea need not be inserted as a second event within this short reminder. Nor must an unnamed later recipient be supplied to make the standard a reference only to the Quran. The words remain about what God gave Moses. His victory displayed God’s power; the Scripture made known the rule by which the people were to live after their deliverance.

**KNOWING THE WAY AND FOLLOWING IT ARE NOT IDENTICAL**

The intended result is ***“that perhaps you would be ˹rightly˺ guided”***. The gift opens a way out of error, but possession of it does not force every recipient to follow. Guidance here includes learning what is true and being enabled to act upon it. A person can know the command and still turn from it through pride or desire. That failure is not proof that the teaching lacked a guiding purpose. It shows why the response of the heart belongs in the account alongside the gift of knowledge. The Book did bear fruit among people who remained faithful: (32:24 — **“We raised from among them leaders, guiding by Our command, when they patiently endured and firmly believed in Our signs”**). Their leadership is joined to patience and firm belief, not to a claim that inherited scripture alone placed them beyond error. Because knowledge supplies a means of guidance, refusing to use it is a serious failure rather than a neutral choice. The verse therefore praises the gift without making its recipients incapable of disobedience. The expected response is a faithful use of this gift.

Moses’ place in this gift also belongs to the wider purpose of the messengers. God speaks of sending them and says, (57:25 — **“and with them We sent down the Scripture and the balance ˹of justice˺ so that people may administer justice”**). Revelation is not detached from the lives people share. Its distinction between right and wrong governs worship, but also the duties by which people deal fairly with one another. The ruler’s wishes are not the final measure, and neither are the claims of a crowd. Those who had known Pharaoh’s rule were given something other than another powerful person’s preference. This is why the standard is itself a mercy. It makes a rightful demand knowable and gives a false demand a measure by which it can be refused. The purpose reaches beyond correcting one episode of calf worship. The people needed a faithful course for the life that continued after rescue and pardon. Remembering the Book as a gift means letting it teach that course. The honour of receiving revelation is fulfilled in following its truth, not in setting the name of its recipient above the command he brought.

---

## Verse 2:54

> And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “O my people! Surely you have wronged yourselves by worshipping the calf, so turn in repentance to your Creator and execute ˹the calf-worshippers among˺ yourselves. That is best for you in the sight of your Creator.” Then He accepted your repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful

Moses’ call to repentance comes as a direct address to the people he serves: ***“And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people”***. His appeal, ***“O my people!”***, retains the bond between them while refusing to conceal their offence. The charge is specific: ***“Surely you have wronged yourselves by worshipping the calf”***. They had harmed themselves by giving worship to what could not be their Lord. Their act did not diminish God; it placed them under a judgement they had brought upon themselves. Al-Ḥasan relates Moses’ rebuke to their recognition that they had gone astray and their plea, (7:149 — **“If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will certainly be losers”**). Since they had begun to recognize the wrong, the speech directs that recognition toward a real return. It does not leave them with shame and no way to respond. At the same time, affection for his people does not make Moses rename calf worship as harmless. He identifies both the deed and the people it has harmed. Their own lives are at stake, and the one addressing them seeks their restoration to the Creator they have forsaken.

**RETURN TO THE ONE WHO GAVE THEM LIFE**

The first demand is ***“so turn in repentance to your Creator”***. Repentance is a return from disobedience to the obedience God requires. For these people, it means abandoning the calf and submitting to the true Lord. Abū al-ʿĀliyah explains the divine title here as the One who created them. Its use is pointed: they had shaped an object for worship, but neither that object nor its maker had given them life. The Creator’s care and power stand against the helplessness of their manufactured god. Elijah raises the same contrast in his rebuke, (37:125 — **“Do you call upon ˹the idol of˺ Ba’l and abandon the Best of Creators”**). The title thus supplies a reason for the required return, not only a name for its destination. Because their being comes from God, devotion belongs to Him rather than to something within His creation. Their regret must become a changed allegiance. It cannot remain an uneasy feeling while the old worship continues. Moses is not asking them to invent a rite that feels severe enough to earn relief. He conveys the form of return required of them in this particular crisis.

**THE SEVERE COMMAND BELONGS TO THIS HISTORICAL JUDGEMENT**

That form includes ***“and execute ˹the calf-worshippers among˺ yourselves”***. The reading followed here is that members of the community carried out the penalty upon those who had worshipped the calf. The reference to themselves describes people of one community acting upon others within it; it is not an instruction that each person take his own life. The account from Ibn ʿAbbās describes the guilty being put to death by those who had not joined their worship. Other early reports describe the event more broadly as members of the people killing one another. They differ over its circumstances, but they do not reduce the event to an inward struggle with desire. The inward need to abandon sinful wishes does not cancel the historical penalty described. Its scope must also be kept clear. This was a command delivered by Moses for that community’s repentance, not permission for later readers to use suicide or private violence as penance. The command to believers is, (4:29 — **“And do not kill ˹each other or˺ yourselves”**). In the law brought by Muhammad, repentance from such worship is a return to God and abandonment of the sin, not a rite of self-destruction.

Moses gives the reason as ***“That is best for you in the sight of your Creator”***. The judgement is measured by the Creator and the final outcome, not by the ease of the act at that moment. The second mention of the Creator directs them back to the authority under which the command was given. It does not make suffering desirable in itself or mean that any harsh demand spoken by a human being must be obeyed. The history concerns a known prophetic command. Ibn ʿAbbās’s account in al-Nasāʾī’s narration of Moses’ trials joins their admission of guilt and response to the command with forgiveness for those involved. Al-Zuhrī’s account also records Moses’ grief over the deaths and the assurance of mercy for the dead and pardon for the survivors. The grief is important: the cost is not treated as slight. The severity shows the gravity of the breach, while the ending shows that the purpose was not to leave the people beyond hope. Their return was accepted, and the killing was brought to an end.

**ACCEPTANCE FOLLOWS THE RETURN TO GOD**

The narrative then states, ***“Then He accepted your repentance”***. It moves from the command conveyed by Moses to the outcome granted by God. The actions between the command and acceptance are not all repeated in the short verse, but the accepted repentance presupposes their response. They did not merely hear the demand and continue to defend the calf. This matters because the mercy recalled earlier was not approval of their false worship. It was God’s acceptance of a return from it. The giver of life was also the giver of pardon. The people could acknowledge their guilt and obey, but they could not declare that God now owed them acquittal. Nor could Moses create forgiveness by his own authority. He conveyed the command and pleaded for his people; the verse attributes acceptance to God. Since that acceptance is plainly affirmed, the account is not an invitation to imagine a punishment continuing without end. It explains the great cost of their return and the mercy by which their relation to God was restored.

The conclusion identifies the Lord as ***“Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful”***. The first name expresses His abundant acceptance of repentance, from many servants and through repeated returns. It does not describe God as repenting of an offence. The servant turns away from sin; God turns toward the servant with pardon and favour. His mercy also precedes and enables the return. Of another group the Quran states, (9:118 — **“Then He turned to them in mercy so that they might repent”**). The opportunity to repent is therefore not a resource a sinner possesses independently of God. His help opens the way, and His acceptance completes it. Joined to the name of the Most Merciful, the title keeps the severe episode within its stated outcome: the people were not denied every path back. The same Lord who judged their wrong accepted their repentance. This offers no excuse to make light of calf worship or of the deaths in its aftermath. It locates the lasting hope in God’s mercy rather than in the people’s ability to erase their own guilt. Repentance is a real change of course, and acceptance remains His gift.

---

## Verse 2:55

> And ˹remember˺ when you said, “O Moses! We will never believe you until we see Allah with our own eyes,” so a thunderbolt struck you while you were looking on

**ASSENT MADE DEPENDENT ON A PRIVATE CONDITION**

The remembered exchange begins with the people’s own words: ***“And ˹remember˺ when you said”***. They address the messenger, ***“O Moses!”***, and declare, ***“We will never believe you”***. Ibn Zayd places this refusal after Moses brought the Tablets and presented their commands as God’s revelation. Al-Suddī relates it to the company who went with Moses to the appointment; another passage records, (7:155 — **“Moses chose seventy men from among his people for Our appointment”**). The precise relation between the accounts need not be forced into this verse, which does not itself number the speakers. Here the demand is read as a challenge to the revelation Moses brought. They are not simply people who have never heard of his mission or seen a sign. They have been confronted with the grounds for trusting him, yet refuse the message unless a further condition is met. Because their words concern what they will accept from him, the difficulty lies in their response to a known messenger, not merely in a lack of information about an unknown claim. The next words expose the condition by which they seek to withhold that acceptance.

They require it to wait ***“until we see Allah with our own eyes”***. Ibn ʿAbbās explains the demand as open, direct sight. They are not asking only for inward understanding or for a dream. The addition about their own eyes makes the intended kind of seeing plain. Their refusal is also bounded by that demand: the force of never believing here is until the claimed condition has been fulfilled, not a separate statement about every possible future. The point is that they make their acceptance of God’s message depend on a form of encounter they can demand for themselves. Yet the chapter has already praised those (2:3 — **“who believe in the unseen”**). Belief in the unseen is not belief with no grounds; Moses had brought signs and revelation. It means that the truth disclosed by God is not confined to what every hearer has personally seen. The speakers reject that relation between messenger and hearer. They seek to make their own sight a condition above the evidence already granted, as though the Lord must be made visible before His word can bind them.

**LONGING TO SEE IS NOT THE SAME AS WITHHOLDING BELIEF**

The fault is not that every desire for greater assurance is wrong. Moses himself asks, (7:143 — **“My Lord! Reveal Yourself to me so I may see You”**). His request arises within faith and longing, not a threat to reject his Lord unless the request is granted. Abraham’s question about the raising of the dead is likewise joined to the affirmation, (2:260 — **“Yes I do, but just so my heart can be reassured”**). The difference concerns the stance from which the request is made. Since the present speakers use their demand to withhold belief from the messenger, their words are not treated as that faithful search for reassurance. Nor does their punishment establish that God can never be seen in the life to come. The blessed are described as (75:23 — **“looking at their Lord”**). That gift belongs to God’s promise and permission, not to a human power to summon it on demand. The account therefore neither condemns honest inquiry as such nor makes sight the only valid ground of faith. It exposes a refusal that tries to dictate the terms on which a known revelation will be accepted.

**THE SIGHT THEY RECEIVED SHOWED THEIR OWN POWERLESSNESS**

The consequence is ***“so a thunderbolt struck you”***. The stroke is overwhelming and fatal. Al-Suddī describes fire, while the report from al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas emphasizes a sound that struck them down. These descriptions bring out the terror of the event; the decisive fact for its outcome is made plain by the following verse, (2:56 — **“Then We brought you back to life after your death”**). Because that statement speaks of death and restoration to life, the event here cannot be reduced to a passing scare. The term for this overwhelming stroke can elsewhere describe a swoon, but the surrounding account determines the sense in this case. They had demanded control over the form of evidence they would receive, yet could not secure even the continuance of their own lives. The power belongs to the Lord whom they sought to place under a condition. The punishment is not the proof that Moses had failed. It follows the refusal of those who challenged him, and leaves him pleading rather than claiming a power to reverse it himself.

The words ***“while you were looking on”*** make the warning immediate. ʿUrwah ibn Ruwaym explains that members of the group saw others being struck. The sight belongs to the event as it overtook them; it does not require the claim that a dead person continued watching after death. They were confronted with what they could neither prevent nor turn aside. Another account makes the link to their offence explicit: (4:153 — **“So a thunderbolt struck them for their wrongdoing”**). The final clause also recalls the earlier rescue, when the Israelites watched Pharaoh’s people drown. Sight had then confirmed deliverance; now those making this demand witnessed judgement among themselves. Having seen an enemy’s fall did not place them outside the duty to trust and obey. Their past privilege could not convert this refusal into a right. Yet the sequence does not end with the thunderbolt. Moses appeals to his Lord for the people, and the next reminder concerns life restored. The severe consequence must be read with that ensuing mercy, not turned into a claim that every path back was closed.

---

## Verse 2:56

> Then We brought you back to life after your death, so that perhaps you would be grateful

**LIFE GIVEN AGAIN TO THOSE WHO HAD LOST IT**

The thunderbolt was not the last act in the account: ***“Then We brought you back to life”***. Moses had appealed to his Lord for the people. His prayer expressed concern for them and for what their loss would mean when he returned to the rest of Israel. Yet the act of restoring life is attributed to God, not to a power belonging to Moses. Qatādah explains that those struck down were raised to complete the remainder of their allotted lives. Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas likewise distinguishes the death that came as punishment from their return to live out their remaining term. The gift was more than release from fear. Life itself, which they could not preserve by their demand or recover by their own effort, was given again. The Quran states the Lord’s power over that whole course: (22:66 — **“He is the One Who gave you life, then will cause you to die, and then will bring you back to life”**). Because the same Lord gives life and governs its end, their revival does not require another power to defeat death on His behalf. Moses’ appeal is heard through God’s mercy, and the restored people are again able to respond to the One whose message they had challenged.

The qualification ***“after your death”*** fixes the nature of the event. They had not merely fallen asleep, lost interest in worship, or received new teaching after being ignorant. The word for raising can elsewhere refer to stirring a sleeper or sending a messenger, but those senses do not cancel the plain qualification here. The Quran can describe loss of consciousness expressly, as when (7:143 — **“Moses collapsed unconscious”**). This account instead speaks of death followed by life. A figurative reading about education would therefore remove the very condition by which the gift is identified. Reading the clause as an appointment to prophethood would likewise add a role that these words do not name. The literal restoration is the reading followed here because it fits both the fatal stroke and the stated return. The verse answers the preceding danger directly. Those who could not bear what overtook them were brought back by the Lord who had power over them throughout. Their weakness was real, and so was the mercy that restored them.

**RETURNED TO LIFE, NOT RELEASED FROM DUTY**

This return belongs to their earthly history, not to the general resurrection for the final judgement. Other extraordinary restorations are also recalled in the chapter. Of those who fled in fear of death it says, (2:243 — **“Allah said to them, “Die!” then He gave them life”**). Such events show the power of the One who will raise all people; they do not mean that every person’s final resurrection has already taken place. The universal promise remains, (23:16 — **“then on the Day of Judgment you will be resurrected”**). An exceptional sign and the general course of human life can therefore be affirmed together. The people restored here returned to a life in which they could receive commands, obey, refuse, and give thanks. They had not passed into a state where earthly duty no longer applied. This distinction also prevents the miracle from becoming a demand that every dead person must now be restored whenever a doubter asks. God chooses the occasion of a sign. The future raising remains His promise, and its certainty does not depend on people being able to bring its time forward for themselves.

The purpose of their return is ***“so that perhaps you would be grateful”***. The same people who had set a condition on belief now owed thanks for a life they could not give themselves. Gratitude in this setting includes accepting the guidance they had resisted. A reading that exempts them from duty because they have witnessed such an event misses this continuing demand. Their unusual experience did not make all obedience needless; the restored life was itself an opportunity to obey. Ibn Zayd’s account records Moses again urging them to take God’s Book after their revival. That fits the purpose stated here more closely than a claim that they had moved beyond commands altogether.
