Since the gift restores the ability to act, the fitting response is a faithful use of that ability. It is not a boast that the experience has placed them above the ordinary servants of God. The story also speaks to the later hearers through their people’s continued life. They inherit the fruits of mercy, not a right to dismiss the message. The renewed life becomes a further reason to heed the Lord whose guidance Moses had brought.

---

## Verse 2:57

> And ˹remember when˺ We shaded you with clouds and sent down to you manna and quails, ˹saying˺, “Eat from the good things We have provided for you.” The evildoers ˹certainly˺ did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves

**CLOUDS, MEAT, AND SWEETNESS IN A BARREN PLACE**

Rescue from Pharaoh did not end the people’s dependence on their Lord, and the open wilderness offered no shelter of its own. The verse turns first to that exposure: ***“And ˹remember when˺ We shaded you with clouds”***. The plain sense of the account is that a cloud cover stood over them through the years of wandering in a land without tree or building. Ibn ʿAbbās states that God shaded the Children of Israel with clouds throughout those years (al-Nasāʾī), and the same reading is transmitted from Ibn ʿUmar, al-Rabīʿ b. Anas, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Suddī. Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah place the shielding in the desert itself, where the sun’s heat was the daily hardship. The construction deserves notice, since the cloud is not the thing shaded but the shade made theirs. That is why the gift stands beside the water struck from stone in the fuller account: (7:160 — **“twelve springs gushed out. Each tribe knew its drinking place. We shaded them with clouds and sent down to them manna and”**). Water from rock and cover from sky answered two needs the people could not supply for themselves.

The provision followed them as they walked: ***“and sent down to you manna”***. Two features of it are transmitted from Qatādah. It fell in the hours before sunrise as snow falls, and it was whiter than milk and sweeter than honey. Any part kept past its day spoiled, so each morning’s collection covered only that day, and on Friday a person collected for two days because the Sabbath barred the search for food. Ibn ʿAbbās adds that the manna descended on the trees and they ate of it as they wished. The desert truffle is tied to the same provision by the Prophet’s words, *"Kam'ah (truffles) is a type of manna, and its liquid is a remedy for the eyes"* (al-Bukhārī), reported by Saʿd b. Zayd. The daily limit carried its own instruction. Because the gift could not be stored, reliance had to be renewed each morning. In other words, a harvest kept in a barn would have made the giver invisible; a fresh fall of food kept the source of every meal in view.

**DAILY BREAD MEASURED BY TRUST**

Meat reached them by the same easy path: ***“and quails, ˹saying˺, “Eat from the good things We have provided”***. What gathered around them was a bird resembling the common quail, a reading transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās and repeated by Mujāhid, al-Shaʿbī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ḥasan and ʿIkrimah. Qatādah records that the birds gathered around them in such numbers that each person took what served him for the day, since meat kept beyond it spoiled. The permission names its object in the moral vocabulary of the Book: what is good, wholesome and lawful. A limit attached to the same provision elsewhere shows that permission is not excess: (20:81 — **“˹saying,˺ “Eat from the good things We have provided for you, but do not transgress in them,”**). What follows from the two halves of the command is a discipline of trust. Food was made easy to gather; storage was forbidden; gratitude was to govern both the taking and the eating. The provision was granted in the wilderness precisely where no field could be sown, so that the hand behind each meal stayed visible.

**NO INJURY REACHES THE ONE DISOBEYED**

The breach turned the gift into a loss. They stored the food against the command and were deprived of it, and the verse draws the line of responsibility with the words ***“for you.” The evildoers ˹certainly˺ did not wrong Us”***. The sentence marks the difference between the one wronged and the ones who suffer. Disobedience adds nothing to God’s estate and takes nothing from it; every effect of it lands on the one who commits it. The closing phrase, ***“but wronged themselves”***, states the settled rule the Book returns to in every account of a punished people: (11:101 — **“We did not wrong them, rather they wronged themselves. The gods they invoked beside Allah were of no help at all”**). The identical provision is recalled in the longer recital of Israel’s journey, where the appointment at the mountain brings the same gift: (20:80 — **“and made an appointment with you on the right side of Mount Ṭûr, and sent down to you manna and quails”**). This is why the story is told at all. The people were shaded, fed, and given water in the sight of wonders, yet a refusal to trust the daily gift brought the harm home to themselves. The verse leaves no room for the thought that disobedience injures God; the injury is a person’s own, and it is named as such on the tongue of revelation.

---

## Verse 2:58

> And ˹remember˺ when We said, “Enter this city and eat freely from wherever you please; enter the gate with humility, saying, ‘Absolve us.’ We will forgive your sins and multiply the reward for the good-doers.”

**A CITY NAMED BY ITS MEANING RATHER THAN ITS STREETS**

The order is brief and its object is left unlabelled: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We said, “Enter this city”***. The wording does not print the city’s name on the page, and the transmitted readings divide on which town stands behind it. Qatādah, al-Suddī and al-Rabīʿ b. Anas take it as the Holy House of Jerusalem, while Ibn ʿAbbās names Jericho; al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqātil name other towns of the same region. The parallel account settles the family of readings by supplying what this sentence withholds: (7:161 — **“And ˹remember˺ when it was said to them, “Enter this city ˹of Jerusalem˺ and eat from wherever you please. Say, ‘Absolve us,’”**). Since the same command reappears with the place identified, the reading followed here is Jerusalem, and the alternative that names Jericho stands as a transmitted report rather than a competing certainty. The command also closes the journey an earlier order began: (5:21 — **“O my people! Enter the Holy Land which Allah has destined for you ˹to enter˺. And do not turn back”**). What was refused at the border of the land is now permitted at its centre, because the wandering had run its appointed length and a generation raised in the desert had come of age to enter.

**EATING FREELY WHERE THE YEARS OF WANT ENDED**

Provision inside the city is promised without the measuring of the wilderness: ***“and eat freely from wherever you please”***. The expression carries the sense of ease and expansion after straitness, and it answers the years in which every meal had been limited to that day’s need. The same formula was spoken to Adam in the garden before any hardship entered human life: (2:35 — **“We cautioned, “O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat as freely as you please,”**). In both places the eating is permission and gift, and in both it stands beside a boundary, since a gift without a limit is not the test that either the garden or the city was made to be. That is why abundance here is paired at once with an act of humility. Bread without command would have suited a people already trained to gather only what the day required; the entry is ordered so that remembrance of the Giver enters along with the gift. The effect of the pairing is a mercy that does not dissolve obligation. Food and land arrive together, and both are held on terms.

**THE PROMISE SPOKEN IN THE SAME BREATH AS THE COMMAND**

The manner of the entry is fixed as carefully as its place: ***“enter the gate with humility, saying, ‘Absolve us.’ We will forgive your sins”***. What the people were told to say is rendered *"Absolve us"* — a single expression carrying the sense of unburdening and pardon. Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it as *"forgive our sins"*, and another early gloss takes it as an acknowledgement that there is no god but God. The posture is named in a word whose reach covers prostration while its use here also covers deep bowing, so the reports of the entry describe people entering bent at the door rather than striding through it. The Prophet relates that God said to the Children of Israel, *"Enter the gate prostrating and say, 'Absolve us,' and We will forgive your sins"* (Muslim). Pardon is therefore offered to a people whose refusal at the border had cost them forty years, and it is offered in the same breath as the command. The reason forgiveness is tied to speech here is that the commanded word is itself an admission of fault, and an admission put on the lips is the first act of the returning heart.

The closing promise divides its gifts by their receivers: ***“and multiply the reward”*** ***“for the good-doers.””***. The increase belongs to those whose conduct answers the gift, and the transmitted gloss explains it as God’s adding to their good deeds. The clause therefore does more than repeat the pardon. Pardon closes the old account because the fault has been admitted; increase belongs to the one who lives afterwards in a way that answers what he has received. A preserved reading recites the pardon in the passive voice, so that the announcement stands settled on its own terms as *"they will be forgiven"*. What turns on the division is plain: entry is open to the whole people, pardon is offered to everyone who says the word, and increase is reserved for the one who then does good. The verse leaves three stations behind it — the gift received, the fault admitted, and the life rebuilt on both.

---

## Verse 2:59

> But the wrongdoers changed the words they were commanded to say. So We sent down a punishment from the heavens upon them for their rebelliousness

**ONE LETTER BETWEEN MERCY AND MOCKERY**

The commanded word was small and its sense was pardon: ***“But the wrongdoers changed the words they were commanded to say.”***. What the people were told to speak carried absolution in a single expression; what they said instead played with letters. The accounts of their substitution differ in its exact shape, and the difference between them is itself instructive. One account gives the mockery as a grain inside a hair, another gives wheat, and another gives a grain in wheat, because the spoken form stood one letter away from the commanded one. Adding that letter turned a plea for pardon into a joke about grain, and the joke was made on the lips that had been offered forgiveness. The verse then marks the guilty party precisely. It does not lay the change on the whole community; it names those who wronged, since not everyone among them took part in the substitution. The effect of that precision is that the punishment attaches to the guilty and no inherited blame is smeared across a lineage. The parallel account states the same division: (7:162 — **“But the wrongdoers among them changed the words they were commanded to say.”**). Abū Hurayrah reports that the Prophet described what followed the change: *"they changed it and entered the gate crawling on their backsides"* (Muslim). The public disgrace answers the private ridicule, and a word spoken in play became the condition of their movement into the city.

**WHAT THE VERSE SETTLES ABOUT WORDS THEMSELVES**

The ruling this event carries concerns wording as such. The people did not abandon the rite; they kept the shape of the ordered entry and tampered with its formula. The jurists of the community therefore hold that a revealed wording is not replaced by another, even where the replacement carries a close sense, because the wording is part of what was commanded and not merely a shell around it. The fixed forms of worship show the same rule in practice. The call to prayer, the testimony of faith, and the words said in bowing and in prostration are transmitted in set forms, and a person is not free to substitute a personal phrasing for them. The reason is not pedantry. A formula taught by revelation carries its ruling in its own letters, and the one who alters it places his own sense where only the revealed sense was ordered. The gravity of the matter is also graded in the reports themselves: a change made to words of repentance drew this answer, so a change made to the descriptions of the worshipped One is graver still. Since the alteration here was small in letters and large in meaning, the answer was large in the same measure. What follows for any age is that closeness of meaning is not a licence for substitution; the words of worship stand as they were given.

**A PENALTY DESCENDING ON THE MOCKERS**

The answer is located above, not in an army on the ground: ***“So We sent down a punishment from the heavens upon them”***. A pestilence struck the camp, and the transmitted count puts the dead at just under seventy thousand within a very short time. Its direction is stated so that no enemy takes credit and no chance event absorbs the blame. The stroke came from the One whose formula had been altered, and it fell on the party the verse had already named. The cause clause is narrow and exact: ***“for their rebelliousness”***. The word the verse spends on their conduct carries the sense of crossing every bound, which is more than an error in speech. They were not mispronouncing through ignorance; they were making light of a commanded word, and defiance of that kind is what the name marks. A warning had already stood over the provision they were living by: (20:81 — **“˹saying,˺ “Eat from the good things We have provided for you, but do not transgress in them,”**). Their transgression here was not in the food but in the speech ordered beside it, and the same law answered both. The event therefore settles a line that runs through the whole account: gifts are given without measure, and mockery of the commanded word is not left unjudged.

---

## Verse 2:60

> And ˹remember˺ when Moses prayed for water for his people, We said, “Strike the rock with your staff.” Then twelve springs gushed out, ˹and˺ each tribe knew its drinking place. ˹We then said,˺ “Eat and drink of Allah’s provisions, and do not go about spreading corruption in the land.”

**WATER ASKED FOR, THEN GIVEN FROM STONE**

Thirst in the open wilderness brought the people to their prophet with a request rather than a complaint: ***“And ˹remember˺ when Moses prayed”***. The form of his praying carries the sense of asking for water to be given, and the setting supplies its cause, since the wanderings were spent in a land without wells or rivers. An account of their questions in that period records them asking first who would shield them from the heat of the sun, then who would give them food, then who would give them water, and each question was answered by a separate gift. The command that answered the last of them is exact and physical: ***“for water for his people, We said, “Strike the rock with your staff.””***. The staff that strikes was itself carried as a sign through the ages before this day. The transmitted account describes it as a rod of a wood of the Garden, ten cubits long, handed down through the prophets until it reached the hand of Moses. What it had already done marks its place among the signs. Cast down, it moved as a living serpent; struck against the sea, it parted the water into standing walls; struck against the stone here, it opened the ground’s own stores. The miracle therefore attaches to the One who commands the rod, not to the wood that moves. The reason the sign hangs on the command rather than on the rod is that the rod itself is created, and every movement credited to it is movement under orders.

**A TABLE SET WITHOUT TOIL**

The result is counted and assigned: ***“Then twelve springs gushed out, ˹and˺ each tribe knew its drinking place. ˹We then said,˺ “Eat”***. Twelve tribes descended from the twelve sons of Jacob, and the springs were divided so that no group crowded another. Ibn ʿAbbās describes the stone as square, with three springs opening on each of its sides, and he reports that each tribe kept its own spring wherever the camp moved, finding the same provision in each new stopping place (al-Nasāʾī). The Arabic verb for bursting forth marks the water at its full force, where the parallel account describes the same springs at their first flow. What gushes from stone answers the doubt that stone can hold water at all; what is assigned tribe by tribe answers the doubt that a single source could serve a whole people. Sustenance then frames the water: ***“and drink of Allah’s provisions”***. The meat, the sweetness and the drink all arrived without sowing or trade, and that is why the gift is named here as belonging to God directly. What follows from the account is the practice it leaves behind. Seeking rain by humble prayer is established practice in the law, since the essential element in it is the prayer itself, offered by a servant who owns nothing of the cloud or the spring.

**THE FAVOUR THAT MUST NOT BE ANSWERED WITH RUIN**

The permission ends where harm begins: ***“and do not go about spreading corruption in the land.””***. The clause stands beside the eating for a reason. A person fed and watered by a gift he did not produce is the person most exposed to the charge of ingratitude, and ingratitude in practice is what corruption means here. The Book states the order of that ruin elsewhere: (7:56 — **“Do not spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order. And call upon Him with hope”**). Provision sets the land in order; disobedience undoes the setting; the warning therefore precedes the harm rather than following it. The verse also turns the stone into a measure of the heart. The same people who drank as springs burst from rock were addressed later in this chapter about a hardness that exceeds stone: (2:74 — **“Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder, for some rocks gush rivers; others split, spilling water;”**). That comparison fixes the difference between the two states. A stone gave way under the command of God while living hearts held out against it, and the yielding of the one measures the defiance of the other. What follows for any community living on unearned provision is that gratitude takes the form of conduct. The land is not corrupted by drought alone; it is corrupted by hands that eat from a gift and then disobey the One who gave it.

---

## Verse 2:61

> And ˹remember˺ when you said, “O Moses! We cannot endure the same meal ˹every day˺. So ˹just˺ call upon your Lord on our behalf, He will bring forth for us some of what the earth produces of herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, and onions.” Moses scolded ˹them˺, “Do you exchange what is better for what is worse? ˹You can˺ go down to any village and you will find what you have asked for.” They were stricken with disgrace and misery, and they invited the displeasure of Allah for rejecting Allah’s signs and unjustly killing the prophets. This is ˹a fair reward˺ for their disobedience and violations

**WEARINESS WITH A GIFT, DRESSED AS A REQUEST**

The turn begins inside the people’s own mouths: ***“And ˹remember˺ when you said, “O Moses!”***. Weariness had replaced gratitude by the time this was said. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī describes them as bored and impatient with the food they had been given, remembering the diet of their old life in Egypt and longing to return to it. What made the complaint sound reasonable to them is the next clause: ***“We cannot endure the same meal ˹every day˺.”***. The meal they call one was in fact two things, and the phrasing is a known Arabic usage in which the dual is spoken of as one; another account gives the reason as their habit of eating each with the other until the two behaved as a single dish. The word they use for endurance also deserves attention, since it carries the sense of holding the self back inside a strait, and their sentence is therefore a refusal to be patient rather than a report of harm. Nothing in the provision was spoiled or scarce. The complaint is that the gift repeated itself, and a gift that repeats itself is still a gift.

**THE MARKET LIST THAT NAMED THEIR OLD LIFE**

The demand follows its complaint immediately: ***“So ˹just˺ call upon your Lord on our behalf, He will bring forth”***. The phrasing already carries its own judgement, because it turns the Lord of the heavens into the arranger of a greengrocer’s stock. What they ask for is then listed item by item: ***“for us some of what the earth produces of herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils”***. The herbs named are plants that grow without a standing stalk, and the fifth item of the list has been read most often as garlic; Ibn ʿAbbās gives that gloss, and the transmitted reading of Ibn Masʿūd pronounces the same word in the form that means garlic outright. Other readings of that item exist, one of them taking it as wheat used for bread, and one taking it as covering every grain and seed that is eaten. The list itself tells the history. These are the foods of settled peasant life, and they are exactly what the people had eaten in the land of their servitude. What follows in the sentence carries their tone back to them: ***“and onions.” Moses scolded ˹them˺, “Do you exchange what is better”***. The question of the rebuke is grammatical as well as moral, since the form of it in Arabic is built for reproach rather than for information.

**A TRADE MEASURED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS**

Moses answers the request by naming what it would cost: ***“for what is worse?”***. Manna and quails descended without sowing or shearing, pure and daily renewed, while the vegetables they asked for would have to be dug from ground that owed them nothing. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī adds that they remembered the food of their forebears and the pull of old habits moved them more than any need. The scolding is therefore also a valuation, and the valuation runs against their own appraisal of their lives. A person who trades descending bread for a field’s labour has not merely changed a menu; he has re-ranked what gift is and what toil is. Moses also shows his measure as a leader in the same movement. He rebukes them sharply and then carries their request to his Lord, since care for a people does not end when their demand is wrong. The answer that follows is itself shaped like their demand. Permission arrives, but the permission is the beginning of the fall they had chosen.

**GRANTED, AND THEN MARKED**

The permission is short: ***“˹You can˺ go down to any village”***. The verb for going down covers entering a place and need not describe a change of elevation, and the town named in the order is indefinite in its grammar, so the reading that takes it as the proper name of Egypt is held back by the shape of the word itself. Ibn ʿAbbās reports two senses for the order: a return to where they had come from, or entry into whatever town would take them. What they find there is only what they asked for: ***“and you will find what you have asked”***. The vegetables were available in towns all along; the wilderness had not deprived them of cucumbers, but of the unearned sweetness they had learned to despise. Granting the request is therefore itself the first stroke of the answer. They are sent down to buy with labour what they had been given without it, and the sending has the shape of exile rather than of favour. The reason the permission grieves a careful reader is that it marks the moment a people moved from being carried to being made to walk.

**STRICKEN WITH WHAT STICKS TO A PEOPLE**

The verse then states the outcome without softening: ***“for.” They were stricken with disgrace”***. The blow is named as a stamp rather than as a passing event. Disgrace of this kind behaves like a dye that has entered the cloth; later washing moves the dirt but the colour remains. The pair of afflictions is completed in the next words: ***“and misery, and they invited the displeasure of Allah”***. The transmitted glosses give the two their shapes. One takes the disgrace as the tribute imposed on the subdued and the misery as the dress of poverty that never left them. The cause clause names two crimes and weighs both: ***“for rejecting Allah’s signs”***. Rejection after seeing the sea part and the stone give water is not ignorance but a decision, and a decision of that kind is what seals the distance between a people and their Lord. The second crime is heavier in the counting: ***“and unjustly killing the prophets. This is ˹a fair reward˺”***. The Book returns to this charge against them in its own ledgers of their covenant: (4:155 — **“rejecting Allah’s signs, killing the prophets unjustly”**). Killing a prophet is the crime that answers mercy with murder, and the word of God given to warn them became the blood they spilled to silence the warning. The closing line then repeats the cause as the verdict: ***“for their disobedience and violations”***. The repetition itself is deliberate, since an account that ends twice on the cause refuses to let the punishment be read as arbitrary. What the verse therefore settles is a pattern that outlives the camp. The same proclamation stands in the record of this people: (7:167 — **“And ˹remember, O Prophet,˺ when your Lord declared that He would send against them others who would make them suffer terribly”**). A stamp set by that much refusal is not removed by wealth or time alone; it is removed only by the return that undoes the cause.

---

## Verse 2:62

> Indeed, the believers, Jews, Christians, and Sabians—whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**A DOOR OPENED AFTER THE VERDICT**

The account has just closed a people under a stamp of disgrace, and the very next line refuses to let that ending be read as a closing of the sky: ***“Indeed, the believers, Jews, Christians”***. The Book pairs warning with promise in this way as its settled practice, so that a hearer who has just watched a punishment is not left with the thought that mercy has run out. The placement answers a misgiving the previous verse could easily leave behind. A whole people has just been marked for conduct of that kind, and the question whether return is still open to anyone has to be settled at once; the verse itself settles it. The door is named again here for every community, and the condition standing at its threshold is set out for all of them together. What the verse promises is also placed against what the previous verse removed. Disgrace was stamped on the wrongdoers there; here the reward waits with the Lord of those who qualify, and the two endings could not stand farther apart. A community is therefore never condemned as a community in this Book; it is condemned for what its wrongdoers did, while its believers are answered by name.

**WHO STANDS INSIDE THE NAMED GROUPS**

The list of names has been read from more than one side, and the differences are transmitted early rather than invented late. The first group, those who believe, is read by the received gloss as those who affirm the Prophet, and it is also read by an early authority, Sufyan al-Thawri, as those whose belief is on their tongues alone, which is why they are counted beside the others and then left to the condition. The name of the second group carries its own history, since the form of it in Arabic is traced to the eldest son of Jacob and to the turning the name records. The third name points back to the town of Jesus and to the disciples’ claim to be helpers of the faith. The fourth name has drawn the widest disagreement: ***“and Sabians whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah”***. Descriptions of them run from a sect that shaves the middle of the head and reads the Gospel while worshipping the angels — Ibn ʿAbbās gives that picture — to people with no scripture or rite at all, and the sounder placement among the transmitted views keeps them inside the Christian fold rather than outside every religion. Later communities claimed the name for themselves, and a claim of that kind settles nothing about what the verse meant when it was sent. The parallel listing elsewhere of the same four groups confirms that these are the communities of the revelation’s own world: (5:69 — **“Indeed, the believers, Jews, Sabians and Christians—whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good,”**). The order of the names shifts between the two passages, and the condition never shifts.

**THE CONDITION GOVERNS THE LABELS**

Everything turns on the qualification: ***“and the Last Day”***. Belief in God is bound here to belief in the final accounting, and deeds are bound to both. The wording then seals the connection: ***“and does good will have their reward with their Lord.”***. The condition is spoken in the singular and answered in the plural, a grammar that lets one person and a whole people hear themselves addressed by the same sentence. The label of a community is therefore not the passport the verse describes; the condition is. That is why the passage must be read with the Book’s own later rule: (3:85 — **“Whoever seeks a way other than Islam, it will never be accepted from them,”**). The report of the sequence is explicit. Ali ibn Abi Talhah transmits from Ibn ʿAbbās that this later verse was revealed after the one under discussion, and the conclusion carried by that sequence is that no deed is accepted from anyone after the final message except on its terms; before it, every people was answered on the terms their own message brought. Two readings have therefore stood in the field. The first takes the verse as the standing rule for every age, so that any sincere monotheist who believes in God and the Last Day and does good is rewarded. The second reads it as the announcement of God’s practice toward the righteous of earlier communities in their own times, with the invitation now answered only by the faith the final message carries. The reading followed here is the second, because the sequence of the two verses is transmitted by a Companion, and because belief in God and the Last Day is measured by what the messengers of God taught and not by the sincerity a person claims for himself. What the first reading guards is not lost in the second: no servant of God in any age was ever wronged, and the righteous of the earlier communities were never refused their reward.

**WITHOUT FEAR AHEAD, WITHOUT GRIEF BEHIND**

The promise closes on the two absences that define peace: ***“And there will be no fear”***. The absence is ordered forward and backward in the transmitted glosses. Fear belongs to what has not yet arrived, and grief belongs to what has already passed; the people of this promise are secured against both directions at once. One early gloss gives the two their furthest reach — no fear when death is overcome and the Fire is closed, and no grief for anything left behind in the world. The same double assurance is given to the close servants of God elsewhere: (10:62 — **“There will certainly be no fear for the close servants of Allah, nor will they grieve”**). And it is placed on the lips of the angels at the moment it is needed most: (41:30 — **“Surely those who say, “Our Lord is Allah,” and then remain steadfast, the angels descend upon them, ˹saying,˺ “Do not fear,”**). The closing clause of the verse under discussion states the same end in plain words: ***“for them, nor will they grieve”***. What follows for the reader who has travelled from the stamp of disgrace to this sentence is the shape of the whole passage. The Book has just shown a people ruin their own standing by refusing guidance; it now shows that the standing itself is offered again to anyone who meets the condition. The reward is held with the Lord, which means no negligence mislays it and no power takes it, and the two absences stand guard over it until the day it is paid.

---

## Verse 2:63

> And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from you and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and observe its teachings so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.”

**A PLEDGE EXACTED WITH ITS OWN SKY**

The record returns to a day of binding: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from you”***. The Arabic form behind the covenant here carries the sense of a firm assurance, a binding that holds by oath or by pact, and the noun is spoken of in the singular because the same pledge was taken from each person there. What the pledge contained is stated at length elsewhere in this chapter: (2:83 — **“And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel ˹stating˺, “Worship none but Allah; be kind to parents, relatives,”**). Monotheism and conduct were sealed together in it, so the covenant was never a bare confession but a course of life. The occasion the accounts give is the return of Moses with the tablets, when the people refused to act on what he brought until they had heard God attest it themselves. Seventy men were then chosen to go and hear, and the account records that they returned as witnesses to the Book but added words of their own to what they had heard, promising themselves ease that God had not promised. A pledge confirmed with words of that kind is exactly the kind a mountain has to settle.

**A MOUNTAIN HELD OVER A REFUSAL**

The confirmation is described without decoration: ***“and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to”***. The mountain was lifted and fixed over their heads like a canopy or a cloud, and the fuller account records their certainty that it was about to fall: (7:171 — **“And ˹remember˺ when We raised the mountain over them as if it were a cloud”**). Ibn ʿAbbās gives the scene its plain shape: the mountain was pulled out and raised above them for the taking of the covenant. A question rises at this point and is settled by the text itself. The Book forbids compulsion in religion: (2:256 — **“Let there be no compulsion in religion, for the truth stands out clearly from falsehood. So whoever renounces false gods”**), yet here force stands over a people’s heads. The reason the two do not contradict is that these were not outsiders being converted. They had already believed in their prophet and already covenanted to act on the Book, and the raising of the mountain is the enforcement of a pledge against a party on the edge of breaking it, which is how every legal order treats the rebel under its own pact. The timing of the two events has been read two ways, and both are transmitted. One reading places the raising after the pledge was broken, so that the mountain is the answer to the breach; another places it with the taking itself, as the verse’s own joining of the two clauses suggests. What turns on the difference is small, because both readings describe the same God and the same severity: a covenant in this history is not a formality that a people may quietly outgrow.

**TWO HALVES OF A DUTY KEPT TOGETHER**

The command given under the mountain is complete in two halves: ***“that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you”***. The holding is charged with strength and seriousness, and the transmitted glosses give the charge its weight. Al-Ḥasan takes the object as the Torah itself; Mujāhid takes the command as strict adherence to it; Abū al-ʿĀliyah and al-Rabīʿ b. Anas fill out the second half in the same direction: ***“and observe its teachings”*** is reading the Book and putting it into practice, not carrying it as a relic. The phrase carries memory and action in one word, so that a scripture observed is a scripture recited, understood and obeyed. The pair of commands also fixes the order of the two halves. Holding the Book without observing it produces the empty witness; observing it without holding to it produces the amended text. The seventy had already shown where the second road ends when they added to what they heard. What the scene demands of any community holding a scripture is therefore double, and the demand does not age: the text is kept as it was given, and it is lived as it reads.

**TAQWĀ AS THE PURPOSE OF THE WHOLE ARRANGEMENT**

The purpose clause names the aim of every part of it: ***“so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.””***. The mindfulness named as the purpose here is given its content by the early glosses as warding off God’s wrath and torment through obedience. That is why the covenant was exacted and the mountain raised. A law secured by awe produces a people who govern themselves when no mountain is visible. The hope is not that they keep the Book under threat; the point is that the discipline of keeping it forms the habit that needs no threat. The later answer of the same people shows how rare that outcome was: (2:93 — **“they answered, “We hear and disobey.””**). Hearing without obeying is the failure this verse was written to prevent. What follows for a reader of any scripture is the measure the verse installs. The gift is the Book; the duty is to hold it unaltered and to practise it; the purpose behind both is a heart that stands in awe of its Lord, and every element that does not serve that purpose has been left out of the arrangement.

---

## Verse 2:64

> Yet you turned away afterwards. Had it not been for Allah’s grace and mercy upon you, you would have certainly been of the losers

**TURNING BACK AFTER THE SEALING**

The verse opens on the motion that undoes a covenant: ***“Yet you turned away afterwards. Had it not been”***. The word it spends on their conduct is the word for turning one’s back, and its plain root is physical; the language extended it to anyone who abandons an order he has been given, so that walking away from a duty is named with the same word as walking away from a person. The sequence marker deserves its weight. The point is that the pledge was complied with first and then left, and that makes the breach worse than a refusal that never accepted anything. The accounts of the mountain day agree with that order. Awe secured the words; the practice that should have followed the words is what failed. The Book marks the same habit in another place, where bounty is followed by withdrawal: (9:76 — **“But when He gave them out of His bounty, they withheld it and turned away indifferently”**). That is why the pattern across these passages is consistent, and the history of this people keeps repeating it: full gifts are answered with half obedience, and half obedience is answered with turning. The terms of their covenant had been itemised elsewhere, from worship of God alone to kindness to parents, and the same covenant is sealed in the Book with its twelve leaders named: (5:12 — **“Allah made a covenant with the Children of Israel and appointed twelve leaders from among them and ˹then˺ said,”**). The charge here is that the whole list was dropped after it was sealed. The reason the verse keeps saying "you" across the generations is that the covenant was taken from the line itself, so every generation that inherits its terms inherits the charge against its own conduct.

**TWO MERCIES STANDING BETWEEN THEM AND RUIN**

The saving clause then names what held the ruin back: ***“for Allah’s grace and mercy upon you, you would have certainly been of the losers”***. The two nouns have been given two readings, and both are transmitted. In one, the grace is the enabling of repentance and the mercy is its acceptance, so that the pair names the whole road back to God in its two halves. In the other, given by Ibn ʿAbbās, the grace and mercy are the sending of the final Messenger and their living to see him, since faith in him is itself part of the covenant they had been given. The two readings meet rather than cancel. Every reprieve in this history is the practice of the same Lord, whether it comes as time given for return or as a message that opens the return. The reading followed here keeps both, and the address of the verse supports it: the second person runs from the people of the mountain to the people standing in the Prophet’s own time, because the covenant’s terms were never withdrawn. What turns on that scope is plain. The warning is not embalmed in the past. The word for loss is drawn from trade, and it means the going of a merchant’s capital rather than the shrinking of his profit, which fixes the grade of what they were saved from. A trader who loses his principal stands with nothing; the people addressed here were one such act away from that position. The Book states the covenant’s weight in the same terms elsewhere: (33:72 — **“Indeed, We offered the trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they ˹all˺ declined to bear it,”**). A trust the mountains refused was held over the heads of this people, and they turned their backs on it. That is why the mercy is named twice in one breath. What follows for any community that has been given a book and a covenant is the reading this verse installs: the turning away is judged as it happened, and the reprieve is counted as what it was, mercy standing between a people and the loss of everything.

The address also runs past the mountain to the people hearing the charge in the Prophet’s own time. The covenant those hearers stand under includes the coming of the final Messenger, so the second person of the warning is not theatre of the past. What was said to the first generation is said to the generation now standing over the same terms, and the mercy that spared them is the same mercy that has held catastrophe back since. The instruction aimed at that audience is therefore precise. A reprieve named as grace is not a guarantee. It is a window that obliges gratitude, and gratitude in covenant terms is compliance with the terms sealed. The losers named at the close are all who let the window pass while their backs are turned.

---

## Verse 2:65

> You are already aware of those of you who broke the Sabbath. We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!”

**A TOWN THAT SET TRAPS FOR ITS OWN LAW**

The address opens as a reminder of what every listener already possessed: ***“You are already aware of those of you”***. The knowledge named here is the knowledge of recognition, and the oath form that carries it marks the story as common property among the people addressed because it was their own history, not a tale imported to shame them. The crime is then named with the word for crossing a limit, which places the act at the level of defiance rather than slip. The phrase that locates the crime has also been read closely, since the transgression fell in the ordinance of the Sabbath rather than in the day as a piece of time. The name of the day itself carries the sense of rest and ceasing, and an early lexicography connects it with the cutting off of work, so the day was a weekly lesson in who governs labour. The setting the reports give is a town by the sea in the age of David, and the fuller account supplies every detail the short verse assumes: (7:163 — **“Ask them ˹O Prophet˺ about ˹the people of˺ the town which was by the sea, who broke the Sabbath. During the Sabbath,”**). Fishing was forbidden to them on that day, and the sea answered the law with its own sign. Fish surfaced in visible abundance on Saturdays and stayed hidden the rest of the week, so the test was made plain before the verdict arrived.

**A PROHIBITION DEFEATED BY ITS OWN FINE PRINT**

What the town did with that sign is the lesson of the whole passage. They did not at first fish on the Sabbath in the open. They set nets and ropes and channels before the day began, let the fish collect themselves against the devices while the law stood, and gathered the catch after the day had passed. The procedure kept the letter and gutted the intent, which is the exact anatomy of every evasion built on fine print. The accounts record that the practice began as pretence and ended as open hunting, and that a company among them warned their people and pressed them to stop. When the warnings were refused, those who forbade the wrong removed themselves to the other end of the town, and the Book gives their fate as the mirror of the other: (7:165 — **“When they ignored the warning they were given, We rescued those who used to warn against evil”**). The division of the town is therefore part of the teaching. A community that splits over a sin is not left to share one fate, because the warners were pulled out of the ruin they had refused to join. What follows for any age is the measure the devices expose. A prohibition answered by engineering proves that the heart behind it never submitted; the difference between obedience and evasion is not the difference between two techniques but between two states of the soul.

**WHEN A VERDICT TAKES THE SHAPE OF THE CRIME**

The sentence of the court is a single line: ***“who broke the Sabbath. We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!””***. The second word of the sentence carries the sense of the driven off, the creature sent away with contempt, and the lexicography of it is drawn from the driving of a dog from a door. The reports describe what followed the word. The young among them were changed into apes, and one account from Ibn ʿAbbās divides the fate by age, the young becoming apes and the old becoming swine. Qatādah describes the apes as howling creatures with tails who still recognised their families and approached them weeping, since the humanity they had debased was not yet out of memory, and the accounts agree that the transformed died within three days. The Prophet was asked about the apes and swine that people see, and Ibn Masʿūd reports his answer: *"when Allah sends down this particular kind of punishment on a people, the race comes to an end with this, and there is no further breeding"* (Muslim). The Book itself keeps the fate in view whenever their later history is counted: (5:60 — **“It is those who earned Allah’s condemnation and displeasure—some being reduced to apes and”**). A verdict that reshapes the body answers a crime that treated the sacred as a technicality, and the symmetry of the two is part of the warning.

**A VERDICT OF BODIES, NOT ONLY OF HEARTS**

Two readings of the sentence have stood in the field, and the disagreement is early rather than modern. One reading takes the command as its words stand, so that the people were changed in form, and it rests on the reports just described: the kinship recognition, the weeping, the death within days, and the Prophet’s own ruling that such a people leave no progeny behind. The other reading, transmitted from Mujāhid, takes the change as one of the heart, comparing the case to the parable of the bearers of the Torah: (62:5 — **“The example of those who were entrusted with ˹observing˺ the Torah but failed to do so,”**). A third treatment makes the line rhetorical, like the address elsewhere that names what a stubborn party may as well become: (17:50 — **“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “˹Yes, even if˺ you become stones, or iron”**). The reading followed here is the first, because the transmitted material about the event is material about bodies and deaths and lineages, and a moral metaphor does not leave corpses or end a breeding line. What the other readings guard is not discarded: in other words, the example teaches with equal force that conduct shapes a person until the shape answers to it, and the Book’s comparison of the unfaithful bearers of a book to a beast of burden is the moral form of the same lesson. The command of the verdict also carries the word of creation itself. At a single utterance forms can change, which is why every ordinance stands for eternity in the custody of the One who says to a thing only that it is.

---

## Verse 2:66

> So We made their fate an example to present and future generations, and a lesson to the God-fearing

**THE OBJECT OF THE SENTENCE, UNPACKED**

A single pronoun in the verse carries the weight of the whole event: ***“So We made their fate an example to present”***. What the pronoun refers to has been settled two ways by the earliest glosses, and both routes run through Ibn ʿAbbās. One takes the pronoun as the punishment itself, the metamorphosis pronounced and performed; the other takes it as the community that was transformed. Further candidates appear later in the lists — the town, and less convincingly the fish that had been the instrument of the test — and the reason the first reading is stronger is that the previous verse ends on the verdict, so that what stands nearest to hand is what a pronoun takes. The word for example then supplies the teaching function of the thing. Its root family belongs to the fetter and the restraint, and the verbal form means to do to one party what holds others back from the same act. A lesson in this vocabulary is therefore not a story told for its own sake. It is a restraint fixed in public view. The making in the sentence is thus a making of the event into a permanent deterrent, and the difference between the event and the example is the difference between a punishment that ended in three days and a restraint that has not ended.

**HELD BEFORE AND BEHIND EVERY LATER AGE**

The reach of the example is drawn in an idiom of place: ***“and future generations, and a lesson to the God-fearing”***. The phrase for present and future generations is literally what stands in front and what stands behind, and the early glosses give the picture its full width. One reading takes it as the people of that time and everyone who came after them; another takes it as the towns near the scene and the towns far from it; the spatial phrase has been applied to both dimensions and both are true of the example’s reach. The Book itself performs the same work when it repeats the verdict of this town in its own ledger of punishments: (7:166 — **“But when they stubbornly persisted in violation, We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!””**). Repetition inside revelation is itself the mechanism of the deterrence. In other words, a story held before and behind cannot be mislaid by a later generation, because every age stands somewhere in front of it or somewhere behind it. The purpose clause that governs the whole arrangement is therefore complete: the event is kept in view so that the fear of it works in advance, restraining a person before he reaches the device that would make a sacred law into a technicality. History in this Book is never decoration. It is instrumentation, set where the living will pass.

**SIGNS THAT BENEFIT ONLY THE GOD-FEARING**

The closing designation narrows the audience of the counsel to those who stand in awe of their Lord. The word it renders has two capacities in the language, counsel and reprimand, and both senses stand here, since the example comforts the obedient and frightens the defiant in one and the same telling. The God-fearing are singled out because they are the party that actually benefits. The point is that a sign meets different hearts differently. In one it settles the fear that keeps a duty intact; in another it passes as news of someone else’s misfortune. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the closing phrase a face rather than a category: the God-fearing named here are the Prophet and his Companions, the generation standing at the example’s far edge and reading it as instruction. The Book states the same division of hearing in its own account of why stories are told at all: (11:120 — **“And We relate to you ˹O Prophet˺ the stories of the messengers to reassure your heart.”**). The same narration that reassures one audience warns another. What the verse therefore settles is the moral economy of history. The example stands in public view for everyone, and it works only where a heart has already chosen to fear its Lord; that is why the verse leaves the counsel with the God-fearing rather than distributing it equally to all who hear.

---

## Verse 2:67

> And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow.” They replied, “Are you mocking us?” Moses responded, “I seek refuge in Allah from acting foolishly!”

**A MURDER WITH NO WITNESS AND A COMMAND WITH NO SENSE**

The story opens on a crime that has already torn the town in two: ***“And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow.” They replied, “Are you mocking us?””***. One man had been killed and the killer was unknown. The deed was done at night, and the body was moved to a stranger's doorstep to be found at dawn. The early account transmitted by Ubaydah al-Salmani gives the crime its face. A man among the Children of Israel who was impotent and had substantial wealth, with only a nephew who would inherit from him. The nephew killed him, moved the body by night, and the next morning the cry for revenge went up. The people took up their weapons and almost fought each other. Each party held the other responsible, and each deflected the charge, until the matter grew between them. The feud had reached the point where each party's grief turned on its neighbour rather than on the killer. The crime was multiplying into a civil war while the murderer stood aside. The first murder in the world is remembered in the book as the lesson against exactly this spiral: (5:28 — **“If you raise your hand to kill me, I will not raise mine to kill you, because I fear Allah—the”**). The wise men among them stopped the feud with one question: why fight one another while a messenger of God stands among you? Moses was asked to expose the killer. The command that answered him was deliberately plain, and Ibn ʿAbbās reads its plainness as the point: any cow would have answered. The murder is recapped at the lesson's other end as (2:72 — **“˹This is˺ when a man was killed and you disputed who the killer was, but Allah revealed what you concealed”**). What turns on their coming questions is already set in the command's form, because the easy answer stood open until their dispute closed it. The next step in their own words shows the narrowing at once: (2:68 — **“They said, “Call upon your Lord to clarify for us what type ˹of cow˺ it should be!” He replied, “Allah says,”**). The sacrifice stands at once as a worldly mercy ending the feud and an otherworldly sign naming the killer.

**THE PROPHET'S REFUGE FROM THE FOLLY OF MOCKERY**

The people's reply to the command is suspicion rather than obedience: ***“Moses responded, “I seek refuge in Allah from acting foolishly!””***. The Arabic noun in their question — are you making us a target of mockery — carries play and mockery alike in its earliest glosses, and that union explains their state of mind. To a people watching a ritual of slaughter proposed as the solvent of an unsolved murder, the command sounded like entertainment at their expense. The fear of ridicule is the fear that sits closest to a humiliated congregation. Moses answers the suspicion at its root. The wording he flees to God from names the ignorant in the sense of the one who speaks useless words and mocks his fellows. The refuge is thus a refusal of the very character they imagined in him. The point is that mockery and messengership cannot occupy the same man. A prophet carrying a people's fate is the one person with nothing to gain from their humiliation. The Prophet's own gloss on the line settles the reading. Ibn ʿAbbās reports the sense as *\"God forbid that I ever mock the believers\"*, a report that turns the grammatical subject of folly into a moral impossibility. In other words, the verse draws the character line of revelation itself: guidance does not entertain itself with its recipients. The neighbouring address to another prophet makes the same register of restraint explicit: (11:46 — **“do not ask Me about what you have no knowledge of! I warn you so you do not fall into ignorance.””**). The lesson for every later hearer follows from the exchange as a practical demand. The one who speaks for God may never amuse himself with the people he serves. The people in turn owe their prophet the reading that takes his words as commands rather than games. The reason the refusal matters is that a mystery invites ridicule of sacred law precisely when it is least understood. For that situation the exchange leaves a standing instruction: the tongue that serves revelation refuses the joke before it answers the question.

---

## Verse 2:68

> They said, “Call upon your Lord to clarify for us what type ˹of cow˺ it should be!” He replied, “Allah says, ‘The cow should neither be old nor young but in between. So do as you are commanded!’”

**A QUESTION THAT BENDS THE OPEN DOOR**

The suspicion of mockery died when the prophet stood by his office, and the people swung from ridicule to bargaining: ***“They said, “Call upon your Lord to clarify”***, ***“for us what type ˹of cow˺ it should be!””***. The request sounds innocent, and that is precisely its cost, because the command had arrived open. Slaughter a cow — any cow, as Ibn ʿAbbās reads the command's bare form — and the answer stood ready. What they asked for was not the essence of the thing; they knew what a cow is. The question is in truth about the attribute, the distinguishing description that would tell one animal from the rest, since a request to clarify what it is only makes sense once the named referent is already known. Their own gloss in the same dialogue confirms the reading, since Ibn ʿAbbās takes the question as asking whether the animal should be large or small. The reply then closes the first door with an instruction rather than a longer description: ***“He replied, “Allah says, ‘The cow should neither be old nor young”***, ***“but in between. So do”***, ***“as you are commanded!’””***. The closing command carries its own gloss from Ibn ʿAbbās as *"and ask no further questions"*, and the effect of their bargaining is already visible in the direction of the text. Each question they add behaves like a doorway being narrowed from both sides, which means the burden of finding the right animal grows with every condition they themselves requested. The next question in their own sequence shows the pattern continuing without pause (2:69 — **“They said, “Call upon your Lord to specify for us its colour.” He replied, “Allah says,”**).

**BETWEEN THE AGED AND THE UNTRIED**

The description given is a span rather than a point: not the aged and not the first-timer, but a middle age between the two conditions. The first designation marks the female that has passed bearing and reached the years of failure; the second marks the untried young that has never borne at all; and the language sets both in the feminine by usage, so that the terms speak of the animal as they would speak of the woman. The middle designation then does the actual work of exclusion. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Mujāhid, Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ b. Anas, and Ibn ʿAbbās stand with al-Suddi, Ikrimah, and al-Dahhak in the wider body of opinion that takes the span as the age when breeding has begun but not yet failed — neither old nor below the age of bearing. On the tightest gloss in the list, al-Dahhak reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that the middle age means *"the age when the cow is strongest and fittest"*, and that report turns an ordinary market category into a search for the animal at the height of its value. In other words, the description is doing two jobs at once: it removes every cow at the edges of life while leaving the whole middle of the herd still in play, so that the search stays long even as the field grows smaller. What turns on this economy is the shape of the trial itself. A single instant judgment would have solved the murder; what their questions have produced instead is a catalogue of conditions that must all be satisfied at once, and the difference between those two outcomes is the lesson the story keeps in view.

**STUBBORNNESS ANSWERED WITH ITS OWN WEIGHT**

Behind the description stands the ruling principle of the whole episode, and the early commentators state it in one line: had they slaughtered any cow, that would have been enough; they imposed hardship on themselves, so hardship was imposed on them. Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū al-ʿĀliyah report the substance in those terms, and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī relates the same balance in a prophetic report — the open command closes exactly as far as the objectors push it. The point is not that clarification is wrong; a seeker of certainty may ask. The point is the motive and the manner, since these questions come not from piety but from the obstinacy that hopes a command will dissolve under scrutiny. Their own later complaint confirms the diagnosis, because the catalogue reaches the place where all cows look alike to them and the trial they engineered has become genuinely hard (2:71 — **“wholesome and without blemish.’” They said, “Now you have come with the truth.” Yet they still slaughtered it hesitantly”**). The narrated outcome follows the same balance to its end: they slaughtered the animal though they were near to not doing it, and the near-miss is the fruit of their own bargaining. The reading passes to the congregation that hears the passage today as an instruction in obedience: when a command is plain, the heart that races to fulfil it keeps the door open, and the heart that negotiates conditions forges the very narrowness it will later complain of.

---

## Verse 2:69

> They said, “Call upon your Lord to specify for us its colour.” He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should be a bright yellow cow—pleasant to see.’”

**A RESTRICTION ASKED FOR A SECOND TIME**

The pattern of the exchange is now plain, and the commentary names it as it is: ***“They said, “Call upon your Lord to specify”***. This is a second stiff-necked ask laid on the first. The people take up the very load that had been lifted from them. The first word of the command left the field wide open. Their first ask closed it to a middle-aged cow. Their second ask closes it again by a colour. The price of the first has taught them nothing. The sequence solves the one question that hangs over the whole scene — why the marks kept coming at all — and the answer in the glosses is that each new clause is a fine charged for the asking. One report puts the whole deal in one frame: had they killed the first cow at hand, that would have been enough for them. So what follows is not a class but a bill, and the reason the bill grows is that each ask distrusts the answer already given. Each needless ask is charged to the asker in the coin of the hunt. In the same key of just deserts, the tales of the two feuding sides of the town end with a rule that outlives the slaying: the one who kills for the inheritance does not inherit, so the gain of the crime is cut off at its root. The tale of the town's rule ends the same way, sealing the seat that bred the feud. Each ask thus shifts the hunt itself, and the shift only grows.

**YELLOW TO ITS DEEPEST DEGREE**

The answer narrows the field by hue, and the words of the answer are thick with force: ***“for us its colour.” He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should be a bright yellow cow”***, ***“pleasant to see.’””***. The line here holds two chains from one voice, and both are worth keeping in view. Ibn ʿAbbās describes the cow as yellow in its hoofs and horns while its hide was black. Al-Awfi hands down from him a second gloss in which the brightness is a deep yellowish white. The heart shared by both is a strength of hue that strikes the eye from far off. Both chains keep the second half of the line in his reading: the brightness is the light of the hue itself, and the joy of those who see her is placed in the eye of the one who looks.

The word-men of the commentary explain why the line doubles the mark instead of naming the hue once. The plain word gives the hue. The strained form puts that hue at its most intense, so the sentence first judges the cow yellow and then judges the hue itself extreme. This is the same build the tongue uses in its hardest colour phrases — whitest bright, blackest deep, reddest blazing — where the second word is there to press the first to its edge. The word for colour in this tongue also bears the sense of kind or type, so a thing once said to shift its hue is a thing that never settles into one character. The picture of the cow thus answers their hunt in both directions at once. The reason the line stacks the two judgements is emphasis: the cow was to be clear at a glance. What turns on that clarity is the fate of the bargaining itself, since a mark a stranger can check is a mark the askers cannot wriggle past.

That check in the open is sealed by the last words of the picture, which hand the hunt to the eye of each onlooker. Al-Suddī reads the close as the cow pleasing those who look at her, and the same stands with Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Qatādah, and al-Rabīʿ b. Anas: her beauty pleasing those that look at it. What this means for their trial is plain and instant. A hue that gladdens the eye is a hue that can be checked without an expert, and the herd grows smaller in each village the hunt enters. Their next complaint shows the narrowing has started to bite: (2:70 — **“for all cows look the same to us. Then, Allah willing, we will be guided ˹to the right one˺.””**). The last specification finishes the choking of the field: (2:71 — **“He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should have been used neither to till the soil nor water the fields;”**). For the reader today the sequence is a warning against bargaining with plain commands. The point is that the door was wide until the askers narrowed it themselves. In other words, the cost of each avoidable ask is paid in the same coin as the ask itself.

---

## Verse 2:70

> Again they said, “Call upon your Lord so that He may make clear to us which cow, for all cows look the same to us. Then, Allah willing, we will be guided ˹to the right one˺.”

**A FOURTH QUESTION AND THE ONE CLAUSE THAT SAVED THEM**

The questioning has become a rhythm, and the fourth round opens exactly as the others did: ***“Again they said, “Call upon your Lord”***, ***“so that He may make clear to us”***. What they ask for now is the animal's occupation rather than its body — does she graze freely or is she used in labour — and that shift explains the shape of the answer waiting in the next verse (2:71 — **“He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should have been used neither to till the soil nor water the fields;”**). The glosses on their question supply the two categories exactly. Does she feed freely from her own pasture, or is she put to work in the fields? The people want to know which occupation would disqualify the animal before they buy. The distinction is not trivial in a farming economy. A working animal would stand in the fields on any day the search passed, while a grazing animal would be loose on the range and harder to claim.

The narrated counting of the exchange puts the matter in order. Had they slaughtered whichever cow came to hand at the beginning, that would have been enough. The first question restricted them by age: (2:69 — **“They said, “Call upon your Lord to specify for us its colour.” He replied, “Allah says,”**). The second restricted them by colour, and each restriction stood as a charge on the asking. The counting in the earliest narrative layer treats this demand as a third failure of understanding after the first two, each one costlier than the last. This third demand seeks disclosure past the disclosure already given, which means the people have decided the first answer did not match their need. The obstinacy reaches the point where the text lets them describe their own difficulty without disguise. Their own words become the evidence of the pattern.

**WHEN CATTLE LOSE THEIR FACES**

Their excuse is stated in the verse as a fact of perception: ***“which cow, for all cows look the same to us.”*** The animal answering the description is abundant in every herd, so the confusion is real rather than invented. The likeness of cattle to one another is a proverb in the language itself — a transmitted saying compares trials to the faces of cows, each resembling the other. The grammar of their complaint keeps the whole species in view. The collective form stands for the entire kind. What has become confused is cattle as such, and not one stray animal. The guidance promise that closes their sentence carries two readings in the earliest glosses. Ibn ʿAbbās takes it as guidance to the fitting description of the cow. A second view in the same transmission takes the guidance as guidance to the exposure of the murderer himself, so that the right one named at the end of their sentence may be the victim's answer rather than the animal. A transmitted reading in this line keeps the confusion open rather than closed. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and al-Araj are reported with a form that turns the likeness into something still arriving, as though the herd would go on losing its faces until the command was obeyed. The point is that the difficulty has been manufactured at every stage. The species was never the obstacle. The obstacle was the catalogue their own questions assembled.

**THE PROVISO THAT OUTLIVED THE QUESTIONS**

Everything in their sentence is bargaining except its last breath: ***“Then, Allah willing, we will be guided ˹to the right one˺.””***. That clause is the one part of the exchange the transmitted account treats as decisive, and the report attached to it is startling in its counterfactual force. Abū Hurayrah transmits the saying in this form: *\"By God, had they not made the proviso, it would never have been clarified for them until the end of time\"*. The reason the clause outweighs the questions is that it concedes the ground the whole exchange had been contesting. Four times they had asked for more, and every request presumed that the matter lay in their hands to specify. The proviso returns the specification to the One who issued the command. Without that surrender the chain of descriptions would have stood as an exhibit of stubbornness with no terminus, and the murder would have stayed buried under the search. That is why the narration marks the utterance as the condition of the clarification itself, rather than a decoration of piety at the sentence's edge. The book lays down the same rider for every plan a mouth will speak: (18:24 — **“without adding, “if Allah so wills!” But if you forget, then remember your Lord, and say,”**).

For the reader today the lesson is exact in its proportions. The phrase attached to plans is not a courtesy. The community that says its clause while doing its work keeps the door of outcomes in the hands of its Lord. A planner who attaches the clause and then bargains with a clear command has learned the words without the surrender they encode, and the narration is careful to separate the two. The entire apparatus of the sign then ends where revelation always ends, in understanding rather than possession: (2:73 — **“showing you His signs so that you may understand”**). The clarification that finally arrived arrived to a people who had, by their own clause, asked to be guided rather than to be satisfied.

---

## Verse 2:71

> He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should have been used neither to till the soil nor water the fields; wholesome and without blemish.’” They said, “Now you have come with the truth.” Yet they still slaughtered it hesitantly

**NEITHER YOKED NOR TURNING THE SOIL**

The last description removes the working class of cattle in one stroke: ***“He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should have been used neither to till the soil”***, ***“nor water the fields”***. The first exclusion is the animal broken to the plough, the kind that churns the earth with its hooves season after season until the work is written into its body. The second is the draught animal kept for carrying water to the crops, the one the language marks with its own designation because watering was its trade. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the pair in its plainest terms: the cow is unyoked and unfettered, not subjugated for the ploughing of the soil, nor for carrying water to irrigate it. The closing seal then disqualifies her by appearance rather than by employment. She is whole, free of any fault and of the effects of toil, with no mark of a colour other than her own on her, so that neither work nor wear may have touched her. Their own question had asked which occupation would disqualify the animal. The answer disqualified both occupations at once and added a purity of hide that no amount of bargaining had put on the list. The specification had escaped their control entirely.

**THE VOWELS THAT SPLIT ONE SHAPE IN TWO**

The first adjective of the description is a small monument of the language, because one written shape divides by its vowels into two different lives. In the reading of the animal the designation means the tamed one, the creature whose wildness has been taken by riding or by labour. Spoken with a different vowelling the same shape describes the abject person whose dignity is gone. The verse takes the first sense entirely, and the narrated gloss on the line makes the causation explicit. The cow is called untamed because work never tamed her. She never churned the soil with her hooves, and no water-course was laid on her for the crops. The grammar of the negation then drew the grammarians into a clean division, and the division is worth recording as evidence of how carefully the line was read. The majority, including al-Akhfash in his insistence on the point, take the negated adjective as an attribute standing to the cow, her own described state. Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami is transmitted with the accusative instead, on the reading that makes the negation its own clause with the predicate left understood. The two readings agree on the sense while dividing on the casing. In other words, what turns on the dispute is small in doctrine and large in attention. The cow's freedom from labour was treated by the readers of the Book as a fact stated in the cow's own description, not as an incidental clause.

**THE MOMENT THE OBJECTIONS RAN OUT**

The people's reply marks the first time their speech carries no objection: ***“wholesome and without blemish.’” They said, “Now you have come with the truth.””***. The admission is glossed from two directions, and both keep the sense of completion. Ibn ʿAbbās renders their words as now we know the cow's right description. The short sense circulating in the glosses is that the Prophet has now explained the matter clearly. The search that follows is one of the tenderest scenes in the episode. The narrations place the animal with a boy known for devotion to his mother, so that the cow marked out by divine description was kept by the hands of filial duty. The two details arrive in the same frame as though the story wanted the reader to see the character of the household that still owned a whole cow. The purchase is reported in two forms that agree on the weight of the price. One transmission has them buying her for her weight in gold. Another has the owner demanding the skin's fill of gold and receiving it. The difference between a weight and a measure does not touch the lesson, since both say the same thing about what the catalogue has done to the market.

**THE PRICE OF THE LAST QUESTION**

The verse ends on the tone of the deed rather than its fact: ***“Yet they still slaughtered it hesitantly”***. The hesitation is glossed twice from one authority, and the two glosses are really one cause seen from two sides. Ibn ʿAbbās takes the hesitation as their first impulse, the drawing back before the act. As it is also said, the hesitation was the price, because the cow had become hugely expensive. The arithmetic of the whole episode is now visible. An open command once carried no price tag at all. The catalogue their questions assembled turned a slaughter into a purchase, and the dearest animal in the market is what obstinacy left in their hands. The proverb against that exact bargain is spoken in this surah by Moses himself: (2:61 — **““Do you exchange what is better for what is worse? ˹You can˺ go down to any village”**). His own line in the earlier exchange keeps its shape against the outcome, (2:67 — **“Moses responded, “I seek refuge in Allah from acting foolishly!””**) — the man who refused mockery now waits while the mockers haggle over their own penance. The instrument of the answer then does its work in a single gesture: (2:73 — **““Strike the dead body with a piece of the cow.” This is how ˹easily˺ Allah brings the dead to life,”**). The extravagance the people feared to spend turns out to have been the solvent of the crime they could not solve. For the reader today the sequence keeps its ordinary shape. Hesitation at the altar of a plain duty is the receipt for the bargaining that came before it, and the price is quoted in the currency the bargaining itself invented.

---

## Verse 2:72

> ˹This is˺ when a man was killed and you disputed who the killer was, but Allah revealed what you concealed

**THE TELLING THAT TURNS BACK TO THE CRIME**

The account now steps behind the scene it has already told: ***“˹This is˺ when a man was killed”***. The verses before this one carried the story from the command to the slaughter. This clause returns to the crime that produced the command, and the arrangement is deliberate rather than accidental. The sentence stands ahead of the tale's first scene precisely because the language permits such inversion freely, and the narrated observation about the sequence is that the telling has not been preserved in chronological order. It has been re-ordered with a subtler purpose. The section has a subject — the transgressions of a people — and the story is placed in service of that subject rather than told for its own delight. What follows from that placement is a rule for reading every narrative passage here. The order of the telling is itself commentary, and the events are arranged where the lesson needs them rather than where the clock left them.

**A KILLING ATTRIBUTED TO A PEOPLE**

The verse addresses the crime to the plural you, and the idiom has its logic. The tongue of the language attributes to a tribe what one member of it does, for blame or praise, and the attribution here carries its own point. A community of excessive greed and formidable audacity is a community from which a killing is never far. The objection that the act belongs to its own hand is true and is not being cancelled. The Book states the individual rule plainly elsewhere: (4:111 — **“And whoever commits a sin—it is only to their own loss. Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise”**). The law of the slain names the weight of the single act in the same terms: (5:32 — **“murder or mischief in the land—it will be as if they killed all of humanity; and whoever saves a life,”**). What the plural you adds is the climate of the crime rather than its fingers, and the narrations about the aftermath confirm the climate directly. The murderer had his supporters, and the dispute the verse names is not a neutral disagreement about evidence. It is a factional defence. One party cries the crime, and the other buries it under accusations aimed at innocent men. The concealment in the last clause is therefore social before it is forensic. A whole population was engaged in keeping the truth down, which means the miracle that follows is addressed to a public conspiracy and not merely to a missing witness.

**THE VERB OF PUSHING BLAME AWAY**

The second movement of the verse is the quarrel itself: ***“and you disputed who the killer was”***.
