The chain of readings on the final verb keeps both parties in view. Whether the sentence reads that He is not heedless of what you do or of what they do, the reach of the watch is the same. The effect on a modern congregation is procedural rather than spectacular. A house today that keeps its charter's comfortable articles and files away the costly ones is standing in exactly this dock, and the closing line is the court's assurance that every article is on the books.

---

## Verse 2:86

> These are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world. So their punishment will not be reduced, nor will they be helped

**THE TRADE THE VERDICT NAMES**

The verse reduces the whole preceding file to a single transaction: ***“These are the ones”***, ***“who trade the Hereafter”***, ***“for the life of this world.”***. The glosses define the exchange without sentiment: purchasing the present life at the price of the next by preferring the first to the second. The transmission from Ibn ʿAbbās pairs the columns by kind — this lower world in place of the world to come, and disbelief in place of belief. The commerce vocabulary is doing the work of a whole theology of value. A trade names two goods and their agreed rates, and the accusation of the verse is not that the men pursued the world but that they priced eternity at the world's rate. The earlier woe had already called the price small and the gain fleeting. The present verse removes even the appearance of shrewdness from the deal, since the merchandise forfeited is named in its full weight before the sentence names the buyers. The books elsewhere draw the same transaction from the other side, where the bargain is written as it should be written: (4:74 — **“Let those who would sacrifice this life for the Hereafter fight in the cause of Allah. And whoever fights in Allah’s cause—whether”**). The difference between the two passages is the difference between a purchase and a sale. In other words, the same exchange runs in two directions. The faithful trade this life for the next, and the men of this verse trade the next for this one. What turns on the direction is everything, since one trade is called sacrifice and the other is called loss. The valuation of the traded good is stated flatly in the lesson of the reckoning: (3:185 — **“and is admitted into Paradise will ˹indeed˺ triumph, whereas the life of this world is no more than the delusion of enjoyment”**).

**DOORS BOLTED FROM BOTH SIDES**

The sentence then closes the two exits of hope in order: ***“So their punishment will not be reduced”***, ***“nor will they be helped”***. The first negative was read in two registers that nearly meet — the punishment will not be lightened, and it will not be lifted — so that neither the discount nor the cancellation is available to the buyers. The second negative withdraws the last resort. No helper will reach them, and the support that would turn the chastisement away is expressly withheld. The doctrine of intercession in the tradition is careful on this point, because the books describe a mercy that reaches the sinful believer after his term while this sentence addresses a class that sold the term itself. The promise of the former does not reach the merchandise of the latter. The reason the two negatives stand together is structural. The first answers the claim that the punishment will be brief. The second answers the claim that someone will intervene. The passage that began with invented arithmetic ends by emptying both calculations at once. The parallel warning against the same bargain in the widest register states the market rule without a parable: (16:95 — **“And do not trade Allah’s covenant for a fleeting gain. What is with Allah is certainly far better for you,”**). The effect of reading the two passages together is to see the covenant treated the way the sellers treated it: an asset with a liquidity date.

**SETTLEMENT DAY WRITTEN INTO THE TERMS**

The summary verse is short because the case is short. The docket of the previous pages is compressed into a bill of sale, and the bill names the two goods and the loss. The reason the compression works is that the whole dispute has been a dispute about rates, and a bill of sale settles rates without debate. The practical demand the compression places on a reader is the demand of valuation. Every age keeps its own exchange floor, its own rate at which the next world is quietly discounted for career, applause, or comfort, and the verse refuses to dignify the rate with argument. The buyers here were not atheists of the marketplace. They were men of a book who kept the articles they liked, and the trading was done with the vocabulary of devotion. In other words, the verdict does not argue the valuation; it publishes the settlement. Any congregation today that has learned to speak of the hereafter in the cadence of a portfolio will find the passage the oldest margin call in the record. The position was marked at the price of the purchase, and the settlement is already written into the terms.

---

## Verse 2:87

> Indeed, We gave Moses the Book and sent after him successive messengers. And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit. Why is it that every time a messenger comes to you ˹Israelites˺ with something you do not like, you become arrogant, rejecting some and killing others

**THE CHAIN THE VERSE LISTS IN ORDER**

The history is laid out as a ledger of gifts before it becomes a bill of charges: ***“Indeed, We gave Moses the Book”***, ***“and sent after him successive messengers.”***, ***“And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs”***, ***“and supported him with the holy spirit. Why is it”***. The first gift is the Torah. One transmitted reading from Ibn ʿAbbās magnifies the scene of its descent. The book came down as a single whole. When Moses was commanded to carry it he could not bear its weight. An angel was appointed for each letter of it, and they could not bear it either. Then the weight was lightened for Moses, and he carried it. The language of succession is drawn from the neck. The verb for following means to come on the heels of what is in front, as the back of the neck follows the head. Al-Suddī hands down the verb of succession in the plain sense of one rank following another. The rhyme-word of poetry is named for the same reason — it follows the speech. The gifts to the son of Mary are then itemized as clear proofs: the raising of the dead, the healing of the blind and the leper, the shaping of the bird, and the foretelling of what is hidden. The same inventory of signs is spoken by the Messiah himself in the account of his mission: (3:49 — **“Allah’s Will. I will heal the blind and the leper and raise the dead to life—by Allah’s”**). The support named in the verse is the subject of its own grammar — an annexation that binds the noun of spirit to the adjective of holiness. The identification the glosses give is the great bearer himself, named for the sanctity of the one he served, who accompanied the Messiah wherever he went. The same title for the same bearer stands in the final revelation's own account of its descent, and the tradition keeps the identification in the line of the community's poet: Gabriel is the messenger among us, and the Holy Spirit has no equal. The pairing of proof and support is stated again in the surah's own later summary: (2:253 — **“son of Mary, We gave clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit. If Allah had willed,”**). The list as a whole is a curriculum of care: a book, a succession, proofs, and a companion — every instrument of guidance delivered before the charge sheet opens. The angel's role through the whole career is remembered in the tradition fourfold: at the conception, at the birth, at the defense, and at the raising: (5:110 — **“how I supported you with the holy spirit so you spoke to people in ˹your˺ infancy”**).

**THE REFUSAL THAT WEARS ITS OWN TENSE**

The charge then arrives, and its grammar was dissected as carefully as the gifts: ***“that every time a messenger comes to you ˹Israelites˺ with something you do not like, you become arrogant, rejecting some”***, ***“and killing others”***. The repeated-time construction carries its own rebuke. The arrogance is the standing response to every arrival. The interrogative form is not a question but an indictment. The tense itself was noted by the language specialists. The verbs of rejection and killing stand in the present while narrating the past. The history is thus staged as still happening while the sentence is read. The named cases fix the register. The ones called liars include the Messiah himself. The ones killed include the prophet of the Baptist house and his father, the aged priest who defended him — the glosses naming the pair as the standing examples of the second clause. The description of the pattern in the tradition is one of worship of desire. Whenever the prophets brought an injunction that did not please them, the injunction was answered with denial or with murder. The covenant of the prophets had bound the opposite behavior into sworn terms, since each prophet was made to promise support for the confirmer who would come after the others: (3:81 — **“if there comes to you a messenger confirming what you have, you must believe in him and support him.” He added,”**). What follows from the tense is the passage's way of making the past an exhibit rather than a memory.

**THE ARROGANCE AS A CONSTANT**

The word for the response is the verse's psychological center, and its force was sharpened by the syntax around it. To disdain following is the meaning the glosses give the arrogance here. It is not the pride of the tyrant alone but the refusal of the pupil — the man who will not sit under a correction. The recurring construction that introduces the clause makes the behavior a constant rather than an event: every time, with what you do not like. The discomfort of the message, not the weakness of the messenger, is named as the trigger. The tradition presses the implication one step further. The selection of prophets to accept and prophets to kill was made by the same faculty — the taste that approved what flattered it and executed what rebuked it. The reason the passage itemizes the gifts first is therefore pedagogical. The charge is not ingratitude in the abstract. It is the specific crime of squandering a curriculum, a succession, and a companion on the same altar of appetite.

**WHEN THE RECORD STAYS OPEN**

Read as a record, the verse closes a section. Read as a diagnosis, it opens one. The pattern it names — accept the scripture that comforts, reject the correction that costs, and settle for the messenger what the message provoked — has no expiry date. The present-tense staging is the text's own device for keeping the exhibit open. Its effect is procedural: the reader is placed in the courtroom rather than in the archive. Any congregation today that prides itself on reverence for the prophets while managing away the parts of the message it dislikes will find the verse's question still standing in its exact register. The arrogance is measured not by the loudness of the denial but by the selection behind it. The closing clause of the charge names the floor of the selection — the killing — so that later audiences cannot file the passage as mere obstinacy. The reason the floor matters is that the passage has already shown where selection ends. The same taste that edits a message will eventually silence a messenger. What the passage finally demands is the one posture the pattern cannot counterfeit: hearing the whole message at the price of the whole self.

---

## Verse 2:88

> They say, “Our hearts are unreceptive!” In fact, Allah has condemned them for their disbelief. They have but little faith

**A WRAP PLEADED IN OPEN COURT**

The excuse arrives in the imperative mood and the mock register: ***“They say, “Our hearts are unreceptive!””***. The noun is one of the strangest in the passage, and the language specialists earned their keep on it. In the common reading it is the plural of a form meaning sheathed — hearts in their covers, as a sword sits in its scabbard and an uncircumcised man is called by the same adjective. These are hearts screened from understanding and discernment. A second reading thickens the vowel of the plural and hears a different plural pattern. On that reading the line becomes a boast rather than a shrug: our hearts are filled with knowledge and need nothing you bring. The transmitted glosses keep the range visible. Mujāhid gives a covering over the heart. ʿIkrimah gives a stamp upon it. Abū al-ʿĀliyah gives a heart that does not comprehend. The mockers' own intent — the claim of satiety, that the vessel is full and the message is surplus — is the reading Qatādah and Ibn ʿAbbās transmit when they render the cry as: our hearts are filled with knowledge and need nothing you bring. The syntax around the cry was itself remarked. The sentence turns from direct address to the third person in the middle of the reproach, a shift the analysts read as deliberate distancing. The speakers are dropped from the honor of being addressed while the quotation of their words is still on the air. The parallel placement of the same cry elsewhere in the revelation keeps the diagnosis consistent: (17:46 — **“We have cast veils over their hearts—leaving them unable to comprehend it—and deafness in their ears. And when”**). What follows from the metaphor is worth pausing on. A wrapped heart is not an empty one. It is a full one under seal, which is precisely the shape of the danger the verse describes.

**THE CAUSALITY THE REPLY REVERSES**

The rebuttal is one particle long and a whole doctrine deep: ***“In fact, Allah has condemned them”***, ***“for their disbelief. They have”***. The particle that turns the sentence is the turn of correction the passage has used before — no, not that — and the correction here is causal as well as factual. The mockers had pleaded the wrapping as the excuse for the disbelief: our hearts were already sheathed, so the message could not enter. The answer reverses the arrow. The disbelief is the cause, and the sheathing is its effect. The phrase for the condemnation places the curse precisely on the disbelief rather than on any original defect of heart. The glosses draw the reversal out. The curse is the removal of mercy and the degradation that follows rejection. Or it is the seal placed on hearts as punishment for what they chose. Or it is the deprivation of every kind of righteousness. None of the readings describes a manufacturing fault. The reply therefore removes the only defense the excuse contained. A man may answer for his capacities; he cannot answer with them. The reason the reversal matters is that it relocates the trial entirely. The question is no longer what the heart was made of but what the will did with what arrived. The passage that recorded the cry of the sheathed hearts in another assembly makes the sequence explicit in its own grammar: (4:155 — **“˹They were condemned˺ for breaking their covenant, rejecting Allah’s signs, killing the prophets unjustly, and for saying, “Our hearts are unreceptive!”—it”**). Note where the saying sits in the list: last, after the deeds. The family of the concealers is named at the condemnation's other end: (2:159 — **“Those who hide the clear proofs and guidance that We have revealed—after We made it clear for humanity in the Book—will be”**).

**WHAT LITTLE BELIEF IS MADE OF**

The closing phrase is a miniature of the whole diagnosis. The faith that remains after the seal is measured, and the measurement itself was debated: ***“but little faith”***. The emphatic particle in the Arabic intensifies the smallness — little indeed is what they believe — and the analysts split on the unit of the littleness. One reading takes the count in persons: only a few of them believe. The other takes it in quantity: their faith is minute, a residue of doctrines held in common — the Lord, the last day, the reward and punishment Moses foretold — while the confirmations that would complete it were refused. The doctrine of faith in the tradition distinguishes the two senses carefully. Lexically the word can name certitude about anything at all. Legally it names the assent that affirms everything the law requires to be affirmed. The satanological parallel is the tradition's coldest illustration. Knowledge of the truth without acceptance of it is the exact condition that intensifies the guilt, since even the adversary knows. The little faith is therefore not a step on the ladder but the rung that was kept while the rest of the ladder was returned. The difference between the two readings is pastoral rather than speculative, since each measures a different kind of small. One counts the faithful; the other weighs the faith. For a congregation today the closing phrase is the sharpest judgment in the verse. Partial belief is not scored as progress here; it is scored as the measure of what was withheld.

---

## Verse 2:89

> Although they used to pray for victory ˹by means of the Prophet˺ over the polytheists, when there came to them a Book from Allah which they recognized, confirming the Scripture they had ˹in their hands˺, they rejected it. So may Allah’s condemnation be upon the disbelievers

**THE DECISIVE OPENING SOUGHT BY PRAYER**

The memory the verse opens is a memory of prayer, and the prayer's own vocabulary is the first exhibit: ***“Although they used to pray”***, ***“for victory ˹by means of the Prophet˺ over the polytheists”***. The verb they used means to seek the decisive opening, the opening of the locked battle and of the sealed judgment. The tradition keeps the companion word in a saying of the Prophet about seeking that same opening through the prayers of the poorest of his emigrants. The scene behind the verse is fixed in the transmitted accounts with names. Before the sending, the scripture-bearers of the city would invoke God for the coming of the awaited prophet so that they might be granted victory over the hostile clans around them. The accounts name the tribes of Asad, Ghatafan, Muzaynah, and Juhaynah as the enemies of that prayer, and the two clans of the city itself as its target in another telling. The taunt that came with the prayer was preserved in the same lines: a prophet is to be sent at the end of time, and we with him shall finish you off as the nations of old were finished off. The whole tableau is worth holding in view. It converts the later rejection into a broken contract of expectation. The prayer asked for the man, the prayer was answered, and the answer was received like a debt collector.

**A BOOK THAT CONFIRMS THEIR OWN SHELF**

The arrival is then described in terms that carry their own compliment: ***“when there came to them a Book from Allah”***, ***“which they recognized, confirming the Scripture they had ˹in their hands˺, they rejected it.”***. The indefiniteness of the noun was read by the analysts as magnification: a Book, meaning a matter of the first rank. The description of it as confirming what they possessed stands second in the sentence's order because the first place belongs to its origin. It is from Him, and its confirmation of their shelf follows from that. The grammar of confirmation is itself pointed. The volume is described as confirming their book and not needing confirmation by it, and the glosses were careful to note the direction of authority. The recognition clause then names the real crisis. The arrival was not a surprise package but a matched description, and the same recognition-metric appears where the revelation says that those who were given the Scripture know the awaited one as they know their own children: (2:146 — **“Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺ as they recognize their own children.”**). The same refusal of plain belief is staged at the head of the surah: (2:13 — **“And when they are told, “Believe as others believe,” they reply, “Will we believe as the fools believe?” Indeed, it is they”**). The effect of the verse's order is prosecutorial: gift, confirmation, recognition, rejection, a chain in which the last link had no cover of ignorance.

**THE REPROACH AND ITS REPLY**

The scene of the denial is preserved down to the dialogue, and it is the passage's most human exhibit. The account handed down from Ibn ʿAbbās records two helpers of the early community, Muadh b. Jabal and Bishr b. al-Bara of the Salamah clan, saying to the men whose praying for victory this passage recalls: *"O Jews! Fear Allah and embrace Islam. You used to invoke Allah for the coming of Muhammad when we were still disbelievers and you used to tell us that he would come and describe him to us."* The reply of a man of the Nadir clan did not dispute the history at all. He declared that the man had brought nothing they recognized and was not the prophet they had described. The sentence about recognition and rejection was then revealed about that statement. Notice what the reply concedes by silence: the prayers, the descriptions, the dates. The dispute moved from the facts of the dossier to the identity of the arrival, which is the last refuge of a foregone decision. What follows from the dialogue's shape is the passage's whole theory of the denial. The evidence was not weighed and found light. The verdict was first, and the weighing was arranged after.

**WHEN RECOGNITION IS THE WORST WITNESS**

The diagnosis beneath the dialogue is named without anesthesia: the disbelieving came out of envy and out of fear for the seat of leadership. The passage's anthropology of faith is therefore starker than a court of evidence. Knowledge of the truth is not the assent the law requires, since if knowledge alone counted, even the adversary would stand among the faithful, and the depth of his knowing would only deepen his case. The sequel of the revelation makes the motive explicit in the verse that follows this one, where the malice is laid down as the cause. In other words, the recognition was not the problem's solution but its aggravation: the better the match, the worse the refusal. The tradition's habit of reading knowledge and acceptance as two separate acts is exactly what this passage was written to teach.

**THE CURSE THAT CLOSES THE DOCKET**

The verse ends with the imprecation the whole section has been earning: ***“So may Allah’s condemnation be upon the disbelievers”***. The syntax of the sequence was noted as compressed. The response to the first arrival-clause is supplied by the response to the second, so that the sentence reads like a court that stops taking evidence mid-trial and pronounces. The list of the condemned's file in the other assembly of the same theme keeps the same order of exhibits, the covenant, the signs, the prophets, and the saying about the sheathed hearts: (4:155 — **“is Allah Who has sealed their hearts for their disbelief, so they do not believe except for a few—”**). The sealing there is placed after the disbelief exactly as the reversal of the last passage demanded, and the head of the surah had already named the class: (2:13 — **“who are fools, but they do not know”**).

**THE PRAYER ANSWERED AND THE DEBT REFUSED**

The verse's afterlife in the tradition is as a warning about answered prayer, and the warning travels well beyond its first audience. A house may pray for the deliverer for generations and still prefer the arrangement that the deliverer's coming would disturb. The city's scripture-bearers prayed for the end of their enemies and were handed the end of their monopoly. The reason the prayer's answer reads as judgment is that the prayer itself was never about the man. It was about the victory he would bring to the prayer's own party. The practical demand on every later audience today is therefore unromantic: the arrival of the long-awaited correction is the test the longing never designed for itself, and the docket of this passage is kept open for every generation that recognizes its prophet and files the recognition under envy.

---

## Verse 2:90

> Miserable is the price they have sold their souls for—denying Allah’s revelation and resenting Allah for granting His grace to whoever He wills of His servants! They have earned wrath upon wrath. And such disbelievers will suffer a humiliating punishment

**THE SALE RECORDED AT ITS TRUE PRICE**

The verse returns to the market image and this time names the asset: ***“Miserable is the price they have sold their souls”***, ***“for denying Allah’s revelation”***. The glosses inventory the sale in three registers. Mujāhid records it as the sale of truth for falsehood together with the concealment of the truth about the awaited prophet. Al-Suddī records it as the sale of the self itself — the worst purchase being what the buyers chose in place of belief, aid, and support. The inherited reading takes the sold asset as the share of reward in the world to come, so that the transaction is priced in the only currency that matters. The grammar of the exclamation was dissected as well. The indefinite noun inside the formula of blame is a specification that singles out the very thing for criticism, as though the verse were pointing the finger at the item on the counter. The denial named as the purchase's content is not ignorance but disclosure. The revelation was recognized and refused, which is why the price is stated in the language of loss rather than of mistake. The market image runs through the whole passage as its accounting system: a small price, a fleeting gain, a trade of the hereafter, and now the souls themselves on the block. The book warns against that trade in its opening pages: (2:41 — **“or trade them for a fleeting gain. And be mindful of Me”**). It draws the same trade again and calls the profit void: (2:16 — **“They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance. But this trade is profitless, and they are not ˹rightly˺ guided”**). What follows from the imagery is the verse's way of making envy look like commerce. The buyers paid with themselves and called the payment profit.

**THE ENVY THAT ARGUES WITH THE GIVER**

The second clause names the motive with a precision that no amount of theology has improved: ***“and resenting Allah for granting His grace to whoever He wills of His servants!”***. The resentful particle in the Arabic is the same word for grudge and for envy, and the glosses read it as the reason-object of the disbelief itself. The denial happened because the gift was given where it was given. The target of the envy is therefore not the message but the Giver's discretion. The tradition states the doctrinal nerve without anesthetics: prophethood is a grace bestowed, not a wage earned, so the grudge against its distribution is a grudge against the discretion of the One who gives. The word for the envy was pressed to its worst case in the transmitted commentary — there is no envy worse than this. Every other envy at least wants what another has. This one disputes the right of the giving itself. The sentence's exclamation mark is placed exactly there: the revelation is to whomever He wills of His servants, and the will is not on trial. The effect of the clause on every later theology of merit is permanent. The grace that arrives unearned is the only kind that was ever on offer, and the grudge against it is the one vice that argues with the treasury rather than with the rival.

**ANGER RETURNING WITH ITS PREDECESSOR**

The judgment then arrives in the verse's heaviest idiom: ***“They have earned wrath upon wrath.”***. The verb for the earning is the verb of returning home, and the glosses hear the buyers coming back from the market carrying anger — an indefinite anger whose very indefiniteness magnifies its weight. The doubling was read three ways, and the readings agree on the arithmetic. One line counts the first anger as the neglect of the Torah and the second as the denial of Jesus. A second counts the denial of the Injil and its prophet as the first, and the denial of the final revelation and its prophet as the second. A third, transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās in flatter currency, reads the pair as curse upon curse. The structure is therefore cumulative by design. The passage's historians have already shown a community that lost one installment of the truth and then refused the next, and the sentence of the verse is that the installments are billed together at the end. The companion decree of the same history keeps the wording close enough to be a gloss: (3:112 — **“for rejecting Allah’s revelations and murdering ˹His˺ prophets unjustly. This is ˹a fair reward˺ for their disobedience and violations”**). The older bill for the same conduct is filed in this surah's own ledger of the wilderness: (2:61 — **“and they invited the displeasure of Allah for rejecting Allah’s signs and unjustly killing the prophets. This is ˹a fair reward˺”**).

**THE DISGRACE THAT IS NOT PURIFICATION**

The closing line names the punishment's species, and the species is the point: ***“And such disbelievers will suffer a humiliating punishment”***. The adjective attached to the torment is the adjective of abasement, and the tradition separates this punishment in kind from the discipline of the believers. The chastisement that awaits the sinful believer is purgative — it is measured to purify — while the disgrace named here is terminal. It is designed to humiliate rather than to mend. The reason for the distinction is stated in the same passages: the disbelief of this class was produced by transgression and envy mastered by arrogance, and the world and the last day answer each part of that chain in its own currency. The same decree elsewhere pairs the scorn of worship with the entry into the fire in humiliation, so that the punishment fits the posture. The pride that refused prostration is sentenced to abasement. The doctrine matters pastorally as well as philosophically, since it keeps the two penitentiaries apart in the reader's mind. The fire of purification and the fire of disgrace are not the same building.

**THE SEQUENCE AS ITS OWN LESSON**

The short verse is a masterclass in sequence-reading. First the sale is priced, then the motive is tried, then the penalty is counted, then its species is named — and each stage excludes the excuse the previous stage might have supplied. The reason the motive-clause stands before the penalty-clause is that the passage is trying the heart rather than the ledger. The envy is what converts the denial from an error into a purchase. Any congregation today that treats divine generosity as a zero-sum rivalry between communities will find the middle clause the corrective in one line. Grace is distributed by will, and the will has never been accountable to the envy. What turns on that corrective is the whole posture of the religious life — gratitude for the neighbor's gift instead of resentment at its address.

---

## Verse 2:91

> When it is said to them: “Believe in what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “We only believe in what was sent down to us,” and they deny what came afterwards, though it is the truth confirming their own Scriptures! Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Why then did you kill Allah’s prophets before, if you are ˹truly˺ believers?”

**THE REPLY THAT FILIBUSTERS THE SUMMONS**

The dialogue of the verse is staged as a summons and a dodge: ***“When it is said to them”***, ***““Believe in what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “We only believe in what was sent down to us,””***. The summons is general. It covers the final revelation and the books before it: (3:3 — **“He has revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ the Book in truth, confirming what came before it, as He revealed the Torah”**). The reply is territorial. What was sent down to us will do. The glosses read the switch as the whole confession. The believers of the reply lock their faith to the shelf that birth assigned them, and the exclusion of the rest is not argued but assumed. They treat revelation as a border rather than a message. The tradition notes the motive inside the grammar of the answer. They denied the other books for the very reason that the books were not addressed to them. That is a piece of reasoning which treats prophecy as mail rather than truth. The reply and the denial land in the same breath. The connective that joins the clauses shows one people assenting to one volume and rejecting what stands beside it. The companion indictment in the revelation's own summary of the case puts the pattern in market language again: (2:146 — **“Yet a group of them hides the truth knowingly”**). Knowing, not unknowing, is the adverb that convicts.

**THE CONFIRMATION THAT BECOMES THE PROSECUTION'S EXHIBIT**

The second half of the exchange delivers the refutation in a single clause: ***“and they deny what came afterwards”***, ***“though it is the truth confirming their own Scriptures!”***. The circumstantial construction is doubled in the Arabic — it is the truth, confirming what is with them — and the grammar specialists marked the doubling as deliberate. The confirming sits as a witness standing inside the defendants' own evidence. The logic the glosses draw out is prosecutorial. The new arrival conforms to the old shelf. Conformity is no threat to the earlier book; it is the earlier book's corroboration. The refusal of the confirmation therefore indicts the shelf it claims to defend. The passage's earlier recognition-metric had already fixed the standard. The descriptions in the inherited books are matched as closely as a man matches his own children: (7:157 — **““˹They are˺ the ones who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whose description they find in their Torah”**). What follows from the doubled circumstance is the reversal the whole passage has been building. The claim to believe only their own revelation becomes, under the confirming clause, a confession of disbelief in their own revelation. In other words, the shield of the reply is the spear of the prosecution.

**THE KILLINGS PUT BACK IN THE DOCKET**

The cross-examination then opens the oldest file in the room: ***“Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Why”***, ***“then did you kill Allah’s prophets before”***, ***“if you are ˹truly˺ believers?””***. The glosses unpack the force of the question in two moves. First the fact. The prophets who were killed came affirming the Torah's own law, and the Torah itself forbade the killing. The deed thus contradicts the very book the reply had claimed as its exclusive faith. Then the inference. If the claim of belief were true, the prophets would have been received rather than removed. The killing stands in the file as the refutation of the claim. The reply of the defendants is preserved in the transmission from Ibn ʿAbbās, who records them saying that their forefathers were believers. His gloss of the final conditional is the flattest available: if your claims are truthful. That the question is put to the living generation about the deeds of their forefathers is itself a legal doctrine the tradition draws out carefully. Those present are addressed because they approve the deeds of the absent. The second person is earned by endorsement rather than by ancestry. The same pattern of messengers answered with violence is stated flatly in the recap of the covenant's history: (5:70 — **“Whenever a messenger came to them with what they did not desire, they denied some and killed others”**). The list of charges in the final accounting keeps the killing beside the sealed hearts: (4:155 — **“˹They were condemned˺ for breaking their covenant, rejecting Allah’s signs, killing the prophets unjustly, and for saying, “Our hearts are unreceptive!”—it”**). The sarcastic conditional at the end — if you are believers — is the last turn of the screw. It invites the defendants to measure their claim against their own exhibits.

**BELIEF TESTED BY ITS BODY COUNT**

The verse's pedagogy is the pedagogy of a courtroom demonstration, and the demonstration travels well past its first defendants. A claim of faith is tested here not by its vocabulary but by its treatment of the messengers its own scriptures promise. The test is administered with the community's own book as the yardstick. The reason the question refuses to argue theology is that the docket already holds the verdict's evidence: the graves of the prophets are the commentary on the reply. Any community today that keeps a constitution of belief while managing away every correction the belief sends will find the passage prescribing the only cross-examination that matters. Read your shelf, then read your record. The pairing of the territorial reply with the open file of the killed has one effect. It makes selective faith look exactly like what the next passage will call it: a covenant cast aside.

---

## Verse 2:92

> Indeed, Moses came to you with clear proofs, then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully

**PROOFS ARRIVING WITH THE HANDS FULL**

The recap opens with a whole prophetic career packed into one clause: ***“Indeed, Moses came to you with clear proofs”***. The proofs named here span the list the tradition keeps whole — the staff that became a serpent, the hand that shone white, the sea that parted into a dry road, the locusts and lice and frogs and flood-years, the manna and quails of the wilderness. One line of analysis takes the word for the proofs as naming the Torah itself with everything it shows. Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the plural in the plainest register he has: commands, prohibitions, and signs. The naming of the signs is itself the point the word-scholars make. They are called by the word for making-plain because they show every onlooker that the claim is a miracle rather than a trick. The analysts of the opening stack count three stresses in a row — an oath-letter, an affirmation particle, and the emphatic form. That is a triple emphasis the passage spends on the one fact nobody disputed. The readings over the scope of the proofs split. Some take them as the evidences of the prophet's truthfulness. Others take them as the evidences of the oneness he came to teach. The wider reading gathers both, since the fuller the light was, the darker the next clause becomes. The reason the list stands first is procedural. The verse is building the delivery receipt before it opens the charge. Its own logic is the logic of an exhibit list: the more signatures on the receipt, the worse the receiving.

**THE INTERVAL THE TURNING USED**

The fall is then dated by its own grammar: ***“then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully”***. The particle of sequence here is heavier than a plain and. The tradition notes that it implies a respite. The calf was taken up after the signs had been pondered and after the prophet had gone to his appointment. That converts the lapse into a decision. The making of the idol is remembered in the glosses with its material detail: the image was cast from their own ornaments and jewelry: (7:148 — **“In the absence of Moses, his people made from their ˹golden˺ jewellery an idol of a calf”**). The idol was therefore minted out of the very wealth God had given. It stands in the record as the first monument financed by its own congregation. The phrase for the absence is the phrase of the appointment itself — the one whose duration the people of the calf later refused to respect. Their words at the height of the episode were kept word for word in the account of the return: (20:91 — **“They replied, “We will not cease to worship it until Moses returns to us.””**). The last word of the verse names the wrong in the language of injustice rather than error, and the earliest glosses press it to its floor: the worship of the calf denied the prophet who had parted the sea and the Lord who had parted it through him. Read the accusation in order and its shape is clear. Proofs delivered, prophet absent, image financed, worship performed, injustice named — no stage of the file is missing its stamp.

**THE APPROVAL THAT SHARES THE GUILT**

The verse's legal reach concerns the second generation, and the tradition states the transfer of blame without embarrassment. The contemporaries of the last prophet did not themselves bow to the calf. What they did was honor the forefathers who had, and take their side. The passage counts the honoring as the sharing. The same mechanism runs the case of the killed prophets in the verse before this one. Those addressed answer for what they endorse, not only for what their hands did. The pattern-prediction in the tradition follows the same shape. A people whose forefathers denied Moses while the sea was still drying under their feet should not be surprised to find their grandchildren denying the final messenger while the descriptions sit unrolled in their laps. Moses himself opened the confrontation with his own people in the words the passage recalls: (2:54 — **“And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “O my people! Surely you have wronged yourselves by worshipping the calf,”**). Note the reflexive form. The wronging of themselves is the wrong's first address, which is why the repair was ordered on themselves too.

**THE EXHIBITS THAT CANNOT BE DISOWNED**

The practical demand the verse makes on later readers is of proof rather than of feeling. A community is not tried on its ancestry but on its docket of endorsements — the causes it funds, the forefathers it crowns, the silences it keeps. The calf's financing from the people's own jewelry remains the passage's picture of how worship is paid for. What follows from the picture is worth stating. The image was not brought in from a foreign cult. It was minted at home in the prophet's week away. Any assembly today that keeps its devotion warm in the intervals between instructions will find the verse dating its danger to the calendar of the absences. The proofs do not expire because the prophet steps out of the room. They stay on the shelf as the exhibits the return will open with.

---

## Verse 2:93

> And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and obey,” they answered, “We hear and disobey.” The love of the calf was rooted in their hearts because of their disbelief. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “How evil is what your ˹so-called˺ belief prompts you to do, if you ˹actually˺ believe ˹in the Torah˺!”

**THE COVENANT SUSPENDED OVER THEIR HEADS**

The scene returns to the mountain, and this time the response is spoken into the record: ***“And when We took your covenant”***, ***“and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to”***, ***“that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you”***, ***“and obey,” they answered, “We hear”***. The account of the raising is given elsewhere in the revelation in its full theater. The mountain stood lifted over them like a cloud while they watched it, certain it would fall: (7:171 — **“And ˹remember˺ when We raised the mountain over them as if it were a cloud”**), and the command spoken from under that threat is quoted in the same scene: (7:171 — **“and they thought it would fall on them. ˹We said,˺ “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you”**). The response clause in this telling is one of the most quoted lines in the whole history, and the tradition of meaning records a subtlety about it. The words stand attributed to the community as speech though they were never voiced in the camp, because the people received the covenant with their conduct, and conduct that answers a command with defiance is speech in the grammar of judgment. The second reading sits beside it. We hear with the ears and disobey with the hearts is simply the anatomy of the first reading spelled out. One language note fixes the covenant's own vocabulary. Obedience is named hearing by adjacency, because hearing is the cause of obedience and the cause lends its name. The parallel covenant-passage closes its version with the softer formula, that they might become mindful: (2:63 — **“that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and observe its teachings so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.””**). The closing surah sets the obedient answer of the faithful beside this one as its mirror: (2:285 — **“and obey. ˹We seek˺ Your forgiveness, our Lord! And to You ˹alone˺ is the final return.””**). The pair of tellings brackets the whole pattern of promise and reply.

**THE ROOT THE CALF LEFT IN THE HEART**

The verse's diagnosis of why the covenant kept failing is botanical: ***“and disobey.” The love of the calf was rooted in their hearts”***, ***“because of their disbelief. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “How evil is what your ˹so-called˺ belief prompts you to do”***. The verb of the rooting is the verb of sinking a well or planting a tree deep enough to stand storms. The calf-affection is a growth grafted onto the heart's stock and not a leaf that fell on it. A second transmitted line reads the figure as drinking rather than planting. The calf's love was poured into the hearts until they had drunk it, and the trial-report of the hearts, transmitted in Muslim, keeps the same metaphor in its own mouth: *"Any heart that is made to drink of them has a black spot placed upon it, and any heart that denies them has a white spot placed upon it"*. The causality named in the clause runs in the direction the excuse-merchants always reverse. The disbelief is the root, and the calf-love is the fruit. An unbelief settled deep enough becomes the taste that then chooses its own gods. The claim of belief that the verse answers is answered in the interrogative of astonishment, the sentence asking what manner of belief this could be. The tradition keeps the sarcasm in its plainest register. The men are citing a Torah that condemns the very calf whose love stands in their hearts. The difference between the covenant's two responses across the two tellings is horticultural. One community heard and became mindful. This one heard and let the old root keep its plot.

**HOW THE TORAH TRIES THE TORAH'S MEN**

The closing challenge is a piece of courtroom arithmetic: ***“if you ˹actually˺ believe ˹in the Torah˺!””***. The conditional invites the defendants to produce their own book as the standard, and the book's own chapters on the calf are the refutation waiting in the margin. The whole method of the passage's last pages condenses here. The appeal is never to a foreign scripture but to the shelf the claimants themselves keep, and the verdict is delivered in their own exhibit's handwriting. The doctrinal generalization under the challenge was stated flatly in the tradition's reading of the earlier reply. The faith that divides the messengers and the books into accepted and rejected parcels is not a lesser faith but the very unbelief the creed names, and the faith that works is the faith that believes in every revelation on the same terms. What turns on the challenge is the testing-method of every later dispute over inherited religion. Bring the book, read the chapter, and let the text try the text's people.

**THE REPENTANCE A ROOT REQUIRES**

The botanical figure carries a pastoral consequence that the passage leaves for the careful reader. If the calf-affection is a root and not a residue, then the repair is gardening and not sweeping. The stock has to be dug at, the graft cut, the soil turned, which is the work the covenant's own formula of turning and mindfulness prescribes. The account of the aftermath reads the same way. The community was commanded to execute the wrong among themselves and turn to their Creator, and the turning was priced as the best purchase in the sight of the One who made them. For a modern house that treats its inherited devotions as untouchable family property, the passage asks the question of roots: what is planted, who planted it, and what the planting stands on. The reply to the covenant at the mountain was heard and recorded in a sentence. The replies of every later generation are still being transcribed.

**THE RESPONSE, THE ROOT, AND THE RECORD**

Read as a unit, the passage is a study in how a covenant dies. The command is delivered over the mountain. The answer is received in conduct. The beloved is discovered growing in the heart. The book is finally put on the witness stand. The effect of the sequence on the reader is to make the religious life legible as a horticulture of the heart. The reason the verse ends with the Torah's own trial rather than a new law is that the passage never needed a new law. It needed the old one read without the root in the way. The evil the verse names as what belief prompts is not the absence of belief. It is the presence of the wrong belief's crop, and the harvest of the record is the only test that cannot be argued with.

---

## Verse 2:94

> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter with Allah is exclusively for you ˹Israelites˺ out of all humanity, then wish for death if what you say is true!”

**THE TEST THAT COSTS ONLY THE TONGUE**

The passage now proposes an experiment, and the experiment's design is the verse's own exhibit: ***“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter with Allah is exclusively”***, ***“for you ˹Israelites˺ out of all humanity”***. The claim being tested belongs to a family of claims the section has already entered into evidence. The fire is said to be limited to counted days; the Garden is said to be reserved for one lineage; the claimants are said to stand as beloved sons. The experiment is built to test the whole family at once. The two conditionals of the sentence are joined so that the first leans on the second. If the world to come is truly yours alone, and if what you say is true, then the desire for it should show itself in the wanting of its door. The logic the glosses draw out is the logic of preference made public. A man inclines toward what is his own. The path to the prize is the door of death. The sincerity of the claim can therefore be read off the wanting. The twin challenge issued later in the revelation to the same claim is worded closely enough to be its own echo: (62:6 — **“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O Jews! If you claim to be Allah’s chosen ˹people˺ out of all humanity, then wish for death,”**). The same exclusive claim is restated a few verses on, in the plainest register: (2:111 — **“The Jews and Christians each claim that none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith. These are their desires. Reply,”**). What follows from the design is the verse's whole way of testing religious claims. The claim is not debated in the abstract. It is priced against the claimant's own preferences.

**THE TONGUE'S TOLL FOR THE TRUTH**

The proposed act is then named in its smallest form: ***“then wish for death”***. The transmitted accounts of the scene frame it as the ancient trial of mutual imprecation — the summons to bring down the sentence on the lying camp of the two parties — and the record states that the offer was declined. The transmitted readings span the range of the wishing: to long for the meeting, to ask for the death, and — in the reading the earliest authority transmits — to invoke God for it outright. In that reading the trial is a prayer as well as a wish. The method deserves its note in the tradition's own commentary on the verse. This is the abnormal method of settling a dispute, chosen precisely because the normal one had been refused. Discussion requires both parties to argue. This test requires only a little strain on the tongue, and the declaration either comes or it does not. The prediction embedded in the offer is part of its design. The passage knows the wish will not be made, and that converts the refusal into the answer sheet before the trial even opens. In other words, the test is one-sided by construction: sincerity would say the word, and the silence is scored. The gate of the wish stands open for every soul in any case: (3:185 — **“Every soul will taste death.”**).

**THE WISH AND ITS DELIVERY MECHANISM**

The third clause carries the conditional's sting — ***“if what you say is true!””*** — and the traditions of the scene report what the wish would have cost in the currency of the world. The transmission through the chain of Ibn ʿAbbās states the outcome three ways, and the statements are recorded with their chains. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and ʿIkrimah both transmit from Ibn ʿAbbās the reading of the wish as an invocation. If the community had invoked for death they would have perished. Had they asked for it, the asker would have choked on his own saliva. The saying of the Prophet transmitted in the same lines confirms that wishing would have brought the death and shown the seats of the wishers. The vividness of the middle report is worth keeping in the account, because it turns an abstraction into an event. The trial was not a thought experiment but a standing order with a delivery mechanism. The earliest gloss on the closing verb of the condition fixes the register. The truthfulness asked for is truthfulness in the claim, the very claim of exclusive inheritance. The scene's archival lesson is procedural. A religious claim that will not be stress-tested by its own terms has already left the courtroom.

**THE DECLINATION AS THE VERDICT**

The verse's afterlife in the tradition is the afterlife of a refused dare. The offer stood on the table — pronounce the wish, establish the claim — and the offer was withdrawn from without a word of rebuttal. The passage then treats the silence as the confession. The reason the silence convicts is the same reason the experiment was designed. The claim of exclusive salvation is a claim about preference, and preference is the one testimony the claimant cannot fake at the moment of truth. The theological family of claims around this one is refuted the same way across the section — not with counter-theology but with a stress test the claimants themselves administer. For a modern reader the method is transferable without remainder. When a community announces that the world to come is reserved to its address, the verse supplies the only question that matters, and it is a question about the community's own desires.

**THE INSTRUMENT THAT NEVER RUSTS**

The closing lesson of the passage is about the portability of the trial, and the portability is total. Every age produces its own version of the exclusive-claim — the blessed class, the guaranteed cohort, the lineage that cannot lose — and the verse keeps the same instrument ready: measure the claim against the claimant's own willingness. The effect of the experiment on the reader is to replace argument with introspection in one move, since nobody has ever needed a debate to know what they love. What turns on that substitution is the whole moral of the section. The honesty of a doctrine is visible in what its men want, and the wish that will not cross the lips is the doctrine's own verdict in advance.

---

## Verse 2:95

> But they will never wish for that because of what their hands have done. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers

**WHAT KEEPS THE WISH OFF THE LIPS**

The forecast of the refusal comes with its own map of the mind: ***“But they will never wish”***. The no carries the full weight of the first word — never at all, on any terms — and the gloss handed down from Ibn ʿAbbās gives the refusers their cause in one line of court logic. They know the prophet they speak to, and they deny him all the same. The men know the prophet they are with. That knowing is in the file from the passage before. The wish for death would be a wish for a meeting their own record has made dreadful. The plain terms of the dare stand in the verse before this one: (2:94 — **“then wish for death if what you say is true!””**). The commentary puts the counter-fact in bare numbers: had the wish been made that day, not one of that people would have lived — and that is just why the tongue stayed still. The shape of the refusal is thus a confession in the grammar of self-guard. A man will not knock at a door he believes opens onto his own trial, and the silence of the lips testifies to the reading of the file. What follows from the never is that the dare of the last verse stands on the table still, undated and unanswered. The wish is not hard to say; it is hard to say honestly.

**THE HANDS THAT FILL THE POCKETS OF FEAR**

The second clause names the brake with the verse's own body idiom: ***“for that because of what their hands have done.”***. The hands send forth what the ledger reads back, and the glosses hear the cause of the cowardice just there. The deeds stand between the man and the door, so the same mouth that claims the world to come refuses to travel toward it. The same men are staged again on the day of the crowd's regret: (2:167 — **“The ˹misled˺ followers will cry, “If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them as they disowned us.””**). The parallel decree of the revelation on the love of this fleeting life draws the same portrait: (17:18 — **“Whoever desires this fleeting world ˹alone˺, We hasten in it whatever We please to whoever We will; then We destine them”**). The mind the two passages share is worth stating without softening. The fear of death in the claimant of paradise is the conscience's own arithmetic. The claim speaks of inheritance; the hands remember the forgery. The reason the verse names the hands and not the heart is that the docket is manual. The deeds were done with these, and the memory of them keeps the wish unmade.

**AWARENESS DIRECTED AT THE WRONGDOERS**

The close of the line attaches knowledge to the class with the care of a charge sheet: ***“And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers”***. The name of the knowing here is the name of the knowledge that holds its objects in full. The elative form in the Arabic does the work of the superlative: a knowledge whole in its grasp of who the wrongdoers are and what the wrongdoers did. The placement of the clause after the refusal is deliberate, since the refusal claimed the cover of anonymity. We are the chosen; we are the beloved; the record is buried in the fathers. The verse answers with a knowledge that names the class by its deeds. The tradition's rendering of the last verb keeps both sides in the frame — whether the line is read as His awareness of what they do or of what the wrongdoers are — because the knowledge does not only watch the act; it files the actor. The effect on the reader standing at the end of this long cross-examination is the effect of a courtroom that has stopped speaking and started writing.

**THE OFFER THAT NEVER EXPIRES**

The two-verse experiment remains the section's most portable instrument, and the tradition treats it as such. The claim of the exclusive home, the counted days, the guaranteed cohort — each family of claims meets the same test, and the test never requires a scholar to administer it. For a congregation today that has quietly replaced the wish for the meeting with a portfolio of postponements, the passage holds the same mirror up and asks the same question in the same register. The difference between the two postures — the faith that would pronounce the wish and the faith that will not — is the difference the whole passage has been building toward, and it is measurable in a single syllable. In other words, the verdict of the experiment does not wait for the last day. It is pronounced in the silence of the wish, on the day the claim was made.

---

## Verse 2:96

> You will surely find them clinging to life more eagerly than any other people, even more than polytheists. Each one of them wishes to live a thousand years. But even if they were to live that long, it would not save them from the punishment. And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do

**THE GREED THE OATH SWORE TO**

The verse opens with an oath's full battery — the oath-letter and the emphatic suffix together — and the content of the sworn statement is a diagnosis: ***“You will surely find them clinging to life more eagerly than any other people, even more than polytheists. Each one of them wishes to live a thousand years.”***. The comparison is chosen with care, and the tradition spells out why the chosen rival matters. The polytheists of the peninsula disbelieved in the world to come altogether, so their clinging to this one is at least consistent. The men named here affirm the other world and claim its joys as their inheritance. They still hold this life tighter than anyone alive. The glosses state the psychology without gloves. The claimants know that the journey's end is the fire, and while the fire is what waits, this life is the only shelter standing between them and the sentence. The parallel portrait of worldly desire elsewhere in the revelation keeps the same market-stall imagery: (3:14 — **“made appealing to people. These are the pleasures of this worldly life, but with Allah is the finest destination”**). What follows from the oath is that the avarice is not incidental to the claim but diagnostic of it. The men who will not wish for death have already testified about their own file. The greed is the confession.

**A THOUSAND YEARS AS THE UNIT OF WISH**

The wish itself is then quoted in its arithmetic, and the number drew the analysts in several directions. The grammar of the conditional was mapped precisely. The if-only particle leans on the verbal noun, and the object of the wish is the being-given-life itself — a thousand years of it. The range of the comparative was argued over the sentence's syntax. One reading holds the whole phrase together, so that the wishers are the ones being compared. Another breaks the report so that the thousand-year wishers are a subset of the polytheists — a reading the language itself resists. The earliest glosses fix the pronoun on the claimants either way. The definition of the thousand divides between the plain figure and the idiom: either the actual number the claimants calculated in their doctrine, or the old way of saying a multitude. The tradition even keeps the folk-cousin of the idiom — the Persian courtesy of wishing ten thousand years at a sneeze — as evidence of how deep the shape of such wishing runs in human speech. The point of the figure is not the calendar but the appetite. The wish is stated at the largest unit the claimant can pronounce.

**THE YEARS THAT MOVE NOTHING**

The third clause answers the wish with physics rather than argument: ***“But even if they were to live”***, ***“that long, it would not save them from the punishment.”***. The verb of saving here is the verb of budging. No millennium will move the man one step from the chastisement. The flatness of the refusal is the sentence's whole force. A thousand years of life does not change a file; it only postpones the reading of it. The wish-death challenge a verse earlier was glossed in the same spirit. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, transmitting from Ibn ʿAbbās, reads the command to wish for death as an invocation: let them call on God for death and see what answers. ʿIkrimah, again from Ibn ʿAbbās, presses the same reading of the challenge. The reality behind both glosses is flatly stated a single verse earlier: (2:95 — **“But they will never wish for that because of what their hands have done. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers”**). The reward the wish was meant to reach early is itself deferred to a fixed day: (3:185 — **“And you will only receive your full reward on the Day of Judgment. Whoever is spared from the Fire”**). The tradition's portrait of this exact psychology is preserved in the report from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī: *\"A hypocrite is more covetous of the world than an idolater\"* — and the reason offered for the paradox is the same gnawing awareness of the consequences of one's own hands. The claimants' certainty of salvation is thus a delusion whose floor the deluded themselves can feel. The clutching at life is the tremor of the diagnosis. The difference between the two populations of the first clause is therefore not faith but foreknowledge. One group fears the fire it believes in; the other ignores the fire it denies. In other words, the greed is proportionate to the dread.

**WATCHFULNESS THAT FILES THE CONCEALED**

The close attaches the divine attribute to the scene with its own precision: ***“And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do”***. The final verb keeps its alternate reading across the transmissions — what they do, and what you do — and the requiting follows the seeing in either register. The earliest authority on the verse extends the scope of the seen past the deeds of hand. The sight files the contraventions, the rebellion, and the concealment — the descriptions and traits of the awaited prophet that were recognized and then buried. That buried knowing is named in its own place in this surah: (2:146 — **“Yet a group of them hides the truth knowingly”**). The attribute of sight in this passage is therefore the attribute of the court reporter rather than of the bystander. The record is taken in full, including the parts the actors believed were never spoken. The effect of the clause after a long cross-examination is to convert the whole section into evidence under oath. Nothing in the file has been missed by the sight that will read it.

**THE CLINGING AS SELF-ASSESSMENT**

The passage's final lesson is the one the experiment of the wish-death challenge already prepared. The claim of inheritance is tested by the claimant's own preferences, and the preferences have now been measured in public. A community that says the world to come is its property while clutching this world above every other people has performed its own cross-examination and lost it on its own answers. Any congregation today that keeps the language of salvation and the portfolio of postponement in the same account will find the verse's diagnostic exact. Watch what the people cling to when the door is described. What turns on the measurement is the honesty of the whole doctrinal claim — the wish for the meeting is the one testimony no liturgy can forge.

---

## Verse 2:97

> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know that he revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah’s Will, confirming what came before it—a guide and good news for the believers.”

**THE BRINGER WHOSE REPUTATION WAS TRIED**

The verse arrives as the answer to a courtroom dodge, and the account of its trigger is preserved in the transmission from Ibn ʿAbbās. A rabbi among the community's notables — the man remembered in the record as Ibn Suriyyah — asked which angel carries the revelation. Told that it was Gabriel, he answered that Gabriel was their enemy, since he brings chastisement in his wake. Had the carrier been Michael they would have believed, he said, since Michael brings fertility and security. The second account of the trigger stands in the report Anas b. Malik transmitted and Bukhārī recorded. A rabbi of their own, named in the record as Ibn Salam, came to the Prophet with three questions that only a prophet could answer, and when the answers arrived he said aloud that Gabriel, among all the angels, is the enemy of the Jews. The verse then opens with the summons that answers the maneuver: ***“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know”***. The inherited readings of the opening keep the sting that the translation folds into the summons — a curse on the enemy of the bringer, dying of his own exasperation — so that the trial of the angel's reputation ends in a verdict on the trial's conductors. The syllogism beneath the sentence was stated by the earliest authority in its bluntest form: whoever is an enemy of Gabriel is an enemy of God. ʿIkrimah even reads the names of the great angels as compounds of worship and divinity, so that the bearers of revelation carry their office in their names. The method of the reply deserves its own observation. The verse does not defend the messenger's character. It makes the messenger's enemies try their own case, and the trial opens with the courier's work on record.

**THE COURIER'S WORK, ENTERED INTO EVIDENCE**

The middle of the verse files the delivery report in four clauses: ***“that he revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah’s Will, confirming what came before it”***. The permissive word in the Arabic is read by the glosses as command rather than mere allowance. The descent was commissioned, not tolerated. The destination is named without ornament: the heart of the prophet. The confirming clause then settles the courier's work in the scheme of the earlier books, and the glosses press the direction of authority once more. The new volume confirms the old shelves rather than standing trial before them. The doctrine of the descent through the holy spirit is stated in the final revelation's own account of the same delivery: (16:102 — **“Say, “The holy spirit has brought it down from your Lord with the truth to reassure the believers, and as a guide”**). The identification of the spirit with the bearer of the revelation is the tradition's constant, and the fruit of that delivery is the split the descent always works: (2:253 — **“succeeding generations would not have fought ˹among themselves˺ after receiving the clear proofs. But they differed—some believed while others disbelieved. Yet”**). What follows from the delivery-report is the refutation's exact shape. The enemy of Gabriel is not a critic of a personality. He is a complainant against the mail route of God.

**THE RECEIPT SIGNED BY THE ERRAND**

The purpose of the delivery is then named in the pair the revelation keeps for exactly this work: ***“a guide and good news”***, ***“for the believers.””***. The same pair marks the book elsewhere as the standing signature of its arrival: (27:2 — **“˹It is˺ a guide and good news for the believers”**). The two nouns mean guidance out of error and glad tidings of the Garden, and their placement at the verse's end is the receipt of the courier's errand. The transmission from Ibn ʿAbbās fixes the second term with its destination: the good news is the news that Paradise is theirs. The pairing matters more than its brevity suggests, because the rabbi's dodge had divided the angels into the angel of comfort and the angel of warning. The verse answers by joining the offices. The same descent that carries the warning carries the good news, and the enemy of the warning has declared war on the comfort as well. The effect on the trial is procedural. The courier's work is now on the record twice, once as a warning and once as a welcome, and no document of the complaint against him is left unaddressed.

**THE PSYCHOLOGY OF CHOOSING YOUR ANGEL**

The scene behind the verse is one of the few places in the passage where the psychology of the refusal is stated out loud by the refusers themselves. The statement is a masterpiece of self-portraiture. The preference voiced in the trial is the preference for the angel of fertility and security over the angel of chastisement. It is a preference for the news that costs nothing over the news that costs the self. The tradition's analysis of the dodge notes its commercial shape. The community was choosing its messenger by the merchandise he carried, and that is the same selective-belief method the passage has been prosecuting for a dozen verses. The structure of the reply is the structure of the whole section in miniature. The courier is not on trial; the shopping is. What turns on the psychology is the modern reader's mirror-image, since every age keeps its own preferred angel — the patron of prosperity, the speaker of comfort — and the verse asks which deliveries the community has been refusing by refusing the courier.

**THE COURT-ROOM RULE THE VERSE ESTABLISHES**

The legal afterlife of the verse is a rule about trying celestial reputations. A complaint against a divine messenger is never a private matter of taste. It is a claim about God's own appointments, and the verse makes the complaint indict its author by its own standard. The tradition generalizes the rule without restraint. The enemy of the bringer is the enemy of the sender, and the animus is measured by which news the complainant wants suppressed. The reason the verse answers with a delivery report rather than a defense of character is that reputations are argued while receipts are produced. Any assembly today that has learned to edit the mail to keep the comfort will find the same counter-examination open. The courier's work is on file, and the file is no longer negotiable.

**THE MESSAGE THAT ANSWERS FOR THE MESSENGER**

The closing lesson is the one the whole trial was staged to teach: the defense of revelation is revelation's own work product. The verse names the descent, the destination, the confirmation, the guidance, and the good news — and then stops, because the courier's case is closed by the courier's account. The reason the account is sufficient is that the trial's question was never about character. It was about authorization, and authorization is documented in delivery. The effect on the reader is to turn every dispute over a prophet into a dispute over the delivered text, and that is the only forum the passage will accept. In other words, the enemies of Gabriel were invited to read the mail, and the reading of the mail is the trial's verdict.

---

## Verse 2:98

> Whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel, and Michael, then ˹let them know that˺ Allah is certainly the enemy of the disbelievers

**THE SUPPLEMENT THAT HONORS BY NAME**

The summons of the last verse widens into a list. Its last names are supplements to a category that already holds them: ***“Whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel”***. The tradition reads the figure as honor. The book names dates and pomegranates after naming fruit in general, so that the specific is called out of the collective for its rank. The two names were mapped in the consonantal tradition in several sound-forms each. The old lexica offer the theophoric shape through ʿIkrimah: the first syllables of both names mean servant, and the last means God. The angels are named as messengers elsewhere in the book as well, so the road from the general to the specific is paved in the book's own usage. The naming is diplomatic as well as doctrinal. The two figures whose reputations were bartered in the market of excuses now stand in the summons by name, so that no later court can claim the sentence was aimed at someone else. The reading that takes the names as the honor-roll of the errand is the reading the sentence's order supports.

**THE STATUS MARKED IN THE SENTENCE**

The second clause closes the syllogism and then does rarer work: ***“and Michael, then ˹let them know that˺ Allah is certainly the enemy of the disbelievers”***. The final noun of the sentence drew the glosses' eye. The line could have ended with the enemy of them. It ends by naming the disbelievers, so the verdict carries the class-status and not only the pronoun. The doctrine of the enmity has two directions, and the tradition lays both out. The servant's enmity toward God is disobedience and hostility to His friends. The enmity attributed to God is the chastising and the display of its effects, since the seeking of harm that defines the word applies to creatures and not to the Creator. The war-rule under the sentence is kept in the tradition's most quoted line on the subject: whoever is an enemy to a friend of God, God makes war on him. The scene that produced the verse was preserved in its full dialogue by the report Anas b. Malik transmitted, in the collection of Bukhārī: *"I am going to ask you about three things which nobody knows except a Prophet"* — the first portent of the Hour, the first meal of the people of Paradise, and the mystery of paternal and avuncular resemblance. When the prophet answered that Gabriel had just told him, the rabbi said: *"He, among all the angels, is the enemy of the Jews."* The prophet recited the summons of the verse in reply.

**THE GRAVAMEN BEHIND THE ANIMUS**

The fuller account of the grievance shows why one angel stood trial and not the angelic order. The same transmission keeps the complaint in its depth. The bringer had come down with punishment and fighting and hardship many times. The hardest of his errands was the prophecy that the Temple would be razed at the hands of a named conqueror at a stated time. The prophecy was delivered and then met its date. The animus toward the courier is therefore the animus toward the docket he kept delivering. The preferred angel of the complaint — the one of rain and fertility and security — was preferred because his mail never rebuked anyone. The selection runs on the same commerce the section has priced since the woe of the writing verse. The merchandise, not the messenger, was always the test.

**A COURIER WHO CANNOT BE SHOPPED**

The refutation's logic is then stated in the tradition's own doctrinal form, and its reach is long. The bringer is a messenger and acts only as a messenger under a command he did not author. The hostility owed to the commission is owed to the commissioner, and the summons names that transfer as its legal effect. The volume the courier carried stands on its own record in any case. It confirms the earlier books instead of contradicting them. It carries the complete guidance out of the kinds of error. It announces the good of both worlds to those who believe. To deny such a volume because of hostility toward the angel who bore it repeats the method the section has named three ways already, the shopping of messages by their cost. The decree against the method is flat where the book rules on defiance: (58:20 — **“˹As for˺ those who defy Allah and His Messenger, they will definitely be among the most debased”**). A caution kept in the later tradition guards the doctrine's other flank. The descent upon the heart is not to be read as a delivery of meanings without words, since the revelation's own verses name the Arabic tongue as its form.

**THE NAMES ENTERED INTO THE SUMMONS**

The closing lesson of the verse is procedural and permanent at once. The two angelic names stand in the summons so that the trial of reputations cannot be retried under new captions. The categories are named. The individuals are named. The transfer of the enmity to its true object is stated in the sentence's final noun. Wherever a modern congregation has learned to resent the deliveries that rebuke it while crowning the deliveries that soothe it, the verse keeps the same court in session. Reading the list slowly shows the whole anatomy of excuse-making laid out for inspection. The courier, the commission, the commissioner, and the merchandise stand named in order, so the blame cannot be parked at the wrong address again.

---

## Verse 2:99

> Indeed, We have sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ clear revelations. ˹But˺ none will deny them except the rebellious

**THE NOTHING-NEW CHARGE ANSWERED**

The last answer in the trial of the courier is an answer about cargo: ***“Indeed, We have sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ clear revelations. ˹But˺ none will deny them except the rebellious”***. The clause is handed down from Ibn ʿAbbās as the reply to the rabbi's parting shot. The charge was that nothing recognizable had been brought, and no clear sign that would justify following. The reply meets a charge of emptiness with a list. The word for the revelations is the word for things made plain, and the gloss handed down from Ibn ʿAbbās runs wide. The name covers the volume itself. It covers the miracles that testified to the bearer. It covers reports of matters kept hidden.
