It covers the concealments of the earlier books, recovered now in public. It covers the laws and duties the descent laid down. That range is the reply's first move. The charge was never about a lack of signs; it was about refusing to know the ones laid on the counter. The descent also carries its own rule of proof. The signs are sent down, not put together by the bearer, and their plainness belongs to the cargo rather than to the court that receives it.

**THE SECRETS THE BOOK NARRATES**

The hardest item in the list is the one the commentary presses hardest. The volume narrates the hidden knowledge that the scholars of the scripture held and buried. It tells the stories of the earlier peoples. It tells the texts known only to the rabbinical shelves. It tells the very sections where the rulings of the Torah had been twisted and redrawn. That material in an unlettered prophet's book is the standing proof in the transmitted gloss, and the same gloss holds it sufficient for anyone true to himself, and unwilling to march into ruin under the colors of envy. The logic is worth stating plainly, since it is the logic of the whole trial: a fake cannot copy the hidden ledgers of the treasury it forges. The earlier recognition-clause had set the standard; this clause brings the goods to match it. A companion point sits close by in the final book, where a group is charged with hiding what they know: (2:146 — **“Yet a group of them hides the truth knowingly”**). The redaction of the rulings is named in its own way a few verses later in the same surah: (3:78 — **“they attribute lies to Allah knowingly”**). What follows is the answer to the charge of nothing-new: the reply prints the plaintiffs' own redactions.

**THE WICKED AS THE ONLY DENIER**

The second half of the verse diagnoses the denial instead of debating it. None will deny except the rebellious. The earliest glosses fix the class-noun on the deniers of the scene, the unbelievers among the scripture-bearers. The doctrinal gloss then widens the class into a law. Denial of known proof is not a stumble of the mind. It is a posture of the will, the standing bent of the willful and the stubborn. The final book states the same law with the same anatomy, the clear revelations kept in the hearts of those given knowledge, and the denial reserved for the wrongdoers: (29:49 — **“But this ˹Quran˺ is ˹a set of˺ clear revelations ˹preserved˺ in the hearts of those gifted with knowledge.”**). The pairing of the two halves is the pairing of the whole section's method. The proof is delivered in public. The refusal is read in private. Not-knowing and not-willing are the two things this passage has drawn apart since the sheathed-heart verse, and here the drawing is finished.

**THE ALIBI THE VERSE REVOKES**

The closing lesson is about the last refuge of the rejecter, and that refuge is the alibi of missing proof. The claim that the proof never arrived is answered by the list. The claim that the proof came but was not clear is answered by the word at the root of the verse. Both claims now stand revoked, and the reason the verse revokes them by list is that the list is checkable. A community of any century that keeps the old alibi on file, the congregation of the unmet standard, meets the counter-filing waiting in this passage: the descent is written down, the cargo is counted out, and the knowing is on record from the plaintiffs' own shelves. The reader today who files the same alibi meets the same counter-filing. What turns on this is the whole law of belief. The signs do not need to be improved; the will needs to be repaired. In other words, the trial ends not with a new sign but with a verdict on the heart. The section closes its case here so that the next can open on the covenant-habit that made the repair so pressing.

---

## Verse 2:100

> Why is it that every time they make a covenant, a group of them casts it aside? In fact, most of them do not believe

**THE COVENANT-CASTING AS HABIT**

The section's last question is asked in the interrogative of exasperation, and its syntax is the syntax of a census taken too many times: ***“Why is it that every time they make a covenant, a group of them casts it aside?”***. The repeated-time construction returns the passage to its oldest rhythm — every time — and the answer hidden inside the question is that the casting-aside is not an incident but a department. The noun for the group is the noun of the faction, and the factional shape of the breach matters. A covenant is not usually broken by a whole house at once. It is discarded by an active third while the rest keep the paper. The verb of the casting is the verb of throwing behind the back, the posture of the man who will not look at what he is abandoning. The earliest glosses on the pattern keep the same two-layer reading the section has used throughout. The deed belongs to the faction, and the responsibility travels to the majority that let the faction carry the mail.

**THE PATTERN ACROSS THE WHOLE DOCKET**

The verse does not name which covenant, and the tradition hears the silence as deliberate. The docket of the section already holds the covenant of the mountain with its seven articles, the civil covenant of blood and homes and ransom, the pledge whose signatories bore witness against themselves, and the standing question of the covenant taken at the origins of the race itself. One line of analysis holds that the pledge was taken from the loins of the first father: (7:172 — **“And ˹remember˺ when your Lord brought forth from the loins of the children of Adam their descendants”**). Another holds that it was sworn in the maturity of every generation on the lips of the prophets. The plural of the unnamed covenants is therefore the section's own archive, and the casting-verse is the archive's index. The transmission from Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the pledge's terms in their plainest form: shed not the blood of your people, nor turn your people out of their dwellings. The two clans whose houses the later fighting emptied are named as the clause's first witnesses. The turn-away of the earlier passage was already counted in the same currency: (2:83 — **“orphans and the needy; speak kindly to people; establish prayer; and pay alms-tax.” But you ˹Israelites˺ turned away—except”**). The witness-clause of the civil pledge is the closing entry: (2:84 — **“you gave your pledge and bore witness”**). Read the index as a whole and the habit appears in its full chronology. The covenants were not forgotten. They were filed and then discarded by the hand that signed them.

**THE MAJORITY-WORD AND ITS WORK**

The second sentence of the verse closes the census: ***“In fact, most of them do not believe”***. The rhetorical question that opened the passage is answered with the flatness of a headcount, and the headcount is the point. The claim of the claimants throughout the section has been a claim about belief. We believe in what was sent to us; we are the beloved; the fire is limited for us. The section's last word withdraws the claim at its root with the majority-verb. The glosses press the arithmetic. The faction breaks the covenant, and the majority do not even reach the threshold the word belief requires. That is the reason the covenant-breaking keeps recurring across the generations. The whole class of such breakers is named at the head of the surah, and the naming keeps nothing back: (2:27 — **“those who violate Allah’s covenant after it has been affirmed, break whatever ˹ties˺ Allah has ordered to be maintained,”**). The doctrine of the earlier reply-verse applies its final turn. The faith that divided the books into accepted and refused parcels was already named as the refusal of belief itself. What follows from the majority-word is the passage's parting verdict on the whole trial. The problem was never a missing signature on the covenant. The problem was a census in which belief itself was the minority report.

**THE VERDICT BEHIND THE STATISTICS**

The placement of the headcount at the section's end deserves its own reading, because the sentence does rhetorical work beyond its arithmetic. The journey from the woe of the writing verse to this census is a journey from the deed to the diagnosis. The pages were forged, the prices were paid, the covenants were discarded, the prophets were killed, the angel was tried, the signs were denied — and the final word explains why the machinery kept running. The disbelief named in the last sentence is the engine, and every covenant-casting was the engine's exhaust. The tradition reads the sequence the way one reads a trial that ends with the defendant's character rather than the defendant's acts. The acts were already entered in evidence. The character is what makes the next acts inevitable. In other words, the section does not end on a crime. It ends on the disposition that manufactures crimes.

**THE CLOSE OF THE HUNDRED-VERSE ARC**

The passage that began with the secret counsels of the pricing-house closes with a public census of belief, and the arc of the hundred verses is the arc of a single trial. The opening questions asked who the custodians were and what they wrote. The closing question asks who believed at all. A later community — including the ones assembled today — that keeps the vocabulary of covenant in its liturgy while managing the covenant's articles by faction will meet the same headcount in advance. What turns on the census is everything the section has built. The covenant is not a heritage to be carried but a belief to be practiced, and the practice is the only signature the last day will read. The next pages of the revelation open on the magic the trial's losers preferred to the message. The book that casts its covenants behind its back always has a sorcerer waiting at the door.

---

## Verse 2:101

> Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them—confirming their own Scriptures—some of the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah behind their backs as if they did not know

**THE RECOGNITION THEY COULD NOT DENY**

The passage opens on the arrival the whole earlier trial has been waiting for: ***“Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them—”***, ***“confirming their own Scriptures—”***. The confirming is the heart of the charge. In Ibn ʿAbbās's own reading, the terms are the plainest available: the messenger came conforming to what their own book carried in traits and in description. The man matched the page. Their Torah had named him, and he stood in front of them named. The received account adds that the good news of his coming had been in the Torah all along, so that the arrival was not a new claim but a kept appointment. The point the verse builds toward is therefore sharp. The refusal at hand is not the refusal of strangers. It is the refusal of readers facing their own text and declining it.

**CAST BEHIND THE BACK**

The reason the gesture matters is that a document placed out of reach is a decision, not an accident. The deed is then drawn as posture, not argument: ***“some of the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah behind their backs ”***. The image is of a man putting a document where his hands cannot reach it. The glosses fix the gesture as refusal in action. They did not act on what the book said about belief in the messenger. The transmission from Ibn ʿAbbās presses the wording further: the flinging was a disbelieving in what the volume contained of the awaited one's traits and description. A second reading heard in the same tradition turns the gesture toward the market: the book was cast behind the back the way goods are disposed of — sold and spent. The book's own rule for that exact trade is short and old: (2:42 — **“Do not mix truth with falsehood or hide the truth knowingly”**). Either way the anatomy is the same. The document was not lost. It was placed out of sight on purpose.

**THE MASK OF THE NOT-KNOWING**

The closing mask is the verse's coldest stroke: ***“ as if they did not know”***. The phrase does not accuse the party of lacking the knowledge. It describes the party wearing the not-knowing as a costume. The gloss from Ibn ʿAbbās puts it in the voice of the scene: they behaved as though they were ignorant people who knew nothing, while the recognition was sitting in their own shelves. The standard of recognition had already been set in this surah in the family image: (2:146 — **“Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺ as they recognize their own children.”**). The description they feigned ignorance of is named in the final book without softness: (7:157 — **““˹They are˺ the ones who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whose description they find in their Torah”**). Doubt and theater part ways here. Doubt stands outside and asks. This stands inside the text and pretends the text is empty. The reason the verse files the posture as the crime is that the knowledge was never the missing piece. The knowing was in the room, and the costume of ignorance was what the knowing wore to work.

**THE HABIT WITH A LATEST INSTANCE**

The placement of this verse right after the covenant-casting refrain is deliberate. The refrain said the casting was a habit. This is the habit's newest face. The same people who signed the papers now stand over the papers and act as if the papers say nothing. The doctrinal weight of the scene is heavy because the alternative was light. Accepting a confirmation of one's own book costs the pride of the shelf. Rejecting it costs the book. The passage makes the trade visible and lets the reader price it. For any reader today who keeps a cherished text at arm's length while quoting its approval of something refused, the mask in this verse has a familiar fit. The habit has a wide reach in households and in study circles both. A verse is quoted with reverence in the morning and shelved by the evening if it recommends an inconvenient step. That is the same back with the same book behind it. The verse answers the costume with one word of daylight. They knew. So do the people who quote and then look away. The page remembers either way.

---

## Verse 2:102

> They ˹instead˺ followed the magic promoted by the devils during the reign of Solomon. Never did Solomon disbelieve, rather the devils disbelieved. They taught magic to the people, along with what had been revealed to the two angels, Hârût and Mârût, in Babylon. The two angels never taught anyone without saying, “We are only a test ˹for you˺, so do not abandon ˹your˺ faith.” Yet people learned ˹magic˺ that caused a rift ˹even˺ between husband and wife; although their magic could not harm anyone except by Allah’s Will. They learned what harmed them and did not benefit them—although they already knew that whoever buys into magic would have no share in the Hereafter. Miserable indeed was the price for which they sold their souls, if only they knew

**THE CHARGE AGAINST A KING**

The next stroke of the passage restores the honor of a prophet and exposes the trade that destroyed the traders: ***“They ˹instead˺ followed the magic promoted by the devils during the reign of Solomon”***. The charge had a shape. The claim ran that Solomon's kingdom was a kingdom of sorcery, that its first forty days were sorcery and white magic, that the throne rested on spells. The gloss from Ibn ʿAbbās records the substance of the slander plainly: the devils wrote of the collapse of Solomon's kingdom and of those forty days of magic. A rumor of that kind does two jobs at once. It degrades a prophet, and it gives magic a royal pedigree. The party in the passage reached for the second job with both hands. If magic was the currency of a prophet's rule, then magic was merchandise with a provenance. The verse's first clause names the tragedy in one word. They followed. The following is the whole engine of the loss.

**THE PARENTHESIS THAT PROTECTS A PROPHET**

The answer comes as the oldest form of defense in this surah, the declaration of separation: ***“Never did Solomon disbelieve, rather the devils disbelieved”***. The separation is made explicit in the sharpest available grammar. The prophet is cleared in the same breath that convicts the devils. The gloss from Ibn ʿAbbās turns each half into its own verdict. Solomon did not write this sorcery and this white magic. The devils disbelieved in that they did write it. The tradition behind the story keeps a second version of the same exoneration. The devils buried their books of sorcery beneath the throne, or fed fabrications to priests who compiled them, until Solomon gathered the volumes and buried them himself. After his death the devils showed people where the books lay. Either version leaves the prophet's hands clean of the trade. The books were the devils' works, kept out of the way by the very king the slander was pinned on. The freedom-of-action doctrine already carried in this surah applies with full weight here, and it is the same freedom the magic verse itself reports from the contest of the magicians: (20:69 — **“Cast what is in your right hand, and it will swallow up what they have made,”**). What the sorcerers could never do is the verse's counter-declaration: (20:69 — **“for what they have made is no more than a magic trick. And magicians can never succeed wherever they go.””**). The parenthesis in the present verse says something about prophethood and something about magic at once. Prophets do not write spells. Spells do not succeed.

**THE TWO AGENTS SENT DOWN AT BABYLON**

The passage then turns from the slander to the market it fed. The teaching is named in the verse's own geography: ***“They taught magic to the people, along with what had been revealed to the two angels, Hârût and Mârût, in Babylon”***. The gloss from Ibn ʿAbbās reads the teaching scene with two lights held up. In one reading the teachers were the devils, and the angels were never taught sorcery at all. In the other, the verse means the people also learned what the angels were inspired with. Both readings protect the same boundary. The angels are not smuggled into the trade as its craftsmen. The verse itself then says the part that governs every account of the descent: ***“The two angels never taught anyone without saying”***, and the warning follows in the angels' own quoted words: ***“We are only a test ˹for you˺, so do not abandon ˹your˺ faith”***. The function of the descent was the exposure of its own buyers. Whoever bought the craft bought the means to harm. The warning in the angels' own mouths is therefore the first consumer-protection notice in the passage. The product was sold with its own hazard label attached. The buyers read the label and signed anyway. The market at Babylon was never a market of the deceived. It was a market of the informed. The reason the verse files the whole scene under testing is that the knowledge was poison in commercial form, and the buyers are exactly the party the passage is prosecuting.

**THE SEAL ON THE CRAFT**

What the craft could and could not do is then sealed with absolute clauses. First the inventory of the learning: ***“Yet people learned ˹magic˺ that caused a rift ˹even˺ between husband and wife”***. Then the ceiling on its power: ***“although their magic could not harm anyone except by Allah’s Will”***. The indictment follows in the accounting word of the passage: ***“They learned what harmed them and did not benefit them”***. The seal matters because the trade in these verses is priced twice, once by its power and once by its outcome. The power was real enough to frighten crowds and to split households. The outcome was harm to the buyer. This is the same asymmetry the trade of the wicked already carried in the surah's marketplace passages. The deal looked like a bargain at the counter and a loss in the ledger. The reason the ceiling clause matters is that it prices the craft as borrowed power, which means the buyer pays for a permission he does not control. The judgment of the passage is therefore not that magic is imaginary. The judgment is that magic is real, borrowed, capped, and expensive. The craftsman of these arts works downward. The one who refuses them loses nothing.

**THE PRICE PAID IN THE SELLING**

The close of the unit reads the loss as self-inflicted, and the verse reaches the accounting by way of what the buyers already knew: ***“although they already knew that whoever buys into magic would have no share in the Hereafter”***. The strangest fact of the trade is its brokerage. The gloss from Ibn ʿAbbās puts the knowing of the buyers at the center of the sale, and the knowing is what makes the brokerage so strange. The buyers traded revelation for rumor. They left the pages that named the awaited one, and they paid for the devils' pages instead. The verdict on the sale is then delivered in the passage's coldest line: ***“Miserable indeed was the price for which they sold their souls”***. The sale had been priced twice over, once in the learning and once in the hereafter, and both invoices were in the buyers' hands before the purchase. The brokerage is therefore the verse's coldest irony. The brokers kept the revelation out of the trade and kept the ruin in it. The final wound is the wish that closes the verse: ***“if only they knew”***. What follows from the knowing clause is the passage's final refusal of the ignorance excuse. The trade of guidance for misguidance has been named in this surah before, and the naming there was clinical. For any reader who has watched a rumor priced above a document — in a family dispute, in the market, in the commentary sections under a news story — the anatomy at Babylon is instructive. The devils still publish. The throne still gets the burial, and the shelf of the two books keeps its labels. The verse keeps the two books on the table and lets the reader choose which one gets cast behind the back. The choice is the reader's own, and the verse has already priced both options.

---

## Verse 2:103

> If only they were faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, there would have been a better reward from Allah, if only they knew

**THE WISH THAT PRECEDES THE VERDICT**

The passage then prices the refusal it has just documented, and it does so in the form of a wish: ***“If only they were faithful”***. The opening is the wish of the witness for the defendant. The faithfulness named is the acceptance of the messenger standing in front of them, the step the preceding unit showed them refusing. The gloss from Ibn ʿAbbās unpacks the wished-for conduct in the vocabulary of this community's own trial. Had they believed in Muhammad and in the Qur'an. The wish therefore stands at the exact point of failure the passage has been prosecuting. The pages were recognized. The man matched the pages. The faithfulness was the one move that would have changed the verdict, and the verse puts the wish in the mouth of the one who watched the failure happen.

**THE SECOND HALF OF THE CONDITION**

The wish's second clause is then added beside the first: ***“and mindful ˹of Allah˺, there would have been a better reward from Allah”***. The same gloss unpacks the mindfulness in its practical form. Had they kept from evil, repented from Judaism and from the sorcery the preceding unit dissected. The condition was therefore not an unscaled wall. The two steps were visible from where the party already stood. The reward clause then turns the wish into an appraisal. A better reward from Allah is set against the trade of the previous verse, the souls sold at a loss and the magic bought at a premium. The tradition heard in the glosses seals the comparison by flipping the direction of the wish. The reward from Allah is better than the faithlessness and the sorcery they settled for. The scale of that better reward is fixed in the final book's own accounting: (3:185 — **“And you will only receive your full reward on the Day of Judgment.”**). The good news of the same scale is set beside it in the verse that promises the gardens under the rivers: (2:25 — **“Give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to those who believe and do good that they will have Gardens under”**). What follows is the difference between a discount and a gift. The sorcery was the discount that costs the store. The reward is the gift that completes.

**THE REPETITION THE VERSE MAKES**

Notice that the verse closes by repeating its own opening mood in sharper form: ***“if only they knew”***. The wish appears twice in one breath of scripture, once over the faithfulness and once over the knowing. The tradition running through the glosses adds the knife's edge to the repetition. The transmission from Ibn ʿAbbās holds that they knew all this from their own book. The not-knowing of 2:101 is therefore worn here a second time, and the fit is just as false. The knowing they discarded was the same knowing that would have made the reward theirs. The repetition of the wish is the passage's accounting of the whole unit. The magic of 2:102 was bought by people who knew its price. The faithfulness of this verse was refused by people who knew its reward. The knowledge was never the missing piece in either case. The knowledge was in the room, and the wish is what the knowing left behind at the scene. The witness of the passage stands over the scene and says the only sentence left to say. If only.

**WHAT THE WISH CANNOT REACH**

The unit's force is that the wish never becomes a prayer. A prayer asks the owner for a change. This wish asks the history to un-happen. The passage has already scheduled the decision at the ownership level, and the schedule does not bend to the wishes of the witnesses. The reward-contrast of the verse is therefore the last mercy of the scene. The better reward stood available at the counter the whole time. The buyers went to the other booth. For any household or forum where the better offer is declined daily for the smaller prize, the appraisal in this verse is the ledger entry that names the loss. The wish is not the cure. The faithfulness and the mindfulness are the cure. The wish is only what the cure looks like when it is observed from the far side of the fence. The verse leaves the reader on the near side of the fence, where the two steps are still open and the wish has not yet been earned.

---

## Verse 2:104

> O believers! Do not say, “Râ’ina.” [Herd us!] But say, “Unẓurna,” [Tend to us!] and listen ˹attentively˺. And the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment

**A WORD WITH TWO FACES**

The passage now polices the smallest unit of the encounter — the word used to address the messenger: ***“O believers! Do not say, “Râ’ina.” [Herd us!]”***. The received record of the mischief is precise. In Arabic the word carries the sense 'be mindful of us', which is why some believers reached for it. In Hebrew the same sound carries an insult. The received gloss traces it to the noun of thoughtlessness and records the amusement the party took when the word landed. The mischief had a design. The trick was to make the cursing public and to make the believers say it themselves, so that the insult would wear a Muslim face. The story is small. The engineering is not. It is a poison pill pressed into a greeting.

**THE REPLACEMENT AS AN ORDER**

The cure is immediate and positive: ***“But say, “Unẓurna,” [Tend to us!]”***, and the posture is commanded with the vocabulary in the next breath of the verse. The gloss from Ibn ʿAbbās gives the replacement in plain speech: say 'look upon us', and hear what you are commanded and obey it. The instruction is worth noticing in its two halves. The vocabulary is corrected, and the posture is corrected with it. Attention is commanded alongside the word, because the word that means attention is useless without the thing itself. The reasoning the passage relies on is simple and worth spelling out. What follows from a language with two faces is that the speaker is responsible for the face the hearer receives. The believers were therefore given a clean word with one face, and the clean word removed the trap without amplifying it.

**THE DISCIPLINE BEHIND THE VOCABULARY**

The verse's warning is then attached to the discipline it belongs to: ***“and listen ˹attentively˺. And the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment”***. The received tradition in this passage files the whole scene under manners in speech and observes that devious words hiding their real meaning were the specialty being answered. The reports that gloss this discipline are of a piece with the verse. Among them is the one Aḥmad hands down from Ibn ʿUmar in connection with the greetings of that period, where the same anatomy of hidden insult in plain sound was being managed by command. The pattern of the passage is therefore continuous with the covenant lessons before it. Words at a counter can be weights and measures, and the weights get checked. The twin command against the word with two faces is recorded in the book's own amendment of the etiquette: (4:46 — **“and “Râ’ina!” [Herd us!]—playing with words and discrediting the faith. Had they said ˹courteously˺, “We hear and obey,” “Listen to us,” and”**). The replacement is named in the very next clause: (4:46 — **““Unẓurna,” [Tend to us!] it would have been better for them and more proper. Allah has condemned them for their disbelief,”**). The general disease behind the trick is diagnosed where the covenant-breakers are sentenced for it: (5:13 — **“But for breaking their covenant We condemned them and hardened their hearts. They distorted the words of the Scripture”**). What the verse installs is the examination of sound as well as sense. The effect is larger than courtesy. A community that watches its vocabulary at the door keeps the poison out of the room.

**THE TOLL AND THE TOOL**

The section's hold on language is practical rather than sentimental. The word that wounds is a tool. The word that heals is the same tool with a different hand on it. The prohibition does not silence speech. It orders speech that can be audited, and it removes the syllable that had been turned into a blade. For the modern reader, the case reads like every community's comment thread where a borrowed phrase cuts on one side and reads as warmth on the other. The verse does not ask the reader to grow suspicious of every greeting. It asks the reader to speak so that the hearer receives the face the speaker owns. That is why the discipline belongs in a passage about scripture sold and words twisted. The same hands that cast the book behind the back also poisoned the greeting. The answer to both is the same habit. Look. Listen. Say the clean thing.

---

## Verse 2:105

> The disbelievers from the People of the Book and the polytheists would not want you to receive any blessing from your Lord, but Allah selects whoever He wills for His mercy. And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty

**THE WELL-WISHERS WHO WERE NONE**

The unit that follows draws the motive behind the refusals already documented: ***“The disbelievers from the People of the Book and the polytheists would not want you to receive any blessing from your Lord, ”***. The verse names the two parties in one breath and gives the shared wish a direction. The received gloss from Ibn ʿAbbās gives the scene its faces. On the side of the People of the Book stand Kaʿb b. al-Ashraf and his companions. On the side of the idolaters stand Abū Jahl and his companions. The good whose descent they dread is spelled out in the same gloss as prophethood, Islam, and the book. The received account of their public posture adds the costume the verse implies. Some of them assured the believers of their goodwill and said they wished the Muslims had received the best of doctrines, so that the wish could be worn openly and the envy kept private.

**ENVY AS THE HIDDEN VETO**

The verse then answers the wish with a matter of ownership: ***“but Allah selects whoever He wills”***. The gloss from Ibn ʿAbbās reads the choosing as the assignment of the mission itself — the sending of revelation to this messenger as the good they wanted withheld. The second clause then widens the answer past this community's hour: ***“And Allah is the Lord of infinite bount”***. The point the verse makes is a point about authority over blessing. The descent of good is not a market decision made by its neighbors. It is a choice made at the level of the ownership of all good. The reminder attached to that choice in the Qur'an's own ledger is worth quoting, because envy never files itself as envy: (4:32 — **“And do not crave what Allah has given some of you over others. Men will be rewarded according to their deeds”**). The craving that this verse exposes is the veto-envy that cannot bear a neighbor's raise. What follows is the difference between a wish and a grudge. A wish asks for the same good. A grudge wants the good withdrawn.

**THE FREEDOM OF THE OWNER TO CHOOSE**

The weight of the declaration sits on the word that follows the envy: ***“He wills for His mercy. And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty”***. The dominion of that bounty is the same survey the previous unit closed on. Ownership of the heavens and the earth includes ownership of the gifts distributed inside them. The reason the passage returns to this here is structural. The envy of 2:105 and the slander of 2:102 share one root. Both refuse a distribution that arrived without the objector's signature. The famous description of the ownership is worth holding next to the envy: (3:26 — **“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O Allah! Lord over all authorities! You give authority to whoever You please and remove it from”**). The companion clause then keeps the hands of the owner open: (3:26 — **“good is in Your Hands. Surely You ˹alone˺ are Most Capable of everything”**). The envy therefore stands outside its competence. It resents a distribution it does not administer.

**THE GESTURE WORN OVER THE GRUDGE**

The passage closes the unit without a command, and the silence is itself instructive. The verse does not answer the pretend-well-wishers with a matching pretend. It answers with the exposure and the ownership clause. The exposure is complete because the wish has been priced. The ownership is complete because the choice has been located. For any reader who has worn the gesture of goodwill over a private grudge, at work or at home or in the rows of a congregation, the anatomy in this verse is the mirror held at the right height. The cure the passage implies is not a vow never to feel envy. It is the relocation of envy at the ownership. The bounty is the owner's to give. The deeds are the servant's to mind. The reader who keeps that division of labor finds the grudge starved of its jurisdiction. That is the division under which every blessing in the surah has been ordered from the first page, and the ordering holds in this verse exactly as it held there.

---

## Verse 2:106

> If We ever abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten, We replace it with a better or similar one. Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything

**THE VERSE THAT COMES LATER**

The passage now answers the mockery that the changes in the law had produced: ***“If We ever abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten”***, ***“We replace it with a better or similar one”***. The received record names the mockery precisely. The disbelievers began to deride the matter outright, saying that one day the messenger enjoins his companions to one thing and the next day he forbids it. The taunt had a sharper edge in this city, because the most visible change in living memory was the direction of prayer. The turn from Jerusalem to the Kaʿbah was fresh, and the taunt attached itself to the turn. The foolish of the people made the question public: (2:142 — **“The foolish among the people will ask, “Why did they turn away from the direction of prayer they used to face?” Say,”**). The verse at hand answers the taunt with a rule of the sending itself rather than with an argument about the turn.

**THE RULE OF THE SENDING**

The rule is stated in the voice of the sender: the verse that is withdrawn or postponed is replaced with what is better or like it. Ibn ʿAbbās opens the unit by noting exactly what the passage is doing. It mentions what was abrogated of the book and what was not abrogated. The same gloss traces the address back to the original challenge, the question of the Quraysh: why do you command us to do something and then forbid it? The answer in the tradition is the answer of administration. A verse may be acted upon for a time and then not acted upon, and the replacement arrives from the same sender with more profit in it. The coherence of the book is therefore not the coherence of a frozen page. It is the coherence of a curriculum whose teacher knows the sequence. A contradiction and a change of schedule are not the same document. A contradiction speaks twice at once. A change of schedule speaks twice in order.

**THE TWO READINGS OF THE WITHDRAWAL**

The tradition of the glosses preserves two technical readings of the same verb, and both are worth naming. In one reading the verse is abrogated together with its recital or with its judgment alone, the recitation continuing while the ruling lifts. In the other, the verb is taken as postponement rather than removal, the ruling deferred to its hour. The point of the pair is that the withdrawal is itself an administered act. Nothing is lost in the process of sending. The verse closed with the capacity that administers all of it: (2:286 — **“Allah does not require of any soul more than what it can afford. All good will be for its own benefit,”**). The replacement of verses and the weighting of souls therefore answer to one policy. The schedule is set by the one who knows the weight of every hour. The closing challenge of the verse puts the whole taunt back in its place: ***“Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything”***.

**THE FAILURE OF THE TAUNT**

The taunt failed for a reason the passage is careful to leave standing. The charge was that the changes came from the messenger himself. The answer is the identity of the one who turns the pages. The verses are sent, withdrawn, and replaced by the owner of the sending. The received account of the qiblah change records the taunt's purpose as well as its words. The aim was to sow the seed of doubt, that the changes were made by the man and not by his lord. The verse answers the purpose, not only the words. For any reader who has watched a curriculum revised at mid-year and heard the charge that the teacher cannot keep his story straight, the case at hand is the same case. The sequence is the method. The maker of the sequence is the one who knows what the next lesson is for. The book's coherence is therefore not the stillness of one page. It is the wisdom of the order in which the pages arrive. The reader who holds that point holds the answer to the mockery at its root, and the answer needs no inventory of the changes at all.

---

## Verse 2:107

> Do you not know that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs ˹only˺ to Allah, and you have no guardian or helper besides Allah

**THE KINGDOM UNDER THE CHANGES**

The passage closes the abrogation question with a survey of ownership: ***“Do you not know”*** ***“that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs ˹only˺ to Allah,”***. The placement is exact. The previous verse answered the taunt about changing pages. This verse answers the question of whose pages they are. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the kingdom here as the stores of the heavens and the earth. The one who holds the stores gives the orders, and the orders follow knowledge. The same gloss puts the reasoning in a single line: He commands His servants with whatever He wills because He knows better what is good for them. The ownership of the schedule therefore rests on the knowledge of the goods. A rule that moves and a rule that wanders part company at the source. The rule that moves is directed from the store. The rule that wanders is directed from the wind.

**NO FRIEND, NO HELPER**

The verse then draws the consequence for the objectors in terms of standing: ***“ and you have no guardian or helper besides Allah”***. Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss gives each missing figure its face. The friend is anyone close enough to benefit or protect. The helper is anyone able to prevent the punishment when it comes. The received gloss frames the two as the safeguard and the shield, the one who keeps the chastisement away when it arrives. The objectors of the passage are therefore short two things at once. They have no title to the schedule they are mocking, and they have no counsel inside the ownership they are addressing. The indictment of the covenant pattern fits them without strain: (2:27 — **“those who violate Allah’s covenant after it has been affirmed, break whatever ˹ties˺ Allah has ordered to be maintained,”**). The breakers of the ties stand outside the ties. The verse simply reads their standing back to them. The reading is not cruel. It is the accurate entry of the parties in the register of the case. No protector steps forward on their side, because the side has no title to present.

**THE PART OF THE TAUNT THE VERSE DOES NOT ANSWER**

Notice what the verse leaves alone. It does not defend the specific changes one by one. It settles the ownership and lets the changes stand as the owner's work. The received account of the taunt explains why this is enough. The doubt being sown was that the changes were made by the man rather than by his lord. Once the kingdom is located, that doubt loses its floor. The pattern of the answer is the pattern used against every slander in this passage. Locate the authority, and the slander runs out of standing. The east and west of the whole question were settled in the answer to the foolish of the people: (2:142 — **“˹O Prophet,˺ “The east and west belong ˹only˺ to Allah. He guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.””**). The question of direction is owned. The question of timing is owned. The ownership is one.

**THE READER WITH A REVISED MAP**

For the modern reader, the section at hand is the answer to every charge that a divinely ordered book must never move. The movement is not a crack in the authority. The movement is a feature of the authority of the one who schedules the lessons. The Kaʿbah turn, the lifted rulings, the replaced verses — all of them are pages being handled by the page-holder. The reader's place in the scene is therefore not the critic of the schedule. The reader's place is the student whose protection clause has already been written, the soul not required to carry more than it can afford. The verse ends the unit with the posture it wants. Look at the kingdom first. The details of the schedule follow from the ownership, and the ownership is not in dispute at home or at work or in the heavens above them. The survey closes the question the mockery opened, and it closes the question by raising the eyes from the page to the one who sends it. The point of the close is worth one more sentence. A kingdom with one owner has one policy, and the policy includes the schedule of every page the kingdom sends.

---

## Verse 2:108

> Or do you ˹believers˺ intend to ask of your Messenger as Moses was asked before? But whoever trades belief for disbelief has truly strayed from the Right Way

**ASKING FOR THE OLD SPECTACLE**

The passage now files the demands themselves as evidence: ***“Or do you ˹believers˺ intend to ask of your Messenger as Moses was asked before? ”***. The received record names the demands twice over. In the city the askers wanted the size of the place enlarged and the hill of Ṣafā made of gold. From the scripture party came the demand for the whole revelation at once, the way the Torah had been said to arrive. The transmission from Ibn ʿAbbās gives the older version its full face. They asked their prophet to show them the Lord outright and to let them hear his speech. The demand of the present hour is therefore not new merchandise. It is the same request wearing the current city's clothes. The second gloss names the Meccan version without ceremony. The ask was spectacle. The answer at hand does not produce the spectacle. It prices the asking.

**THE PRECEDENT OF THE MOUNTAIN**

The comparison to Moses does its work by recalling how that asking ended. The children of Israel had asked their prophet the same kind of question, and the answer arrived as a mountain raised over the covenant-party: (7:171 — **“and they thought it would fall on them. ˹We said,˺ “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you”**). The precedent is instructive because of the shape of the exchange. The askers wanted God on their terms. The answer put the covenant back in their hands. The sign for the sincere and the spectacle for the demanding serve opposite ends. The sign settles the truth for the one ready to submit. The spectacle feeds the appetite that will ask again tomorrow. The received tradition of this passage notes that the demands of this period repeated the pattern exactly. The promise of the revelation would be held hostage to the theater.

**THE TRADE NAMED AT LAST**

The verse then drops the pricing hammer: ***“ But whoever trades belief for disbelief has truly strayed from the Right Way”***. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the straying in plain terms: the trader has relinquished the path of guidance. The verb of trading is the surah's own accounting word, the one used at the market stalls of the wicked. The trade of guidance for misguidance has already been itemized in this passage's ledger, and the naming there was clinical. The demand for spectacle is therefore not a neutral question at the counter. It is the offer of belief in exchange for a demonstration on the buyer's terms. The verse marks the offer as the trade it is. The revelation can be removed at will, and the power behind the removal was noted in this surah's own defense: (2:20 — **“and sight. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything”**). The terms of the supply are set by the supplier. The demand that forgets this fact has already left the Right Way by the door marked disbelief.

**THE SELF-ANSWERING QUESTION**

The unit works because the demand is self-incriminating. The askers stand inside a tradition that records the mountain, the tablets, and the punishment of the askers, and then they ask again in the same shape. The reason the verse references the older episode is that the pattern needs no new refutation. The demand for proof on demand is the refusal of the proof already sent. The passage therefore files the question under the trade rather than under the inquiry, and the filing is precise. An inquiry opens the book. The demand opens the account. The reader who wants the doctrine in one line has it here. Revelation arrives by the schedule of the one who owns the demonstrating, and the schedule is set at the level of the ownership. Everything else is the marketplace of the spectacle. The trader leaves that market with the book under one arm and the wish under the other, and the wish is the heavier load by the verse's own accounting. The whole unit is therefore a price list with one entry. The spectacle costs the belief. The belief costs the spectacle. The exchange rate is published in the verse itself, and no third booth opens along the road. The list never changes its prices.

---

## Verse 2:109

> Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you ˹believers˺ back to disbelief because of their envy, after the truth has been made clear to them. Pardon and bear with them until Allah delivers His decision. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything

**ENVY WITH A POLICY**

The passage then names the motive force behind the whole campaign of demands: ***“Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you ˹believers˺ back to disbelief because of their envy, after the truth has been made clear to them.”***. Ibn ʿAbbās paints the wish with its faces again. Kaʿb b. al-Ashraf and his companions, Finhāṣ b. AbīʿAzūrah and his companions — the wish had offices and committees. The same gloss names the addressees of the warning, the men being recruited back: ʿAmmār, Ḥudhayfah, and Muʿādh b. Jabal. The envy is then located with the precision the sentence deserves: it is of their own account, resentful envy, arising after the truth had become manifest. The older gloss puts the manifesting in the right venue. The truth about this messenger had become clear to them in the Torah. The envy is therefore not the envy of the uninformed. It is the envy of the informed.

**THE COMMAND TO STAND DOWN**

The command that follows is one of the hardest in the passage: ***“ Pardon and bear with them until Allah delivers His decision”***. The instruction has two halves, and the tradition hears both. Pardon names the hands kept off. Bear names the tempers kept still. The command is not consent. It is the disciplined stand-down of a community that has been armed with the truth and ordered to wait for the verdict. The reminder attached to that verdict is the patience-anchor of the passage: (2:214 — **““When will Allah’s help come?” Indeed, Allah’s help is ˹always˺ near”**). The help being near is the reason the stand-down is possible. A community governed by its wounds and one governed by its verdict keep different calendars. The first retaliates on schedule. The second pardons on schedule. The point of the verse is that the timetable of the retaliation is not the community's to set.

**THE FREEDOM OF THE VERDICT**

The closing clause of the unit is the ownership survey again, in the sharpest possible wording: the decision is delivered by the one who does what he wills. The companion of that freedom has been stated in this surah without softness: (2:253 — **“if Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another. But Allah does what He wills”**). The envy of the wishers is therefore answered twice. The truth they resent was manifest in their own shelves. The decision they dread is scheduled at the ownership level. The tradition of the passage adds the detail that makes the envy legible. The stratagems kept arriving even after repeated failure, because envy does not retire. The modern reader meets the same personality in every comment section where a clear answer is met with a wish that the answer were otherwise. The verse replies to the wish with the stand-down and the verdict. Pardon now. The judgment is booked.

**THE WISH AND THE WILL**

The point of the balance is worth stating plainly. Notice the balance the passage builds between two verbs. The wish belongs to the enviers. The will belongs to the owner. The wish wants a reversal that has already been answered by the manifest truth. The will delivers a decision that cannot be lobbied. The balance is the surah's answer to every campaign of turning-back. The recruiting is old. The names change. The armory is always the same: spectacle at the door and envy at the desk. The verse files both under one accounting and then orders the believers to spend their day elsewhere. Prayer, alms, patience — the work of the verdict is not the servant's overtime. That is the relief inside the hardest command of the unit. The case is not being neglected. It is simply above the pay grade of the street. The stand-down is therefore not the silence of the defeated. It is the schedule of the confident. The community ordered to pardon is a community whose case has already been heard in the court that decides without the lobbyists. The envoy of the verdict is on the road. The campaigners can retire their wish at the door. The wish they retire has been fully itemized in the passage. It began with the informed shelves and the manifest truth. It continued through the spectacles and the stratagems. It will end at the decision already calendared at the ownership level. The envier keeps the calendar of the grievance. The servant keeps the calendar of the owner. Only one of the two calendars ends.

---

## Verse 2:110

> Establish prayer, and pay alms-tax. Whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will ˹certainly˺ find ˹its reward˺ with Allah. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do

**TWO VERBS AND A BANK**

The unit that answers the envy-campaign is an order to keep working: ***“Establish prayer, and pay alms-tax.”***. In the gloss of Ibn ʿAbbās, each verb carries its full instruction. The establishing is the perfection of the five daily prayers. The paying is the poor-due, the share owed from the wealth to the poor. The reason the pairing answers the campaign is structural. The pairing is the passage's answer to the strategists of the previous verse. The envy-campaign wants the believers' attention. The order sends the attention to the timetable and to the account. The structure is worth naming. Prayer governs the day. The alms govern the wealth. Between the two, the whole of the believer's estate is scheduled, and the schedule leaves no opening for the recruiters.

**WHAT THE ACCOUNT KEEPS**

The verse then opens the ledger of the sending: ***“Whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will ˹certainly˺ find ˹its reward˺ with Allah.”***. The glosses hear the sending in the language of the market. Whatever of good, of righteous deeds and charitable works, the servant saves for himself by sending it ahead, he will find its reward stored with the owner. The tradition's gloss widens the good beyond the two verbs to include observing kinship and every obedience. The position of the verse in the passage is therefore deliberate. The envy of 2:109 wants the believers turned back. The bank of 2:110 keeps the believers turned forward. The goods sent ahead are goods nobody can envy away. The recipients of the poor-due are then described in the passage where the charter is given: (2:273 — **“˹Charity is˺ for the needy”**), and the needy are the people whose dignity the same passage protects. The vow and the charity are likewise inventoried in the passage that keeps the full books: (2:270 — **“Whatever charities you give or vows you make are surely known to Allah. And the wrongdoers will have no helpers”**). What follows from the ledger is a difference of time. The envy-campaign works in the present tense. The account works in the settlement tense.

**THE SEEING OF THE SPENDING**

The closing clause files the whole economy under one observation: ***“Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you ”***. The companion's tradition turns the seeing into the knowing of the innermost thing: he knows your intentions, what you spend in charity and the rest of it. The seeing of the spending is the inspection that makes the bank trustworthy. The goods sent forward are recorded in their full weight, including the intention that gave them their weight. The discipline of the patience needed to keep working under fire was commanded in this surah's first page of practice: (2:45 — **“And seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is a burden except for the humble—”**). The verse therefore answers both halves of the situation at once. The recruiters keep scheming. The worker keeps shipping. The one who sees the shipping keeps the books.

**THE WORK AS THE ANSWER**

For any reader who has been the target of a campaign — a household dispute, an office faction, a theological fight that runs on momentum — the order in this verse is the withdrawal of fuel. The campaign feeds on attention and reply. The prayer and the alms remove both from the table. The reason this is the passage's answer rather than a change of subject is structural. The envy wants a reversal of the truth. The prayer keeps the truth standing on the day's own feet. The alms keep the truth standing in the wealth. The reversal has nowhere to begin. The verse leaves the recruiters with the truth on its timetable and the reward in its bank, and the two together close the door the strategy was trying to open. Keep the schedule. Keep the account. The verdict arrives on its own hour. The spending that went forward keeps arriving too, at the hour when the books are opened and the goods are weighed. Nothing shipped to the owner's account is ever lost in the mail. The two verbs of the verse are the whole estate of that mail service. The prayer stamps the day. The alms stamps the wealth. The owner of the account sees the sending and keeps it. That is the full economy of the verse, and the economy runs without the permission of the envy-campaign.

---

## Verse 2:111

> The Jews and Christians each claim that none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith. These are their desires. Reply, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof if what you say is true.”

**THE EXCLUSIVE-ENTRY CLAIM**

The passage now turns from the campaign to the claim that fed it: ***“The Jews and Christians each claim that none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith.”***. The tradition behind the claim gives it its venue and its two halves. The Jews of Medina and the Christians of Najrān disputed with the messenger, each party claiming Paradise for its own membership exclusively. Ibn ʿAbbās hears the claim in the words of its makers. None enter unless he dies as a Jew, said one party, and the Christians likewise claimed their own. The structure of the claim is the same in both mouths. Membership is the ticket. The verse then labels the claim in its own vocabulary: ***“These are their desires.”***. The same gloss notes what the labeling costs the claim. They are wishing from Allah even though it is not in their books. The wish is therefore not even loyal to the shelves it stands on.

**THE PROOF CHALLENGE**

The reply is the shortest legal move in the passage: ***“ Reply, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof if what you say is true.””***. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the challenge its jurisdiction. Bring your proofs from your own respective books. The demand is fair in the highest degree. The claim is about an entry rule. The books are where the entry rules were said to be written. The received account of the wider failure explains why the challenge lands where it does. The parties had identified religion with affiliation, with a racial and social membership, instead of with the authentic doctrines and the deeds the revelations actually prescribe. The universal rule of the entry has already been stated in this surah's own table: (2:62 — **“Indeed, the believers, Jews, Christians, and Sabians—whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah and the Last Day and”**), and its completion governs the claim at hand: (2:62 — **“does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve”**). The entry rule is belief and deed. The membership card belongs to the office of the unproven.

**THE BURDEN NOBODY MET**

Notice the procedural effect of the challenge. The claim was made without its exhibit. The verse records the claim and the demand for the exhibit in adjacent breaths. A promise and a promissory note are separated by the signature. The promise is found in the books and read in the light of the messengers. The note is printed at the counter of the affiliation. The next verse of the passage then writes the rule the parties were asked to exhibit, the statement of the submitted face and its reward. The reason the exhibit-order is the perfect reply is that the claim was printed on the book's own letterhead, which means the proof belongs to the shelf the claim stands on. The exhibit therefore exists. It simply sits in the wrong name on the shelf of each exclusive claim.

**THE CLAIM IN MODERN DRESS**

For the reader of this age the scene is older than the sects and as current as the morning. The exclusive-entry claim survives wherever a community has confused its address with its deeds. The verse's reply is the same in every century. Produce the proof. The proof from the book. The doctrine and the deed are the entry rule, and the book that names them was never read for the exclusivity clause, because the clause is not printed there. The verse leaves the challenge standing where it can be heard at every desk where the question is asked again. The claim is cheap. The exhibit is dear. The passage bills accordingly. The claimant who brings the exhibit finds the rule waiting in the book's own words. The claimant who cannot bring it has printed the sign at his own counter. The passage simply reads the sign back to its author and keeps the challenge on the table until somebody brings the page. The claimant who returns with the page finds that the page names the belief and the deed. The claimant who returns with a membership card finds that the card is not a page of the book. Either way the challenge has done its work. The exclusive-entry claim cannot survive the exhibit, and the verse records the claim and the exhibit-order in the same breath so that the failure is visible in the margin of the text itself.

---

## Verse 2:112

> But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**THE ADMISSION RULE**

The passage answers the exclusive claims of the previous verse with the rule as written: ***“But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah and does good will have their reward with their Lord.”***. Ibn ʿAbbās hears the submitting in its two halves. The surrender is made sincere to Allah in the religion. The good is worked in words and in deeds. The rule is therefore not the rule of a lineage. It is the rule of a posture and its output. What follows from the substitution is the end of the membership argument. A second gloss gives the claiming-part of the claim its own anatomy. The face is named in the Arabic as the most noble part of the body. When the face has submitted, the rest of the frame has its captain. The point of the phrasing is the point of the whole passage. Submission is not a badge worn on the sleeve. It is the direction of the person.

**THE FACE AS THE SURRENDERED PART**

The imagery of the surrendered face is worth holding. The face is where recognition lives, where the gaze is set, where the self is presented. The submission of the face is therefore the submission of the aim. The tradition of the glosses makes the following-action explicit. The face surrenders, and the limbs follow in the good of words and deeds. The reward clause then opens the second half of the rule: the reward is with the Lord, stored at the level of the ownership rather than at the counters of the world. The reversal of the exclusive claim is total. The entry was never the property of a party. The entry is the property of the surrender and the deed, and both are available at every address. A passport and a posture are different kinds of document. A passport is printed by a state. A posture is chosen at the door.

**FEAR AND GRIEF, BOTH ANSWERED**

The verse's closing assurance is drawn against the two sharpest pains of the afterlife: ***“And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve”***. The old tradition names each pain in its juridical place. The fear is the fear of staying eternally in the fire. The grief is the grief of missing the garden. The twin negation is the passover of the two terrors. The reward clause and the twin negation together are repeated in the passage of the shared ledger: (2:62 — **“does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve”**), and the reward's completion in the final accounting was named in this passage's own reward-discipline: (3:185 — **“And you will only receive your full reward on the Day of Judgment. Whoever is spared from the Fire”**). The good news of the same reward was offered to the working believer at the gates of the garden: (2:25 — **“Give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to those who believe and do good that they will have Gardens under”**). The rule of the admission and the promises of its reward are therefore one continuous policy. Submit the face. Work the good. Collect at the settlement.

**THE RULE READ BACK TO THE READER**

The theology at the counter of this verse is the passage's answer to every exclusive-entry sign ever printed. The sign says: our address, our membership, our name. The rule says: the face and the deed. The exclusivity claim has no exhibit in the books. The admission rule is printed in the plainest terms of the books, and it is printed twice. For any reader who has sat through the argument of the exclusive claim at work or at home or in the rows of a sanctuary, the rule at hand is the document to hold up. The claim is about who belongs to whom. The rule is about who has submitted what. That is the jurisdiction the verse restores, and it restores it with one line of the admission policy. No membership card is named. The surrender and the deed are the only credentials the passage reads. The credentials are also the only ones the settlement will cash. Every other card is printed at a desk with no window at the settlement. The verse keeps the window and the policy in one line.

---

## Verse 2:113

> The Jews say, “The Christians have nothing to stand on” and the Christians say, “The Jews have nothing to stand on,” although both recite the Scriptures. And those ˹pagans˺ who have no knowledge say the same ˹about people of faith˺. Surely Allah will judge between them on the Day of Judgment regarding their dispute

**THE CROSS-DISQUALIFICATION**

The passage then widens the lens on the exclusive claims to show the parties disqualifying each other: ***“The Jews say, “The Christians have nothing to stand on” and the Christians say, “The Jews have nothing to stand on,” ”***. The old gloss gives each verdict its venue. The Jews of Medina say the Christians follow nothing as a religion from God, and there is no true religion except Judaism. The Christians of Najrān say the same of the Jews, and there is no true religion except Christianity. The two verdicts land in the same grave. Each party buries the other's claim while standing on its own. The reason the geometry matters is that the two claims cannot both stand. The geometry of the passage is worth naming. Two exclusive claims that annihilate each other are not two truths in tension. The reason the third voice matters is that it shows the claim traveling downhill, which means the verse is diagnosing a temperament rather than a doctrine. They are two unproven notes failing at the same counter.

**THE BOOKS THEY SHARE**

The verse's next clause is the quietest and the deadliest: ***“ although both recite the Scriptures”***. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the clause its weight. Both are readers of the book. The reading is the indictment. The transmitted gloss traces the mutual recognition inside the two volumes themselves. In the scripture of the Jews there is the confirmation of the prophet who came after Moses. In the scripture of the Christians there is the confirmation of Moses before. The shelves each party stands on therefore carry the refutation of the other's exclusivity and the admission of the shared line. The passage of the shared recognition has already been quoted in this surah's family image: (2:146 — **“Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺ as they recognize their own children.”**). The knowing is in both rooms. The cross-disqualification is performed anyway. Reading and reciting are not the same verb. Reading lets the book address the reader. Reciting lets the reader parade the book.

**THE THIRD PARTY OF IGNORANCE**

The verse then folds a third voice into the exchange: ***“And those ˹pagans˺ who have no knowledge say the same ˹about people of faith˺.”***. The claim of the knowing has become the claim of the knowing-nothing. The unlettered party of the city picked up the same exclusive grammar without even the books to recite. The development is the verse's warning about how the claim travels. It starts as doctrine in a committee. It ends as a slogan in the street. The judgment reserved for the whole exchange is then attached to the ownership of the judgment: the arbiter is the one whose freedom of decision has been the passage's standing survey: (2:253 — **“if Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another. But Allah does what He wills”**). The verdict on the reciprocal disqualifications is therefore booked above all three parties. The arguments are filed here below. The finding arrives from the desk of the owner.

**THE ARGUMENT THAT PREEMPTS THE JUDGMENT**

For the modern reader, the scene is a complete map of every trialogue in which the communities recite and nobody reads. The verdicts cancel. The books confirm. The street amplifies. The verse's answer is to defer the finding to the day of the finding and to mark the pre-judgment as the error it is. A party that disqualifies the other's book while its own book confirms the other's lineage has tried to sit in the chair reserved for the ownership. The passage keeps the chair empty on purpose. For any household or forum where the same cross-verdicts are pronounced every year, the discipline of the empty chair is the medicine. Recite less. Read more. Leave the finding to the finder. The books have carried their confirmations for centuries across the same shelves. The reciprocal silencing has never once moved a syllable of either page. What travels forward is the claim that one committee can clear the docket of the day of the finding. The verse answers that travel with its own geometry. Two cancelled verdicts leave one chair, and the chair is not on the road between the two houses. It is at the end of the road where the owner of both houses receives the case whole. The books will speak at that hearing. The verdicts of the street will not. The docket is therefore kept by the owner of the shelves, and the shelves have outlasted every committee that ever tried to move them.

---

## Verse 2:114

> Who does more wrong than those who prevent Allah’s Name from being mentioned in His places of worship and strive to destroy them? Such people have no right to enter these places except with fear. For them is disgrace in this world, and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter

**THE GATEKEEPERS OF THE NAMES**

The passage now files the worst case of the whole campaign: ***“Who does more wrong than those who prevent Allah’s Name from being mentioned in His places of worship and strive to destroy them? ”***. The question is the passage's rhetorical maximum. Nothing exceeds the deed at hand. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the case its history-book face. The reference is to the ruler of the Byzantines, Tātūs, who destroyed Jerusalem. The same gloss records the manner of the profanation: carrion thrown into the sanctuary, the call to prayer stifled, the declaring of the oneness made a crime in its own house. The received tradition preserves the second reading of the case alongside the first. The verse was revealed to inform of the Byzantine destruction of the holy house, and it was also read as covering the idolaters' barring of the messenger from Mecca. The two readings agree on the anatomy. The gatekeepers of the names are the worst offenders in the passage's own scale.

**TATUS AND THE CARRION**

The historical case deserves its own look, because the deed it records is the deed the verse is measuring. A conquering power takes a city and then works on its house of worship. The name is removed from the walls. The carrion is thrown in to make the floor unclean for prayer. The endowments are cut. The received record notes how long the ruin lasted until the Muslims recovered the city and restored the house to its work. The effect of the ruling is to weigh the function of the house above its walls, which means the silenced mention is the deeper ruin. The judgment of the passage on the deed is the judgment of a building code written in the ownership of the names. The houses are the places where the name is mentioned. The preventer of the mention is therefore the arsonist of the function, not merely the occupant of the address. A damaged building and a silenced house are losses of different orders. The building can be repaired in a season. The silenced house needs the name returned to the tongue. The covenant judgment of the tie-breakers fits the deed without alteration: (2:27 — **“those who violate Allah’s covenant after it has been affirmed, break whatever ˹ties˺ Allah has ordered to be maintained,”**). The destroying of the houses is the breaking of the ties in mortar.

**THE HOUSES AND THEIR RIGHTS**

The verse then legislates the standing of the houses: ***“Such people have no right to enter these places except with fear.”***, and the penalty stands on both sides of the settlement: ***“For them is disgrace in this world, and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter”***. The received tradition of the passage widens the protection to the whole estate. The mosques of the world stand in one respect. The sanctity of the two sanctuaries and the mosque of the prophet is the sanctity of every mosque where the name is mentioned. The destruction the verse condemns is therefore never local news. The fire clause of the penalty is written in the passage of the refusers without variation: (2:81 — **“and are engrossed in sin will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever”**), and the order that the houses were built to keep is the order the corrupters reverse: (2:11 — **“When they are told, “Do not spread corruption in the land,” they reply, “We are only peace-makers!””**). The house of the name is the land at its most ordered. The defiler of the house spreads the corruption at its source.

**THE HOUSES AROUND THE READER**

The case at hand reaches past the history-books into the ordinary estate of every reader. The houses of the name are not only the famous addresses. They are the rooms where the name is mentioned at home, the circles where the book is read at work, the quiet corners of a neighborhood mosque whose roof nobody budgets for. The verse's question stays open across the estate. The verse's question names the one who silences the mention and unmakes the house as the worst case on the scale. The preventer of the mention is the worst case on the passage's own scale because the mention is the function of the whole address. The place stands for the name. The name does not stand for the place. The reader who keeps that order keeps the building code of the passage, and the code holds in this world's estate exactly as it will hold at the settlement of the next. Let the name be mentioned. Let the house stand.

---

## Verse 2:115

> To Allah belong the east and the west, so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah. Surely Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing

**THE COMPASS THAT RELAXES**

The unit that answers the worship-house cases returns to the question of direction itself: ***“To Allah belong the east and the west, so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah.”***. The tradition behind the verse gives it two occasions, and both are worth holding. The Jews had criticized the change of the prayer-direction. And a group of companions had prayed while traveling at night without knowing which way the direction lay. The transmission from Ikrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, places those travelers at the center of the scene. The verse to them is a relaxation, not a repeal. The east and the west are named as the entire earth's two handles, the pair of directions that between them stand for the whole. The ownership of both handles is then read as the permission the travelers needed. Their prayer faced the pleasure of the one who owns every face's turning.

**A DIRECTION THAT SURVIVES THE TRAVEL**

The design of the rule deserves its own look, because a rule that survives the road is a rule built for human life. The reason the relaxation can exist is that the ownership of the direction never sat in the servant's hands. What follows is a rule that survives every road and every night. The house stands with its wall. The traveler moves without one. The verse keeps both situations inside one ownership clause. The face turns as commanded, and where the command cannot fix the wall, the owner of the walls takes the face as it comes. The gloss of the received text takes the clause in exactly this key: whithersoever you turn your faces in prayer by his command, there is the face of God, the direction of prayer in his pleasure. The logic at work is the logic of the previous unit's building code. The houses stand for the name. The name owns the ground the houses stand on. So when the ground itself turns under a traveler's feet, the name has not moved.

**THE FACE AND THE COUNTENANCE**

Notice the two faces in the verse's vocabulary. There is the face the servant turns. There is the countenance the turning meets. The pairing is the passage's summary of the whole direction-question. The servant is responsible for the turning as commanded. The reception belongs to the owner of the east and west. The ownership of the compass has been settled in the answer to the foolish of the people: (2:142 — **“˹O Prophet,˺ “The east and west belong ˹only˺ to Allah. He guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.””**). The sustaining behind the ownership is the sustaining of the keeper who never sleeps: (2:255 — **“All-Sustaining. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.”**). The two verses of the book stand as the survey lines of the present verse. The same pairing governs the ownership surveys that have run through the passage since the abrogation unit. The schedule of the law moves as the lawgiver directs, and the lawgiver's ground includes every road the law will ever be kept on. The travelers of the first occasion therefore teach the standing rule to every later journey. Keep the command where the command is clear. Where the road takes the clarity away, the owner of the road keeps the prayer. The relaxation is thus a door built for the weather of real travel. The hinge is the ownership. The critics can stand at the hinge all day without closing the door.

**THE CLAUSE AFTER THE HOUSE CASES**

The placement of this relaxation directly after the worship-house verses is deliberate. The houses were defended as the homes of the mention itself. The verse now widens the mention beyond the house's walls. The name is mentioned on the road. The name is mentioned in the dark. The east and west belong to the same owner the houses belong to, and the mention travels on the owner's ground without a permit from the critics. The received record of the occasion shows the critics doing exactly what the passage has catalogued. A change in the schedule is treated as a defect in the authority. The verse answers by locating the authority over the compass itself. The critics own neither needle. The traveler prays. The owner receives. That is the geometry of the relaxation, and it holds wherever the journey goes.

---

## Verse 2:116

> They say, “Allah has offspring.” Glory be to Him! In fact, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth—all are subject to His Will

**THE SON-CLAIM IN THREE MOUTHS**

The passage now answers the theology that the scripture parties had carried into the argument: ***“They say, “Allah has offspring.” Glory be to Him! ”***. Ibn ʿAbbās names the claim in each of its historical mouths. The Jews said it of Ezra. The Christians said it of the Messiah. The polytheists of the city said it of the angels, the daughters they assigned. The claim therefore arrives in the passage wearing three sets of clothes at once, and the verse answers the wardrobe rather than the outfit. The exclamation in the middle of the sentence is the verdict before the argument. Glory be to him.
