The distance between the claim and the majesty is measured in the exclamation itself, and the measurement is infinite.

**GLORY AS THE VERDICT**

The argument then lands in one line of estate law: ***“In fact, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth—all are subject to His Wi”***. The companion's reading turns the ownership into the servitude of the whole estate. Whatever is in the heavens and the earth are his servants, linked to him by the bond of servitude. The second tradition notes the grammar of the inclusion. The little word that gathers all things is chosen precisely to leave nothing outside the estate. The reasoning is then plain enough to state as a syllogism. The owner of the whole estate is served by the whole estate. A son of the owner would stand inside the estate as one of the served. The claim arriving from all three mouths therefore fails on its own paperwork. The sovereignty and the sonship cannot both be registered at the same desk. The verse of the oneness that the whole book keeps in view is the verse the claim collides with: (2:255 — **“Allah! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him, the Ever-Living,”**). The living that needs no successor is the living that takes no child.

**THE SUBJECTED UNIVERSE**

The closing clause of the verse is the survey of the whole estate under one will: ***“—all are subject to His Wil”***. The subjection is total and it is personal. The heavens are subject. The earth is subject. The claim of the three mouths is answered by the register of the three realms. The passage has used this form of answer before, against the slander of the prophet and the envy of the wishers. Locate the ownership. The slander runs out of standing. For the doctrine of the son-claim the answer is therefore not a quarrel with any one sect's wording. The answer is the estate. The register lists the whole creation on one side of the ledger. The claim of the offspring asks the ledger to add a line that the ownership cannot sign. The verse closes the registry and the exclamation closes the verse. Glory be to him. The registrar's office belongs to the owner alone, and no committee of the three mouths holds a pen at that desk.

**THE COUNCIL AND THE REGISTRY**

The three claims of the three mouths are documented at the level of the book's own report as well. The scripture party's version names Ezra in one chair and the Messiah in the other, and the sentence the passage reports is the sentence the council of the claim has always passed: (9:30 — **“The Jews say, “Ezra is the son of Allah,” while the Christians say,”**). The second half of the report names the other chair: (9:30 — **““The Messiah is the son of Allah.” Such are their baseless assertions,”**). The passage of the estate answers the council before the council rises. Also within the heavens and earth's ownership, the registry was opened and the servants were counted, and the seat of the sonship was found empty. What the three mouths call a household, the register calls an estate. The difference is not a matter of taste. The household assumes an owner with a successor. The estate assumes an owner with servants. The register in this verse lists servants alone, and the counting of the servants is the argument. The council of the claim never adjourns, because the claim is cheap to reprint. The registry closes after one reading. That asymmetry is the passage's final mercy to the argument.

---

## Verse 2:117

> ˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens and the earth! When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, “Be!” And it is

**THE ORIGIN WITH NO PRECEDENT**

The answer to the son-claim then moves from the estate to the act of originating: ***“˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens and the earth! ”***. The tradition from Ibn ʿAbbās gives the originating its plainest description. He originated them when they were nothing before. The received tradition adds the precision of the Arabic. The making here is a making without any exemplary precedent. Nothing stood before the heavens and the earth to copy. Nothing stood beside them to assist. The claim of the previous verse imagined a household with an heir. The originating answers the household with the workshop that has no family business. The estate came into the register by being spoken into it. The reason the decree is narrated in one word is that the workshop needs no apparatus, which means the son-claim is answered by the absence of a family business.

**THE DECREE OF TWO SYLLABLES**

The verse then narrates the method of the workshop: ***“ When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, “Be!” And it is”***. Ibn ʿAbbās turns the illustration to the exact case the son-claim had been built on. When he wants to create a child without a father, like the Messiah, he says to it only: be. The parallel in the tradition is older than the Messiah and larger than him. Adam was created without a father or a mother. The claim had treated a birth without a father as the proof of a divine sonship. The verse treats it as a Tuesday in the workshop. The decree of the two syllables is documented at the level of the whole creation in the verse of the command: (36:82 — **“All it takes, when He wills something ˹to be˺, is simply to say to it: “Be!” And it is”**). The same power to bring back what has gone is recorded in the passage of the restoration: (30:50 — **“Surely That ˹same God˺ can raise the dead. For He is Most Capable of everything”**). The operating word of the workshop is therefore one word, used at the beginning and at the return.

**THE VARIANT THAT WITNESSES THE GRAMMAR**

The tradition of the glosses preserves a small reading-variant at the verse's close, and the detail is worth its own sentence in the record. The responding verb is read in two ways, one settling into the indicative and one hanging in the subjunctive after the command. The variant is the kind of detail the scholars of the reading have always kept, and its presence in the record is itself instructive. The workshop's speech is so exact that even its grammatical shadows are inventoried. The variant does not change the doctrine. It deepens the impression of the precision. The point of the variant is the precision of the record itself. A claim that would rearrange the estate deserves an answer given in the grammar of the estate.

**THREE REASONS THE CLAIM COLLAPSES**

The unit's answer to the son-claim now stands on three legs, and the passage has hammered each one. What follows from the three legs is the collapse of the whole anatomy of the claim. First the estate. All that is in the heavens and the earth serves the owner. Second the method. The creating is done by decree, without household, without precedent. Third the exclamation. The glory is the distance the claim cannot cross. The tradition of the passage adds the rational frame to the three. The assertions are absurd on their own ground before the revelation ever speaks. For the reader of the bookshelf where the three claims still circulate, the verse is the workshop tour. Ask how the estate is owned. Ask how the matter is decreed. The claim answers its own question when the two answers stand side by side. The owner of the decree has no need of an heir to keep the shop. The shop keeps itself by the word that keeps everything. The tour of the bench is therefore the answer the passage keeps in circulation. The estate register stands at the door. The decree stands at the bench. The exclamation stands at the roof. The three together are the whole answer to the three mouths. A doctrine that would add a fourth station to the workshop must first produce that station in the register. The register is closed. The word remains. The workshop answer stands at that closed door with its three stations staffed. Nothing in the claim of the three mouths survives the tour. The tour is short on purpose. The doctrine is one question deep. The benches were never crowded. The word was always enough.

---

## Verse 2:118

> Those who have no knowledge say, “If only Allah would speak to us or a sign would come to us!” The same was said by those who came before. Their hearts are all alike. Indeed, We have made the signs clear for people of sure faith

**TWO REQUESTS, ONE TEMPERAMENT**

The passage then hands the whole case of the refusers its portrait: ***“Those who have no knowledge say, “If only Allah would speak to us or a sign would come to us!” ”***. The two requests are the temperaments of the same refusal. Ibn ʿAbbās hears the speakers as the Jews asking for direct speech and for a confirming sign, with the promise hiding behind the request: then we would surely believe. The attribution of the speakers in the sources runs both ways, and the spread is itself a finding. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, al-Rabīʿ b. Anas, Qatādah, and al-Suddī hear the statement as the statement of the Arab disbelievers. The speakers named in one reading and the speakers named in the other are separated by a peninsula and a library. The verse has an answer for the separation, and the answer is the next clause.

**THE HEARTS THAT MATCH**

The portrait closes with the line that completes the portrait: ***“The same was said by those who came before”***. The likeness-clause follows as the verse's verdict on the whole exchange: ***“Their hearts are all alike. Indeed, We have made the signs clear for people of sure faith”***. The reason the census-word matters is that it moves the problem from the evidence to the receiving organ. The companion's tradition compresses the likeness into one stroke: their words and their hearts are the same. The likeness is the verse's jurisprudence of temperament. A demand framed as inquiry and a demand framed as mockery are the same demand when the receiving heart is sealed against the answer. The likeness has been described in this surah at the level of the organ itself: (2:18 — **“They are ˹wilfully˺ deaf, dumb, and blind, so they will never return ˹to the Right Path˺”**). The storm of the metaphor was drawn in the same passage's image-table: (2:20 — **“It is as if the lightning were about to snatch away their sight. Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light,”**). The corruption that matches across the two readings is the corruption the covenant-passages already itemized: (2:75 — **“then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it”**). The request for one more sign is therefore filed under the temperament rather than under the evidence.

**THE EVIDENCE THE REQUESTS REJECT**

Notice the closing clause of the verse in its full force: the signs have been made clear for a people who know. The clarity is not the missing piece of the exchange. The requests arrive after the clarity. The glosses of the passage describe the demands as the devices of a malevolence that has run out of arguments and taken up scheduling instead. If the sign is one century late, the demand will be made in the next century. The modern reader watches the same two requests circulate in every comment section that asks for a demonstration before it will read a document. The sign has been sent. The document is open. The temperament is the variable. The verse's census counts the hearts, not the signs, and the census is why the passage can promise the clarity to the knowing while the requests continue their rounds.

**THE AMBIGUITY THAT SERVES THE PORTRAIT**

The double attribution in the tradition is worth keeping rather than resolving, because the portrait is bigger than any one party. The verse says their hearts are all alike. The likeness is then demonstrated by the sources themselves. Two committees of historians name two different sets of speakers for the same sentence, and the sentence survives both attributions unchanged. The claim of the request is portable. That is the point. It traveled from the old communities to the new city without losing a syllable. The portrait also explains the address of the clarity clause. The knowing people are not the ones making the requests. The requests come from the temperament. The clarity is delivered to the temperament's opposite. The exchange is therefore not an auction of signs. It is a census of hearts with the signs as the constant. The census runs in every generation, and the census-word in the verse is the one verdict the two committees share. Alike. The request for the sign is the sign that the temperament has closed. The porters of the request keep moving it between the cities. The census stays at one number. The verse keeps both facts in view at once, the movement of the request and the stillness of the count.

---

## Verse 2:119

> We have surely sent you with the truth ˹O Prophet˺ as a deliverer of good news and a warner. And you will not be accountable for the residents of the Hellfire

**THE COMMISSION, FULLY WRITTEN**

The passage then hands the messenger his own case-file: ***“We have surely sent you with the truth ˹O Prophet˺ as a deliverer of good news and a warner.”***. Ibn ʿAbbās unpacks the file by its three clauses. The sending is with the truth, which is the book and the declaration of the oneness. The good news is the promise of the garden for the believers. The warning is the warning of the fire against those who disbelieve. The commission is therefore complete at the level of both its message and its audience. The truth names the cargo. The good news and the warning name the two destinations the cargo separates. The version of the commission that names its audience by their response is recorded in the passage of the guidance-bearers: (27:2 — **“˹It is˺ a guide and good news for the believers”**). The carrier of the truth is a courier, and the courier's route runs between two addresses.

**THE ACCOUNTABILITY CLAUSE**

The file's next line is the relief of the office: ***“ And you will not be accountable for the residents of the Hellfire”***. The old gloss hears the line twice. In one reading it is not befitting that he should ask about the dwellers of the fire. In the other, the line is the prohibition of asking forgiveness for them. The received gloss states the underlying doctrine in its plainest form: his responsibility is only to deliver the message. The reading tradition then preserves the variant of the verb, one reading carried as the passive of the asking and the other as the imperative of the prohibition. The reason the accountability clause exists is that the office of delivery has a boundary, which means the courier's grief has an edge. The variant agrees with the doctrine from two directions. The point of the variant is that the boundary is documented two ways. The office is delivery. The verdict is not in the courier's bag. The address-list of the fire is drawn in the passage of the refusers without variation: (2:81 — **“and are engrossed in sin will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever”**). The residents of that home are the residents the commission will not answer for. The courier's books close at the delivery.

**THE DESCRIPTION ASKED OF THE EARLIER SCRIBE**

The case-file of the commission carries one more exhibit in the received record, and the chain of the exhibit is worth naming. The report of the description asked of ʿAbdullāh b. ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ comes through ʿAṭāʾ b. Yasar, and the transmission is recorded by Aḥmad. The old scribe read the seal of the description from the pages he guarded, the prophet whose coming the Torah had named. The companion's report of the sealed description is the one al-Bukhārī alone preserved in his book. The exhibit does exactly the work the commission needs. The truth of the sending was documented before the sending arrived. The warner and the bringer of good news had been on the earlier shelves with both titles written.

**THE CONSOLATION AFTER THE REFUSAL**

The placement of the file at this point in the passage is its own kindness. The preceding verse had shown the refusers in full temperament, the hearts alike, the requests on their rounds. The received record of the passage reads the present verse as consolation for the sadness of the messenger at the incorrigible. The thought that any soul would persist in denial weighed on him, and the file answers the weight. The truth has been sent. The good news has been opened. The warning has been sounded. The residuum of the refusal belongs to the court of the fire, and the courier of the passage does not carry that case. What follows from the boundary is the consolation the file was written to deliver. The office is therefore relieved of the one burden it was never assigned. The audience owns its response. The response does not own the messenger.

**THE ROUTE AND THE TWO ADDRESSES**

The whole unit is best read as a route with two termini. The courier leaves the owner's desk with the truth in the bag. One address opens to the good news. The other is filed under the warning. The route is walked every day the commission stands. The packages are delivered by tongue and by book and by the patience that continues after the refusal. The reader who meets the courier on the route meets the commission's full sentence. Sent with the truth. Good news and warning. Accountable to the sender. The three clauses are the courier's standing orders, and the orders have never been revised. The route stays open. The addresses stay real. The books close at the sender's desk where the case-file began.

---

## Verse 2:120

> Never will the Jews or Christians be pleased with you, until you follow their faith. Say, “Allah’s guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance.” And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, there would be none to protect or help you against Allah

**THE PLEASING THAT NEVER COMES**

The passage closes the unit with a fact of social physics: ***“Never will the Jews or Christians be pleased with you, until you follow their faith.”***. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the parties their addresses again. The Jews of Medina and the Christians of Najrān stand behind the plural. The same gloss gives the following its concrete content: their religion and their direction of prayer. The pleasing is therefore not asking for a better argument or a kinder sentence. The pleasing asks for the surrender of the religion and the compass both. The received record of the passage reads the refusal beneath the pleasing as pride. Each group believes its own religion is superior, and the belief is not listening for a reply. The pleasing is the door-prize of the conversion, and the conversion is the only ticket the counter sells. The reason the pleasing never comes is that its price is the surrender of the creed, which means the counter is closed before the negotiation begins.

**THE ONLY GUIDANCE**

The reply is the passage's shortest creed: ***“ Say, “Allah’s guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance.””***. Qatādah's gloss on the line expands the creed into its three dimensions. The guidance is the straight, the perfect, and the comprehensive religion. Straight in its direction, perfect in its measure, comprehensive in its address. The creed is worth holding beside the pleasing of the first clause. The pleasing wants a faith approved by a committee. The guidance is a light approved by its owner. The two approvals cannot share a desk. The companion-clause of the creed has been spoken in the passage of the submitted faces: (2:256 — **“Let there be no compulsion in religion, for the truth stands out clearly from falsehood. So whoever renounces false gods”**), and its completion names the grip that the guided take: (2:256 — **“and believes in Allah has certainly grasped the firmest, unfailing hand-hold. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing”**). The creed is therefore not a slogan of the sect. It is the description of the hand-hold.

**FOLLOWING AFTER KNOWLEDGE**

The verse's closing warning is priced like the trade-verse of the earlier passage: ***“if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, there would be none to protect or help you against All”***. The transmission from Ibn ʿAbbās names the knowledge in its two forms, the knowledge of the oneness and the knowledge of the proof in the books. The tradition of the glosses notes the oath built into the Arabic of the conditional. The following is hypothetical, and the warning is certain. The knowledge that has arrived is the knowledge the whole passage has been itemizing. The recognition of the named prophet is documented on the shelf of each party: (2:146 — **“Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺ as they recognize their own children.”**). The knowledge is therefore not the missing exhibit of this trial. The knowledge is the evidence the pleasing asks the defendant to burn.

**THE COUNTER THAT SELLS ONE TICKET**

The full unit is the passage's closing price-tag on every courtship of approval. The pleasing is offered at one price. The creed is held at another. The warning invoices the difference. The pride beneath the pleasing is pride in a possession that was never owned. The guidance beneath the creed is a light that was always owned and lent. For the reader of any century standing at the counter of the pleasing, the verse is the ledger card. The pleasing of the committee is not receivable at the settlement. The hand-hold is. The knowledge has come. The following is optional. The protection clause is what the following would cancel. The ledger card is worth keeping in the wallet of the passage. The pleasing invoices the creed. The creed invoices nothing. The warning closes the account of the following. Between the three lines any offer of approval can be priced, and the price-tag is older than the merchandise. The merchandise never changed. The counter at the pleasing sells the same ticket it sold at Najrān and Medina. The guidance counter sells the same light it has always sold. Two counters, two tickets, one settlement. Between the ticket of the pleasing and the ticket of the guidance, the passage keeps one counter open, and the keeper of that counter has never once asked a committee for its stamp.

---

## Verse 2:121

> Those We have given the Book follow it as it should be followed. It is they who ˹truly˺ believe in it. As for those who reject it, it is they who are the losers

**THE FOLLOWING THAT COUNTS**

The verse opens on a class of readers. It grades their reading. ***“Those We have given the Book follow it”*** ***“as it should be followed. It is they who ˹truly˺ believe in it.”*** The gift is not in dispute. These people already hold the Book. The whole weight of the sentence therefore falls on the manner of the following. A reading can be syllables moving over a tongue. It can still fail to be the real thing. Which means a walking and a holding fall apart from each other here. In Ibn ʿAbbās's own gloss the proper following is *"the Book, and acting upon it and following it"*, then *"belief in me and in my mission."* The reading has a destination. It was always walking toward a man. The parallel verse names the failure that makes this rare (62:5 — **“The example of those who were entrusted with ˹observing˺ the Torah but failed to do so,”**). The entrustment came. The following did not.

**THE WITNESSES OF THE FAVOUR**

The tradition about who the verse means runs on names. The names are worth the space. In the transmission of Ibn ʿAbbās: *"Those who were given the Book and follow it as it should be followed — they are the believers from among the People of the Book: ʿAbdullāh b. Salām, Asad b. Zurārah, Thaʿlabah b. Sāʿid, Sallām b. Mishkam and their companions; and the ones who believed with them from among the People of the Book, and every believer in Muhammad ﷺ from his Companions and his community, up to the Day of Resurrection."* The list is not a library roll. It is a cohort of witnesses. They read and then signed the reading with their lives. The reason the same gloss ends on the mission is plain. The following announces a face. An earlier generation is named at the head of the group: ʿAbdullāh b. Salām and Asad b. Zurārah walked first. So the chain runs through the school of revelation itself. The Book. The following. The face the following was addressed to. The difference between owning a text and walking its way is exactly what this verse grades.

**THE LOSERS' SIDE OF THE LEDGER**

The verse closes both cases in one line. ***“As for those who reject it, it is they who are the losers”***. Qatādah fixes the losing in its precise form: *"the losers are the losers against themselves."* The parallel closes on the same side of the ledger (62:5 — **“For Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people”**). The losing is not an accident that befalls a reader. It is a verdict that follows a refusal. Notice what the verse does not say. The rejecters do not lose their books. They lose themselves. The books stay in their hands as the evidence that was once on the table. The report of Ibn ʿAbbās places the horizon of the sentence at the Day of Resurrection. The ledger does not close inside the lifetime of the claim. The reading a person lives remains attached to that person. Everything else gets redistributed. For a reader today the same grading runs over any inherited scripture. The test of a reading is not its tone of reverence. It is the belief and the follow-through. The loser here is not the person who reads little. It is the person whose reading never becomes a walked way. The two outcomes sit in one class of people. The difference between them is made entirely by what the reading does when it lands. The grading is public and it is personal at once. A reader can carry the Book for a lifetime. The carrying is not the following. The following walks where the Book walks. It believes where the Book points. It signs the reading with the life. The witnesses of the favour did exactly this. Their names stay in the verse's shadow. Their deeds bring them into the light. The difference is small on paper. It is total on the Day. The point of the whole passage is therefore practical. Read to walk. Read to believe. Read to sign. The losers lose themselves because the reading never left the shelf. The winners are the ones whose reading grew legs. That is the whole ledger of the verse.

---

## Verse 2:122

> O Children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you and how I honoured you above the others

**THE FAVOUR TO BE REMEMBERED**

The verse turns the appeal from a crowd to a class. ***“O Children of Israel!”*** ***“Remember My favours upon you”*** ***“and how I honoured you above the others”***. Favours plural. Honoured singular. The address keeps its family name. The parallel passage states the same honour in its active form (2:47 — **“O Children of Israel! Remember ˹all˺ the favours I granted you and how I honoured you above the others”**). In Ibn ʿAbbās's account the remembering has a date and a face: *"When they came out from Egypt, there was no human being in the world more honoured by Allah than the Children of Israel, until they worshipped the calf."* The honour is past tense twice over. So the verse is not offering a promotion. It is reading back a receipt. The command to remember is a command to audit an account already settled in the reader's favour. The address keeps its family form because the favour did come in a family line. The verse never pretends otherwise. The choosing is even stated in its own historical shape (44:32 — **“And indeed, We chose the Israelites knowingly above the others”**).

**THE DELIVERANCE IN THE MEMORY**

The honour being remembered is concrete. The crossing is concrete. The rescue is concrete. Gratitude in this verse is given a history rather than a mood. That is why the Quran can command a remembering at all. The remembering has an object. The object is a night of rescue and a morning of honour. Ibn ʿAbbās's account keeps the two turning points of the story in one frame. The honour held. Then the calf arrived. Both points turn on the same hinge. One is the remembering this verse commands. The other is the worshipping that replaced it. A favour remembered and a favour merely inherited are different things. An inherited favour is a story one tells. A remembered favour is an account one stands in. For the modern reader the logic holds without adjustment. A community that cannot name its favours will not recognise its debts. This age is fluent at accumulation. It is illiterate at gratitude. The verse's remedy is old. Name the favour. Name the favourer. Let the honour order the life that follows.

**THE ORDER OF THE MEMORY**

The imperative is the whole engine of the verse. Remember. A favour delivered is not automatically a favour held. Memory here is an act of maintenance. The maintenance is what keeps the honour from becoming a museum piece. What follows is that the children of the favour are addressed, not the makers of it. The generation being called to remember inherited the crossing without having carried it. The report from Ibn ʿAbbās marks where the honour held and where it broke. The two points share a hinge. Remembering on one side. A calf on the other. The difference is stark and it is the verse's own. To remember the favours is to stand where the honour puts you. To forget them is to stand in the crowd that asks for a calf. The honour sits above the others because the measure of the honour is the measure of the responsibility on top of it. That responsibility never localises. Neither does the obligation. The memory is the favour's last form. It is also the only form the reader can still refuse. The command has a target and the target is a memory. Not a monument. Not a festival. A memory that reorders the week. The honour above the others was never a decoration to display. It was a duty to carry. The carrying looks like obedience. It looks like gratitude that changes behaviour. The family of the favour learned both sides of this. The remembering held them. Then the forgetting undid them. One calf is enough to tell the whole story. For the reader now the same story has a quiet form. A favour named is a favour kept. A favour unnamed is a favour already leaving. The verse puts the naming in the imperative voice because the leaving is so slow no one feels it go. Remember. The word is small. The work of it fills a life. The honour stands above the others so that the responsibility can be seen from a distance. The distance is exactly where the forgetting begins.

---

## Verse 2:123

> And guard yourselves against the Day when no soul will be of any help to another. No ransom will be taken, no intercession accepted, and no help will be given

**THE DAY OF NO EXCHANGES**

The verse turns the address a second time. ***“And guard yourselves against the Day”***. The occasion is named in the next breath: ***“when no soul will be of any help to another.”*** The report of Ibn ʿAbbās is direct about the span. The verse was revealed about everyone up to the Day of Resurrection. The address keeps its historical audience. The meaning leaves the address behind. It settles on every soul that will ever be audited. So the Day here is not an event on a family calendar. It is the name of the accounting itself. Mujāhid reads the opening as the guarding of one's own Day. The discipline is the one the book's caller teaches those who call morning and evening. The reason the guarding comes first is simple. The accounting will be exact whether or not anyone prepared for it. The effect is a Day named by its refusals. The refusals are one refusal wearing three coats. Nothing moves between the accounts.

**THREE REFUSALS IN ONE BREATH**

The verse names the refusals one by one. First, the refusal of help. No help passes from soul to soul. Second, the refusal of price: ***“No ransom will be taken, no intercession accepted”***. The parallel address states the same block in its own shape (2:48 — **“Guard yourselves against the Day on which no soul will be of help to another. No intercession will be accepted,”**). Third, the refusal of every remaining remedy: ***“and no help will be given”***. The block is total. The parallel of the ransom states it harder still (2:48 — **“no ransom taken, and no help will be given”**). In the record of Ibn Abī Ḥātim the report of Ibn ʿAbbās marks the verse as running to the end of the days. No generation folds into another's account. Every ordinary hope of the guilty closes in one line. No borrowed merit. No rigged verdict. No adjournment. The difference between this accounting and the world's courts is not severity. It is completeness. The kindness and the severity of the verse are the same statement read twice. The wronged are also on this ledger. The swiftness finally serves them.

**THE ACCOUNT THAT STANDS ALONE**

The verse closes where it opened. The guarding is personal because the accounting is personal. Not the family's earning. Not the crowd's. The horizon note from Ibn ʿAbbās makes the same point from the other direction. The verse runs to the Day of Resurrection precisely so that no one can hide inside a generation. The Day is neither collective nor negotiable. There is a strange privacy about the end. The nearest people to a person on that Day are the very people the verse just named. The only currency is what the hands and hearts have actually made. For the modern reader this age offers many soft ledgers. Reputations. Narratives. The comfort of being on the right side of history. The verse answers all of them with one accounting shape. The earned stays with the earner. The reader is being taught to stand alone on the account now. The standing is still cheap. The openings for making are still open. The reason the verse keeps returning to the Day is that the remembering is the preparation. The account stands alone. The getting ready happens here. The guarding has a shape and the shape is attention. Attention to the Day named in the first line. Attention to the refusals named in the middle. Attention to the account named at the end. The soul learns to stand alone early. Then the standing at the end costs nothing. That is the wisdom of the verse's order. The guard is worn now. The account is opened later. Between the two lies the only stretch of time the person controls. The earned remains. The given-back remains. Everything else in the sentence is subtraction. No help. No ransom. No intercession. The subtraction is not cruelty. It is clarity. The courts of the world blur the ledger with favours and faces. This court does neither. The reason the verse can promise no injustice on the Day is that the Day has no back rooms. The ruling is public. The paying is exact. The mindfulness named at the opening is the only currency that gains value before the account is opened. Spend it now.

---

## Verse 2:124

> ˹Remember˺ when Abraham was tested by his Lord with ˹certain˺ commandments, which he fulfilled. Allah said, “I will certainly make you into a role model for the people.” Abraham asked, “What about my offspring?” Allah replied, “My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers.”

**THE TEST THAT MADE THE MODEL**

The verse gives the account a face. ***“˹Remember˺ when Abraham was tested by his Lord with ˹certain˺ commandments”*** ***“which he fulfilled.”*** In the counting of Ibn ʿAbbās the commandments are ten. Everything the Prophet ﷺ suffered in his message, Abraham suffered before him. The verse does not say Abraham was honoured and then tested. It says the honour was built out of the tests kept. So the model here is not a natural greatness that happened to obey. It is an obedience graded in real events and passed. The reason the tester is named as his Lord matters. The tests came from the same hand that would give the title. The title is therefore a response to the keeping. Each commandment is a moment where the fulfilling could have failed. None did. The effect is a life that reads like a series of kept decisions. The tradition around the House carries the same instruction. The people are told to take Abraham as their pattern. His example is what the community recites and follows. The parallel portrait states the pattern plainly (16:120 — **“Indeed, Abraham was a model of excellence: devoted to Allah, ˹perfectly˺ upright—not a polytheist—”**).

**TEN COMMANDS IN TWO GROUPS**

The ten are not listed here. The tradition sorts them into two groups of five. The sorting is its own teaching. The transmission from Ibn ʿAbbās gives the shape of the first five. The test of hunger. The test of the desert and what the traveller carried. The test of the two journeys of the infant. The test of the two sacrifices. The test of the fire. The second five fall on the side of the face and the body. The shaving of the head. The letters of the revealed chapter of Abraham. The touch. The heart. The smile. The two groups cover the whole of a person. Provisions and routes. Family and sacrifice. Head and heart and face. The difference between a biography and a model is exactly the counting. The verse counts the commandments kept so the fulfilling can be seen decision by decision. The reason the tradition bothers to count is that the number never came from one glowing night. The keeping was a life.

**THE MODEL AND THE OFFSPRING**

The verse hands down the title the tests earned. ***“Allah said, “I will certainly make you into a role model”*** ***“for the people.”*** The father's question arrives at once: ***“Abraham asked, “What about my offspring?””*** The answer is one of the coldest and kindest lines in the passage: ***“Allah replied, “My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers.””*** The leadership is not passed by blood. It is passed by the keeping. The covenant ties the offspring to fulfilled commandments. So the title is earned into a lineage rather than poured into one. In the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās the model reaches the prophets of this community and the followers who keep to the path the trials carved. What follows is that the model is approachable. The test sets are given. The fulfilments are given. The human incidents along the way are given. The choosing of Abraham becomes a choosing anyone can walk toward. For the modern reader this age admires outcomes and forgets tests. The verse corrects the order. The tests make the outcomes. The chain runs from the fire to the furthest believer. The reason the verse can promise a role model for the people is that the model was made of kept commandments first. The revealed instruction still names the same faith to follow (16:123 — **“Then We revealed to you ˹O Prophet, saying˺: “Follow the faith of Abraham, the upright, who was not one of the polytheists.””**). The tests were public and private in turn. Hunger in the desert. A son on the altar. A fire that turned to safety. The record does not flatter the model. It shows him being graded. The reason the tradition counts the tests is that counting makes the model honest. Ten kept decisions are not one lucky night. The covenant then narrows the family line to the keepers. Blood does not pass the title. Obedience does. The father heard the news about his son and smiled. The smile is one of the tests. It is the smallest one and the hardest. So the model walks toward the reader without a pedestal. He walks on kept ground. The reader today can count the tests in an ordinary week. The count is rarely ten. It is rarely zero. The difference between the two counts is the difference between the model and the crowd.

---

## Verse 2:125

> And ˹remember˺ when We made the Sacred House a centre and a sanctuary for the people ˹saying˺, “˹You may˺ take the standing-place of Abraham as a site of prayer.” And We entrusted Abraham and Ishmael to purify My House for those who circle it, who meditate in it, and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺

**THE HOUSE AS CENTRE**

The verse gives the House two jobs in one breath. ***“And ˹remember˺ when We made the Sacred House a centre”*** ***“and a sanctuary for the people ˹saying˺, “˹You may˺ take the standing-place of Abraham”*** ***“as a site of prayer.””*** A centre gathers. A sanctuary protects. The parallel chapter states the same design in its social form (22:26 — **“And ˹remember˺ when We assigned to Abraham the site of the House, ˹saying,˺ “Do not associate anything with Me ˹in worship˺”**). The other passage names the centre's own character (3:96 — **“Surely the first House ˹of worship˺ established for humanity is the one at Bakkah—a blessed sanctuary and a guide for ˹all˺ people”**). Through Ibn Jurayj from ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn ʿAbbās defines the bond God Himself takes with the site: *"Allah's ʿAhd is His command."* The founding was made before the founding party arrived. So the centrality is not a city's achievement. It is a decree the city serves. The reason the sanctuary can sit in the same line is that the decree carries its own protection.

**THE SANCTUARY'S CONTRACT**

The standing-place command arrives as architecture and ethic at once. The verse then converts the site into a contract with a crowd. ***“And We entrusted Abraham”*** ***“and Ishmael to purify My House”*** ***“for those who circle it”*** ***“who meditate in it”*** ***“and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺”***. Mujāhid reads the purifying in its first object: *"Purify it from the idols."* Qatādah reads the meditating as the staying. Al-Rabīʿ b. Anas names the committing at the House and the visiting of it. A House defined by its users' postures is a different thing from a monument. The monument wants the visitor to stand back. The centre wants the visitor to move, stay, and kneel. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk adds the shaving of the head to the picture of those who enter. The contract even reaches the hair of the one who arrives. The sanctuary clause is not merely religious either. The killer of a soul there is warded off from the House. The same peace that holds the birds of the Ḥaram holds the person who walks in with clean hands.

**THE ENTRUSTED PAIR**

The command is addressed to two names at once. The pair is the point. Abraham and Ishmael are entrusted to purify the House for crowds that do not yet exist. The entrustment names the users before the users arrive. Through ʿAṭāʾ the defining of the House and its people stands as God's own ʿAhd. So the pair's work is the working-out of a covenant. It is not the design of a family. What follows is that the standing-place is not a relic to admire. It is a method to take up. The one who takes it as a site of prayer joins the set of postures the House was purified for. The modern reader may travel to the House once or never in a lifetime. The contract still reaches the one who reads it. The purifying entrusted here is the same purifying the opening of this surah asked of the heart. For the people of this age the sanctuary's ethic travels as far as the crowd does. What is sacred in the House is the peace the House exists to keep. The reason Abraham and Ishmael appear together is that the work needed two hands and two biographies. The House is a centre because someone purified it. The reader inherits the purifying as much as the House. The decree arrives before the builders and outlasts them. That is what makes the House a centre rather than a landmark. A landmark is dated. A centre is decreed. The sanctuary's rules follow the decree like a shadow. No blood. No prey. No injustice. The rules are not suggestions pinned to a wall. They are the sanctuary in practice. The purifying commanded to the pair is therefore ongoing work. Every generation of guests arrives with new idols to clear. Some are stone. Some are schedules. The circling, the staying, the bowing and the prostrating are the forms the cleaning takes. The entrustment named two builders because the work was never meant to die with one. The reader who lives far away still receives the contract. Keep the heart's House clean. Walk the ethics of the sanctuary in the household. The peace the House exists to keep is portable. It travels in the behaviour of the ones who read about it.

---

## Verse 2:126

> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord, make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure and provide fruits to its people—those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day.” He answered, “As for those who disbelieve, I will let them enjoy themselves for a little while, then I will condemn them to the torment of the Fire. What an evil destination!”

**THE PRAYER FOR THE CITY**

The verse moves from the House to the city that holds it. ***“And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord, make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure”*** ***“and provide fruits to its people”*** ***“those among them who believe in Allah”*** ***“and the Last Day.” He answered, “As”***. The prayer is for the city in its double life. The settled and the passing through. In the record of Ibn ʿAbbās the prayer is answered in the city's own stones. The place was made a sanctuary in which no human blood is shed. No injustice is done to anyone. No prey is hunted. The provision arrived the same way. Itinerants came from as far as Syria into a valley that had held no vegetation or water. The reason the prayer starts with security is simple. The city's value is the safety of the lives inside it. The first gift Abraham asks for is not splendour. It is peace. The House was made a sanctuary before this prayer. The prayer asks the sanctuary to cover the households as well.

**AN ANSWER IN TWO HALVES**

The prayer's second limb is aimed. The fruits are explicitly for those who believe in the Last Day. The answer splits the crowd in one breath. ***“for those who disbelieve, I will let them enjoy themselves”*** ***“for a little while”***. The disbeliever's share is measured. The believer's share is not capped in the verse's own wording. In the gloss of Ibn ʿAbbās the provision has a double object. The city is to be fed in its earth and fed in its faith. The effect is an answer that refuses to bless a peace leaving the theology untouched. The city is secure. Its people are fed. The feeding is aimed at the believing. The same sentence that says yes to the city says a counted yes to the wrong belief's party. The difference between Abraham's two sentences is the whole theology of the passage. The first asks for the city's goods. The second asks for the city's hearts.

**THE RESPITE AND THE DESTINATION**

The verse closes the disbeliever's branch in two moves. Enjoyment first. Fire second. ***“then I will condemn them to the torment of the Fire. What an evil destination!””*** The parallel prayer of the patriarch states the city's security in its own shape (14:35 — **“˹Remember˺ when Abraham prayed, “My Lord! Make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure,”**). The same prayer reaches past the city to the household's altars (14:35 — **“and keep me and my children away from the worship of idols”**). The respite is real. The destination is real. The two do not cancel each other. The closing line does the work of a compass. What an evil destination the fire is. How measured the enjoyment that precedes it. What follows is that the reader is asked to pray the way Abraham did. For the city's security. For the people's goods. For the belief that makes the goods a blessing. For the modern reader the prayer is a template this age keeps mislaying. It asks for safety and provision and faith in one breath. The destination closes the verse because the prayer was always about where the city is going. Even the old proverb about the fathers runs through the same theology. The sins belong to the sinners. The families are not charged with them. Inheritance sits outside the verse's claim. It speaks only of sins. The city receives security first and fruit second. The order matters. Lives before produce. Peace before plenty. The prayer then aims the fruit at the believing. The answer separates the branches without apology. The enjoyment of the disbeliever is timed. The fire after it is named. The destination does the accounting the respite delays. Abraham's prayer is therefore a double petition. Save the city. Save the hearts. The modern reader can pray the same petition over any town. The petition asks for streets without fear and tables without idols. The provision that arrives without belief is the respite's own category. It is measured. It runs out. The evil destination at the verse's end is the second half of the answer. It is not an afterthought. It is the horizon the provision sits inside. The prayer for the city is answered in full. The full answer includes the fire.

---

## Verse 2:127

> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael, ˹both praying,˺ “Our Lord! Accept ˹this˺ from us. You are indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**THE RAISING OF THE FOUNDATION**

The verse's verb is the whole architecture. ***“And ˹remember˺ when Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael”***. Raised, not laid. As if the work were being lifted into its use rather than merely set down. The pair's prayer runs under the building: ***“˹both praying,˺ “Our Lord!”*** ***“Accept ˹this˺ from us. You are”*** ***“indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing”***. In the chains that carry the verses of the prophets, Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the recital of the prophets is this. Abraham and Ishmael raised the foundation and prayed while the raising continued. The House is built twice then. Once in stone. Once in the prayer said over the stone. The verse counts the prayer as part of the construction. It is not decoration. The reason the verse can say with Ishmael in one breath is that the raising needed two biographies. The father's and the son's. Both were already on the site. Every later builder of the House builds on top of a sentence spoken while the work was going up. The parallel chapter states the entrustment beside the assigning (22:26 — **“and purify My House for those who circle ˹the Ka’bah˺, stand ˹in prayer˺, and bow and prostrate themselves”**).

**THE ACCEPTANCE-PRAYER**

The prayer at the foundation is short and exact. Accept this from us. The completion names the two attributes that make accepting possible. The ear that receives the prayer. The knowledge that knows the hands behind it. For Ibn ʿAbbās the prayer is the practice of the prophets themselves. The standing-place of Abraham was taken as a site of prayer. The prayer of acceptance was said over the work. The effect is a theology of effort. The pair build the building and hand it over in the same breath. The accepting is not their department. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk's gloss on the city's origin runs in the same direction. The House's matter is the Lord's matter. The builders raise. The Lord hears. The difference between a project and an act of worship is exactly this sentence. The project ends when the stone is set. The act of worship ends when the acceptance is asked for. The reason the two names close the prayer is that the work will be judged. The ear misses nothing. The knowledge cannot be argued with.

**HEARING AND KNOWING AT THE SITE**

The verse ends on two names. Both are site-names in this context. The All-Hearing hears the prayer spoken over the foundation. The All-Knowing knows the hands that raised it and the hearts that raised with the hands. The record of Ibn ʿAbbās leaves the pair's prayer answered by the same two names that heard it. So hearing and knowing at the House are not abstract attributes. They are the working conditions of the building. Every later circumambulator walks inside a prayer that was heard. For the modern reader the same two names travel beyond the site. The work a person raises in any city is raised before an ear and a knowledge named at the first foundation. This age builds loudly and asks acceptance rarely. The verse shows the order the builders used. Raise. Then ask. Then trust the names. The effect of the closing titles is a construction site that is also a prayer room. The reason the verse stops on the two names is that the House was built to be heard in. The parallel prayer of the family shows where the asking leads (14:37 — **“so that they may establish prayer. So make the hearts of ˹believing˺ people incline towards them and provide them with fruits,”**). The hands lift the stones. The hearts lift the acceptance. The verse keeps both movements in one scene. A building that is prayed over is different from a building that is only built. The prayer is the second foundation. It holds the first one up. The two names at the close are the working conditions of the site. An ear for the asking. A knowledge for the hands. Every later builder inherits the conditions along with the stones. The construction site becomes a prayer room by the words said above it. The reader who builds anything in any city can follow the same order. Raise the work. Ask for the accepting. Trust the names. The order is short enough to memorise. The practice of it is a lifetime. The foundation of the House was a prayer. The prayer is still doing its work.

---

## Verse 2:128

> Our Lord! Make us both ˹fully˺ submit to You and from our descendants a nation that will submit to you. Show us our rituals, and turn to us in grace. You are truly the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful

**THE SUBMISSION-PRAYER**

The pair's second prayer asks for the religion itself. ***“Our Lord! Make us both ˹fully˺ submit to You”*** ***“and from our descendants a nation”*** ***“that will submit to you. Show us our rituals”***. Two submissions are requested at once. The father's and the family's. In the report of Ibn ʿAbbās, Abraham and Ishmael prayed it together while raising the House. The verse treats submission as a gift to be requested. It is not a temperament to be discovered. The first phrase is the whole theology. Make us. The submitting is made in the one who receives it. The reason the prayer reaches past the two names to a nation is that the House was never built for a private devotion. It is a station for whoever comes after the builders. The descendants clause turns the construction into a request for a future congregation. The parallel passage of the family states the settling in its human form (14:37 — **“Our Lord! I have settled some of my offspring in a barren valley, near Your Sacred House, our Lord,”**).

**THE RITUALS TO BE SHOWN**

The prayer's second half asks for the rites themselves as a teaching. ***“and turn to us in grace. You are truly the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful”***. The report of Ibn ʿAbbās defines the rituals that were to be shown. The stoning of the pillars. The standing at ʿArafah. The rapid walking between Ṣafā and Marwah. The throwing of the pebbles. Through Ibn Jurayj the stayer's own station joins the picture. The one staying for worship is the one in retreat. The rituals include the staying. The effect of the prayer is that the rituals are requested as revelation. They are not invented as culture. The builder of the House asks to be taught how the House is used. A rite remembered and a rite shown are different things. One is a custom. The other is a teaching. Qatādah and al-Rabīʿ b. Anas read the staying and the visiting as the acts of the one who commits himself at the House and comes to it. The prayer covers the resident and the traveller. The reason the rituals need showing is that the submission asked for in the first half has to walk. The walking has a pattern. The pattern is part of the answer to the prayer. The parallel closes on the hope of the grateful (14:37 — **“so perhaps they will be thankful”**).

**THE TURNING IN GRACE**

The verse ends where every sincere request ends. On the turning one. The accepting is named at the close of the prayer that asked to be turned toward. In the report of Ibn ʿAbbās the pair's prayer is answered in the very names that close it. The accepting and the mercy are the two handles the builders hold. The rituals and the turning are asked for in the same breath for a reason. The rituals are the body of the repentance. The repentance is the soul of the rituals. For the modern reader the closing title is the most portable line in the passage. Whatever has been built or broken, the accepting is still being named at the end of the prayer. This age is fluent in self-improvement. It is mute about repentance. The verse keeps the second word in the pair's own vocabulary. The builders of the House are thus shown as people who needed turning. They are not finished saints. The reason the verse closes on mercy rather than stone is that the stone was only ever the visible half. The requested nation is made of people who ask to be shown the rituals. That asking is already a submission. The father wanted the submitting made in the children. The making happens through the showing. The rituals then walk the submission through the body. The feet circle. The knees bow. The forehead touches the ground. The turning closes the sequence with mercy. The pair prayed for the turning because the rituals need it. A ritual without repentance becomes a routine. A repentance without ritual becomes a mood. The verse asks for both in one breath. The breath is the pattern of the House. Submit. Be shown. Turn. The modern reader can run the pattern anywhere. The pattern does not require the stones. It requires the same asking. The builders of the House asked for a nation. The nation is made of askers. The mercy named at the close is the answer already given.

---

## Verse 2:129

> Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger who will recite to them Your revelations, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed, You ˹alone˺ are the Almighty, All-Wise.”

**THE MESSENGER PRAYED FOR**

The verse puts a name-less request in the builders' mouths. ***“Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger”***. From them. From the valley's own households. And to them. Back into the same households. In the answering of Ibn ʿAbbās each phrase finds its man. The raising is Muhammad ﷺ, the one who prayed at the standing-place of Abraham and settled the House. The reciting of the revelations is his reciting of the book. The teaching of the Book and the wisdom is his teaching of the book and of the rulings and the law. The point lands quickly. The prayer of the builders includes the school the building will host. The House and the curriculum were commissioned in the same sentence. The request is plural in both directions because the mercy of the teaching runs along family lines. The parallel verse states the same commission from the sender's side (2:151 — **“Since We have sent you a messenger from among yourselves—reciting to you Our revelations, purifying you, teaching you the Book and wisdom,”**). The messenger's work is named before the messenger is named.

**FOUR VERBS OF THE TEACHING**

The commission has four verbs and the tradition keeps them in order. Recite. Teach the Book. Teach the wisdom. Purify. ***“who will recite to them Your revelations, teach them the Book”*** ***“and wisdom, and purify them.”*** In the transmission of Ibn ʿAbbās the reciting reaches its distance. The truth sounded across the Hijaz and the lands with the mission of Muhammad ﷺ. The rest of the commission stayed in the households the prayer was made for. The same gloss leaves the cleaning to the heart itself. The purifying is the work of the teaching on the one who receives it. Four verbs together define a school. Reading. Ruling. Shaping. Cleansing. The difference between information and revelation is exactly the fourth verb. A messenger who only recites delivers sounds. A messenger who purifies delivers people. The reason wisdom sits beside the Book is that the reading needs a ruling mind to become practice. What follows is that the prayer's answer is not a scripture dropped from the sky. It is a teacher raised from the family and set among the people of the house. The believers' own verse names the raising as their favour (3:164 — **“Indeed, Allah has done the believers a ˹great˺ favour by raising a messenger from among them—reciting to them His revelations, purifying them,”**).

**THE PRAYER'S ANSWER**

The verse closes the commission with the names that make it reliable. ***“Indeed, You ˹alone˺ are the Almighty, All-Wise.””*** The Almighty makes the raising certain. The All-Wise places the raising where it belongs. Ibn ʿAbbās's account puts the son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib at the place where Abraham and Ishmael had prayed. The prayer was answered in his mouth and his mission. The builders' request and the sender's promise meet in one figure. The closing names hold both halves of the meeting. The power that raised the messenger. The wisdom that taught him what to teach. For the modern reader the commission still describes the only school the House was built to host. A recitation read aloud. A book explained. A wisdom that judges. A purity that lands in the chest. This age has many teachers and few purifiers. The verse keeps the fourth verb in the curriculum. The effect of the ending is a prayer answered but not finished. The commission runs until the reciting stops. The reason the verse closes on the two names is that the school needed a power behind it and a wisdom inside it. The commission outlives the commission's first audience. The messenger died. The reciting did not. The teaching moved from the valley to the world. The purifying moved with it. Four verbs still describe the school. Nothing has been added. Nothing has been taken away. The reading aloud still opens the work. The explaining still follows the reading. The wisdom still judges the practice. The cleaning still lands in the chest. A modern reader can test any religious school by the four verbs. Where the reciting stops, the school is closed. Where the purifying stops, the school is decoration. The commission's return address is still in force. Raised from among them. Sent back to them. The teaching runs in both directions. The prayer of the builders was answered in a person. The person left a curriculum. The curriculum is still taking students. The two names behind the commission still hold. The power raises. The wisdom places. The school continues.

---

## Verse 2:130

> And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool! We certainly chose him in this life, and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous

**REJECTION AS SELF-DEGRADATION**

The verse answers the standing question with a counter-question. ***“And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool!”***. The rejection is self-degradation in the verse's own grammar. The one who rejects the faith of Abraham does not ascend out of the family. He walks out of the raised footing the faith gives. The parallel passage states the witness in its first shape (60:4 — **“You already have an excellent example in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people,”**). In Ibn ʿAbbās's definition the patriarch's standing has a name of its own: *"Khalīl, i.e. a friend."* The faith of Abraham is not a mood. It is a relationship. The friend of the Merciful. The one who rejects it rejects the standing the relationship gives. So the verse's word fool is a measuring word. The rejection is a loss of footing before it is a loss of doctrine. The reason the verse does not name the rejecters by tribe is that foolishness is portable. The faith is the fixed point.

**THE CHOOSING THAT NEVER ENDS**

The verse's answer is a choosing in two tenses. ***“We certainly chose him in this life”*** ***“and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous”***. Through al-Kalbī, the report of Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the monuments of the old world inside the same frame. The houses and pillars and palaces of ʿĀd were built in the land. The one who passed like the passing of the wind took the whole of it. The measuring word says he did not attain so much as a foothold. The choosing runs through the same whole life. The friend of the Merciful. The chosen one. The one whose house was chosen before him and whose place was made a sanctuary. The choosing in this world and the placing in the next are one decision read across two horizons. The reason the verse can promise the Hereafter in the same breath as the choosing is that the choosing is a covenant. It is not a compliment. The other passage names the patriarch as the one who followed the way (37:83 — **“And indeed, one of those who followed his way was Abraham”**).

**THE CREED THAT HAS A FACE**

The faith of Abraham is named as a creed with a person inside it. The person is the proof. In the definition of Ibn ʿAbbās the friend and the chosen one are the same man at different stages of one life. The creed is not a list of propositions with a biography attached. It is a biography that carries the propositions on its back. For the modern reader the difference matters. This age is comfortable with ideas and suspicious of lives. The verse puts the life first. What follows is that the faith of Abraham is something a reader can walk into. The walking was done before the reader arrived. The parallel of the family's prayer shows the pattern. The building. The asking. The submitting. The showing of the rituals. The reason the verse keeps returning to the name of Abraham is that the name works as a standard. The one who believes in him joins the path he walked. The effect of the face inside the creed is visible. The rejection named at the opening becomes a refusal of a person. It is not merely a refusal of a text.

**THE BRACKETS OF THE SURVEY**

The verse's closing tenses do the survey work. The choosing in this life is already done. The Hereafter's placing is already promised. The brackets sit around the life of the chosen one. The reader stands between them. The choosing that has happened. The placing that is promised. The faith of Abraham is the way across. For any reader now the brackets hold around every life being measured. The world's choosing is temporary. The Hereafter's is the standing one. This age reads history as a sequence of winners. The verse reads it as a sequence of keepers. The reason the verse can call the faith of Abraham the only worth answering is that the brackets were closed by the same hand that opened them. The foolishness of the rejection is that it trades the standing promise for a standing that ends. The survey is complete. The answer is older than the question.

---

## Verse 2:131

> When his Lord ordered him, “Submit ˹to My Will˺,” he responded, “I submit to the Lord of all worlds.”

**TWO WORDS OF THE SUBMISSION**

The verse is one of the shortest in the Book. It works like a hinge. ***“When his Lord ordered him”***. The command itself is barely spoken. ***““Submit ˹to My Will˺,” he responded”***. The answer arrives before the sentence ends. Ibn ʿAbbās compresses the whole theology into the reply: *"A Muslim boy to a Muslim father; he said: 'I submit to the Lord of all worlds.'"* The submission here is not a decision made after deliberation. It is an answer given while the command is still in the air. So the verse measures the religion by its response time. The reason the order names His Lord rather than a set of rules is that the command has a face. The submitting is to the face. The first half of the verse is the pattern of the Book in miniature. An order. A Lord. A person who says the word before the echo has faded. The parallel states the same word as the entry itself (6:161 — **“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Surely my Lord has guided me to the Straight Path, a perfect way, the faith of Abraham, the upright,”**).

**THE REPLY THAT NAMES THE LORD**

The answer inside the verse is a full creed in six words. ***““I submit to the Lord of all worlds.””***. In the report of Ibn ʿAbbās the response is a formula that travels. The father says it. The son says it. The saying itself is the inheritance. The same transmission names the two speakers of the scene. A Muslim boy answering a Muslim father. The verse holds two generations in one breath and gives both the same word. The effect is that the creed arrives as a reply. It does not arrive as a thesis. The Lord is named inside the submitting. The submitting knows whose it is. The difference between a surrender without a name and a submission to the Lord of the worlds is the difference between despair and religion. The reason the verse puts the response in the past tense is worth noticing. He responded. The answering has already happened. The verse reads it back as a completed act. Every later order of the same Lord is met the same way. The first word. Then the life. The summons to the community states the same word as its entry rule (2:208 — **“O believers! Enter into Islam wholeheartedly and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. Surely he is your sworn enemy”**).

**THE RELIGION WITHOUT A CENTURY**

The verse closes on a name that outlives every clock. The Lord of all worlds. The report of Ibn ʿAbbās leaves the response standing where it was given. At the moment of the order. The early tradition marks it as the first submission of the first family. The point is that the religion in this verse has no century. The order and the answer are the same in every age. The Lord of the worlds does not age out of His own lordship. For the modern reader the portability is the challenge. This age rewrites its answers by the decade and calls the rewriting maturity. The verse answers an order with a word that has never needed updating. The parallel's command closes the same circle. The first to submit. The rest told to do the same. What follows is that the submission is not a mood of surrender. It is a named act with a named Lord. The naming is what keeps the act from becoming mere resignation. The reason the verse is short is that the answer is short. The religion was never meant to take longer than the responding. The response time is the verse's quiet measurement. The order is still in the air. The answer has already landed. A faith that waits for the echo is a different faith from this one. The naming of the Lord inside the answer keeps the submission from drifting. It is not surrender to the weather. It is submitting to the Lord of all worlds. The father-son pair of the report shows the word passing across a table. The passing is the whole method of the religion. One generation says it. The next repeats it. The repeating is not laziness. It is inheritance. For a reader now the six words stand at the door of every decision. The door is the same in every century. The order arrives. The answer names the Lord. The life follows the answer. The shortness of the verse is its own instruction. Do not decorate the answer. Give it.

---

## Verse 2:132

> This was the advice of Abraham—as well as Jacob—to his children, ˹saying˺, “Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this faith; so do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission.”

**THE ADVICE OF TWO FATHERS**

The verse names the speakers before it names the speech. ***“This was the advice of Abraham”*** ***“as well as Jacob”*** ***“to his children, ˹saying˺, “Indeed, Allah has chosen”***. Two fathers. One advice. Delivered across the generations of the House. In the gloss of Ibn ʿAbbās the advice is the standing charge of the family. Abraham and Jacob both said it. Both said it at the end, when the saying costs something. The verse counts the advice as inheritance. It is not opinion. What passes from the fathers to the children in this line is a religion with a dying instruction attached. The grammar does the theology. The advice is singular even though the speakers are two. The reason both names sit on the sentence is that the path was walked twice. Once at the raising of the House. Once at the deathbed. The children of the House receive the faith with a timestamp. It is the last hour of the fathers who held it. The parallel command states the dying-instruction in its open form (3:102 — **“and do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission ˹to Him˺”**).

**THE LAST WORDS AS AN INHERITANCE**

The content of the advice is a choosing and a dying-instruction. ***“for you this faith”*** ***“so do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission.””***. For Ibn ʿAbbās the choice is the family's own measurement. The faith is chosen for the children. It is not invented by them. The father's last words hand the choosing over as property. Qatādah reads the dying-instruction as the summary of every instruction. Whatever else the fathers taught, the state of the final hour is the state they asked for. The verse turns a deathbed into a curriculum. The advice is the whole religion compressed into its last required form. The difference between advice given at leisure and advice given at death is the weight the verse puts on it. The dying man's speech is his ledger read aloud. The reason the faith is named as chosen is that the choosing settles every later argument. The children do not have to discover the religion. They only have to die in it. What follows is that the submission named here is not a mood. It is a state. The state has a name and a Lord.

**DYING IN THE STATE OF SUBMISSION**

The verse's final clause is a deadline written as a hope. Do not die except in the submission. The report of Ibn ʿAbbās leaves the fathers' words standing over the whole family. The clause completes the covenant's circle. The House is built by submitters. It is inherited by people asked to die submitters. The point is that the verse places the proof of the religion at its very end. The last breath is the exam. The advice is the exam preparation. For the modern reader the clause is comfort and instruction at once. This age hides death from view. It therefore loses the deadline that organises a life. The verse puts the deadline back at the centre of the family's speech. The verse of the last hour states the same horizon in its open form (29:57 — **“Every soul will taste death, then to Us you will ˹all˺ be returned”**). The advice of the two fathers is not nostalgia. It is logistics. The children will die. The fathers want the state ready. The reason the verse keeps both names on the charge is that two witnesses are needed for a last will. The submission is asked for as the final form of a life. The life is what the House was built to hold. The advice is singular because the faith is singular. Two fathers agree at the end of two different lives. The agreement is the inheritance. The children receive a chosen faith and a final instruction. The choosing settles what to hold. The dying-instruction settles how to end holding it. The two charges fit together like a hand and a glove. The deathbed is not a place of new ideas. It is a place of kept ones. The verse dates the advice to the last hour on purpose. The dating gives the words their weight. For the reader the weight transfers. The faith is still chosen. The hour is still coming. The state is still asked for. The advice of the fathers is therefore a standing charge. It is read again at every deathbed in the line. The charge names the faith. The charge names the state. The two names are the inheritance entire.

---

## Verse 2:133

> Or did you witness when death came to Jacob? He asked his children, “Who will you worship after my passing?” They replied, “We will ˹continue to˺ worship your God, the God of your forefathers—Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac—the One God. And to Him we ˹all˺ submit.”

**THE DEATHBED QUESTION**

The verse stages its whole theology inside one family hour. ***“Or did you witness”*** ***“when death came to Jacob?”***. The witness question works as a summons. The reader is put at the bedside before the answer is given. The father's question is the smallest creed in the passage. ***“He asked his children, “Who will you worship after my passing?””***. In the account of Ibn ʿAbbās the hour is the last test of the family line. The father does not ask about property or burial. He asks about the worship that will outlive him. The inheritance that matters is the altar. The point is that the deathbed question is a curriculum check. Every teaching of the House is compressed into the one word worship. The children are asked to answer with their mouths. What follows is that the verse treats the moment of death as the moment of maximum clarity. It is the hour when a family says what it actually holds. The reason the verse opens in the witness form is that the reader is being enrolled. Not as an audience. As a witness. The prayer of the dying prophet of the family states the same form (12:101 — **“and the earth! You are my Guardian in this world and the Hereafter. Allow me to die as one who submits”**).

**THE NAMES IN THE ANSWER**

The children's reply names its object before it gives its verb. ***“They replied, “We will ˹continue to˺ worship your God, the God of your forefathers”*** ***“Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac”***. The list is the answer's evidence. The God being named is the God of a chain. The chain is named link by link so no one can claim the worship is an innovation. From Ibn ʿAbbās the family's speech stays attached to the patriarchs themselves. The forefathers are named so that the worship has a history. The history has a family. The effect is that the reply is a legal statement as much as a devotion. The God of our forefathers is a title of continuity. The difference between a private faith and an inherited faith is exactly this naming. The private faith must introduce its god. The inherited faith names the god with three patriarchs standing behind it. The reason the list stops at Isaac is that the verse counts the line the deathbed holds. The naming is the family's way of answering with its own records open.

**THE SUBMISSION OF THE WHOLE HOUSE**

The answer ends with the verb the whole passage has walked toward. ***“the One God. And to Him we ˹all˺ submit.””***. The plural is the point. The father asked a single question. The household answered with a single word. The word is the one the first father gave when his Lord ordered him. The account of Ibn ʿAbbās leaves the scene standing as the family's public record. The deathbed question. The patriarchs named. The submission spoken in the plural so that no child stands outside the answer. The verse closes the family's theology in the exact shape the earlier verse asked for. Die in the state of submission. Let the submission be a household word. For the modern reader the scene models how a religion is passed. Not by argument at the table. By a question at the end and an answer in the plural. This age plans its estates. It rarely plans its altars. The verse keeps the altar in the last will. The effect of the scene is that the reader learns what the House was built to produce. A family that answers worship questions in one voice. The reason the verse can end on the submit word is that the submitting is what the deathbed was checking for. The prophet's own prayer closes the circle (12:101 — **“and join me with the righteous.””**). The household answers in one word because the household learned one word. The learning took a lifetime. The saying takes a second. The list of names inside the answer is the household's evidence file. The God of the forefathers is a title with records attached. Abraham. Ishmael. Isaac. The line is short and the claim is large. The claim is that worship has a genealogy. The genealogy runs through a family that answered a question the same way at the end. The submission spoken in the plural is the family's signature. No child is outside the answer. No child is outside the verb. The altar named in the question is the altar kept in the will. The scene travels past the family to any household that plans its end. The planning is the inheritance's final form. The deathbed question is still being asked. The answer is still one word. The word still has a plural.

---

## Verse 2:134

> That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done

**THE PASSED COMMUNITY**
