The verse turns from the deathbed to the ledger. ***“That was a community”*** ***“that had already gone before.”***. The sentence is a verdict and a boundary at once. The community named in the previous scene is finished. The verse closes its file before opening the reader's. In the span marked by Ibn ʿAbbās the verse covers the generations that came and went. Each with its own hour. Each with its own account. The past tense does the theology. Had already gone means their making time is over. The only open accounts are the ones still being written. So the verse teaches the reader how to hold history. With respect and without transfer. The reason the verse opens with the past community is that the reader's temptation is old. To live inside someone else's record. To claim the fathers' faith as a deposit or pay the fathers' debts as a penalty. The verse separates the files with one word. The separation is a mercy.

**TWO LEDGERS, NOT ONE**

The verse states the arithmetic plainly. ***“For them is what they earned”*** ***“and for you is what you have earned.”***. The parallel states the same earning as the whole horizon of the person (53:39 — **“and that each person will only have what they endeavoured towards”**). The reading of Ibn ʿAbbās is the closing of the collective ledger. The deeds do not migrate. The earning stays where it was made. The effect is a doubled accounting. Two ledgers. Opened at the same time. Closed at the same time. Never merged. The difference between a family name and a personal account is exactly what this verse draws. The name travels down the line. The deeds do not. The prayer of the closing passage of the Book puts the same theology in its merciful form (2:286 — **“and all evil will be to its own loss. ˹The believers pray,˺ “Our Lord! Do not punish us”**). The evil made is charged to its own maker. The charge is the same rule that keeps the good with its own earner. What follows is that the ledger's logic is symmetrical. Neither guilt nor righteousness crosses the line.

**THE DEEDS THAT DO NOT TRANSFER**

The verse closes the boundary from the other side. ***“And you will not be accountable”*** ***“for what they have done”***. The reader is freed from the past's file. The reader is confined to the present's. From Ibn ʿAbbās the family's own rule of accounts stands in the open. The fathers answer for the fathers. The children for the children. The verse protects in both directions. No one inherits another's guilt. No one spends another's righteousness. For the modern reader the two protections are equally needed. This age is fluent in inherited blame and inherited credit. The verse cancels both currencies. The effect of the boundary is that the reader stands alone before the earning. Exactly as the Day's verse promised. No help from soul to soul. What follows is that the only responsible posture toward a passed community is the one the next verse will name. Follow the faith that was right. Do not claim the faith of the dead as a substitute for the work of the living. The accountability clause closes the verse because the clause is the reader's own horizon. The deeds do not transfer. The making is yours. The boundary holds in both directions and both directions are mercy. The dead are not charged with the living's file. The living are not charged with the dead's. The two rules together make history safe to study. The studying then stops being prosecution. A passed community becomes a lesson rather than a verdict. The earning stays with the earner. The lesson stays with the learner. The verse frees the reader from the ancestor's account and confines the reader to the present one. The confinement is the freedom. One open column is lighter than a family archive. The modern reader meets the same boundary in every old argument. The argument wants to move the deeds across the line. The verse refuses. The refusal is the mercy named twice. Their earning. Your earning. The two ledgers close at the same hour. The hour does not accept transfers. The making is the only entry that counts.

---

## Verse 2:135

> The Jews and Christians each say, “Follow our faith to be ˹rightly˺ guided.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “No! We follow the faith of Abraham, the upright—who was not a polytheist.”

**THE PAIR OF INVITATIONS**

The verse stages a public argument in one line. ***“The Jews and Christians each say, “Follow our faith to be ˹rightly˺ guided.””***. Two parties. One invitation each. The claim is not disputed as an invitation. Both parties offer guidance. The claim is disputed as a claim of exclusive standing. The scene behind the verse is public and specific. The delegations of the Jews and the Christians of Najrān stood before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Each party claimed to be upon the religion of Allah. So the verse puts two house-names on the table. It prepares to answer both with one name. In the account of Ibn ʿAbbās the saying is the standing claim of the two groups. The effect of the stage direction is audible. The reader hears the claim in its polite form first. Then the answer in its blunt form. The reason the verse quotes the invitation rather than paraphrasing it is that the reply must fit the exact words on offer. The stage direction then turns the reply into a public instruction: ***“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “No!”***.

**THE ANSWER WITH A NAME IN IT**

The instruction refuses the pair and returns to a face. ***“We follow the faith of Abraham, the upright”*** ***“who was not a polytheist.””***. The parallel chapter states the same faith as the revealed instruction (16:123 — **“Then We revealed to you ˹O Prophet, saying˺: “Follow the faith of Abraham, the upright, who was not one of the polytheists.””**). The other passage names the patriarch in his exact state (3:67 — **“Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian; he submitted in all uprightness and was not a polytheist”**). For Ibn ʿAbbās the faith of Abraham is older than the two invitations. It stands as their measure. The reply does not argue with the two houses on their own ground. It resets the ground to the father of the houses. The difference between following a community and following a faith is the whole answer. The community is a later shape. The faith is the original one. What follows is that the upright one becomes the standard by which every later claim is tested. The test is simple enough to be named in one adjective.

**THE ADJECTIVE THAT IS NOT A SECT**

The verse ends on a negative description. It does more work than a title would. ***“who was not a polytheist.””***. The description carries the weight. The upright is defined by what he refused. The refusal is the first boundary of the faith. In the reading of the early authorities the uprightness is the shape of the religion before any later century named it. The adjective is portable across every age. Whoever is not a polytheist stands where Abraham stood. The standing does not require a passport from any later community. For the modern reader the verse is a lesson in answering confident invitations. Go back past both of them to the father who was neither. This age treats labels as identities. The verse treats one negative as the identity that matters. The faith of Abraham is therefore defined by a boundary. It is not defined by a brand. The reason the verse closes on the polytheist refusal is that the refusal is the one thing both invitations had quietly left out of their claims. The invitations offered a guidance. The answer names a father. The two invitations are confident and the confidence is the point. Each party arrives with a shelf of evidence. The answer does not attack the shelves. It moves the whole case to a father both parties claim. The father is older than the shelves. His faith is older than the names of the houses. The adjective at the end then does the boundary work. Not a polytheist. The negative is clean and it is portable. It fits in any century. It fits beside any bookshelf. The upright one defined himself by what he refused. The refusal was the first wall of the faith. A reader in this age can hold the same wall. The wall is not a brand. It is a boundary. The invitations can be answered without raising the voice. Name the father. Name the adjective. The two names end the meeting. The meeting began with two claims. It ends with one patriarch.

---

## Verse 2:136

> Say, ˹O believers,˺ “We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us; and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants; and what was given to Moses, Jesus, and other prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them. And to Allah we all submit.”

**THE CREED'S FULL ROLL**

The invitation is answered with an inventory. ***“Say, ˹O believers,˺ “We believe in Allah”*** ***“and what has been revealed to us”*** ***“and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob”*** ***“and his descendants”*** ***“and what was given to Moses, Jesus”***. The roll of names is deliberately crowded. The names arrive in families and in sequences. No prophet can be used as a wall against another. The parallel of the sending names what the teaching adds (2:151 — **“and teaching you what you never knew—”**). In the recitation of the believers reported by al-Bukhārī from Abū Hurayrah from Ibn ʿAbbās, the Torah stands in its own shape. In Hebrew, of course. The point of the roll is that the books are honoured in the languages they came in. The believing named in the first line expands into a history. The history is the believer's property. The reason the roll is crowded is that the religion is crowded with messengers. The honour is the roof they all share.

**THE PROPHETS WITHOUT A RANKING**

The roll's second half refuses the very thing the invitations were built on. A ranking. ***“and other prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them.”***. Qatādah names the collection behind the descendants' line. The twelve sons of Jacob. Every one of them a community in the counting. So the prophets are presented as one faculty of one teaching. They are not competitors for a single chair. The difference between honouring a prophet and ranking the prophets is exactly the distinction the verse refuses to make. The same chapter's warning names the cost of the refusal (4:136 — **“Indeed, whoever denies Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day has clearly gone far astray”**). The tradition of the books and the names leaves the roll as a statement of belief in a chain. It is not a scoreboard. The reason the verse lists the unnamed ones after the named ones is that the chain is longer than the list. Other prophets from their Lord. What follows is that the believer's creed is measured by its breadth of honour. Not by its exclusivity of name.

**THE SURRENDER AT THE END OF THE LIST**

The verse closes its inventory with the verb the deathbed used. ***“And to Allah we all submit.””***. The roll and the surrender stand in one sentence. The effect is a creed that ends where it began. In the submitting Abraham gave and Jacob's children echoed. The roll of names was never the destination. The destination is the verb at the end. The verb is plural. For the modern reader the structure is the instruction. This age collects affiliations the way the roll collects prophets. The verse says the collection must end in a surrender common to all of them. The obligation of the parallel ends in the same place. Faith in Allah and the Messenger and the books. Then the life that follows. What follows is that the believer who recites this verse has signed a document. Its final clause is a posture. The reason the verse can hold so many names without collapsing into a committee is that the names all end on the same word. The surrender is the list's conclusion. It is also its summary. The reader who believes believes in the whole faculty at once. The roll is spoken in the first person so that it can be recited rather than studied. The believing is not a report about other people. It is the community standing inside its own sentence. The names then do their quiet work. Abraham and his line. Moses and Jesus. The unnamed ones after the named ones. The roll refuses the ranking the invitations implied. Every prophet is honoured in his own tongue. Every book is honoured in its own language. The twelve sons of Jacob each stand as a community in the counting. The counting widens the creed past every later faction. The final verb then gathers the whole roll into one posture. Submit. The posture is plural because the creed is plural. A modern reader reciting the verse joins the plural. The joining is the point of the inventory. Believe in all of them. Distinguish between none of them. Submit with all of them. The roll ends where the deathbed ended.

## Verse 2:137

> So if they believe in what you believe, then they will indeed be ˹rightly˺ guided. But if they turn away, they are simply opposed ˹to the truth˺. But Allah will spare you their evil. For He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**TWO BRANCHES OF THE TEST**

The verse converts the creed of the previous passage into a test. The test has exactly two outcomes. ***“So if they believe in what you believe”*** ***“then they will indeed be ˹rightly˺ guided.”***. The condition is deliberately flat. The guidance requires no new deed. It requires only the joining of the belief already stated. In the public recitation of the believers reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim, the roll of the previous verse was spoken as the community's own confession. The test of the others is whether they will stand where the confession stands. So the verse refuses to grade belief by antiquity or sophistication. The only grade is the alignment. The reason the verse offers the two branches before it names the costs is that the reader must see the fork first. What follows is that guidance in this verse is a state. The state of being aligned with what was revealed. The alignment is offered to anyone still standing.

**THE GUIDANCE-CONDITION**

The second branch is stated without softening. ***“But if they turn away, they are simply opposed ˹to the truth˺.”***. The parallel chapter states the same opposition as a matter of settled record (3:19 — **“Certainly, Allah’s only Way is Islam. Those who were given the Scripture did not dispute ˹among themselves˺ out of mutual envy”**). The report collected by Muslim keeps the same grammar of colouring. The faith was given as a colouring. The turning away is a refusal of the colour. The effect of the verse's middle is diagnostic. The turning away is described before it is priced. The difference between an argument and an opposition is what the verse marks. An argument engages the belief. An opposition simply faces the other way. The reason the condition is stated twice in the verse's own structure is that the fork is real. The two branches never meet.

**THE SCHISM-NAMING**

The verse's third move takes the pressure off the believer. ***“But Allah will spare you their evil.”***. The parallel continues the diagnosis (3:19 — **“until knowledge came to them. Whoever denies Allah’s signs, then surely Allah is swift in reckoning”**). Qatādah reads the sparing as a standing promise. The one who holds the confession is covered. The evil of the opposition is real. It is also bounded. The effect is a strange calm in the middle of a dispute. The believer is told the outcome of the hostility before the hostility finishes. What follows is that the heat of the dispute transfers to the ledger where it belongs. The reckoning is swift. The sparing is already in effect. The reason the verse names the sparing before it closes on the two names is that the servant needs the shelter before the theology. The covering arrives first. The explanation arrives second.

**THE SUFFICIENCY THAT COVERS THE SERVANT**

The verse closes on the two names that make the promise hold. ***“For He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing”***. The ear hears the opposition's words. The knowledge knows its ends. The recitation reported by al-Bukhārī places the community's own confession in the open beside the verse. It is recited in the open. It is heard in the open. The closing names turn the sparing into a relationship rather than a policy. The servant is covered because the covering One hears and knows. For the modern reader the same structure survives every public dispute. This age argues about guidance as a branding problem. The verse answers with a fork, a diagnosis, and a shelter. The effect of the ending is that the reader stands between the two branches with the covering already named. The reason the verse ends on hearing and knowledge is that the opposition's loudest threat is that no one is listening. The promise is that the hearing is total. The knowledge never blinks. The fork in the verse is honest about its two branches. The first branch is open to anyone still standing. The second branch is described before it is priced. The opposition has a shape and the shape is a turned face. The sparing then arrives before the explanation. The servant is covered first. The theology arrives second. The two names at the close carry the covering. The ear hears the threats. The knowledge knows their ends. The dispute is therefore bounded on both sides. The believer is not asked to win it. The believer is asked to hold the confession and walk on. The opposition's evil is real and it is fenced. The fence is the sparing named in the verse's third move. A modern argument about guidance wants the believer to panic. The verse gives a fork and a shelter instead. The shelter is older than the argument. The covering name never stopped listening. The knowing never looked away. That is enough to walk with.

---

## Verse 2:138

> This is the ˹natural˺ Way of Allah. And who is better than Allah in ordaining a way? And we worship ˹none but˺ Him

**THE WAY THAT IS A COLOURING**

Against the schism-naming the passage raises a name for the religion itself. ***“This is the ˹natural˺ Way of Allah.”***. The tradition behind the word is richer than any single translation. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Mujāhid report that the sibghah is the colouring. The colouring is the religion of Allah with which Allah colours the people of Islam. In the report collected by Muslim the nature and the colouring sit in one teaching. Every child is born upon the nature. Then the colouring is laid on. So the religion here is a finish on the person. It is not an outfit over the person. The colouring goes down to the surface it colours. The reason the verse prefers the colouring image to the path image is structural. A path can be left behind. A colour cannot be peeled off without tearing. The effect is a faith that marks the person it saves.

**THE QUESTION NO ONE ELSE ANSWERS**

The verse's second line is a challenge in the form of a question. ***“And who is better than Allah in ordaining a way?”***. The question is rhetorical in the strongest sense. It names the standard and dares the opposition to name a better one. The question of Ibn ʿAbbās's reading stands over every dispute about the way. The ordaining belongs to the one who coloured the creation in the first place. The effect is that the argument of the previous passage moves to a higher court. The dispute is not between two communities. It is between every community and the ordainer. The difference between a way invented and a way ordained is the whole force of the question. What follows is that the reader measures every claimed way by its ordainer. The measuring is quick work when the ordainer is named. The reason the question sits in the middle of the passage is structural. The surrender at the end needs the ordaining at the front. The parallel chapter states the steadfastness in its imperative form (30:30 — **“So be steadfast in faith in all uprightness ˹O Prophet˺—the natural Way of Allah which”**).

**THE WORSHIP THAT FOLLOWS THE WAY**

The verse ends with the worship the colouring produces. ***“And we worship ˹none but˺ Him”***. The plural is back. The plural is the community the way has coloured. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Mujāhid keep the colouring and the worship in one image. The one coloured by the religion worships in the colour. The point is that the verse closes with the deed that proves the colouring. The deed is singular. Worship none but Him. The same passage guards the colouring from alteration (30:30 — **“He has instilled in ˹all˺ people. Let there be no change in this creation of Allah. That is the Straight Way, but”**). For the modern reader the sequence is the instruction. The way is named. The ordainer is named. The worship follows without an intervening committee. This age treats religion as a preference. The verse treats it as a colouring. The difference shows up in the last verb. The passage thus closes on worship in the plural. The deathbed scene closed on submitting in the plural. The two closes rhyme. The reason the verse ends on the worship is that the colouring is verified by what the coloured hands do. The passage closes on the width of the miss (30:30 — **“most people do not know”**). The colouring goes deeper than any uniform. It marks the surface it covers. The ordaining question then settles every dispute before it restarts. No ordainer compares. No way competes. The worship at the end is the colour made visible. The hands worship in the hue they were given. The community around the worship is the plural the verse collects. The straightness of the way is guarded from alteration. The guarding is the same decree that fixed the House. Nothing in the creation is to be remade by the created. The change is the refusal named in the previous verse. The refusal of the colour. A modern reader can test every claim of spiritual fashion by the ordaining question. Who ordained the way? The answer settles the claim in one line. The worship that follows the answer is the proof. The proof is done with hands. The miss at the end is the width of the crowd. The crowd never checks the ordainer.

---

## Verse 2:139

> Say, “Would you dispute with us about Allah, while He is our Lord and your Lord? We are accountable for our deeds and you for yours. And we are devoted to Him ˹alone˺

**THE DISPUTE PUT IN ITS PLACE**

The verse takes the argument running through the passage and reshapes it. ***“Say, “Would you dispute with us about Allah”*** ***“while He is our Lord”*** ***“and your Lord?”***. The question is not who has the better claim. It is whose Lord is in question. The answer collapses the two sides into one sovereignty. The parallel invitation states the same ground in its constructive form (3:64 — **“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O People of the Book! Let us come to common terms: that we will worship none but Allah,”**). Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Mujāhid keep the dispute inside the same frame as the colouring-verse. The way is His. The ordaining is His. The disputing is therefore conducted on His ground. So the verse does not forbid the dispute. It relocates it. Everything said must be said before the one Lord both parties already name. The reason the possessive is doubled is that the common ground is the whole court. Our Lord and your Lord. The verse is a rule of procedure as much as a creed.

**THE LEDGER OF THE DEEDS SPLIT**

The verse then settles the accounting exactly as the passed-community verse did. ***“We are accountable for our deeds”*** ***“and you for yours.”***. The splitting of the deeds is the same boundary drawn a second time. This time in the middle of a live dispute. The reading of Ibn ʿAbbās leaves the clause as the standing rule of argument. The deeds stay with their makers. The disputing cannot move them. The effect is that the argument loses its favourite weapon. The trading of ancestries. The charging of one generation's file to another. The difference between a dispute about truth and a dispute about records is what the verse marks. The truth is argued before the Lord. The records are closed per person. What follows is that the disputers learn where their energy will actually be spent. Not on moving the ledger. On filling it. The reason the verse splits the deeds in the middle of the dispute is that the split is the mercy. Everyone gets to work with what is still open.

**THE DEVOTION THAT CLOSES THE CASE**

The verse ends not on a verdict but on a posture. ***“And we are devoted to Him ˹alone˺”***. The devotion closes the case the way the submission closed the roll of names. The parallel's summons runs to the same ending (3:64 — **“that we have submitted ˹to Allah alone˺.””**). Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Mujāhid keep the colouring and the devotion in one image. The one who wears the religion's colour devotes the worship to the one who ordained the colour. The point is that the last word is not about winning the dispute. It is about the devotion that outlives it. For the modern reader the ending is the instruction this age most needs. Arguments end. The posture continues. The posture is what the ledger records. The effect of the close is that the disputers stand with their own deeds, their own Lord, and their own devotion. The three together are enough to live on. The reason the verse stops on the devotion rather than the argument is that the argument was only ever the doorway. The case closes in the posture. It does not close in the last word. The relocation of the dispute changes its temperature. The argument is no longer between enemies. It is conducted before a shared Lord. The shared Lord hears both sides in one ear. The deeds then split the case into two files. Each file has one name on it. The name is the maker's. The dispute cannot move the entries between them. The devotion at the end closes the case without a verdict. The posture outlives the argument. The argument is a doorway. The posture is the room. A modern reader arguing across a divide can follow the verse's procedure. Keep the shared Lord visible. Keep the deeds separate. Close in a posture. The procedure is old and it is undefeated. The defeated thing is the appetite for prosecution. The appetite wants the other file. The verse returns every maker to their own. The return is merciful. The devotion named last is the only part of the exchange that survives it. The survival is the point. The case is closed in worship.

---

## Verse 2:140

> Do you claim that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants were all Jews or Christians?” Say, “Who is more knowledgeable: you or Allah?” Who does more wrong than those who hide the testimony they received from Allah? And Allah is never unaware of what you do

**THE PATRIARCHS' IDENTITY CARD**

The verse names the claim in its full historical form. ***“Do you claim that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob”*** ***“and his descendants were all Jews”*** ***“or Christians?” Say, “Who is more knowledgeable”*** ***“you or Allah?””***. The roll of names is the verse's own evidence. The same names the creed listed a few verses ago now stand as witnesses against the claim. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Mujāhid read the question as the refutation of both parties at once. The patriarchs predate the two names being claimed for them. So the dispute of the previous passages is settled by chronology as well as by theology. The verse treats the claim as a paperwork error. The identity cards are dated. The dates do not work. The reason the verse lists the descendants along with the patriarchs is that the claim covers whole families. The refutation has to cover them too. The reader sees the claim measured against the calendar it invokes. The question then moves the case from identity to testimony. The testimony belongs to the one who knows what no party to the dispute can know.

**A QUESTION OF GREATER KNOWLEDGE**

The counter-question is devastating in its simplicity. Who is more knowledgeable, you or Allah? In the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās the question stays attached to the Book's own record of the patriarchs. The names are in the revelation. The revelation's author is the one being asked about. The effect is that the claim's real weakness is exposed. It is not only old. It is unauthorised. The difference between a claim of inheritance and a claim of knowledge is what the question draws. Inheritance can be argued in a family dispute. Knowledge is settled at its source. What follows is that the parties are asked to weigh their certainty against the certainty of the Book. The weighing is quick work for anyone who believes the Book has an author. The reason the question is asked in this exact form is that it leaves the disputers two options. Confess the gap. Or claim the knowledge of the Lord. The claim about the patriarchs cannot survive the second option.

**THE HIDDEN TESTIMONY**

The verse then names the act the claim required. ***“Who does more wrong than those”*** ***“who hide the testimony they received from Allah?”***. The parallel verse states the hiding in its full shape (2:159 — **“Those who hide the clear proofs and guidance that We have revealed—after We made it clear for humanity in the Book—will be”**). Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Mujāhid mark the hiding as the pivot of the whole dispute. The testimony was received. The receiving is what makes the hiding wrong. So the disagreement is a concealment problem. It is not a comprehension problem. The patriarchs were known. The knowing was kept in a drawer. The effect is that the wrong is measured by the evidence in hand. The one who hides more testimony does more wrong. What follows is that the claim of the previous verses is read back as an act of hiding. The hiding has a witness that never stops watching.

**THE AWARENESS THAT NEVER BLINKS**

The verse closes the whole passage on a name of the Lord. ***“And Allah is never unaware of what you do”***. The parallel's sentence ends on the punishment of the hiders (2:159 — **“condemned by Allah and ˹all˺ those who condemn”**). The account of Ibn ʿAbbās leaves the ending standing over every later generation of claimants. The testimony is in the Book. The Book is with the Lord. The Lord is never unaware. The point is that the closing name answers the hiding with the one thing the hiding cannot survive. Total awareness. For the modern reader the ending is the passage's final comfort and its final warning. This age hides testimony in plain sight. Behind institutions and vocabularies. The verse says the unawareness is entirely one-sided. The effect of the close is that the reader leaves the dispute with the Lord's own name as the last word. The Abraham-arc ends here because the arc was always about the testimony. The House. The faith. The roll of names. The way. The devotion. The awareness that keeps the record of every one of them. The dispute ends. The watching does not.

---

## Verse 2:141

> That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done

**A LEDGER OF TWO COLUMNS**

History closes a file here with a three-part verdict. ***“That was a community”*** ***“that had already gone before.”***. The refrain of the patriarchs returns to shut the long dispute over the direction. The people named through that dispute have finished their term. Ibn ʿAbbās's account reports the date-stamp plainly: *"a group of people who have passed away; perished."* Their making-time is over. The reading of the sentence is therefore a boundary marker rather than a boast. The verse does not celebrate the ending of a rival. It records an ending that any community can have. What follows is that history becomes safe to study. A closed file can be read without being inherited. The dispute with the People of the Book over prophets, qiblahs, and merit is now behind the community. The verse itself stands at the door of the archive and reads the label aloud. The effect of the placement is structural. Everything the previous pages established is filed under the names of people who no longer walk the street. The archive of the dispute is thereby closed to further editing.

**THE EARNED AND THE EARNED**

The second sentence splits the record into two ledgers. ***“For them is what they earned”*** ***“and for you is what you have earned.”***. Two columns. Two owners. No crossings. The reading of Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the columns strict. The earnings of the dead stay with the dead. The earnings of the living stay with the living. The point of the paired clauses is that no one inherits an account. A father's faith does not post to a son's book. A teacher's work does not post to a student's book. Each ledger is opened in its own name. The same strictness shows up at the seat of judgment itself (99:6 — **“On that Day people will proceed in separate groups to be shown ˹the consequences of˺ their deeds”**). Separate groups. Shown deeds. The ledger language of the earth's courts is taken up and perfected at the throne. The two columns are therefore not a metaphor invented by commentators. They are the accounting policy of the final court, announced in advance so that no litigant arrives surprised.

**THE VERDICT WITHOUT CROSSINGS**

The closing clause removes the last fear. ***“And you will not be accountable”*** ***“for what they have done”***. The boundary of accountability is drawn at the self. In the transmitted reading of Ibn ʿAbbās the clause comforts the Prophet against the charge of failing with the dead. He was not their keeper. Their accounts closed with their breath. The same accounting is stated in its smallest unit at the scales (99:7 — **“So whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it”**). Atom-weight. Seen. Nothing crosses between the two columns because nothing is lost inside them. For the modern reader the discipline is double-edged. It releases the living from the guilt of the dead and it loads the living with their own file. This age loves inherited praise and hates inherited blame. The verse refuses both packages. The good of the previous generation is honoured in the archive, and the present generation writes its own pages with its own hands. The verdict has no crossings. The columns stand open until they close.

**A FILE CLOSED, A FILE OPENED**

The practical force of the passage lands in the ordinary rooms where ledgers are kept. A household that studies its ancestors inherits lessons and never balances. A congregation that retells its founders inherits honour and never discipline. The verse separates the two inheritances with surgical care, and the separation is a mercy in both directions. The dead are released from the anxiety of their successors' deeds. The living are released from the credit of their predecessors' names. Every generation stands at its own counter with its own book. The reason this matters at the close of the qiblah section is structural. The community has just been re-pointed, re-sent, and re-commissioned. The temptation of the moment would have been to lean on the borrowed light of the older houses. The verse refuses the loan. The light of this community is the deed-book it writes under the new direction. For the modern reader the double release is news worth hearing twice. This age markets ancestry as identity and forgets the counter. The verse keeps the counter open and the ancestry in the archive where it belongs. The file of history is closed. The file of the present is still accepting entries.

---

## Verse 2:142

> The foolish among the people will ask, “Why did they turn away from the direction of prayer they used to face?” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “The east and west belong ˹only˺ to Allah. He guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.”

**A JEER AT THE TURN**

The jeer arrives on schedule. ***“The foolish among the people will ask, “Why did they turn away from the direction of prayer they used to face?””***. The verse names the askers before it answers them. The foolish. The lightweight of the city now files a question about sacred law. Ibn ʿAbbās ties the jeer to the moment of the change. The hearts that carried no weight treated the turn as material for mockery. The point of the naming is that the question was never a question. It was a taunt with a question mark. What follows is that the answer is pitched over the heads of the askers. The verse does not argue with the jeer. It reopens the doctrine of divine ownership instead. The effect is a hard lesson in audience selection. Some questions deserve a teacher. Others deserve a sentence. This one receives the sentence first, and the teaching rides behind it for everyone still listening. The arrangement is a mercy to the sincere of the city, who get the doctrine without having to sit through the mockery.

**THE EAST AND THE WEST**

The answer begins with geography and ends with ownership. ***“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “The east”*** ***“and west belong ˹only˺ to Allah. He guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.””***. The east and the west are the two doors of the horizon. The verse deeds both of them to one owner. The gloss of Ibn ʿAbbās marks the clause as a dismissal of the jeer's premise. No direction belongs to a people. The directions belong to the one who raised the sky over all of them. The same dismissal had already been filed against the claimants of exclusive guidance (2:120 — **“Never will the Jews or Christians be pleased with you, until you follow their faith. Say,”**). Their displeasure is scheduled. The verdict answers the claim to monopoly (2:120 — **““Allah’s guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance.” And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge”**). The guidance is His to give. The turn of a prayer-direction is His to command. The difference between a shrine and a Lord is the difference between a rented room and the owner of the street.

**A QUESTION WITH TWO AUDIENCES**

The closing sentence of the answer is a policy for the Prophet's own table. He guides whoever He wills to the straight path. The clause is mercy and warning in one line. Mercy for every convert who arrives late. Warning for every family that assumes a birthright. Ibn ʿAbbās's reading exposes the two audiences of the jeer in one glance. The foolish who asked for sport. The sincere who heard an answer. For the modern reader the scene replays whenever a practice changes in public. The lightweight asks why. The weighty ask what the owner has said. This age treats every change as a scandal and every custom as a deed of ownership. The verse corrects both habits. The horizons are leased. The guidance is granted. The straight path is the only possession worth competing for, and it is distributed by the one who holds the title to both doors of the sky.

**JEERS AS AN ADDRESS PROBLEM**

The scene also grades the way a community handles its public questions. The foolish of the verse are not people who lacked information. They are people who addressed the question to the wrong department. The question of sacred law was aimed at the Prophet's back as a taunt, and the answer was mailed over their heads to the sincere. The effect of that routing is a standing policy. Public mockery receives a doctrine. Honest inquiry receives a teacher. The reason the distinction matters is that the two audiences are usually standing in the same room. The verse trains the ear to hear which one has spoken. For the modern reader the training is urgent in the square of the platforms. This age rewards the loudest question with the largest audience and calls the exchange a debate. The verse keeps the two mail-rooms separate. The jeer is answered with ownership. The sincere question is answered with guidance. The east and the west remain the property of the one who made both horizons, and the mail of the mockery never changes his address.

---

## Verse 2:143

> And so We have made you ˹believers˺ an upright community so that you may be witnesses over humanity and that the Messenger may be a witness over you. We assigned your former direction of prayer only to distinguish those who would remain faithful to the Messenger from those who would lose faith. It was certainly a difficult test except for those ˹rightly˺ guided by Allah. And Allah would never discount your ˹previous acts of˺ faith. Surely Allah is Ever Gracious and Most Merciful to humanity

**A COMMUNITY OF THE MIDDLE**

The verse builds a standing structure out of the turn. ***“And so We have made you ˹believers˺ an upright community”***. A community is made, not merely mustered. The word is wa-saṭan. The hadith that al-Tirmidhī reports from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī takes the middle to mean just, in the sense of the best of its kind. The gloss of Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading. The middle is the balanced rank. ***“so that you may be witnesses over humanity”*** ***“and that the Messenger may be a witness over you. We assigned your former direction of prayer only to distinguish those”***. The witnesses are stacked in two layers. The community over the peoples. The Messenger over the community. What follows is that the qiblah-student now stands inside a legal structure. The direction was never only about faces. It was about testimony. The effect of the design is a chain of custody for the message itself. The parallel of the gathering-day makes the first layer concrete (4:41 — **“So how will it be when We bring a witness from every faith-community and bring you ˹O Prophet˺”**). Every community gets its witness. The middle community carries the standing witness for the rest.

**THE MARKER INSIDE THE TEST**

The verse then explains the interval that hurt. ***“who would remain faithful to the Messenger from those”*** ***“who would lose faith. It was certainly a difficult test except”*** ***“for those ˹rightly˺ guided by Allah.”***. The former direction was a marker. The reading of Ibn ʿAbbās makes the design explicit. The temporary rule sorted the hearts before the final rule arrived. Those who held their prayer behind the Messenger through the awkward months proved their attachment. Those who treated the turn as a chance to jeer showed their fracture. The point is that the test was a sorting instrument, not a punishment. It was certainly a difficult test. The verse admits the weight out loud. The guidance named as the exception is the thing that made the weight bearable. The parallel completes the witness-chain at the second layer (4:41 — **“as a witness against yours”**). The Messenger testifies that he delivered. The community testifies that it received. The marker inside the test therefore became evidence inside the trial. The awkward months did their work as a laboratory of attachment, and the results were entered into the record the moment they appeared.

**THE FAITH NEVER DISCOUNTED**

The closing mercy answers the anxious question of the graveyard. ***“And Allah would never discount your ˹previous acts of˺ faith. Surely Allah is Ever Gracious”*** ***“and Most Merciful to humanity”***. The companions who died under the former direction had prayed well and died unsure. The verse settles their account. The narration collected by al-Bukhārī puts the whole scene in one room. The first congregation that prayed toward the House was still in its bowing when the news reached another mosque. One man among them narrates the moment and reports his own words to the room: *"By Allah, I bear witness that I have offered prayer with the Prophet facing Makkah"* The bowing rows turned in place. Then the question rose about the dead. The verse answers with a policy. No sincere act is ever discounted. The grace named at the end is not a soft extra. It is the accounting standard of the whole book. For the modern reader who fears that a changed instruction erases past obedience, the promise stands. The faith was recorded when it was lived. The mercy of the examiner keeps the books from losing it.

**A TESTIMONY THAT TAKES STANDS**

The witness-structure of the verse deserves a second pass, because it organises the whole mission. A witness is not a spectator. The community is appointed to testify over humanity, which means the deeds of the community become evidence in the trial of the message. The effect of that appointment is that the middle community is on the stand at every hour. Its prayer is evidence. Its patience is evidence. Its justice in the market is evidence. The reason the former direction was used as a marker is that the trial needed exhibits before the testimony began. The faithful through the awkward months and the jeerers of the turn were entered into the record in real time. For the modern reader the appointment is sobering and energising at once. This age puts communities on trial in the press every morning. The standing was made official by the verse itself. The testimony is scheduled, the exhibits are the conduct, and the witness over the witnesses is the one who never discounts the sincere act. The stand is taken daily. The record is kept by the mercy that closes the passage.

---

## Verse 2:144

> Indeed, We see you ˹O Prophet˺ turning your face towards heaven. Now We will make you turn towards a direction ˹of prayer˺ that will please you. So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque ˹in Mecca˺—wherever you are, turn your faces towards it. Those who were given the Scripture certainly know this to be the truth from their Lord. And Allah is never unaware of what they do

**A FACE LOOKING UP**

The heaven itself was watching the picture the verse frames. ***“Indeed, We see you ˹O Prophet˺ turning your face towards heaven. Now We will make you turn towards a direction ˹of prayer˺”*** ***“that will please you.”***. The Prophet's face searched the sky for the order. The answer to the search arrives as a gift with a preference attached. A direction that will please you. Ibn ʿAbbās's account puts the longing in the Prophet's prayer across a long season. He loved the House of his father Abraham. The verse now announces the return as a granting. What follows is that the change of qiblah is framed as an answered yearning, not an arbitrary decree. The effect of the framing is intimate. The law arrives inside a relationship. The one who legislates the direction is the one who noticed the upturned face. The point of the sighting is theological. Nothing about the Prophet's heart was lost on the sky.

**TURNING TOWARD A PLACE**

The command then lands on the whole assembly. ***“So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque ˹in Mecca˺”*** ***“wherever you are, turn your faces towards it. Those”*** ***“who were given the Scripture certainly know this to be the truth from their Lord.”***. One face is turned first. Then every face follows. The singular becomes a plural inside a single sentence. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the ordering as deliberate. The Prophet turns, and the rows of the believers turn with him. Then the verse turns to the People of the Book with a startling aside. They know this address. The recognition is not a matter of debate. It is a matter of their own shelves. The awaited prophet's description and the standing of the House were already written in the material they guarded. The parallel of the House's founding places the address in its own archive (2:125 — **“And ˹remember˺ when We made the Sacred House a centre and a sanctuary for the people ˹saying˺,”**). The House was made a centre before the jeer was made. The aside about the Scripture-knowers is therefore a citation of the other side's own records.

**A LORD WHO NEVER MISSES**

The closing line holds the whole redesign under one gaze. ***“And Allah is never unaware of what they do”***. The turn of a thousand faces is not a logistics problem. It is a watched act. The gloss of Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the closing line aimed at every party in the scene. The Prophet who longed is seen. The believers who turned are seen. The scholars who recognised and stayed quiet are seen. The same custody of the House is stated in its liturgical form (2:125 — **““˹You may˺ take the standing-place of Abraham as a site of prayer.” And We entrusted Abraham and Ishmael to purify My House”**). The standing-place of Abraham is the pivot of the turn. The purification of the House is the condition of the meeting. For the modern reader the aside about the recognisers is the sobering half of the verse. Recognition without response is a documented state. This age keeps archives of the truth and departments for ignoring them. The closing gaze covers both. Nothing done at the turning is missed by the one who ordered the turn.

**A GIFT WITH A PREFERENCE**

The phrase that shapes the whole passage is the smallest one. A direction that will please you. The law of the qiblah arrives inside a relationship, and the relationship names the Prophet's own delight as part of the design. The effect of the phrasing is that obedience is not flattened into machinery. The one who commands the turn is the one who noticed the longing. The reason the detail is preserved in the verse is theological. The sky pays attention to hearts. The longing of the Prophet was seen before it was answered, and the answer was shaped to fit the longing. For the modern reader the pattern corrects a cold reading of religious law. This age separates the rule-book from the heart-book and sells both. The verse keeps them bound in one sentence. The turn is commanded. The pleasure is promised. The seeing covers the whole transaction. The direction that pleased the Prophet still gathers the faces of the world toward the house of his father, and the gaze that watched him look up has not moved away from the ones who follow.

---

## Verse 2:145

> Even if you were to bring every proof to the People of the Book, they would not accept your direction ˹of prayer˺, nor would you accept theirs; nor would any of them accept the direction ˹of prayer˺ of another. And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, then you would certainly be one of the wrongdoers

**PROOFS THAT CHANGE NO MINDS**

A policy of stubbornness receives its diagnosis. ***“Even if you were to bring every proof to the People of the Book, they would not accept your direction ˹of prayer˺”***. The verse removes the burden of proof from the Prophet's shoulders. The proofs have already done their work. The recognition of the House and the traits was filed in their own shelves long before the turn. The description of the awaited messenger was written in the material they guarded. The proof itself was acknowledged (26:197 — **“Was it not sufficient proof for the deniers that it has been recognized by the knowledgeable among the Children of Israel”**). The knowledgeable recognised. The proof was sufficient. What follows is that the refusal downstream of recognition is not an information problem. It is a posture problem. ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read the refusal here as the partisanship of the market-stall. Each party will not accept the qiblah of the other. The effect of the verse is to stop the Prophet from exhausting himself over a verdict already reached.

**THREE REFUSALS AND ONE PRICE**

The verse then stacks the refusals so the pattern is unmistakable. ***“nor would you accept theirs”*** ***“nor would any of them accept the direction ˹of prayer˺ of another.”***. Your direction is refused. Their own rival's direction is refused. The third clause shows the disease has no owner. The seal of bias sits on the heart before the argument begins. Ibn ʿAbbās marks the clause as a description of the scene rather than a command. The clause describes how the ground lies so that the planting can go where the soil is open. The point is that refusals of this kind predate the discussion. They survive every proof because they were never produced by a shortage of proofs. The difference between an honest question and a sealed verdict is the willingness to accept an answer. The sealed verdict is recognizable by its allergy to evidence. The clause therefore becomes a diagnostic tool. Watch what a claim does with proof. The posture tells the truth before the words finish. A sealed verdict announces itself by the way it handles the exhibit. The diagnostic therefore costs nothing to use and never misreports.

**KNOWLEDGE OVERRULED**

The closing conditional names the price of overriding the known. ***“And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge”*** ***“that has come to you”*** ***“then you would certainly be one of the wrongdoers”***. The knowledge has arrived. The desires remain. Following the second after the first is named as wrongdoing with no softening. The same word against the desires was filed against the claimants of exclusive guidance (2:120 — **“that has come to you, there would be none to protect or help you against Allah”**). No protector. No helper. The sentence of the wrongdoer is handed down at the end of the line. For the modern reader the conditional is a school policy and a household policy. Knowledge is given to be obeyed, not traded for the comfort of the room. The markets of direction keep their stalls open late, and every stall sells its own east. The verse forbids the trade that overrides the known. The price is named in advance. Wrongdoing. And the absence of anyone who can protect the trader from the owner of the horizons.

**WHEN THE ARGUMENT ENDS**

There is a quiet mercy hidden inside the diagnosis. Once the refusal is recognised as pre-decisional, the faithful disputant is released from the spiral of re-argument. The verse does not ask the Prophet to win the sealed verdict. It asks him to keep his own account clean and to keep the knowledge un-traded. The effect of the release is enormous in practice. Energy that would have been spent on the unmoveable is redirected toward the teachable. The reason the closing conditional is addressed to the Prophet is that he is the one most exposed to the pressure of the room. The desires of the loudest can bend a speaker even after the knowledge has arrived. The verse installs the rule against the bending. For the modern reader the diagnostic has a workday form. The committee that will not accept any direction, the forum that re-litigates settled facts, the family that refuses every proof on principle — these are the sealed verdicts of today. The verse names the posture and frees the worker to walk on. The knowledge stands. The trader stands warned. The owner of the horizons keeps the register.

---

## Verse 2:146

> Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺ as they recognize their own children. Yet a group of them hides the truth knowingly

**RECOGNITION WITH NO DOUBT**

The verse states a recognition so clear it names its own standard. ***“Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺”*** ***“as they recognize their own children.”***. The standard of certainty is the family's own certainty. A father does not need a document to know his son. The scholars of the People of the Book knew the traits of the awaited prophet with that same clarity. ʿAbdullāh b. Salām reports his own case in one line: *"I recognised him the moment I saw him as I would my own son; but my recognition of Muhammad was more intense."* The parallel verse states the same recognition in its own words (6:20 — **“Those to whom We gave the Scripture recognize him ˹to be a true prophet˺ as they recognize their own children. Those”**). The comparison is fixed across the two passages. The point of the comparison is that no ambiguity survives it. The traits were in the shelves. The man stood in front of the shelves. The matching was immediate. What follows is that the problem of the next clause is not epistemic. Everyone in the scene knows what the scene is. The comparison is therefore the verse's own way of closing the door on every later excuse of confusion.

**THE HIDING THAT IS KNOWING**

The second sentence delivers the verdict on the knowing. ***“Yet a group of them hides the truth knowingly”***. The adverb is the indictment. Knowingly. The gloss from Ibn ʿAbbās names the thing hidden as the description and the traits themselves. They guarded the pages and buried the conclusions. The same crime is named in the covenant they had already signed (3:187 — **“˹Remember, O Prophet,˺ when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture to make it known to people”**). The covenant ordered a publishing. The group chose a withholding. The effect of the adverb is that the hiding is classed as a deed rather than an oversight. An honest man can fail to see. A knowing man can only fail to act. The verse grades the second failure as the heavier crime because it was committed with the lamps already lit and the map already open. The truth was not missing from their account. It was missing from their counter.

**SHELVES THAT STILL SPEAK**

The closing application is for every generation that inherits documents. The recognition clause proves the shelves were sufficient. The hiding clause proves the shelves are not self-executing. The early commentators read the pair as a standing law of religious scholarship. The book on the shelf requires a hand at the counter. For the modern reader the two sentences bracket the whole vocation of knowledge. To recognise the truth in the sources is the first duty. To publish it with the tongue is the second. This age keeps more archives than any age before it and runs more counters that withhold. The verse shows both states in a single household. The scholars who recognised and the group that hid shared the same shelves. The difference between them was made entirely in the choosing. The shelves still speak. The hand at the counter still decides what the room hears.

**THE CLARITY STANDARD**

The family-comparison of the verse sets a standard that no courtroom can improve. A father knows his son in a crowd without a document and without a debate. The verse grants the scholars of the Scripture that level of clarity about the awaited prophet, and the granting is itself the condemnation of what followed. The hiding came after the knowing. The effect of the comparison is that the standard of excuse collapses. No one in the scene can claim that the lamps were dim. The reason the verse repeats the comparison in another passage is that the claim of ambiguity would outlive one mention. The second mention closes the exit. For the modern reader the clarity standard applies wherever a source is guarded rather than followed. The archive that knows and the hand that withholds are described here as two different moral states. This age produces more recognitions than it publishes. The verse keeps the two verbs apart and grades both. Recognition is a gift. The publication of the recognition is a debt. The debt is paid at the counter.

---

## Verse 2:147

> ˹This is˺ the truth from your Lord, so do not ever be one of those who doubt

**CERTAINTY FROM THE LORD**

A single sentence arrives to steady the whole design. ***“˹This is˺ the truth from your Lord”***. The truth is addressed to the Prophet first. The turn of the qiblah, the witnesses, the community of the middle, the recognition and the hiding — all of it stands under one label. The truth from your Lord. Mujāhid's comment keeps the line short and final. The clause is a verdict on the preceding pages. Everything filed before this sentence is now certified by the office that issued it. The certification covers the design, the marker, the mercy, and the whole preceding argument about the House. The passage does not reopen the case at this point. It signs the verdict instead. The signature itself is the teaching, because a signed argument and an open argument live different lives in the heart. What follows is that doubt loses its footing at the signature. A claim can be debated while its origin is unsettled. Once the origin is named, the debate changes shape. The effect of the naming is that the Prophet's heart is set down on solid ground before the closing instruction arrives. The truth has an address. The address is the Lord of the Prophet.

**THE COMMAND AGAINST DOUBT**

The second half of the verse is an instruction and a guardrail. ***“so do not ever be one of those who doubt”***. The wording is future-facing. Not ever. The reading of Ibn ʿAbbās places the command against the noise of the jeer and the counter-claims of the shelves. The doubt being forbidden is not the honest question. It is the doubt manufactured by the marketplace after the certification has landed. The parallel passage states the same truth from the same address in its own words (3:60 — **“This is the truth from your Lord, so do not be one of those who doubt”**). The repetition across the passages is itself the teaching. The truth from the Lord is stable enough to be stated twice in two places without wear. The difference between a question and a doubt is the posture toward the answer. The question leans in. The doubt leans away. The command guards the posture of the heart.

**PROMISES KEPT ON SCHEDULE**

The verse closes the qiblah section, and the closing ties the design to the character of God. The one who moved the direction is the one who keeps the promise. The challenge of the impatient had been raised before in the city (22:47 — **“They challenge you ˹O Prophet˺ to hasten the torment. And Allah will never fail in His promise.”**). The torment runs on the clock of the promise-keeper. The design of the qiblah runs on the same clock. For the modern reader the guardrail is aimed at the waiting season. Instructions land. Fulfilment lags. The gap between the two is the breeding ground of the forbidden doubt. This age trains the heart to expect same-day delivery of every promise. The verse trains the heart to read delay as scheduling, not absence. The truth is from your Lord. The promise belongs to the same name. The one who certified the design can be trusted with the calendar.

**THE SIGNED ARGUMENT**

The signing of the truth is what turns the whole preceding section from argument into foundation. A city had spent its months jeering at a turn, counting directions as property, and weighing prophets by market-share. The verse ends the weighing with a label and a prohibition. The label names the address of the truth. The prohibition guards the heart against the after-tremors of the jeer. The effect of the pair is a settled table on which the next section can be built. The community is about to be commissioned as witnesses and sent a curriculum. The curriculum cannot rest on a debatable turn. It rests on the truth from the Lord. The reason the prohibition is future-facing is that the doubting industry does not close with the first verdict. It reopens at every new instruction. For the modern reader the guardrail is installed exactly where the noise is loudest. Between the certified decision and the arriving fulfilment there is a corridor, and the corridor is where the forbidden doubt breeds. The verse closes the corridor with the two names. The truth is signed. The promise is kept.

---

## Verse 2:148

> Everyone turns to their own direction ˹of prayer˺. So compete with one another in doing good. Wherever you are, Allah will bring you all together ˹for judgment˺. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything

**EVERY FACE TURNS SOMEWHERE**

The verse files the whole qiblah dispute inside one observation. ***“Everyone turns to their own direction ˹of prayer˺.”***. Every party in the city has a facing. The claimants of exclusive direction are answered with a landscape. The turn is universal. The ownership of the turn is not. The comment of Ibn ʿAbbās reads the sentence as a settling of the argument. The faces will keep turning. The verse now turns the page from facing to doing. What follows is that the qiblah is recast as a starting position rather than a trophy. The point of the placement is that the dispute over directions was always a doorway. The door opens onto the street of deeds. The effect of the sentence is a demotion of the polemic. The jeerers can keep their geography. The believers are handed a race. The demotion is itself a gift, because the energy spent on the argument returns to the arms of the good where it belongs.

**A RACE WORTH ENTERING**

The command that follows is the surah's most athletic sentence. ***“So compete with one another in doing good.”***. The grammar is a summons to the front. Race one another. The good is the track. The parallel of the forgiveness-promise names the prize at the end of the track (3:133 — **“And hasten towards forgiveness from your Lord and a Paradise as vast as the heavens and the earth, prepared”**). Hasten. The verb of the race appears again in the promise. The reading of Qatādah keeps the racing here in the register of deeds rather than words. The arms of the good are the arms of the obedient. Compete in the prayer. Compete in the fasting. Compete in the charity and the patience. The same racing-heart is described where the front-runners are named (23:61 — **“it is they who race to do good deeds, always taking the lead”**). The race has lanes. The lanes are the deeds. The winning is measured by the one who owns the track.

**GATHERED BY THE CAPABLE**

The verse closes the competition with a guarantee and a name. ***“Wherever you are, Allah will bring you all together ˹for judgment˺.”*** ***“Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything”***. The gathering is certain. The scattered runners on their scattered lanes finish at one ground. The capability named at the end is the reason the certainty can be absolute. For the modern reader the two closing clauses fix the ethics of competition itself. Every race of the market ends at a boardroom of one. This age runs a thousand races and posts no finish line. The verse installs one. The good is competed in here. The gathering is administered there. The capable one handles both the track and the tape. The faces turned in one direction this season will stand on one ground in the next. The race is worth entering because the gathering is guaranteed by the name that ends the sentence.

**THE FINISH LINE INSTALLED**

The demotion of the direction-dispute at the opening of the verse is the permission slip for the race. Once the faces are free to turn, the hands are free to work. The effect of the sequence is a full re-orientation of religious energy. The argument about the map is closed so the traffic can move. The point of the gathering-clause is that the race is timed by an organiser who also holds the results. The runners do not certify their own finish. The clock of the race is held by the one who also names the medals at the entrance. The same economy of deeds is drawn in its smallest unit at the scales of the last day, and the same certainty is kept for the front-runners named elsewhere in the book. For the modern reader the finish line is the missing piece of every competing culture. This age runs endless races with the finish line edited out, and the runners discover the omission at the edge of exhaustion. The verse installs the line and posts the organiser's name above it. The good is competed in now. The gathering is administered later. The capability at the end of the sentence covers both halves of the schedule. The runners of the market and the runners of the mosque answer to the same organiser in the end.

---

## Verse 2:149

> Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. This is certainly the truth from your Lord. And Allah is never unaware of what you ˹all˺ do

**FACING THE HOUSE FROM ANYWHERE**

The command now speaks to the Prophet in his own geography. ***“Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque.”***. Wherever. The word dissolves the map. The Prophet is released from the calculation of place. The same release was already standing at the House's founding (2:125 — **“for those who circle it, who meditate in it, and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺”**). The circle of the worshippers was designed for bodies in motion. The meditating and the bowing were always portable around a fixed point. The point of the wherever is therefore a design principle rather than a concession. The centre is fixed so the edges can move. What follows is that the believer's prayer-life acquires a spine. Every location hangs on the same point. The effect of the command is felt most in travel, in exile, in the hospital room and the work site. The face has somewhere to go in every place.

**TRUTH AT THE QIBLAH**

The sentence that follows labels the whole arrangement again. ***“This is certainly the truth from your Lord.”***. The certainty lands on the direction itself. Not merely on the book that orders it. The reading of Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the label attached to the redesign. The truth from the Lord is the standing-place of Abraham, the House, and the facing from anywhere. The parallel verse had certified the same in fewer words. The certification is repeated because the scene repeats its doubts. The effect of the repetition is a double lock. The Prophet's heart is locked to the truth. The believers' map is locked to the House. The difference between a custom and a truth is the address of the one who set it. A custom can be moved by a room. A truth is moved only by its Lord. The qiblah is therefore held at the rank of truth in the plainest grammar of the passage.

**A LORD WHO SEES THE TURNING**

The closing line covers the new design with the old gaze. ***“And Allah is never unaware of what you ˹all˺ do”***. The doing includes the turning. The turning is seen wherever it happens. The same custody clause had closed the command to the Prophet himself (2:144 — **“Allah is never unaware of what they do”**). The address widens from the Prophet to the whole community. For the modern reader the portability of the facing is the verse's practical gift. The prayer of the office and the prayer of the road share the address of the prayer of the city. This age schedules its devotions around its movements. The verse schedules the movements around one point. The unawareness is excluded from the arrangement. Every face that turns is noted. Every turn taken at the edge of the map is seen at the centre. The truth stands. The gaze holds. The facing goes on wherever the servant stands.

**ONE POINT, EVERY PLACE**

The portability clause deserves its own second look, because it re-engineered the geography of devotion. Before the turn, the direction was a possession of place. After the wherever, the direction is a possession of the person. The face carries the point with it into the ship and the field and the borrowed room. The effect of the portability is that the prayer-life acquires a spine that no itinerary can bend. The truth named in the verse is the pin that holds the map together. The reason the closing gaze is attached to the portable facing is precise. The servant is most exposed to forgetfulness exactly where the map is unfamiliar. The gaze covers the exposure. The servant walking in an unfamiliar city carries the whole apparatus of the prayer inside a single intention. The point does not move when the person moves, and the gaze does not thin at the edges of the map. For the modern reader the arrangement is the answer to the oldest complaint of the busy life. This age moves its people across cities and time-zones and calls the movement progress. The verse gives the movement a fixed point and the fixed point a watched address. The House stands. The faces turn. The turning is noted in every place.

---

## Verse 2:150

> Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. And wherever you ˹believers˺ are, face towards it, so that people will have no argument against you, except the wrongdoers among them. Do not fear them; fear Me, so that I may ˹continue to˺ perfect My favour upon you and so you may be ˹rightly˺ guided

**AN ARGUMENT REMOVED**

The command repeats itself and then widens its circle. ***“Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque.”*** ***“And wherever you ˹believers˺ are, face towards it”*** ***“so that people will have no argument against you, except the wrongdoers among them. Do not fear them”***. The Prophet turns. The rows turn. The result is stated as a courtroom outcome. No argument remains. The reading of Ibn ʿAbbās names the people of this clause in the city around him. ʿAbdullāh b. Salām and the believers who stood with him were the standing answer to the claim of error. The recognition of the traits had already closed the scholarly dispute. What follows is that the qiblah itself becomes evidence. A community praying on one line across a city is a document. The point of the exceptive clause is surgical. The wrongdoers keep their argument because they were never missing an argument. They were missing a heart that accepts one. The effect of the design is that the Prophet is freed to pray rather than to litigate.

**FEAR IN THE RIGHT PLACE**

The verse then manages the fear that the argument carries. ***“fear Me, so that I may ˹continue to˺ perfect My favour upon you”***. The redirect is absolute. Do not fear them. Fear Me. The two fears cannot share one heart. The smaller fear starves when the larger one is fed. The same redirect had been issued against the prompting of the enemy in the field (3:175 — **“That ˹warning˺ was only ˹from˺ Satan, trying to prompt you to fear his followers. So do not fear them;”**). The prompting that magnifies the crowd is named at its source. The command follows the naming (3:175 — **“fear Me if you are ˹true˺ believers”**). Fear Me. The clause is the hinge of every public stand. The crowd is loud. The owner is near. The early commentators read the pairing here as a promise attached to a posture. The favour is perfected for the ones who redirect the fear. The perfection of the favour is the thing the wrongdoers' noise is trying to interrupt. The point is that fear is never removed from the human heart. It is re-addressed.

**A FAVOUR STILL BEING PERFECTED**

The closing clause carries the design into the future. ***“and so you may be ˹rightly˺ guided”***. The favour is still in progress. The guidance is its delivery method. The turn of the qiblah was one instalment. The sending of the messenger is the next. The facing of the whole community is the visible proof that the instalments are real. For the modern reader the pair of fears is the practical core of the passage. Public pressure invents fears that the heart then feeds. The verse starves the wrong fear and feeds the right one. This age calls the crowd's mood the verdict. The verse calls it noise around a verdict already entered. The favour stands at the stage of perfecting. The guidance is the road of the delivery. The one who ordered the face to turn can be trusted with the rest of the schedule.

**THE ARGUMENT THE QIBLAH REMOVES**

The courtroom clause is worth a slow read, because of what it actually deletes. The people of the city had kept an argument against the Prophet as their last reserve of leverage. The unity of the facing drains the reserve. A community praying on one line across a city is not a sect with an eccentricity. It is a document signed by the sky. The effect of the document is that the remaining complaint is exposed as the wrongdoer's private property. The exceptive clause names the owners precisely. Those who keep the argument after the argument has been removed are the ones whose posture pre-dates the evidence. The reason the fear-redirect sits inside the same verse is that the wrongdoers' only remaining power is the power to frighten. The redirect starves that power at its root. For the modern reader the passage is a manual for public stands. The evidence is assembled. The conduct is unified. The fear is re-addressed to its owner. This age calls the crowd's volume a verdict. The verse enters a different verdict and posts it above the noise.

---

## Verse 2:151

> Since We have sent you a messenger from among yourselves—reciting to you Our revelations, purifying you, teaching you the Book and wisdom, and teaching you what you never knew—

**THE SENDING THAT COMPLETED THE FAVOUR**

The qiblah passage closes by naming the gift that crowns it. ***“Since We have sent you a messenger from among yourselves”***. The sending is the perfection of the favour. From among yourselves. The mercy is packaged as family. Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss ties the clause back to the verse of perfecting. The favour of the direction was completed with the favour of the messenger. The prayer of the builders of the House had asked for a messenger raised from among them. The verse now delivers the messenger and names the work. What follows is that the redesign of the prayer is joined to the arrival of a teacher. A community is given a direction and a curriculum at once. The effect is a favour in two halves. The faces have somewhere to turn. The hearts have someone to teach them why. The placement of the verse at the close of the qiblah section is itself a commentary. The turn was always going somewhere. The messenger names the destination.

**THE CURRICULUM'S FOUR MOVES**

The work of the messenger is stated in four verbs. ***“reciting to you Our revelations, purifying you, teaching you the Book”*** ***“and wisdom, and teaching you what you never knew”***. Recite. Purify. Teach the book. Teach the wisdom. The unknown is added at the end as an open door. Ibn ʿAbbās unpacks the verbs as a system. The reciting carries the commands and the prohibitions. The purifying is the growth that cleanses. The teaching covers the scripture and the rulings that stand beside it. The wisdom named beside the book is the prophetic practice that shows the book in motion. The parallel account of the believers' favour states the same verbs in the plural (3:164 — **“and teaching them the Book and wisdom. For indeed they had previously been clearly astray”**). The other passage states the same sending in its own register (62:2 — **“teaching them the Book and wisdom, for indeed they had previously been clearly astray—”**). The commission is therefore fixed across the book. Four doors open into one room. The difference between a preacher and this messenger is the range of the verbs.

**THE RECEIVING THAT NEVER STOPS**

The final clause keeps the curriculum open at the far edge. Teaching you what you never knew. The receiving is designed to continue. The gloss of Ibn ʿAbbās marks the clause against the pride of the shelf. The People of the Book held a scripture and recognised the traits. The community is handed what no shelf held alone. What follows is that the community of the qiblah is a community of students by constitution. The direction gathers the bodies. The teaching gathers the minds. For the modern reader the four verbs test every religious claim in public. Where the reciting stops, the claim closes its source. Where the purifying stops, the claim becomes decoration. This age keeps teachers of the book and few teachers of the wisdom. The commission refuses to separate them. The unknown is where the mercy of the sending is felt most, because the receiving is still in progress. The messenger came to open the door, and the door has no plan to shut.

**A TEACHER, NOT ONLY A LAW**

The pairing of the sending with the qiblah is the verse's deepest structural claim. A direction without a teacher is a wall with a doorway painted on it. A teacher without a direction is a voice in a storm. The verse delivers both at once, and the effect is a complete apparatus. The faces are gathered by the law. The hearts are gathered by the curriculum. The reason the four verbs are listed rather than summarised is that each one repairs a different damage. The reciting reconnects the speech of the people to the speech of the sky. The purifying addresses the character. The teaching addresses the mind. The unknown at the end addresses the future. Each verb is a repair-job on a different layer of the same damage, and the four together rebuild the whole house.
