For the modern reader the apparatus is the measure of every school and every mosque in this age. Where the verbs are split apart, the institution thins. Where they stand together, the institution can carry the weight of a community. The sending is the favour that perfects the turn. The teacher is the mercy that explains it.

---

## Verse 2:152

> remember Me; I will remember you. And thank Me, and never be ungrateful

**THE REMEMBRANCE THAT RETURNS**

A covenant in miniature stands at the centre of the passage. ***“remember Me; I will remember you.”***. Two verbs. Two sides. One circuit. Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss reads the remembering as the performance of acts of obedience. The return of the remembering is the granting of the garden. The same transmission gives the harder form of the bargain. Remember Allah in the season of ease. He remembers you in the season of hardship. The circuit is therefore not decorative. It is a supply line, and the supply is drawn against a promise written in the first person. What follows is that the smallest phrase spoken on a tongue has an address at the other end. The addressing is the mercy of the design. The point of the paired pronouns is intimacy with procedure. The remembering goes up. The remembering comes down. The effect is that the servant's dhikr is a meeting rather than a technique. The comfort-clause states where the returned remembering is first felt (13:28 — **“whose hearts find comfort in the remembrance of Allah. Surely in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find comfort”**). The comfort is the receipt of the circuit.

**THE THANK THAT CLOSES THE CIRCUIT**

The gratitude clause completes the loop. ***“And thank Me, and never be ungrateful”***. The thank is the remembering in its social form. The rejection named at the end is the verse's single prohibition. The gloss of Ibn ʿAbbās takes the thank as thanks for the blessings bestowed and the rejection as the stopping of that thanks. al-Bukhārī and Muslim both record the return-promise in the report of the Prophet: *"whoever remembers Me in himself I will remember him in Myself and whoever remembers Me in an assembly I will remember him in an Assembly more excellent than his"*. The private and the public remembering both draw a matching return. The circuit has two switches. The heart can open it. The tongue can open it. The bargain of gratitude is proclaimed with its stakes in full elsewhere (14:7 — **“And ˹remember˺ when your Lord proclaimed, ‘If you are grateful, I will certainly give you more. But if you are ungrateful,”**). The increase follows the thanks. The circuit is economic in the strictest sense. The supply grows with the gratitude.

**THE INGRATITUDE THAT IS A THEFT**

The closing prohibition deserves its own warning-post. Never be ungrateful. The early commentators keep the warning lashed to the blessings just delivered. The qiblah. The messenger. The direction and the teacher. To receive the favour and withhold the thanks is the theft the verse names. For the modern reader the small verse is a complete manual of the inner life. Remember. Thank. Do not cut the circuit. This age is fluent in mindfulness and mute about the one being remembered. The second clause fixes the address of the practice. A memory technique returns calm. A meeting returns a gaze. The difference between the two is the difference between an exercise and a prayer. The returned remembering is the proof that the meeting is real. The covenant stands open at both ends. Remember Me. I will remember you. The circuit is older than the reader, and the line is still live.

**TWO SWITCHES, ONE LINE**

The engineering of the covenant is simple enough to carry in a pocket and deep enough to spend a life on. The remembering is the current. The thanks is the load. The prohibition at the end is the fuse. The effect of the three together is a complete circuit diagram of the inner life. The point of the assembly-clause in the transmitted report is that the circuit is not embarrassed by company. The private meeting draws its return. The public meeting draws its matching return. The reason the gratitude is paired with the remembering is that the two are the same act in two registers. The tongue remembers. The conduct thanks. For the modern reader the diagram replaces a whole shelf of manuals. This age runs on forgetting, and its industries are tuned to interrupt the current. The verse installs the practice that survives the interruptions. The line is old. The switches are in the reader's hands. The promise at the other end is written in the first person.

---

## Verse 2:153

> O believers! Seek comfort in patience and prayer. Allah is truly with those who are patient

**THE COMFORT IS ASKED FOR**

The address turns to the believers with a two-handed prescription. ***“O believers! Seek comfort in patience”*** ***“and prayer. Allah is truly with those”*** ***“who are patient”***. Two tools and one presence. Patience. Prayer. Allah with the patient. Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss unpacks the seeking of help as the seeking of strength for the obligations. The patience is the abstaining from contraventions and shameful works. The prayer named beside it is the abundant prayer of the night and the day. The point is that the comfort is not wished for in the verse. It is sought in two instruments. The instruments are the strength of the limbs and the strength of the schedule. What follows is that the suffering believer is handed work to do, and the work is the door of the presence. The older passage in this surah states the same prescription with its weight attached (3:200 — **“O believers! Patiently endure, persevere, stand on guard, and be mindful of Allah, so you may be successful”**). Endure. Persevere. Stand guard. The verbs are the handles of the instrument.

**PATIENCE AND THE PRAYER THAT HELPS**

The two tools are joined because neither is complete alone. Patience without prayer becomes a clenched jaw. Prayer without patience becomes a complaint with candles. The transmission of the son of Zayd divides the patience into two parts. One part turns away from the prohibitions. The other endures the afflictions when they arrive. The pairing with the prayer supplies both parts with fuel. The early authorities read the night prayer as the purifier of the day's books, and the patience as the guard of the day's boundaries. The two hands hold the instrument together. The patriarch's own words under pressure state the pairing from inside a crisis (12:18 — **“So ˹I can only endure with˺ beautiful patience! It is Allah’s help that I seek to bear your claims.””**). Beautiful patience. Sought help. One sentence carries the whole prescription. The effect is that the method is ancient and portable. The father of the prophets used it under a false-blood shirt. The method scales down to an ordinary week without losing its physics.

**THE HUMBLE ONES**

The closing promise has a named recipient. Allah is truly with those who are patient. The with-ness is the reward that arrives before any ending. The gloss of Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the presence practical. The patient ones are helped into the obligations and kept from the shameful works. The keeping is the presence made visible in conduct. For the modern reader the verse is a standing instruction for the hard seasons. Seek the comfort in the two tools. Expect the presence, not the exemption. This age sells comfort as a product and calls patience a defect of the brand. The verse reverses both prices. The comfort is sought in the patient posture. The prayer is the meeting that steadies the posture. The waiting is therefore never empty time. It is an activity with two handles. The remembering of the covenant supplies the patience. The patience spends the supply where it counts. The presence is the standing balance of the account.

**TWO HANDS ON THE INSTRUMENT**

The genius of the pairing is that it covers both the ambush and the siege. The patience handles the affliction that arrives without warning. The prayer handles the slow weight of the ordinary week. The effect of holding both is a resilience that does not depend on the shape of the trouble. The reason the promise is attached to the posture rather than the outcome is that the outcome is scheduled by the one who sends the touches. The with-ness is given now. The ending is given later. For the modern reader the prescription fits the two most common crises of this age. The ambush of bad news is answered with the creed-posture of patience. The siege of the crowded calendar is answered with the appointment of prayer. This age prescribes distraction for both and wonders at the fatigue. The verse prescribes two handles and promises a presence. The comfort is sought, not wished. The seeking is rewarded with the company of the one who counts the patient among his own. The presence arrives with the practice and stays past the season.

---

## Verse 2:154

> Never say that those martyred in the cause of Allah are dead—in fact, they are alive! But you do not perceive it

**THE MARTYRS NOT DEAD**

A forbidden sentence is filed at the top of the verse. ***“Never say that those martyred in the cause of Allah are dead”***. The sentence was circulating in the streets of the city. Ibn ʿAbbās's account reports the speakers and their script over the martyrs of the battles in these words: *"So-and-so has died and lost all comfort and happiness."* The aggravation of the sincere households was the purpose. The reason for the ban is the falsity of the sentence itself, not merely its cruelty. The correction arrives in the sharpest available form. ***“in fact, they are alive!”***. The life is not a metaphor in the grammar of the passage. It is the reality the death-talk obscures. What follows is that the language of the marketplace is placed under a veto. The dead of the cause are not available for the agitators' arithmetic. The effect is a public correction of the record, spoken over the graves themselves.

**THE SAYING OF THE AGITATORS**

The forbidden sentence has a motive and the motive is named in the tradition. The mourning was to be loud. The cause was to look costly. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the aggravation in view as the engine of the wording. The verse answers the motive as well as the words. ***“But you do not perceive it”***. The perception clause is a rebuke dressed as a description. The living of the martyrs sits outside the audience's instruments. The instruments of the market cannot see it. The point of the rebuke is that the failure is located in the eyes rather than in the martyrs. The life continues. The audience lacks the lens. The difference between a hidden fact and a denied fact is the whole drama of the verse. The agitators denied. The verse asserts. The parallel of the provision-promise asserts with the same confidence (3:169 — **“Never think of those martyred in the cause of Allah as dead. In fact, they are alive with their Lord,”**). Alive with their Lord. The dictionary of the cause has its own vocabulary for the grave.

**THE GREEN BIRDS**

The tradition of the living martyrs gives the life a shape the eyes can hold. al-Bukhārī and Muslim both transmit the report that describes the spirits in *"green birds that take wing freely wherever they wish in Paradise"*. The image is not decoration. It is a citizenship. The birds move where they wish and the wish is granted. The provision runs beside the throne. The emigrants' promise states the same accounting from the entry-side of the ledger (22:58 — **“As for those who emigrate in the cause of Allah and then are martyred or die, Allah will”**). The provision is promised by the best of providers. For the modern reader the veto on the death-sentence is a lesson in language discipline. The words used about the dead of a cause shape the living of the cause. This age speaks of loss and of cost at the graveside. The verse speaks of life and provision. The two dictionaries disagree about the ending, and only one of them is filed at the throne. The birds keep flying. The provision keeps arriving. The words of the agitators expire.

**A LANGUAGE POLICED AT THE GRAVE**

The veto on the death-sentence is finally a lesson in the power of vocabulary. The agitators chose their words to instruct the market. The verse chooses its words to instruct the sky-side of the same market. The effect of the correction is that the bereaved are given a grammar that can survive the grave. The point of the perception-clause is that the living martyrs are outside the instruments of the crowd, not outside the care of the Lord. The instruments of the market measure breath and payroll. The instruments of the promise measure provision and presence. For the modern reader the choice of dictionary is daily work. This age speaks of loss and cost and closure at every graveside, and the words do their quiet work on the living. The verse offers the older vocabulary. Alive. Well provided. Seen by the one who keeps the birds flying. The speech of the cause is policed at the grave because the speech of the cause is the inheritance of the household. The words of hope are not decoration. They are equipment.

---

## Verse 2:155

> We will certainly test you with a touch of fear and famine and loss of property, life, and crops. Give good news to those who patiently endure—

**THE PROMISED TOUCHES**

The verse announces a policy with its schedule already printed. ***“We will certainly test you with a touch of fear”***. The testing is not an accident of the world. It is administered. The touch of fear is itemised first. Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss reads the fear here as the fear of the enemy at the door. The famine named next is the hunger of the drought years. The point is that the list is itemised because the preparation must be itemised. A generic warning equips nobody. The verse names the instruments of the test by name. Fear. Hunger. What follows is that the believer who reads the verse receives a map of the terrain, and the terrain includes the valleys. The effect of the announcing is strangely stabilising. The shock is never evidence of abandonment. The policy was filed in advance. The earlier challenge to the tested ones states the same policy as a question (2:214 — **“Do you think you will be admitted into Paradise without being tested like those before you? They were afflicted with suffering”**).

**THE LIST OF LOSSES**

The itemisation continues and grows specific enough to budget around. ***“and famine and loss of property, life”*** ***“and crops. Give good news to those”*** ***“who patiently endure”***. Property. Lives. Crops. The three columns the world counts as wealth. The verse places all three under the touch. The gloss of Ibn ʿAbbās marks the mechanics of each column. The wealth is hit through destruction. The lives are hit through killing, death, and illness. The crops are hit through the damage of the harvest. The list covers the household and the field in one sweep. The effect is that no category of loss is left unprinted on the map. The shaken scene of the tested shows the weight in historical units (2:214 — **“and adversity and were so ˹violently˺ shaken that ˹even˺ the Messenger and the believers with him cried out,”**). The Messenger himself cried out. The weight of the test is measured by that single detail. What follows is that the good news arrives inside the warning rather than after it.

**GOOD NEWS FOR THE ENDURING**

The closing phrase turns the whole list toward a named group. The patient ones. The good news is not a soft ending to a hard verse. It is the verse's purpose. The early commentators read the glad tidings here as the tidings of the mercy and the garden. The bearers of the good news are the ones who endure the listed touches without renouncing their Lord. For the modern reader the sequence is the instruction itself. Expect the touches. Prepare the itemised back. This age reads every loss as an indictment of the cause and every hardship as bad marketing. The verse reads the loss as the announced curriculum. The difference between the two readings is the difference between a shock and a scheduled lesson. The good news waits at the end of the schedule with the names of its bearers attached. The reward is prepared before the famine is finished. The policy stands. The map is in the reader's hands.

**A SCHEDULE THAT STABILISES**

The announcement of the test is the strange mercy at the heart of the passage. A world that tests without warning produces households that read every hardship as abandonment. A world whose tests are itemised in advance produces households that can budget the grief. The effect of the printing is that the shock is removed from the encounter. The famine is still a famine. The fear is still fear. But neither arrives without a label. The reason the good news is placed inside the list rather than after it is structural. The promise must be read in the same breath as the loss. The two clauses stand shoulder to shoulder so the reader cannot finish the inventory without meeting the reward. For the modern reader the schedule is the difference between panic and preparation. This age sells resilience as a product and leaves the map in the warehouse. The verse hands the map over the counter with the good news printed on the same sheet. The touches are promised. The patience is prescribed. The reward is signed at the bottom of the page.

---

## Verse 2:156

> who, when faced with a disaster, say, “Surely to Allah we belong and to Him we will ˹all˺ return.”

**THE WORDS SAID AT THE DOOR**

Two sentences land at the door of every disaster. ***“who, when faced with a disaster, say”*** ***““Surely to Allah we belong”*** ***“and to Him we will ˹all˺ return.””***. Ownership and return. One breath. One creed. Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss unpacks both clauses at their full weight. We are the slaves of Allah. He does with us as He pleases. We are returning to Him after we die. The transmission adds the condition that governs the acceptance of the sentence. If we are not pleased with His decree, He will not be pleased with our works. The point is that the sentence is spoken before the grief is finished. It is a door-sentence. The disaster knocks. The believer answers with the creed. What follows is that the ownership clause reframes the loss itself. What was owned has gone home to the owner. The return clause reframes the mourner. The mourner is also on the road. The effect is a theology of property that covers the whole crisis.

**THE OWNERSHIP CONFESSED**

The first clause is the constitution of the believer's world. To Allah we belong. The belongings travel back to the owner without injustice. The provision-promise states what the return includes on its receiving-side (22:58 — **“indeed grant them a good provision. Surely Allah is the Best Provider”**). The return is not a repossession. It is a reception by the best of providers. al-Bukhārī and Muslim both record the report attached to this phrase. Its promise covers the moment of the saying. The report gives the sentence its terms: *"when an affliction befalls him God will reward him and compensate him with what is better"*. The grief is real. The transaction is also real. The difference between the two is the difference between the world's arithmetic and the verse's. The world counts the loss. The verse counts the saying. For the modern reader the creed is portable past every border of sorrow. The sentence fits the hospital door and the graveside in any city.

**A RETURN THAT ORGANISES**

The second clause does the future's work. And to Him we will return. The return organises the rest of the life. The early commentators read the patience here as the child of that single sentence. The disaster is not the end of the road. It is a bend on the road. The reward of the doers waits at the bend's far side (39:10 — **“who do good in this world will have a good reward.”**). The patient ones are the doers in the season of the disaster. What follows is that the creed works as a compass in six words. The first three set the ownership. The last three set the destination. The middle of the life is walked between the two. This age sells a thousand sentences for the hard hour and ships them in bright packaging. The verse keeps one. The sentence has survived every century because the two facts inside it have never changed. The belonging is real. The returning is real. The door opens onto both.

**A CREED BUILT FOR CRISIS**

The placement of the creed at the door of the disaster is deliberate psychology and deliberate theology. The sentence is short enough to survive the shock. The two facts it carries are large enough to organise the shock. Ownership re-labels the loss. The return re-labels the mourner. The effect of the re-labelling is that the grief is given a frame that does not collapse under its own weight. The point of the acceptance-clause in the transmitted gloss is that the creed is a submission as well as a speech. The heart is asked to agree with the sentence it speaks. The reason the report of the reward is attached to the formula is that the sentence is heard at the other end. The one who receives the owned is also the one who records the saying. For the modern reader the six words are the most portable equipment in the passage. This age offers a thousand therapies for the hard hour and forgets the address of the owner. The creed supplies the address and the destination in one breath. The crisis arrives. The sentence is spoken. The door holds.

---

## Verse 2:157

> They are the ones who will receive Allah’s blessings and mercy. And it is they who are ˹rightly˺ guided

**THE BLESSING AND THE MERCY**

The promised account now pays out in named currencies. ***“They are the ones”*** ***“who will receive Allah’s blessings”*** ***“and mercy. And it is they”***. Two payments. Blessings and mercy. Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss itemises the pair across the two horizons. The blessing is the forgiveness in this world. The mercy is the protection from torment in the world to come. The account of the patient therefore pays in both currencies at once. The current world clears the record. The coming world clears the fear. The point is that the promise of the disaster-verse is shown to be solvent. The promise has a treasury. The treasury pays in the exact shapes the testing threatened. What follows is that the good news announced before the famine is now receipted after the creed. The effect of the itemisation is that no horizon is left unpaid. The one who sends the touches sends the payments.

**GUIDED ON THE STRUCK ROAD**

The closing clause names the third payment. ***“who are ˹rightly˺ guided”***. The guidance is given to the struck ones as equipment. The reading of the early authorities ties the guidance here to the sentence the struck ones keep saying. The return-creed is the compass, and the compass is the guidance made portable. The opening supplication of the book states the same guidance as the family's daily request (1:5 — **“You ˹alone˺ we worship and You ˹alone˺ we ask for help”**). Worship and asking. The guided life has this shape as its grammar. The struck ones keep the shape under pressure. That keeping is the guidance in action. The difference between guidance as information and guidance as posture is the quiet revolution of the clause. The information arrives once. The posture is held daily. For the modern reader the third payment is the one the hard season needs most. The forgiveness is welcome. The safety is welcome. The guidance is what makes the next disaster survivable.

**THE PAYMENT WITHOUT A CEILING**

The account closes on a promise of scale. The spaciousness of the earth is placed beside the spaciousness of the reward (39:10 — **“And Allah’s earth is spacious. Only those who endure patiently will be given their reward without limit.””**). Without limit. The payment carries no ceiling. The point of the pairing is generosity measured against geography. The earth itself is the unit of the reward's vocabulary. Ibn ʿAbbās's reading keeps the guidance as the first instalment of the whole deposit. The guided one walks with the compass in hand, and the compass arrives early. What follows is that the group of the creed-verse stands fully equipped. They belong. They return. They are blessed, kept, and guided. This age measures its recoveries in quarters and calls a good year a triumph. The verse measures the recovery in horizons. Both horizons are solvent. The payment without a ceiling is the reason the good news could be printed before the test was delivered. The treasury does not run on the schedule of the drought.

**RECEIPTS FOR TWO HORIZONS**

The double payment is the answer to the oldest complaint about the patient life. The complaint says that the patient are paid late. The verse answers that the patient are paid twice and in both currencies. The forgiveness clears the books in the current world. The mercy clears the fear in the coming one. Neither payment is deferred to the other's horizon, and neither horizon is treated as a rounding error in the account. The effect of the itemisation is that no horizon is treated as an afterthought. The reason the guidance is named as the third payment is that the second disaster is already scheduled in a world of tests. The guidance is the equipment for the next season, and the equipment arrives early. The compass is handed over before the storm is scheduled, and the hand that schedules the storm is the hand that issues the compass. For the modern reader the receipting is the missing half of every hard season. This age counts only the losses of the current quarter and calls the rest theology. The verse counts both horizons and issues receipts for each. The blessing is posted. The mercy is posted. The compass is in the hand. The account of the patient carries no ceiling and no shortage.

---

## Verse 2:158

> Indeed, ˹the hills of˺ Ṣafa and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah. So whoever performs the pilgrimage or minor pilgrimage, let them walk between ˹the two hills˺. And whoever does good willingly, Allah is truly Appreciative, All-Knowing

**TWO HILLS AS SIGNS**

The rites of the House receive two standing landmarks. ***“Indeed, ˹the hills of˺ Ṣafa”*** ***“and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah.”***. Two hills near the House. Two waymarks among the waymarks. Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss places the walking among the rites that Allah commanded for the pilgrimage. The geography of the House is folded into the ritual itself. The point is that the terrain is consecrated by decree. The body of the pilgrim walks through a theology. The two hills carry the memory of a searching mother and a family. The walking between them makes the memory in the feet. What follows is that the rites of the pilgrimage are given an address in the world rather than in the air. The symbols are named by the one who raised the mountain. The effect of the naming is that the practice survives every retelling. The pilgrim circles the House and paces the hills on the map of the same owner.

**THE WALK THE IDOLS ONCE WATCHED**

The permission to walk arrives with a history attached. ***“So whoever performs the pilgrimage”*** ***“or minor pilgrimage, let them walk between ˹the two hills˺.”***. The believers had disliked the walking. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the reason in view. The idols stood at the two hills and the pagans used to stroke them there. The conscience of the converts said this practice belonged to the old world. The verse removes the veto and re-consecrates the stones. The point of the reveal-context is that the symbols never belonged to the borrowers. The idols had leased the hills for a season. The report of the pacing's own status keeps the ruling inside the prophetic practice. The Prophet said: *"Begin with what God has begun"* meaning the first hill, as the report is recorded by Muslim. Another report gives the pacing its rank: *"God has prescribed for you the pacing"* in the collection of al-Bayhaqī. The effect is that the walk stands with a deed and a date. The pilgrimage's ethics stand beside the walk itself (2:197 — **“the best provision is righteousness. And be mindful of Me, O people of reason”**). The feet walk. The character supplies the provision.

**A GOOD THAT IS APPRECIATED**

The verse closes the rite with the names of the one who receives it. ***“And whoever does good willingly, Allah is truly Appreciative, All-Knowing”***. The willing good is seen and appreciated at the address of the two names. The fear of the unaccepted act is answered by the appreciative one. The fear of the unseen act is answered by the knowing one. The early commentators read the willing clause as covering the extra walk and every extra kindness beside the obligation. The volunteer's good is not surplus. It is received, and the smallest of it is accepted. The rites of the House are named in their pilgrim's form elsewhere (22:29 — **“Then let them groom themselves, fulfil their vows, and circle the Ancient House.””**). The grooming and the vows and the circling stand in one line. For the modern reader the closing names reframe the whole rite. The walk between two hills is not a hoop. It is a gift delivered to an appreciative address. This age counts its rituals as obligations and its hobbies as gifts. The verse counts the willing good as both, and the knowing one keeps the count.

**STONES WITH DEEDS ATTACHED**

The re-consecration of the two hills is the passage's model for all inherited practice. The stones stood in the old world under borrowed names. The verse re-titles the stones by decree and attaches the walking to the rites of the House. The effect of the re-titling is that the geography of the pilgrimage becomes a walking archive. Every circuit of the House is a memory. Every pacing of the hills is a memory made in the feet. The reason the prophetic practice is cited beside the permission is that the rite is a handover, not an invention. The handover carries the deed and the date. For the modern reader the model settles the anxiety of borrowed forms. This age inherits practices the way it inherits furniture, and the dust makes people nervous. The verse shows the procedure. Re-title by the owner's word. Attach the deed. Walk it with the willing good in the heart. The hills stand. The deeds are recorded. The appreciative one keeps the register open.

---

## Verse 2:159

> Those who hide the clear proofs and guidance that We have revealed—after We made it clear for humanity in the Book—will be condemned by Allah and ˹all˺ those who condemn

**THE CONCEALED PROOFS**

The concealment now receives its courtroom. ***“Those who hide the clear proofs”*** ***“and guidance that We have revealed”*** ***“after We made it clear for humanity in the Book”***. The objects of the hiding are named before the verdict. Proofs and guidance. Both were revealed. Both were made clear in advance of the hiding, so that no appeal of confusion remains available at the trial. Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss itemises what was buried. The commands and the prohibitions and the signs written in the Torah. The guidance here is the description and the traits of the awaited prophet. The narration of Abū al-ʿĀliyah states the occasion plainly. These verses came down about the People of the Scripture who hid the description. The point is that the crime is named as concealment rather than ignorance. The material was in the shelves. The clarity was delivered in advance. What follows is that the hiding is graded as a deed done against the light. The effect of the naming is forensic. The verse opens an evidence file before it opens a verdict.

**CURSES FROM TWO COURTS**

The verdict arrives with two courts in session. ***“will be condemned by Allah and ˹all˺ those who condemn”***. The court above and the court below pronounce one sentence. Ibn ʿAbbās's reading marks the two condemnations in their places. The condemnation from Allah is the torment that meets the concealer in the grave. The condemnation from the created order is the cursing that answers the screams. The parallel warning states the same verdict at its origin (2:174 — **“Indeed, those who hide Allah’s revelations, trading them for a fleeting gain consume nothing”**). The trading is the motive underneath the hiding. The revelation was exchanged for a price. The verdict matches the trade. The difference between a private grudge and a licensed curse is the presence of the proofs. The proofs were clear. The concealing was deliberate. The courts speak because the evidence is complete. What follows is that the ordinary conscience is granted a place in the judgment. The cursers of the earth repeat what the throne has already said.

**A PROFIT OF FIRE**

The account of the trade closes the passage with its payment. The revelations were traded for a fleeting gain. The payment is filed in the other currency (2:174 — **“but fire into their bellies. Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment, nor will He purify them.”**). Fire for the belly. Silence at the speaking. No purification at the end. The early commentators read the sequence as the economy of the shelf made visible. The knowledge was bought to be kept. The keeping returned as a payment no bank recognises. For the modern reader the verse is a lesson in the ethics of information. The proofs are given to be shared, not stored behind a counter. This age has invented new hands to lay over the light. Noise departments. Burial by volume. The verse's verdict has a modern application because the deed is old. The hand over the light is still the same hand. The courts still speak in the same order. The gain still flees before the payment arrives.

**THE SHELF ON TRIAL**

The trial of the concealers is finally a trial of every keeper of sources. The proofs were named first so that the verdict could be read as a document case. The courts were named second so that the sentence could be heard as a public act. The trade was named last so that the motive could be filed with the evidence. The effect of the sequence is a complete prosecution with exhibits. The reason the modern application is unavoidable is that every age produces shelf-keepers. The archive is always tended by hands that can either publish or bury. The burial has a market. The gain is always fleeting. The payment is always posted to the other currency. For the modern reader the passage is a warning posted above the archive door. This age keeps the proofs in volumes and pays the hiding hands in full view. The verse reads the docket aloud. The truth was made clear. The hiding was a deed. The fire is the trade's own coin returned to the trader.

---

## Verse 2:160

> As for those who repent, mend their ways, and let the truth be known, they are the ones to whom I will turn ˹in forgiveness˺, for I am the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful

**A REPENTANCE THAT OPENS**

The exception arrives in three movements. ***“As for those who repent, mend their ways, and let the truth be known”***. Repent. Repair. Publish. The verse that follows the widest verdict installs the narrowest door. Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss unpacks the three movements at their full size. The repentance turns back from the old course. The mending is the worship of Allah alone without partners added to the household of the heart. The publishing is the making-manifest of the very traits that were hidden. The point of the third movement is surgical. The crime was a hiding. The repair includes a showing. What follows is that the repentance is not a private mood. It has a public limb. The effect of the verse is a door that opens onto the street. The one who buried the description is invited to publish it. The turn is accepted, and the accepting is announced in the first person at the end of the line.

**THREE MOVEMENTS BACK TO HIM**

The structure of the offer deserves its own ledger. The first movement is the exit from the old allegiance. The second is the repair of the conduct. The third is the letting of the truth be known. The early commentators read the third as the un-doing of the concealment's own effect in public. The hidden word returns to the market-stand. The same invitation is issued to the despairing servants in the plainest terms (39:53 — **“Do not lose hope in Allah’s mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins. He is indeed the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”**). Do not lose hope. The mercy is addressed to the ones who have exceeded the limits against their own souls. The difference between the two passages is the audience, not the door. One speaks to the concealers of proofs. The other speaks to the over-doers of sins. The mercy covers both addresses. What follows is that no one in the two crowds is standing outside the offer. The movements are available in every city.

**MERCY FOR THE SHOWING**

The closing names complete the offer's paperwork. ***“they are the ones to whom I will turn ˹in forgiveness˺”***. The turn of the Lord answers the turn of the servant. The names at the close are personal and open: ***“for I am the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful”***. The closing summons of the book places the same work in the servant's hands as a practice (110:3 — **“then glorify the praises of your Lord and seek His forgiveness, for certainly He is ever Accepting of Repentance”**). Glorify. Seek. The seeking is the movement the door is built for. For the modern reader the third movement is the hardest and the most modern. This age runs apology industries and hiding industries side by side. The verse refuses the apology without the publication. The mend is counted only when the truth is let out. The two names at the end hold the account open for the reader still walking. The acceptance is His profession. The mercy is His nature. The showing is the servant's remaining work, and the work is light.

**THE DOOR WITH THREE STEPS**

The design of the exception is the practical heart of the whole passage. The verdict of the previous verse was wide enough to cover a generation of concealers. The door of this verse is built to fit a human being. Turn. Repair. Show. The three steps scale from a single convert to a whole household of teachers. The effect of the publishing-clause is that the repentance reaches the same public square where the concealment once stood. The truth that was buried is walked back into the light by the same people who buried it. The reason the first-person promise closes the verse is that the steps are heavy enough to need a promise. The accepting is announced by the one who receives the turning. For the modern reader the three steps are the whole curriculum of repair. This age runs apology industries that skip the publishing and mend industries that skip the turning. The verse keeps the three in one line and refuses to sell a shorter version. The door is narrow. The steps are clear. The work at the end of them is light because the accepting is done by the master of the door.

---

## Verse 2:161

> Surely those who disbelieve and die as disbelievers are condemned by Allah, the angels, and all of humanity

**CONDEMNED AT THE HOUR OF DEATH**

***“Surely those who disbelieve”*** opens a sentence that is not argued but closed, and its timing is precise. The verse continues, ***“and die as disbelievers are condemned by Allah,”*** so the state recorded is the state death finds. Life is the workshop where the state can change; death is the door that locks it. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the report that the participle is read over people who persist in unbelief of Allah and His Messenger to the end. The sentence attaches to that final condition, which means every breath before it remained an open opportunity. The condemnation is not pronounced over a life still in motion. The sentence waits at the door of the final breath, which means the ground of hope and the ground of warning occupy the same moment.

**THREE PRONOUNCEMENTS**

The verdict is issued by three parties at once. The verse itself names the court: ***“the angels”*** take their share of the pronouncement, and ***“and all of humanity”*** closes the list. The reason for the threefold shape is coverage — nobody in creation pronounces the opposite. Ibn ʿAbbās transmits the substance of the third layer: the curses which believers direct through history at wrongdoers settle upon these people as well, so even human judgment is folded into the verdict. The point is that the condemned stand without advocate anywhere, because every level of the moral universe has spoken the same sentence. The order of the list also runs downward from the source of law to its last witness, which is how verdicts are published: authority first, confirmation last. Because the angels are named before humanity, the sentence is dated in the register before any human mouth repeats it. No one can then treat the verdict as a rumour started by enemies; it is a judgement copied from the register and read aloud by creation. (33:64 — **“Surely Allah condemns the disbelievers, and has prepared for them a blazing Fire”**)

**WAITING FOR THE LAST BREATH**

A hearer may ask whether the sentence is not too final for people who sinned for a limited time. The objection has force only if the condemnation were pronounced before death, and the text refuses that timing. Because the record is made at the last breath, no one can claim the sentence was rushed, and no one can claim the opportunity was hidden. The threefold pronouncement mirrors a threefold offer, since prophets, books, and natural testimony all spoke while testimony could still move the heart. This is the difference between a judge who condemns at the first offence and a judge who waits at the door. The period of sin is limited precisely because the period of repentance is limited too, and the verse keeps both limits visible at once. The threefold list also does the work of a formal verdict sheet, because a sentence read by one judge can be argued with while a sentence confirmed by every level of the court cannot. That is why the passage places the angels between Allah and humanity in the list: the highest authority and the lowest witness agree, and the middle of the universe is filled with confirmations. The dying are addressed rather than the dead, which means the warning is still a mercy while it is being read. Every hearer of the verse is standing in the only hour the verse leaves open. The warning is therefore addressed to the living in the grammar of the dead, and the tension between the two is the mercy of its tone.

**SEALED BY ALL CREATION**

The Book states the same logic in its own register: (3:12 — **“˹O Prophet!˺ Tell the disbelievers, “Soon you will be overpowered and driven to Hell—what an evil place to rest!””**). The report of Ibn ʿAbbās holds that the torment itself is the curse of Allah named first in the list, so the order runs from the highest court downward. I read the scope of "people" as either all humanity or the believers; both readings leave the condemned without cover, and the second adds a layer — the very community that warned them confirms the sentence. The scope is therefore total in either case, which is the rhetorical point of naming all three parties in one breath. The application is immediate and narrow: the decisive question is never how a person lived in the middle of the story but in what state the story ends. Those who die in unbelief are marked by all creation.

---

## Verse 2:162

> They will be in Hell forever. Their punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be delayed ˹from it˺

**BOTH EXITS CLOSED**

***“They will be in Hell forever. Their punishment will”*** opens the account of duration and intensity together. The two negatives that follow close both doors a prisoner would try: ***“not be lightened”*** removes mitigation, and ***“nor will they be delayed ˹from it˺”*** removes postponement. The previous verse delivered the sentence; this one describes its administration. Because relief and adjournment are named and denied, the horror is not only that the punishment is severe but that its administration is constant. Ibn ʿAbbās's report has it that the doom will not be lifted or reduced, and that it will not be deferred.  Every form of hope the punished might form is answered by name, and the naming is done before the hope can be spoken.

**NOT EVEN A BLINK**

The denial of lightening is total in my reading — not an instant of relief separates them from the doom. Human courts normally offer exactly the two mercies this verse removes: sentences shortened for good conduct, and starts postponed pending appeal. The stacking of the negatives therefore anticipates the precise hopes of the punished and forecloses each one. In the administration described here the hours count the same on the first day and the ten-thousandth, and no season brings the matter to a close. The horror is the removal of every curve in the graph. Ibn ʿAbbās's wording is stark: the doom is neither lifted nor reduced, and no deferral is granted once the matter is settled. The smallest unit of relief the mind can invent is the unit reported as refused, so the verse closes the door on the microscopic as well as on the infinite. Both denials are administrative rather than descriptive: they speak of what will be done with the sentence rather than of what the Fire is like. An administration without a schedule of grace is the state the two negatives describe. (33:65 — **“to stay there for ever and ever—never will they find any protector or helper”**)

**WHERE HOPE BELONGS**

A hearer may ask whether "forever" can be reconciled with a mercy said to embrace everything. The two statements are reconciled by their different addresses, because the mercy is offered inside a life where it can be received; this verse describes the account after the offer has been refused at its last door. That is why the severity is announced alongside verses of hope rather than instead of them. The pair of passages prices the present correctly. This is the difference between medicine available at the pharmacy and medicine at the post-mortem — the same substance, differently timed, is either gift or memory. No hearer can claim the text was unclear about which side of the door hope belongs to. The verse also settles the question of whether the punishment might be imagined as a series of episodes with rests between them; the denial of delay removes the rests along with the end. Because the two denials stand in the same breath, neither can be read as an exaggeration of the other — lightening and deferral are separate mercies, and each is refused separately. In the administration described, the punished find no season of relief and no procedural gap to enter. The steadiness is the horror, and the horror is meant to be read while steadiness is still available on the other side.

**THE ADMINISTRATION DESCRIBED**

The companion verses fix the same steady state, and the renewal of torment is drawn out in (4:56 — **“Surely those who reject Our signs, We will cast them into the Fire. Whenever their skin is burnt completely,”**). The verse also answers the fantasy of gradual cooling, since a punishment that could taper might be imagined as finite; the denial of lightening removes the taper along with the end. The mind's last refuge — that the sentence might soften by attrition — is closed by name. What remains is the same intensity repeated without interruption. The verse thus describes eternity in the only way a temporal reader can grasp it: as a rate that never changes. Ibn ʿAbbās reports that no respite is granted in which to repent or to prepare a defence. The application is sober: every day of life is the only period in which the administration of mercy is still possible. The two closed exits make the open door of the present valuable beyond measure.

---

## Verse 2:163

> Your God is ˹only˺ One God. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him—the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful

**DESCRIBING THE LORD**

***“Your God is ˹only˺ One God. There is no”*** strips the answer to its skeleton: one object of worship, without division of essence or rank. The confession completes itself with ***“god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him”***, stated both positively and negatively, because nothing else holds a position that is singular by definition. I take the question behind the verse to be the demand to describe the Lord — the answer arrives as description rather than as argument. From Ibn ʿAbbās comes the report that the unbelievers denied this very oneness, so the verse answers a live dispute. What remains is the character of the One, and the verse adds it in two words of mercy. The creed is completed in the same breath in which it is introduced.

**THE SHORTEST CREED**

The answer refuses both errors floating in Mecca: the division of the divine into parts, and the shrinking of the divine into an idol's share of power. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the confession in these terms — one God without son or partner, the Beneficent as the Tender and the Merciful as the Compassionate. The reason the description stops at mercy rather than continuing into majesty is instructive, because the questioners wanted a handle they could grasp; the text gives them a relation they must enter. The creed is short enough for a child and deep enough for a theologian, and the verse intends both readers at once. Because the description is revealed rather than negotiated, the mercy named at the end stands on the same footing as the oneness named at the start. (112:1 — **“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “He is Allah—One ˹and Indivisible˺”**)

**ONE STANDARD, ONE ADMINISTRATION**

A hearer may ask whether a God described only as One and Merciful governs anything as serious as the warnings before this verse. The objection dissolves once mercy and judgment are read as one policy, because the One who seals the condemned at death is the same One who holds the door open for the whole of life. Severity in the earlier verses is mercy's property boundary, not a rival to it. The oneness of God includes the oneness of His administration: one law of return, one hour of closing, one standard applied to every soul. The tender description is therefore not decoration placed between warnings; it is the ground of both the warnings and the offers. Fear and hope share one root. The objection can also be turned around: it is precisely because the One is merciful that the warnings are terrible, since a universe governed by indifference would have no need of them. The breath spent on the warning is itself a form of the mercy named at the close. Because the same names govern both passages — the warnings before this verse and the tenderness inside it — the reader is invited to hold them together rather than to choose between them. A creed that keeps only the mercy becomes sentiment, and a creed that keeps only the severity becomes despair; the verse supplies the proportion in ten words.

**RECEIVED, NOT COMPOSED**

The exaltedness of the One is named again in (39:4 — **“He is Allah—the One, the Supreme”**), and the two statements together fix the confession's register. Ibn ʿAbbās narrates that the unbelievers denied the divine oneness because it excluded son and partner, which means the verse answers the objection at its root. The application is simple and permanent: whoever worships one God lives under one standard, and the mercy at the verse's end is the mercy to which every reader of the warnings is invited while there is still breath to answer with. The invitation is dated by the same grammar that dates the warnings. The hearer is not asked to compose a theology but to receive one. The creed's brevity is itself an argument against the alternatives on offer, because the divided divine of Mecca required a priesthood to manage its contradictions while the One requires only a servant to answer. Because the answer is short enough to carry into every prostration, the verse gives the worshipper a creed that survives travel, fear, and the hour of death. The theology is received in the same posture the prayer demands. The confession closes on the character of the One: ***“the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful”***.

---

## Verse 2:164

> Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth; the alternation of the day and the night; the ships that sail the sea for the benefit of humanity; the rain sent down by Allah from the skies, reviving the earth after its death; the scattering of all kinds of creatures throughout; the shifting of the winds; and the clouds drifting between the heavens and the earth—˹in all of this˺ are surely signs for people of understanding

**THE OPEN-AIR CATALOGUE**

***“Indeed, in the creation of the heavens”*** begins a catalogue that never leaves the observable world. The verse moves through ***“and the earth”*** and into ***“the alternation of the day”***, ***“and the night”***, then turns to human commerce itself with ***“the ships that sail the sea”*** and their cargo, ***“for the benefit of humanity”***. Nothing in the list is hidden or rare, which means the demand for one spectacular sign is answered by an inventory of spectacles already in every eye. The catalogue reads as an answer to a demand for proof, and the answer is given in kind: the proof asked for is the proof already standing in the open air. The demand for the exotic is answered with the essential.

**SIGNS STACKED IN ORDER**

The arrangement walks from the largest frame down to the household table. As Ibn ʿAbbās reports, the alternation of night and day includes their increase and decrease through the seasons, so even time is shown to be administered rather than automatic. After the ships the verse turns skyward with ***“the rain sent down by Allah from the skies, reviving the earth after its death”***, and then to the population of the revived land with ***“the scattering of all kinds of creatures throughout”***. The earth needs the rain, the rain wakes the soil, the soil spreads the creatures, and the system is kept running by ***“the shifting of the winds”*** and ***“and the clouds drifting between the heavens”*** and ***“and the earth”***. The summary is compressed into ***“˹in all of this˺ are surely signs”*** for ***“for people of understanding”***. Comprehension is the response the signs require, and the verse names the reader's task as plainly as it names the signs. (31:31 — **“Do you not see that the ships sail ˹smoothly˺ through the sea by the grace of Allah”**)

**WHY NO SINGLE MIRACLE**

A hearer may ask why no single miracle is granted instead of this long inventory. The objection assumes that one miracle would be more persuasive, but a wonder is witnessed once while a sign is read daily. The catalogue functions so that nobody stands outside the evidence; the alternation of day and night witnesses at every moment, and the loaded ship witnesses at every port. Because each item is ordinary, the excuse of rarity is removed; because each item is essential, the excuse of irrelevance is removed as well. The reader who cannot find a sign in the ship's cargo or the rain's return would not find one in a splitting moon either, because the problem would be the eye and not the evidence. This is the difference between an event that startles a crowd and a system that educates a lifetime. The verse would rather teach than startle. The inventory also answers the demand for signs at the right scale, because the demand was for a private spectacle while the answer is a public system. A private spectacle can be denied by the witnesses who missed it; the alternation of night and day cannot be missed by anyone alive. The catalogue therefore shifts the question from the availability of proof to the disposition of the reader, which is the only variable the verse leaves open. The signs themselves are unanimous, and the comprehension named at the close is the reader's contribution.

**READING THE ORDINARY**

The dead ground is drawn as evidence in its own right in (36:33 — **“There is a sign for them in the dead earth: We give it life, producing grain from it for them to eat”**). Ibn ʿAbbās transmits the note that the clouds are subservient between heaven and earth, moving wherever the command sends them, and that the winds change direction by the same ordinance — sometimes carrying torment and sometimes mercy. The application is practical: look at the ordinary with the attention others reserve for the extraordinary, because the ordinary is where the administration of the One is most continuously visible. The signs were never hidden; what changes is the eye that reads them. The verse trains the eye rather than supplying the missing object. The comprehension the verse names is available to anyone willing to think through what they already see. The verse leaves the willing reader with no missing evidence and the unwilling reader with no available excuse.

---

## Verse 2:165

> Still there are some who take others as Allah’s equal—they love them as they should love Allah—but the ˹true˺ believers love Allah even more. If only the wrongdoers could see the ˹horrible˺ punishment ˹awaiting them˺, they would certainly realize that all power belongs to Allah and that Allah is indeed severe in punishment

**TWO KINDS OF LOVE**

***“Still there are some”*** introduces the people whose religion is attachment. The verse names it in two movements: ***“who take others as Allah’s equal”*** and then ***“they love them as they should love Allah”***. Against them stand the believers, ***“but the ˹true˺ believers love Allah even more.”*** The comparative is the hinge of the verse, because it does not merely rank the two loves; it predicts their behaviour. The difference between them is discovered in what each love survives, and the verse stages the discovery as a public test. The ranking that hides in the heart in this world becomes the visible order of the next. The verse therefore refuses to let the ranking stay private, and the public test becomes the means of the discovery.

**WHAT PRESSURE REVEALS**

The devotees of equals love them as God is loved, yet when hardship arrives those same equals are abandoned, while the believers never reject God — so the claim of love is weighed by its endurance. The verse stages a courtroom for loves: each one testifies under pressure, and the counterfeit witness collapses. Ibn ʿAbbās reports the substance of the warning — those who take equals to Allah love them with a love owed to Him alone. The exposure continues in the verse's closing wish: ***“If only the wrongdoers could see the ˹horrible˺ punishment ˹awaiting them˺, they would certainly realize”*** that the betrayal has a price. The clause ***“that all power belongs to Allah”*** names what the wrongdoers fail to see, and the weight lands in the final beat: ***“and that Allah is”***, ***“indeed severe in punishment”***. Power and punishment are two faces of one seriousness. (9:24 — **“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If your parents and children and siblings and spouses and extended family and the wealth you have acquired”**)

**GIFTS VERSUS ALTARS**

A hearer may ask whether loving what God gives can become a form of loving equals. The verse does not condemn affection; it condemns rank. Loving family or wealth as gifts is gratitude, but loving them as the decisive loyalty of one's life installs them at the altar, and that installation is what the verse calls taking equals. Enjoying the warmth of a fire is one act; bowing to it is another. The test is not how strong the affection is but what it does when it collides with obedience. The moment of collision is where the ranking appears. The verse's severity therefore targets the ranking rather than the feeling, and its comfort is that the believers' love is not weaker — it is simply placed correctly. The pressure-test explains the verse's setting: the ranking of loves decides the ranking of outcomes, and the outcome the verse names is severe. The image of the courtroom is therefore not decoration; it is the literal shape of the Day in which the ranking becomes visible to everyone at once. The heart cannot keep two supreme loyalties, because the moment they collide one of them is obeyed and the other is revealed as second. The verse describes the second love exactly, and its description doubles as a diagnosis: the equals are loved in the place reserved for Allah, which means the love is real but its address is wrong. Because the believers' love is proven by what it survives, the comparative is falsifiable — it can be checked against the hardest day of one's own life. The check is the application the verse asks for.

**THE EMPIRICAL TEST**

The condition of true love is stated plainly in (3:31 — **“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If you ˹sincerely˺ love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you and forgive your sins.”**). The transmission of Ibn ʿAbbās adds that the equals are loved with the magnification owed to the One alone. I read the comparative as evidence rather than ornament: measure the loves by their behaviour on the hard day, when obedience costs something, because that is the only scale the verse trusts. The comparative therefore invites the reader to check the data of his own loyalty. The check costs nothing and settles the ranking of the heart in one sitting. The evidence of love is what it refuses to abandon. The heart that keeps its ranking keeps its peace, and what Allah is to the heart is shown by what the heart will not give up.

---

## Verse 2:166

> ˹Consider the Day˺ when those who misled others will disown their followers—when they face the torment—and the bonds that united them will be cut off

**LEADERS DISOWNING FOLLOWERS**

***“˹Consider the Day˺ when those”*** opens a courtroom scene in which the relationship of leader and follower is taken apart publicly. The first act is the repudiation: ***“who misled others will disown their followers”***, and the reason arrives at once with ***“when they face the torment”***. The verse then widens the collapse from one relationship to all of them with ***“and the bonds that united them will be cut off”***. The entire network of loyalty that made the misguidance possible is switched off in full view. Influence is a loan, and the Day calls it due. The verse insists on the timing: the bonds are cut at the moment the torment is seen, which is the moment the borrowed trust can no longer produce anything for its borrower.

**BONDS CUT IN PUBLIC**

The cutting of the bonds is grammatically joined to the act of disowning, so the leaders do not merely speak against their followers — the affection and kinship that bound them on earth are severed in front of them. The horror is the exposure: the loyalties that felt permanent are shown to have been conditional all along. Ibn ʿAbbās reports that "all their aims" means the pledges and congeniality between them in this world, so even the private warmth of the group is entered as evidence. The leader who borrowed the follower's trust to purchase compliance must answer for the account. Since the cutting precedes the accusations, neither party's excuse survives the opening of the scene. The network that carried the lie is displayed as the mechanism of the lie. (33:67 — **“And they will say, “Our Lord! We obeyed our leaders and elite, but they led us astray from the ˹Right˺ Way”**)

**SHARED PROJECT, SHARED TRIAL**

A hearer may ask whether the followers are not also victims of their leaders and therefore excused. The verse refuses the excuse without refusing the leaders' guilt, because the follower's will is not destroyed by influence — it is courted by it. Every follower chose the pleasing answer over the true one, so the disowning exposes a shared project rather than a one-sided fraud. The leaders receive the heavier charge for initiating; the followers answer for their willing participation. Both are told the truth at the same moment, which is itself a form of justice. The scene is not two trials but one, with the bonds of conspiracy displayed as exhibits. The verse also removes the comfort of anonymity from the misguiders, because a bond severed in public is a relationship confessed in public. Each party is shown holding the end of the rope that tied the other to the ruin. The exposure is social because the crime was social; the group that carried the lie is gathered as a group to answer for it. Because the cutting happens before the accusations begin, the excuses of both parties are answered in advance. The network that carried the lie is displayed as the mechanism of the lie. The verse's own sequence draws the line: the leaders disown first, and the followers' cry comes next. This is the difference between victim and partner.

**INFLUENCE AS A LOAN**

The followers' counter-charge is recorded in (34:31 — **“The lowly ˹followers˺ will say to the arrogant ˹leaders˺, “Had it not been for you, we would certainly have been believers.””**). Ibn ʿAbbās reports that both the leaders and the lowly behold the doom together. The scene also explains why the choice of companions matters so much in the passages around this one: the bonds of a group are the transmission lines of its judgment, and when the lines are cut, each person stands alone with what he chose to believe. The application is sobering for anyone with influence and honest for anyone under it. Use the bond while it exists for the truth, because the bond itself is temporary property. The two audiences are addressed by the same scene: the leader answers for what he taught, and the follower answers for what he agreed to hear. Because the bonds are severed at the door of the torment, the partnership is proven to have been real and to have ended exactly where its usefulness ended. Every chain of influence will be measured by where it ended.

---

## Verse 2:167

> The ˹misled˺ followers will cry, “If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them as they disowned us.” And so Allah will make them remorseful of their misdeeds. And they will never ˹be able to˺ leave the Fire

**A CHANCE ASKED TWICE**

The previous verse showed the leaders repudiating their followers; this one gives the reply. ***“The ˹misled˺ followers will cry, “If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them”*** is the exact shape of their wish — not to escape the Fire outright, but merely to change sides in the argument. The verse closes their sentence with ***“as they disowned us.””***, so the repudiation they request is the same act they have just suffered. The wish is symmetrical to the injury, and that symmetry is the verse's quietest cruelty: they want only a matching revenge. The cry is recorded in the followers' own words, so the record cannot be suspected of exaggeration by their sympathisers. Their vocabulary of regret is the proof that comprehension arrived too late to become guidance. The verse therefore counts comprehension as a resource with an expiry date attached.

**WISH GRANTED AS REGRET**

The particle at the head of the wish is optative — a wish for what cannot be — and its grammatical answer is the repudiation they would perform if granted the return. God's actual answer is named in the next clause: ***“And so Allah will make them remorseful of their misdeeds.”*** The counterfactual is granted as anguish rather than as travel, and the deeds are shown to them wrapped in regret. Ibn ʿAbbās reports that both the leaders and the followers see their deeds in this state, so the exposure is shared even though the wish belongs to the followers. The clause that ends the matter is absolute: ***“And they will never ˹be able to˺ leave the Fire”***. Return requires the world, and the world is closed. The permanence is not a verdict imposed on the wish; it is the condition of the place where the wish is spoken. The wish travels backward to a door that has already been shut, which is why the verse calls the deeds anguish rather than calling the punishment the cause of their pain. The regret is informational as well as painful — the deeds are shown as they are, without the story the followers used to tell about them. (6:27 — **“If only we could be sent back, we would never deny the signs of our Lord”**)

**KEPT ON RECORD FOR THE LIVING**

A hearer may ask why the wish is recorded at all if it can never be granted. Recording it serves two purposes at once. The first is documentary: the followers' complaint is entered so that no party claims the record was edited by the victors. The second is pedagogical: every reader still inside a life holds the second chance the dead now beg for, and the verse prices that possession by showing the empty hands on the other side of the door. The wish appears in the perfect position — between the disowning and the permanence of the Fire. This is the difference between envying the dead nothing and envying the living everything; the hearers are meant to realize which side of the exchange they stand on. Recording the wish also closes every excuse of imitation, because the alternative is exactly what they wish for. A hearer who copies the followers after reading their wish cannot claim the road was unmarked.

**ENVIED BY THE DEAD**

The mutual blaming is drawn again in (34:31 — **“when the wrongdoers will be detained before their Lord, throwing blame at each other!”**), and Ibn ʿAbbās reports from his side that the leaders and followers alike will not emerge once they have entered. The application is to spend the possession the dead envy: the second chance is not a promise for later but an inventory for now, and the repudiations worth performing today are the ones the verse's speakers would give anything to perform. The wish on record is therefore an asset belonging to the reader, and its value rises with every breath. Their own mouths certify the case. The wish is on record so that the living can spend it. The door is open where they are standing, and the door is priced by the hands shown reaching for it too late. The inventory of the present is therefore the reader's possession, counted in breaths.

---

## Verse 2:168

> O humanity! Eat from what is lawful and good on the earth and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. He is truly your sworn enemy

**EAT WHAT IS LAWFUL AND GOOD**

***“O humanity! Eat from what is lawful”*** addresses all people with an order to eat, which is itself the answer to a piety that forbids what God has given. The permission is doubled by quality: ***“and good on the earth”***, so the lawful is not merely permitted but wholesome and pleasant. Then the verse names the source of the invented prohibitions with ***“and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. He is truly your sworn”*** and closes with the single word ***“enemy”***. In the reading transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, the embellishments of the enemy concerned exactly these goods — the cultivation of land and the raising of cattle — declared forbidden by whispering rather than by revelation. The structure is gift, boundary, and diagnosis. The order matters, because the gift comes first: the people are fed before they are warned, so the warning arrives from a generous hand rather than from a grudging one.

**ANSWERING INVENTED TABOOS**

The distortion had taken the form of piety: the more a person forbade, the holier they appeared, and the only cure for that competition is a divine permission that cannot be outbid. Ibn ʿAbbās reports the setting in concrete terms — the claim covered cultivation and cattle alike, and the verse reopens what the whisperings had closed. The reason the verse answers with permission rather than argument is that the additions were not a heightening of devotion but an insult to the Lawgiver. A law that grows without its author is a law that has found a new author, and the verse names the new author as the enemy. The order to eat is therefore an act of legislation as much as an act of kindness: it restores the boundary of the law at the same time as it fills the table. That is why the enemy's method is named as footsteps: a path walked step by step, so that each small prohibition leads the walker further from the open ground of the gift. The permission is also a test of gratitude, because the person forbidden everything can perform holiness at no cost while the person permitted everything must practise thankfulness all day. The lawful is also named good, which places pleasure and piety on the same side. The earth is a table set by a host, and the meal is one of its invitations. (16:114 — **“So eat from the good, lawful things which Allah has provided for you, and be grateful for Allah’s favours,”**)

**DISCIPLINE VERSUS LEGISLATION**

A hearer may ask whether refusing food cannot be a legitimate discipline of the soul. Discipline is legitimate as a choice and blasphemous as a law. The one remains inside the permission and simply uses it lightly; the other rewrites the permission, and that rewriting is the enemy's work. Fasting today is discipline; declaring bread unlawful forever is legislation. Because the permission is God's to give, it is also God's to revoke, and a servant's veto cannot register in His register. The verse protects both gratitude and authority: gratitude by ordering the good to be eaten, authority by reserving the definition of lawful to its source. The lawful is called good as well, so pleasure and piety are not rivals. The earth is a table set by a host.

**NAMED AS AN ENEMY**

The enmity named here is expanded in (35:6 — **“so take him as an enemy. He only invites his followers to become inmates of the Blaze”**), and Ibn ʿAbbās's transmission states that the devil's whisperings against cultivation and cattle are the specific content of the footsteps to avoid. The application is to treat the good as good: to eat gratefully, to work honestly, and to hold every prohibition to the standard of the text that enacts it. The footsteps to avoid are the ones that trade a generous law for a flattering strictness. The trade flatters the trader and starves the household, and the verse reopens the table it closed. Because the enemy is named, the reader can refuse him by name. The table is reopened as a gift, and the gratitude is its reply. The verse keeps both sides of that answer in view: eat from the good, and remember the hand that made it good.

---

## Verse 2:169

> He only incites you to commit evil and indecency, and to claim against Allah what you do not know

**THE ENEMY'S CURRICULUM**

***“He only incites you to commit evil”*** names the first item of the enemy's programme in its broadest form, and the second narrows the field: ***“and indecency, and to claim against Allah what you”***, closing with ***“do not know”***. The list is exhaustive in its logic. The first item covers what harms the self, the second covers what harms the community, and the third covers the corruption of the standard by which both are judged. The claim of what is not known turns the whole curriculum into forgery: the speaker cites a source that has not spoken. Ibn ʿAbbās reports the three items in these terms — evil works, foulness, and a lie about Allah of which the claimer knows nothing.

**FORGERY AS THE SEAL**

The first two items are ordinary crimes; the third is treason in the court itself, because it forges the judge's signature. The forbidden and the permitted cannot be corrected until the source of the list is trusted, so the forgery disables the reader's entire moral instrument. I read the word that caps the list as doing this work: the curriculum is bounded, there is nothing else in the enemy's school. The pairing of evil and indecency also covers the private and public faces of harm, so the list leaves no corner of conduct unaddressed before it turns to the forgery that blesses both. The effect of the third item is that the sinner takes comfort in a permission that was never given, which is a heavier ruin than sin committed knowingly. The forgery is worse than the crime because it recruits the standard itself into the defence. A sinner who knows he sins may yet repent; a sinner who has been told God permits his sin has been robbed of the alarm that makes repentance possible. Because the third item corrupts the measuring instrument, the first two items can be repeated without felt cost. This is why the curriculum is named as one programme rather than three temptations: the items support each other, and the third one licenses the other two. (4:119 — **“I will certainly mislead them and delude them with empty hopes. Also, I will order them”**)

**CHECKING THE CLAIM**

A hearer may ask how a claim about God can be checked at all, since nobody hears the divine voice directly. The claim is checked the same way the earlier verses checked their signs — by the received text and the transmitted standard, which is why the passage keeps returning to what God has actually said. The Book defines the permitted and the forbidden in explicit passages, so an added prohibition is not a mystery but a mismatch, and the mismatch is visible to anyone comparing the claim with the source. The test is textual and public: the forgery is caught at the register of revelation, not by private intuition. The unknowing claim is answered by the knowing recitation. Because the forger needs the first two sins to populate the world he invents, the claim about God seals the curriculum and makes it look legitimate.

**THE FORGERY SELF-DOCUMENTED**

The content of the enemy's command is drawn again in (24:21 — **“then ˹let them know that˺ he surely bids ˹all to˺ immorality and wickedness. Had it not been”**). Ibn ʿAbbās reports that what is claimed is a lie of which the claimer knows nothing, and the sequence of the list explains the placement: the claim is the seal that makes the whole programme look legitimate. Because the claim is of what the claimer knows not, it carries its own refutation inside its grammar — the speaker certifies his ignorance in the same sentence in which he speaks for the divine. The lie is therefore self-documenting. The application is a habit of verification: before accepting any prohibition or permission attributed to God, ask for the text that enacts it. The habit is small enough to practise on every claim and sharp enough to end the enemy's third item on contact. Evil, indecency, and forgery form one curriculum, and the entry fee is attention. The exit fee is the habit of verification, which costs the reader a question and saves him a creed, and the fee is paid in full the first time the habit is kept.

---

## Verse 2:170

> When it is said to them, “Follow what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “No! We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.” ˹Would they still do so,˺ even if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance

**INHERITED PRACTICE**

***“When it is said to them, “Follow what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “No!”*** stages the whole argument in one line: a revealed command is met with a refusal that offers no text in return. The substitute appears next: ***“We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.” ˹Would they still do so,˺ even”***, and the verse cuts the defence at its root with ***“if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance”***. Inheritance of a practice proves nothing about its truth, which means the verse separates the two questions the reply had fused: how old a thing is, and how true it is. Ibn ʿAbbās reports the double question in three forms, all of them pressing on the fathers' lack of religion and guidance.

**AN ADMISSION OF POSITION**

The addressees kept the practices of the dedicated camel and the slit ear, dedicating animals to their gods by custom rather than by revelation. The reply "we follow our fathers" is therefore not neutral conservatism; it is the specific defence of a ritual economy.
