Because the promise of response is attached to the call, the discipline of asking is itself an act of faith in the nearness. The one who stops asking has quietly stopped believing in the reply. The two conditions are therefore one habit in two directions.

**GUIDANCE AS THE OUTCOME**

The verse ends where the Qur'an's invitations usually end: perhaps they will be guided ˹to the Right Way˺. The guidance is the product of the whole exchange — the nearness believed, the call made, the obedience returned — and the particle of hope leaves the door open. The application is to treat every prayer as the conversation the verse describes: addressed to the near, answered by the near, and closed with obedience. The listener who keeps a record of answers will find the nearness confirmed by experience as well as by text. Because the answer comes in the first person, the believer's private address is met by a personal reply. The One who proclaimed the invitation has guaranteed the channel. The guarantee is worth testing in the smallest cases as well as the largest, because the verse's promise is attached to the call and not to the size of the need. The servant who asks for help in an ordinary hour is standing inside the same nearness as the servant who asks in the worst one. Because the response is promised before the servant speaks, the silence of the moment is never evidence of the absence of the answer. The response can arrive as a gift, as a redirection, or as strength to endure, and the verse does not narrow the forms it may take. The servant's part is to keep the channel open in all three shapes of the reply. The keeping is the obedience the verse names, and it is measured in the prayer that continues after the first unanswered hour.

---

## Verse 2:187

> It has been made permissible for you to be intimate with your wives during the nights preceding the fast. Your spouses are a garment for you as you are for them. Allah knows that you were deceiving yourselves. So He has accepted your repentance and pardoned you. So now you may be intimate with them and seek what Allah has prescribed for you. ˹You may˺ eat and drink until you see the light of dawn breaking the darkness of night, then complete the fast until nightfall. Do not be intimate with your spouses while you are meditating in the mosques. These are the limits set by Allah, so do not exceed them. This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to people, so they may become mindful ˹of Him˺

**PERMITTED IN STAGES**

Read in sequence, the passage's phrases release the night and fence the day: ***“It has been made permissible”***, ***“for you to be intimate with your wives during the nights preceding the fast. Your spouses are a garment”***, ***“for you as you are”***, ***“for them. Allah knows”***, ***“that you were deceiving yourselves.”***, ***“So He has accepted your repentance”***, ***“and pardoned you. So now you may be intimate with them”***, ***“and seek what Allah has prescribed”***, ***“for you. ˹You may˺ eat”***, ***“and drink until you see the light of dawn breaking the darkness of night”***, ***“then complete the fast”***, ***“until nightfall. Do not be intimate with your spouses”***, ***“while you are meditating in the mosques. These are the limits set by Allah”***, ***“so do not exceed them. This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to people”***, ***“so they may become mindful ˹of Him˺”***. The sequence releases first and fences second, which is the order mercy keeps: the gift of the household arrives before the boundary of the retreat. The permissions and the fences alternate exactly as the day and the night alternate in the month governed here. The report on Ibn ʿAbbās's side keeps the same order of permissions and fences.

It has been made permissible for you to be intimate with your wives during the nights preceding the fast. reads like a simple permission, but its shape is a history. The ruling arrived after an earlier practice in which the fasting person ate, drank, and slept only at night and left the intimacy of the night as well, and the permission is recorded as a release from that harder discipline. The movement of the law is from strictness to ease, and the ease is dated to the nights that surround the fast rather than to the fast itself. The night is given back to the household, and the day is given to the discipline. The verse keeps both halves visible so that neither can swallow the other. Because the permission is placed at the head of the passage, the month of fasting is established as a month of households and not of retreat alone. The lawful boundaries of the household's days are drawn with the same care as the fences of the retreat (2:222 — **“and do not have intercourse with your wives during their monthly cycles until they are purified. When they purify themselves,”**)

**GARMENT FOR BOTH SIDES**

The verse's most quoted line — Your spouses are a garment for you as you are for them — describes the marriage with the image of the closest covering a person owns. The garment hides the body's faults from the world, keeps warmth inside, and is worn rather than displayed, which is three qualities of a good marriage in one noun. Ibn ʿAbbās's wording on the image is brief: the spouses are a repose for one another, which is the interior of the garment — the comfort no one outside sees. The symmetry of the phrasing refuses the household where one side is clothed and the other bare; each covers the other or neither is dressed. Because the image is placed in the fasting month's legislation, the discipline of the day is answered by the mercy of the night. The garment image also settles the question of priority inside the household, and the mercy named beside the comfort keeps the priority gentle (30:21 — **“so that you may find comfort in them. And He has placed between you compassion and mercy. Surely in this are signs”**): the covering runs in both directions or the household is undressed. A marriage where one spouse is the garment and the other is merely worn is not the marriage the verse describes, and the month of fasting will expose it quickly. The one who spends the days hungry and the nights cold has misread the permission that opens the passage. The verse hands the night back to the household with both hands.

**SECRETS THAT WERE KNOWN**

Allah knows that you were deceiving yourselves. So He has accepted your repentance and pardoned you. places the permission in the language of forgiveness, which is where its history is kept. The believers had been living under the stricter practice and testing its edges, and the verse announces that the testing was known and is now pardoned. The pardon is not a verdict on desire but on the self-deception that hid behind the stricter rule — the habit of pretending to be stronger than the law's mercy required. Because the acceptance is announced before the new permission, the permission arrives as pardon rather than as concession. The sequence teaches the reader how revelation works with the conscience: the weakness is named, the pardon is given, and the ruling is changed. The household enters the month forgiven and released.

**THREADS AT DAWN**

The timing of the fast is drawn as a visible boundary: and drink until you see the light of dawn breaking the darkness of night and then then complete the fast until nightfall. The dawn is described in the image of its threads — the white thread of light against the black thread of night — and the report preserved in al-Bukhārī puts the metaphor in the Prophet's own practical terms: each person has a white thread and a dark thread before the eyes, and the fast begins when they can be told apart. The rule is written for the eye rather than for the clock, so the boundary is public and the month keeps one time across a whole city. Because the nightfall closes the fast rather than the sunset's afterglow, the discipline ends in the darkness where the permission began.

**RETREAT BEHIND A LIMIT**

The retreat in the mosques is drawn with its own boundary: Do not be intimate with your spouses while you are meditating in the mosques. The retreat is a state of devotion with edges, and the edges are the doors of the mosque. The one who enters the retreat steps out of the permissions of the household for the days of the devotion and steps back in when the retreat ends. The verse does not abolish the household but sequences it, and the sequence is the meaning of the limit. Because the retreat and the intimacy are both lawful in their seasons, the unlawful act is only the overlap. The practice of the retreat, preserved in the reports of the month's final days, keeps the boundaries exactly where this verse places them.

**LIMITS THAT TEACH**

The close of the passage names the whole system: These are the limits set by Allah so do not exceed them. The permissions and prohibitions of the month are presented as one architecture — the night given, the day kept, the dawn measured, the retreat fenced — and the architecture is a revelation like the verses read at night. The application is to keep the month in its pieces: to eat at the lawful hour, to return to the household at the lawful hour, and to leave the retreat at the door the verse draws. The one who exceeds the limits is not more pious than the law; he is outside the mercy that made the law's shape. Because the limits are made clear to people, the failure to keep them is never an accident of geography. The month is a set of doors, and the doors are instructions. There is one more lesson in the passage's architecture worth naming: every permission arrives with its hour, which trains the believer to think of rulings as schedules rather than moods. The person who treats the law as a schedule keeps it when the mood fails. Because the schedule is published, the household can plan its worship and its tenderness together, and the planning is itself an act of devotion. The month ends with its limits intact and its members closer to the One who drew them. The passage as a whole is one of the clearest demonstrations in the chapter of how the law works: a permission, a purpose, a boundary, and a reminder, all in one breath. The four elements belong together, and the household that keeps them together keeps the month as it was designed. The household that keeps them discovers the same trust the legislation assumes: a law drawn in this detail is a law meant to be lived in. The passage also answers the person who complains that the month's rules are complicated: the rules are few, and each one protects a good the reader already values — the body, the marriage, the worship, and the calendar. Because every rule names its good, the complexity dissolves the moment the household reads the purposes aloud.

---

## Verse 2:188

> Do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly, nor deliberately bribe authorities in order to devour a portion of others’ property, knowing that it is a sin

**WEALTH UNDER A NAME**

The verse's phrases name the property, the trick, and the knowledge in order: ***“Do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly”***, ***“nor deliberately bribe authorities in order to devour a portion of others’ property, knowing”***, ***“that it is a sin”***. The walk moves from the ownership to the courtroom to the conscience, and each phrase deepens the charge by naming one more layer of the act. The anatomy of the crime is the indictment's evidence, and every phrase adds a layer to the charge. The event named on Ibn ʿAbbās's authority stands behind the whole sequence. The property named first is somebody's actual livelihood, the trick named second steals it through the courthouse, and the knowledge named third convicts the hand that signed the paperwork.

Do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly is a negative built on an ownership the passage admits before the prohibition starts: the wealth belongs to one another, which means the household is full of property with names attached. The consumption prohibited is the quiet kind — the margin taken without a contract, the share reduced without a witness. The second prohibition sharpens the first by adding the courtroom: nor deliberately bribe authorities in order to devour a portion of others’ property. The bribe is described as deliberate and the target as a portion, so the corruption is calculated rather than impulsive. The verse refuses the whole pipeline from theft to verdict, because the verdict is where theft acquires a document. Because the command is addressed to believers, the corruption being policed is the corruption inside the community's own transactions.

**THE BRIBE DISGUISED AS LAW**

The bribe's particular evil is its costume: the money moves in the dark and returns as a ruling, so the victim is robbed by an authority he is required to trust. The verse sees through the costume by describing the purpose — to devour a portion of others' property — which is theft's purpose wearing judgment's clothes. The legislation of trusts and judgment stands against exactly this exchange, commanding that trusts be returned to their owners and that people be judged with justice (4:58 — **“Indeed, Allah commands you to return trusts to their rightful owners; and when you judge between people,”**). The bribed judge is the anti-witness of the previous passage: instead of standing firm against payment, he stands for sale. Because the ruling family of verses calls judgment a trust, the purchased verdict is a double theft — the property and the law at once. The corruption cannot be repaired by the ruling it produced; the money must go back and the case be heard again.

**KNOWING MAKES IT WORSE**

The verse's last words carry the indictment: knowing that it is a sin. The knowledge is part of the act, so the corruption is done with the scale in the doer's hand. This is the difference between the ignorant transgressor and the calculating one, and the verse addresses the second. The report of Ibn ʿAbbās names the event behind the law — two men and an estate dispute in which the property was consumed in vanity — and the law refuses to let the paperwork of such cases stand. Because the sin is known, the excuse of confusion is removed before it is offered, and the only remaining question is the doer's repentance. The One who counts the portions counts the knowledge with them.

**FIRE AS THE ACCOUNTANT**

The threatened account is drawn in the imagery the Qur'an reserves for the devourers of other people's property: the consumption of the unjust is answered with consumption of another kind. The orphan's wealth, swallowed without right, is described as fire carried in the belly, and the image returns in the legislation of the vulnerable's property (4:10 — **“Indeed, those who unjustly consume orphans’ wealth ˹in fact˺ consume nothing but fire into their bellies.”**). The equality of the image is the justice of it: the mouth that swallowed the wrong share receives the share it deserves. The application is therefore practical and not poetic — to examine the estate, the contract, and the courtroom before the money moves, because the examination done in this world is cheaper than the one prepared for the next. The honest man's margin is small and his fear is large; the corrupt man's margin is large and his account is fire. The verse's warning therefore works in both directions at once: it discourages the bribe and it comforts the victim, since the verdict purchased in this world is scheduled for reversal in the next. Because the sin is known at the moment of the payment, the repentance must include the money returned and the case reopened. The estate that was devoured is owed its portion back before the bellies are emptied of anything else. The verse's audience includes the officials as well, since a marketplace without bribes is built by the refusals of the judges as much as by the honesty of the traders. The one who refuses the envelope protects the whole street's faith in the courthouse.

---

## Verse 2:189

> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the phases of the moon. Say, “They are a means for people to determine time and pilgrimage.” Righteousness is not in entering your houses from the back doors. Rather, righteousness is to be mindful ˹of Allah˺. So enter your homes through their ˹proper˺ doors, and be mindful of Allah so you may be successful

**PHASES IN THE SKY**

From first phrase to last, the answer moves from the sky to the doorway: ***“They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the phases of the moon. Say, “They are a means”***, ***“for people to determine time”***, ***“and pilgrimage.” Righteousness is not in entering your houses from the back doors. Rather, righteousness is to be mindful ˹of Allah˺.”***, ***“So enter your homes through their ˹proper˺ doors”***, ***“and be mindful of Allah”***, ***“so you may be successful”***. The order of the walk is itself the argument: the phases are demoted to a calendar before the doorway is commanded, so the reader carries no omen to the door. The reader who walks these phrases leaves with two commands and one definition to live by. Ibn ʿAbbās's reading of the moon-question follows the same route.

They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the phases of the moon. records a question about irregularity: the moon thins, swells, and vanishes, and the questioners want to know what the irregularity means. The answer removes the omen and installs the instrument: Say, They are a means for people to determine time and pilgrimage. The phases are a clock and a calendar, not a message about anyone's fortune. The sun and the moon run by measure everywhere the Qur'an describes them, and the measuring is the point (10:5 — **“He is the One Who made the sun a radiant source and the moon a reflected light, with precisely ordained phases,”**). Because the question came from a people who read irregularity as portent, the reply is a liberation: the sky keeps time and the believer keeps his deeds. The moon is demoted from oracle to clock, and the demotion is a mercy.

**TWO DOORS OPEN**

The verse then pivots to a practice of the questioners themselves: they entered their houses from the back doors during the ritual state, treating the front door as ritually charged. The reply dismantles the superstition at its root — the ritual state does not reverse architecture — and the command is stated plainly: So enter your homes through their ˹proper˺ doors. The practice shows how a piety of taboos grows: a prohibition nobody legislated becomes a custom, and the custom becomes a test of devotion. The verse answers the whole trajectory by pointing to the doorway of the house and saying, in effect, that the pious person enters normally. The cosmos and the household are governed by one law, and the law is not startled by a door. Because the superstition is corrected alongside the moon-question, both are examples of one error: reading divine meaning into things God has made functional.

**PIETY IS NOT A RITUAL WALK**

The verse's definition is among the most quoted in the chapter: righteousness is not the back-door entrance but the character described after it. The ritual gesture is displaced by the interior disposition — mindfulness — and the displacement is complete enough to change the layout of the house. The companion tradition preserved in al-Bukhārī warns against inventing rituals the law never legislated, and the back-door practice is exactly such an invention. The piety of taboos flatters its practitioner because the taboos are visible; the piety of mindfulness is quieter and harder. Because the verse keeps the definition negative first — righteousness is not this — the reader learns to suspect his own theatrical habits before trusting them. The test of a ritual is whether it makes the person kinder at the door he walks through every day.

**ENTERING WITH INTENTION**

The close gathers the passage into one instruction: and be mindful of Allah so you may be successful. The mindfulness named at the end is the same element the fasting legislation names as its purpose, and the consistency is the reader's map. The application is to enter — the house, the month, the marketplace — as one person, with the same face at the door and behind it. The phases keep the calendar, the doors keep the house, and the mindfulness keeps the person; the three lines of the verse are one system. Because success is attached to mindfulness rather than to ritual dexterity, the poorest practitioner can be the most successful. The moon does not know your name; the One who set its phases does. The verse's two answers therefore share one theology: the sky is made functional and the person is made moral. The reader who consults the phases for his calendar is doing exactly what the verse teaches, and the reader who consults them for his fortune has wandered into the error the verse corrects. Because the correction arrives as a command about doors, the superstition is defeated by the ordinary — the most reliable weapon the revelation owns. The same weapon answers the modern superstitions that dress themselves in the language of science while reading the sky for luck. The verse sends the reader back to the clock and the conscience. The two returns are the verse's whole method: the sky is demoted to a clock so that the conscience can be promoted to the judge.

---

## Verse 2:190

> Fight in the cause of Allah ˹only˺ against those who wage war against you, but do not exceed the limits. Allah does not like transgressors

**PERMISSION WITH A BOUNDARY**

The permission's phrases stand in a deliberate order of cause, target, limit, disposition: ***“Fight in the cause of Allah ˹only˺ against those who wage war against you”***, ***“but do not exceed the limits. Allah does not like transgressors”***. Reading the permission in this order keeps the fence attached to the verb, since the limit arrives before the disposition that guards it. A permission memorized without its fence is a different permission entirely, and the walk keeps them together. Ibn ʿAbbās's wording on the condition is confirmed by the order of these phrases. The commander who holds the four elements in one memory holds the permission as it was granted and not as the campaign's momentum would prefer to remember it.

Fight in the cause of Allah ˹only˺ against those who wage war against you grants a permission and fences it in the same breath. The cause is Allah's, the targets are defined by their own aggression, and the second clause — but do not exceed the limits — turns the permission into a legal category with edges. The verse was revealed in the setting recorded after the pact of Hudaybiyya, when the community was prevented from the House and then promised its return, and the permission to fight belongs to that refusal and the pressures that followed it. The permission is granted to the wronged rather than to the strong, which is the logic of the legislation on fighting everywhere it appears (22:39 — **“Permission ˹to fight back˺ is ˹hereby˺ granted to those being fought, for they have been wronged.”**). The cause and the target are both required; the one who fights the wrong enemy has left the permission's fence.

**AGAINST THE AGGRESSORS ONLY**

The defining phrase is doing the work of the entire law of war: the criterion is aggression, not identity. Ibn ʿAbbās's wording keeps the condition in view — the command is against those who initiate fighting against you, and the prohibition follows: begin not hostilities. Because the criterion is behavioral, it can be applied by anyone with eyes, and the soldier is spared the task of sorting peoples instead of sorting acts. The permission's fence is therefore practical: the one who has not waged war is outside the verse's target, whatever his other faults. The same logic appears in the prohibition against killing those who do not fight, and in the treaties the mission honored even with its enemies. The defining phrase functions as a standing court for every commander.

**DISLIKED AND NAMED**

The close of the verse gives the limit its theology: Allah does not like transgressors. The dislike is named in a sentence attached to the boundary, so the one who exceeds the limit does not merely break a rule — he acts against the divine taste. The phrase returns in the legislation on the lawful and the forbidden, where the same dislike guards the boundary from the other side: do not forbid what God has made lawful, and do not transgress (5:87 — **“Allah does not like transgressors”**). The two boundaries — the battlefield's and the table's — are therefore guarded by one disposition of God toward the transgressor. Because the dislike is stated in the middle of the permission's verse, the permission itself is to be exercised with fear. The soldier who reads the closing words fights differently from the one who stops at the middle.

**A LIMIT INSIDE THE ORDER**

The verse's arrangement — cause, target, limit, dislike — is a compressed manual, and each element corrects the one before it. The cause corrects the target, the target corrects the cause, and the limit corrects the strength. The application is to read the whole sentence before acting on the verb: the fight belongs to a cause that is not the fighter's ego, against an aggressor the fighter did not choose, within limits the fighter did not draw. The one who cannot find all three elements in his situation stands outside the permission. Because the permission is granted in the cause of Allah, the fighting is a duty of protection rather than a sport of conquest. The boundary is the meaning of the permission. The verse is worth reading against the war-songs of every age, because the permission is written for the wronged and the songs are usually sung by the strong. The one who quotes the first clause without the second has purchased a weapon the verse does not sell. Because the limit is stated by the same voice that grants the permission, the soldier's discipline is a matter of obedience and not of taste. The permission travels with its fence. The verse is short enough to be memorized in a minute and strict enough to govern a campaign, which is the standard proportion of the chapter's laws. The one who memorizes the verb and forgets the fence has memorized half a verse and armed himself with the dangerous half. The chapter's method is to give permissions their boundaries in the same breath, and this verse is the clearest instance of the method.

---

## Verse 2:191

> Kill them wherever you come upon them and drive them out of the places from which they have driven you out. For persecution is far worse than killing. And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque unless they attack you there. If they do so, then fight them—that is the reward of the disbelievers

**RETURNING TO THE HOMES**

The command's phrases trace the map from the first return to the last reward: ***“Kill them wherever you come upon them”***, ***“and drive them out of the places from”***, ***“which they have driven you out.”***, ***“For persecution is far worse than killing.”***, ***“And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque”***, ***“unless they attack you there.”***, ***“If they do so”***, ***“then fight them”***, ***“that is the reward of the disbelievers”***. The walk runs from the homes to the sanctuary and ends at the payment owed to the one who refuses the peace, which is the whole map in miniature. The orientation between two cities and one sanctuary is the discipline the command requires of its reader. The condition Ibn ʿAbbās records is visible in the order of the phrases.

Kill them wherever you come upon them and drive them out of the places from which they have driven you out. reads as an order of restoration: the verb of the second half answers the verb of the first, and the city's map is being put back. The expulsion of the believers from their homes is the wound the verse addresses, and the return is the closing of that wound. The report of Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the condition in view — the slaying is for those who start the fighting — and the expulsion is measured against the one already suffered. Because the verse names the places of the driving-out, the return is not conquest but restitution: the evicted come back to what was theirs. The command's symmetry is its justice, and the symmetry is the reason the verse can be read as the end of an exile rather than the beginning of a war.

**EXPELLED AND REPLACED**

The two expulsions — theirs of the believers, the believers' of them — are stated in one verse so that no memory can keep only one. The verse that follows names the deeper conflict beneath the physical one, since the persecution the believers endured was designed to separate them from their worship. The scripture's complaint against the persecutors is therefore theological before it is territorial: the crime of the expulsion is that it was aimed at the religion. Because the believers were driven out for their worship, the return restores the worship along with the homes. The community that re-enters the city carries the mission that was being suppressed, and the restoration is complete only when the mission stands where it stood. The geography of the verse is measured in the direction of the worship.

**PERSECUTION WEIGHS MORE**

The verse states its own hierarchy in the middle of the command: For persecution is far worse than killing. The comparison is deliberate — the killing of a body ends, while the persecution of a religion continues inside every life it touches. The claim returns in the later legislation on the sacred months, where the same weights are used to answer the question of fighting during them (2:217 — **“For persecution is far worse than killing. And they will not stop fighting you until they turn you away from your faith—if”**). Because the hierarchy is stated twice in the chapter, it is meant to govern the reader's judgment in every case where the two goods are weighed. The one who forbids resistance to persecution has inverted the scales the revelation has calibrated twice. The verse does not glorify killing; it locates it on the lesser pan.

**A SHIELD AROUND THE SANCTUARY**

The command carries its own sanctuary law: And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque unless they attack you there. The mosque is granted a peace that overrides the general permission, and the exception is only the attack that breaks the peace first. The arrangement shows the mission's own priorities — the sanctuary is sacred even to those who denied its sanctity — and the restraint is the verse's proof of the point. Because the permission is limited by the sanctuary, the army of the verse is an army with a conscience and a map. The application is to read the permission together with its exceptions before quoting its verbs, since the exceptions carry the mercy the verbs lack. The one who fights inside a sanctuary after reading this verse has read half of it. The careful reader keeps the shield in place. The shield's existence is the proof that the permission was designed by a mind that also designs sanctuaries. The verse's restoration logic also answers the accusation that the mission was a war for territory: the territory named is the territory lost, and the verb that governs the map is the verb of return. Because the exile is the wound, the return is the healing, and the healing is the verse's purpose. The one who re-reads the passage from the first expulsion will find the whole command standing on one injury. The injury is named in the verse itself, and the naming is what keeps the permission from becoming a mood.

---

## Verse 2:192

> But if they cease, then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**IF THEY CEASE**

The short verse divides cleanly into its two phrases, and both are needed: ***“But if they cease”***, ***“then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”***. The first phrase is the condition and the second is the promise, and neither phrase can stand in the verse without the other. Both halves of the short verse carry the mercy together, and the walk spends a breath on each. The two destinies Ibn ʿAbbās draws out are the two phrases in sequence. The mercy of the short verse is the mercy of a gate that stays open while the person can still walk, and the walk keeps the gate visible from both sides. The two halves of the verse hold the condition and the promise in one breath.

The whole verse is one condition and two names: But if they cease, then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful. The brevity is the mercy's posture — the gate is stated without decoration so that the one who turns can see it at once. The cessation named is the cessation of the conflict described in the surrounding passage, and the forgiveness is aimed at those who stop and turn. On Ibn ʿAbbās's reading, the short verse carries two destinies: forgiveness for the one who turns to Allah in life, and mercy for the one who dies in the state of repentance. The pairing of the names covers the whole path of the return — the turning and the ending alike. Because the condition is placed between two commands to fight, the reader cannot mistake the war's purpose: the purpose is the cessation.

**FORGIVENESS IN THE SHORT VERSE**

The verse's placement does the argument: it follows the permission to fight and precedes the command to end the persecution, so the war is bracketed by mercy on both sides. The structure answers the accusation that the passage loves violence — the passage gives violence a stopping point in the very center of its grammar. The forgiveness offered is not a reward for defeat but a door for reform, and the door stays open while the person can walk. The application is to read the two names as the war's intended end-state: the fighting is a medicine whose health is the forgiveness. Because the names are all-forgiving and most-merciful, the returning enemy is treated as a guest rather than as a prisoner of the verse. The short verse is the passage's conscience. Its brevity is worth imitating in the moments the reader must offer an exit to an opponent: the shorter the sentence, the sooner the door is seen. The verse models the speech of mercy as much as the doctrine of it. The reader who offers an exit in the verse's own economy — short, open, and unconditional in tone — is imitating the rhetoric the revelation uses for repentance.

**THE SWORD OF TWO EDGES**

The verses on either side give the stopping condition its teeth: the fight continues until the persecution ends, and the moment it ends the hostility must end with it. The community's adversary in the spiritual register is described in the same period as the party that causes the forgetting of remembrance, and the forgetting is the persecution of the heart (58:19 — **“causing them to forget the remembrance of Allah. They are the party of Satan. Surely Satan’s party is bound to lose”**). The one who fights to restore remembrance cannot then fight the one who has remembered. Because the sword's second edge cuts the warrior's own aggression, the verse trains an army that can stop. The stopping is the harder skill and the one the verse rewards with the divine names.

**CEASEFIRE AND REPENTANCE**

The close of the reading returns to the condition: the ceasefire is the political act, and the repentance is the interior one, and the verse treats them as one motion. The one who stops the outward persecution but keeps the inward enmity has met half the condition; the forgiveness is attached to the whole of it. The application is to offer the exit before the battle as well as after it, because the gate named in the verse does not depend on who is winning. Because the names are attached to the condition rather than to the battlefield, the mercy is available on the day of weakness as well as the day of strength. The verse keeps the light on for the returning. Because the condition is placed at the center of the military passage, the war's own scripture dates the peace, and the dating is the mercy's appointment. The two names at the end are also the answer to the shame that keeps people from returning at all. Because the forgiveness is all-forgiving and the mercy is most-merciful, the one who turns is met by an attribute rather than by a grudge. The gate is small in words and total in reach. The application is to believe the names as they stand: to treat the returning person as the person the names describe, and to leave the verdict to the One who signed it.

---

## Verse 2:193

> Fight against them ˹if they persecute you˺ until there is no more persecution, and ˹your˺ devotion will be to Allah ˹alone˺. If they stop ˹persecuting you˺, let there be no hostility except against the aggressors

**UNTIL THE PRESSURE ENDS**

The phrases of the command run from the persecution to the aggressor in order: ***“Fight against them ˹if they persecute you˺”***, ***“until there is no more persecution”***, ***“and ˹your˺ devotion will be to Allah ˹alone˺.”***, ***“If they stop ˹persecuting you˺, let there be no hostility except against the aggressors”***. The walk keeps the destination in view while the exception is stated, so the aggression is answered and the war is never left without its stopping rule. The phrases are drawn tightly enough to hold in memory when the road gets loud. Ibn ʿAbbās's transmission keeps the condition in view throughout the sequence. The war is dated by its purpose because the purpose is the only element of the command that can outlast the campaign and judge it afterwards.

Fight against them ˹if they persecute you˺ until there is no more persecution sets a destination rather than describing a pleasure. The end of the fighting is written into the fighting's purpose: the command runs until the persecution stops, which means the war is a means with an expiry date built in. The second phrase supplies the definition of the peace that follows — and ˹your˺ devotion will be to Allah ˹alone˺. — so the destination is a state of worship rather than a map of territory. The fight is therefore aimed at a condition of the soul: the persecution that blocks devotion must end so the devotion can stand. The verse's logic answers those who read the passage as an open license, since the license expires at the moment the persecution expires. The pressure is the measure of the command.

**DEVOTION AS THE DESTINATION**

The verse's goal — devotion to Allah alone — is the same goal the whole chapter has been building since its creed. The persecution named here is the pressure that prevents the devotion, and the relief of the pressure is the purpose of the fighting. The later legislation on guardianship in the community states the alternative in social terms: if the believers do not hold together, great oppression and corruption spread in the land (8:73 — **“As for the disbelievers, they are guardians of one another. And unless you ˹believers˺ act likewise, there will be great oppression”**). Ibn ʿAbbās's transmission keeps the condition in view throughout: the fighting answers the persecution and stops at its end. Because devotion is the destination, the army is a construction crew as much as a defense force, and the building is the freedom to worship. The one who fights for any other destination has wandered outside the verse's sentence.

**NO HOSTILITY AFTER VICTORY**

The condition of the peace is stated with the same precision as the condition of the war: If they stop ˹persecuting you˺, let there be no hostility except against the aggressors. The hostility is cut off at the moment the persecution is cut off, and the remainder is reserved for those who continue to aggress. The arrangement protects the returning party and disciplines the victorious one, which is the double duty of a just ceasefire. Because the exception names the aggressors, the hostility cannot be generalized to their families, their cities, or their posterity. The application is to date the end of the enmity by the end of the persecution and not by the mood of the crowd. The verse's army knows when to stop because the stopping date is written inside the purpose clause. The date of the ceasefire is written into the purpose clause, which is the most civilian thing about this military law. The one who keeps the purpose in view keeps the calendar in view too. The verse is also a standing correction to every army that forgets its purpose clause in the heat of its success.

**THE AGGRESSOR EXCLUDED**

The final clause is the ceasefire's police force: the aggression that continues after the peace is answered within the law, and the answer is limited to the aggressor. The crying of the oppressed elsewhere in the legislation is what the whole system exists to end — the children who ask to be delivered from the land of oppressors have their answer in this verse's freedom (4:75 — **“And what is it with you? You do not fight in the cause of Allah and for oppressed men, women,”**). Because the oppression of the vulnerable is the persecution the war targets, the peace that follows must not contain a new oppression. The application is to hold both clauses with one hand: to stop when the pressure stops, and to pursue the aggressor who refuses to stop. The verse keeps its eyes open until the road is safe. The safety is the point of every line of the passage: the persecuted freed, the devotion restored, and the road watched. Because the three goods are named in order, the commander can audit the campaign against the verse rather than against the momentum. The application is to write the purpose clause at the top of every decision made under pressure. The purpose clause is the verse's gift to the commander and the citizen alike, and it outlasts the campaign it governs. Because the pressure ends at a stated line, the decision made under it can be audited after the road is safe.

---

## Verse 2:194

> ˹There will be retaliation in˺ a sacred month for ˹an offence in˺ a sacred month, and all violations will bring about retaliation. So, if anyone attacks you, retaliate in the same manner. ˹But˺ be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is with those mindful ˹of Him˺

**SACRED AGAINST SACRED**

Read phrase by phrase, the ruling settles the sacred month and the violation together: ***“˹There will be retaliation in˺ a sacred month”***, ***“for ˹an offence in˺ a sacred month”***, ***“and all violations will bring about retaliation.”***, ***“So, if anyone attacks you, retaliate in the same manner. ˹But˺ be mindful of Allah”***, ***“and know that Allah is with those mindful ˹of Him˺”***. The sequence answers the hesitation first, generalizes the retaliation second, and offers the patience third, which is the shape of a ruling addressed to a conscience. The ruling meets the doubt at the level it was raised, which is the level of law. The account of Ibn ʿAbbās on the companions' hesitation matches this order. The companions' conscience is treated as an asset of the community rather than as a nuisance, and the ruling answers it in the currency of law.

˹There will be retaliation in˺ a sacred month for ˹an offence in˺ a sacred month answers the question the companions raised about fighting in the sacred months. The objection behind the question was pious — the month is sacred, so how can the sword enter it? — and the reply makes the sanctity symmetrical: the aggression in the sacred month is answered in the sacred month, and the holiness is not a shield for the one who violates it. The third clause generalizes the principle: and all violations will bring about retaliation. The sacred is thus protected by the sacred law of retaliation rather than exempted from law. Because the companions' hesitation is recorded in the reports, the verse addresses the conscience that fears being unjust inside a holy season. The reply honors the conscience by giving it a rule instead of a rebuke.

**THE COMPANIONS' HESITATION**

The occasion is preserved in the reports of the year the verse answered: the believers had fought a party during one of the sacred months and the doubt arrived with the news. The response was measured in the cause as well as the calendar, since the enemy's aggression had begun in the month and the fight was the answer to it. The reported wording of Ibn ʿAbbās keeps both halves of the ledger: the month of the ʿumra they were prevented from is answered in the month of the prevention. The doubt itself is a sign of the community's conscience, and the revelation answers it with the equality of the sacred months. Because the answer is procedural rather than emotional, the conscience is given a way to act without being told to stop feeling. The doubt of the companions is therefore part of the verse's meaning: a community that doubts its own violence is a community fit to carry the permission. The revelation answers the doubt with a rule and keeps the doubters as the verse's first audience. Because the answer respects the conscience, the rule is obeyed by people who understand it.

**EQUAL MEASURE**

The retaliation rule is stated twice — the sacred month for the sacred month, and the attacks in kind — and the repetition is the law's symmetry. The principle appears in the general legislation of recompense: if you retaliate, the retaliation must equal the injury (16:126 — **“If you retaliate, then let it be equivalent to what you have suffered. But if you patiently endure, it is certainly best”**). The equality is the boundary that separates retaliation from revenge, and the boundary is drawn by the injured party's own restraint. Because the measure is fixed, the punishment cannot grow as it travels down the family line, and the feud is stopped by arithmetic. The application is to count before answering: the answer is permitted in the measure of the injury and not in the measure of the anger. The one who answers beyond the measure has entered the verse's prohibition.

**PATIENCE AS THE BETTER VERDICT**

The close of the verse offers the second path alongside the first: ˹But˺ be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is with those mindful ˹of Him˺. The patience named in the legislation of recompense is placed here as the better verdict for the one who can carry it, and the promise attached is the company of Allah. The forgiveness of the strong is praised in the system's economics as the higher exchange, since reconciliation is repaid by the One who does not like wrongdoers (42:40 — **“The reward of an evil deed is its equivalent. But whoever pardons and seeks reconciliation,”**). Because both paths are offered, the verse treats the injured person as a moral agent rather than a mechanism of revenge. The application is to weigh the two verdicts in the hour of the injury — the equal answer and the pardoned one — and to know that the scales are held by Allah. The mindful person retires the case in the better court. The verse's double offer is also a discipline for the one who retaliates: the equal measure is the ceiling and the patience is the invitation. Because the ceiling is enforced by the reminder of Allah, the retaliator answers his own anger before he answers his enemy. The two verdicts of the verse — the equal answer and the pardoned one — are both lawful, which is the range the conscience is trusted to navigate. The application is to know the range before the hour of the injury arrives.

---

## Verse 2:195

> Spend in the cause of Allah and do not let your own hands throw you into destruction ˹by withholding˺. And do good, for Allah certainly loves the good-doers

**SPENDING AS SURVIVAL**

The verse's three phrases move from the spending to the ruin to the love: ***“Spend in the cause of Allah”***, ***“and do not let your own hands throw you into destruction ˹by withholding˺.”***, ***“And do good, for Allah certainly loves the good-doers”***. The walk is a complete economy in three moves: the command to release, the warning against the hold, and the valuation of the character the release builds. Any household budget can be checked against these three moves in a single afternoon. The warning Ibn ʿAbbās unpacks is the sequence read aloud. The three phrases are worth reading before every pledge of money, because the pledge sits between the ruin and the love whichever way the hand decides. The hand decides in the pledge's very hour.

Spend in the cause of Allah is written in the imperative of survival rather than of charity. The clause that answers it — and do not let your own hands throw you into destruction ˹by withholding˺. — identifies the withholding as the danger, so the person who keeps everything is the person at risk. The destruction named is the ruin that arrives when the community's defense, its poor, and its worship have no funding. The report transmitted through Ibn ʿAbbās unpacks the warning in the setting of the mission's expenses: the one who withholds from the cause risks the ruin the verse names. Because the hands are named as the instruments of the destruction, the withholding is an act and not a state. The verse's accountancy is long-term: the treasure kept is the person endangered, and the treasure spent is the person saved.

**YOUR OWN HANDS**

The verse blames the hands the money sits in, which is the chapter's most economical description of how wealth destroys its owner. The hand that refuses to release the dinar is the hand that throws the person into the ruin, and the causation is stated as a single motion. The surrounding legislation of spending returns to the rhythm of the donation — day and night, secretly and openly — and the rhythm is the opposite of the hoarder's freeze (2:274 — **“Those who spend their wealth in charity day and night, secretly and openly—their reward is with their Lord, and”**). Because the danger is self-inflicted, the verse's warning can be heard before the crisis arrives. The application is to practice the release while the hand is steady, so the hand learns the motion before it is needed. The one who waits for the emergency to be generous has practiced his whole life for the wrong act.

**WITHHOLDING AS DESTRUCTION**

The definition of destruction here is social as well as personal: the community that cannot fund its obligations begins to lose them one by one, and the loss is the destruction moving through the body. The verse's order — spend first, warn second — puts the command at the head of the sentence so the warning is heard as its explanation. The close of the passage converts the warning into character: And do good, for Allah certainly loves the good-doers. The good-doer is the person whose hands have learned the motion of release, and the love attached to the character is the verse's highest valuation. Because the doing of good is placed after the spending, the spending is the first exercise of the character. The destruction and the love are separated by one habit.

**LOVE FOR THE GOOD-DOERS**

The closing word of the verse is a love, and its placement is the argument's last move. The one who spends in the cause is described as a good-doer and loved, and the one who withholds is described as standing near destruction. The pairing refuses the accountancy of the miser, where the money kept is the self kept; the revelation counts the kept money as the thrown self. The cooperation the wider legislation commands — in goodness and righteousness rather than in sin and aggression — makes the same judgment in social terms (5:2 — **“who once barred you from the Sacred Mosque provoke you to transgress. Cooperate with one another in goodness and righteousness,”**). Because the love is named at the end, the motive of the spender is allowed to include it: the servant may spend to be among the loved. The application is to set the budget of the cause before the budget of the appetite, and to let the hands practice the verse's verb every month. The destruction is avoided by the same hands that could have caused it. The symmetry of the verse is complete: the hand that threw the person toward the ruin is the hand that pulls him back. The verse's budget of the person is worth reciting when the accounts are drawn at the year's end: what was spent on the cause is listed beside what was spent on the appetite, and the two columns tell the truth. Because the hands are named, the budget is a moral document as well as a financial one. The verse's warning is addressed to the community's accounts as well as its souls, since a cause with empty hands is a cause at the edge of the ruin the verse names. The application is therefore organizational as well as personal.

---

## Verse 2:196

> Complete the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage for Allah. But if prevented ˹from proceeding˺, then ˹offer˺ whatever sacrificial animals you can afford. And do not shave your heads until the sacrificial animal reaches its destination. But if any of you is ill or has a scalp ailment ˹requiring shaving˺, then compensate either by fasting, charity, or a sacrificial offering. In times of peace, you may combine the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage then make the sacrificial offering you can afford. Whoever cannot afford that ˹offering˺, let them fast three days during pilgrimage and seven after returning ˹home˺—completing ten. These offerings are for those who do not live near the Sacred House. And be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is severe in punishment

**CONTRACTS OF ARRIVAL**

The contracts of the passage are drawn phrase by phrase, from arrival to the reminder: ***“Complete the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage”***, ***“for Allah. But if prevented ˹from proceeding˺”***, ***“then ˹offer˺ whatever sacrificial animals you can afford.”***, ***“And do not shave your heads”***, ***“until the sacrificial animal reaches its destination.”***, ***“But if any of you is ill”***, ***“or has a scalp ailment ˹requiring shaving˺”***, ***“then compensate either by fasting, charity”***, ***“or a sacrificial offering. In times of peace, you may combine the pilgrimage”***, ***“and minor pilgrimage then make the sacrificial offering you can afford. Whoever cannot afford”***, ***“that ˹offering˺, let them fast three days during pilgrimage”***, ***“and seven after returning ˹home˺”***, ***“completing ten. These offerings are”***, ***“for those who do not live near the Sacred House.”***, ***“And be mindful of Allah”***, ***“and know that Allah is severe in punishment”***. The order of the contracts is the order of the traveller's day: the intention, the blockage, the animal, the hair, the combination, the counting, and the mindfulness. Each phrase meets the pilgrim at the hour of the journey it actually governs. The purpose Ibn ʿAbbās states for the two rites governs the whole sequence.

Complete the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage for Allah. opens a passage of contracts, and the first contract is completion. The two rites are named together and aimed at Allah, so the intention is the offering's first ingredient. Ibn ʿAbbās states the purpose of the two rites in exactly those terms: they are performed sincerely for Him and carried to their full completion, and the completion is what the imperative demands. The verse does not describe arrival as the achievement; arrival is where the contract begins. The pilgrim who reaches the precinct and quits the rites has entered the contract without finishing it, and the law follows the unfinished contract with its remedies. Because the two rites share the verse, the minor pilgrimage borrows the major one's discipline and the major one keeps its own completion. The worship is a promise with a shape.

**PREVENTED BY ENEMY**

The first remedy answers the pilgrim who is stopped on the road: But if prevented ˹from proceeding˺, then ˹offer˺ whatever sacrificial animals you can afford. The prevention named in the reports is the prevention by an enemy — the community was held back from the House — and the law responds to the blocked pilgrim with an offering rather than a reproach. The offering is measured by capacity, so the poor traveler is inside the ruling as well as the wealthy one. The sequence preserves the contract by substituting its object: the journey ends, the offering continues it. Because the prevention is not the pilgrim's fault, the remedy carries no blame, only the animal. The blocked traveler learns that the law has a place for him at the very moment the road refuses him.

**HAIR AND ITS RANSOM**

The ritual of the hair is fenced with a timing rule: And do not shave your heads until the sacrificial animal reaches its destination. The shave is the rite's completion signal, and the offering must arrive before the signal is given. The verse then answers the pilgrim whose body breaks the rule's patience — illness or a scalp ailment — with a ransom measured in the familiar three: fasting, charity, or a sacrifice. The ransom formula appears in the legislation of violations at the House, where the penalty for the broken discipline of the ihram runs through the same three currencies (5:95 — **“fasting so that they may taste the consequences of their violations. Allah has forgiven what has been done. But those”**). Because the ransom is available, the ailment is a case and not a catastrophe. The hair waits for the offering or is bought back; the two paths keep the rite intact.

**COMBINING THE TWO PILGRIMAGES**

The verse turns to the case of peace, where the pilgrim can perform both rites together: In times of peace, you may combine the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage then make the sacrificial offering you can afford. The combination is legislated as an economy of travel, and the offering remains the constant that both rites share. The permission to combine arrived with the practice preserved in the reports of the farewell pilgrimage, where the Prophet taught the rites to the assembled thousands. Because the combination is offered in times of peace, the war's prevention and the peace's ease are both answered inside one verse. The application is to plan the rites by the verse's ladder — completion, prevention, combination — and to know where the traveler stands before the first step. The rite that is designed with its exceptions is a rite the whole community can keep.

**COUNTING THE FASTS**

The pilgrim who cannot afford the offering receives his own arithmetic: let them fast three days during pilgrimage and seven after returning ˹home˺, completing ten. The counting is stated in full so that nobody has to guess, and the split — three on the road, seven at home — respects the traveler's condition. The verse's numbers are a mercy of precision: the penance is bounded, dated, and completable, which is the shape of every ease in the passage. Because the ten are divided by the state of the person, the law legislates around the body rather than against it. The one who reads the numbers as a burden has missed their direction: they are the ceiling of the obligation, not its floor. The fasts are a bridge the poor pilgrim walks home on. The three-and-seven arrangement is also a lesson in the sequencing of duty: the road's share is kept on the road, and the home's share waits for the home. The verse treats the traveler's energy as a real quantity, and the legislation bends around it without cancelling the debt. The arrangement is one of the clearest demonstrations in the passage that the law measures people before it measures them against the law. Because the counting is done for the traveler, the duty arrives as a schedule rather than as a burden. The one who keeps the ten days in their two homes has kept the whole contract.

**SEVERITY ALONGSIDE MERCY**

The close of the passage refuses to end in softness alone: And be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is severe in punishment. The severity is placed beside the mercy of the remedies so that the rulings are kept for their Giver's sake and not only for their convenience. The reminder of the punishment is the verse's final instrument, aimed at the pilgrim who would skip the offering once the rites are done. Because the mercy and the severity share the close, the pilgrim leaves the passage with both hands full: the remedies of the law and the fear of the Lawgiver. The application is to settle the contract before leaving the precinct — to shave only when the offering is safe, and to count the fasts before counting the days home. The rites end where the verse ends, in mindfulness. The reminder of the punishment at the close is the verse's final service to the pilgrim: it keeps the contracts alive in the memory after the road has emptied. Severity at the end and mercy in the middle is the passage's whole architecture, and the pilgrim who has walked it once will recognize the shape in every ruling that follows. Because the contracts outlast the rites, the journey is judged after the traveler is home. The passage's protections — the blocked pilgrim's offering, the ailment's ransom, the poor traveler's counted days — form one policy of accommodation that runs from the road to the doorway. The policy exists because the rites were designed for real travelers with real bodies, and the design is visible in every exemption. The one who finishes the rites in any of these forms has finished them lawfully.

## Verse 2:197

> ˹Commitment to˺ pilgrimage is made in appointed months. Whoever commits to ˹performing˺ pilgrimage, let them stay away from intimate relations, foul language, and arguments during pilgrimage. Whatever good you do, Allah ˹fully˺ knows of it. Take ˹necessary˺ provisions ˹for the journey˺—surely the best provision is righteousness. And be mindful of Me, O people of reason

**MONTHS WITH NAMES**

The verse's phrases frame the journey: the months, the tongue, the sack, the reason: ***“˹Commitment to˺ pilgrimage is made in appointed months. Whoever commits to ˹performing˺ pilgrimage, let them stay away from intimate relations, foul language”***, ***“and arguments during pilgrimage. Whatever good you do, Allah ˹fully˺ knows of it. Take ˹necessary˺ provisions ˹for the journey˺”***, ***“surely the best provision is righteousness.”***, ***“And be mindful of Me, O people of reason”***. The frame runs from the calendar at one end to the conscience at the other, and the provisions are named between them so nothing travels outside the frame. Every item on the packing list is named before the departure date arrives. The months named in the account Ibn ʿAbbās transmits open this sequence. The tongue's discipline during the rites is legislated beside the body's discipline, and the pairing shows the ihram covering the person from both directions at once.

˹Commitment to˺ pilgrimage is made in appointed months. gives the rite a place on the calendar and the calendar a purpose in worship. The transmission of Ibn ʿAbbās names the months precisely — Shawwāl, Dhū'l-Qaʿda, and the first ten of Dhū'l-Ḥijja — so the consecration of the ihram has named doors rather than vague seasons. The naming matters because the rites are public: the whole community travels on the same schedule, and the schedule is the beginning of the discipline. The appointed months answer the one who would keep the pilgrimage as a private errand; the rite arrives with a crowd. The obligation of the House is stated in the same public terms (3:97 — **“and the standing-place of Abraham. Whoever enters it should be safe. Pilgrimage to this House is an obligation by Allah upon whoever”**) Because the months are known, the preparation is possible — the traveler can free his calendar and his debts before the ihram begins. The worship is dated by the One who set the phases that measure the dates.

**SILENCE OF THE PILGRIM**

The verse defines the ihram of the tongue as sharply as the ihram of the dress: let them stay away from intimate relations, foul language, and arguments during pilgrimage. The prohibition covers the body and the conversation at once, which is the pilgrim's double dress. The reports of the farewell pilgrimage preserve the same teaching in practical form, where the assembled thousands were taught the rites and warned against the lewdness the verse names. Because the arguments are forbidden in the rite, the journey to the House is a rehearsal of the peace the House represents. The one who cannot hold his tongue has entered the ihram with his clothes and left his character at home. The verse's discipline is therefore social as well as personal: the crowd is kept holy by the words its members do not say.

**PROVISION THAT DOES NOT WEIGH**

The verse then mentions the traveler's sack and gives it a surprising content: Take ˹necessary˺ provisions ˹for the journey˺ and then surely the best provision is righteousness. The provision is not abolished but ranked, since the physical sack is necessary and the moral sack is best. The ranking answers the two failures at once: the pilgrim who travels with no food and the pilgrim who travels with no fear. Because the best provision is named, the traveler is taught to check his bags twice — once for the road and once for the heart. The application is to pack the verse's two provisions in the order it gives them: enough for the body's journey and the righteousness that makes the journey a worship. The one who carries the best provision cannot be stranded. The provision-image also corrects the modern habit of treating the pilgrimage as a travel product: the verse counts the sack and the character in one packing list. Because the best provision is named, the traveler can weigh his bags against the verse before the departure date. The rites the traveller keeps are valued on the same scale (22:30 — **“That is so. And whoever honours the rituals of Allah, it is best”**) The weighing is the first rite of the journey, and the verse sets the scale before the road begins.

**REASON AS THE AUDIENCE**

The close addresses the audience by its capacity rather than its rank: And be mindful of Me, O people of reason. The address is to the intellect the journey is meant to sharpen, since the rites are a curriculum of remembrance for people who think. The pilgrimage's geography — the standing, the walking, the stoning — is designed for the mind that can read it. Because the audience is the people of reason, the ritual is not a mystery to be endured but a text to be understood. The application is to arrive at the rites with questions and to leave with answers, since the verse expects the reason to be used. The mindfulness asked for at the end is the provision named in the middle. The two halves of the verse frame the journey: the calendar at the head and the conscience at the close. The application is to travel inside that frame — dated and mindful — and to let the rites teach the reason rather than silence it. The pilgrim who returns with more questions than he left has used the verse's equipment. Because the equipment is provision and righteousness together, the journey is measured twice — once by the sack and once by the soul. The application is to travel inside that frame and to let the rites teach the reason.

## Verse 2:198

> There is no blame on you for seeking the bounty of your Lord ˹during this journey˺. When you return from ’Arafât, praise Allah near the sacred place and praise Him for having guided you, for surely before this ˹guidance˺ you were astray

**TRADE IS NOT BLAMED**

Read in its phrases, the passage permits the trade and blesses the descent: ***“There is no blame on you”***, ***“for seeking the bounty of your Lord ˹during this journey˺.”***, ***“When you return from ’Arafât, praise Allah near the sacred place”***, ***“and praise Him for having guided you”***, ***“for surely before this ˹guidance˺ you were astray”***. The walk balances the marketplace against the plain: the bounty is permitted in the first phrases and the gratitude is commanded in the last. The pilgrim carries both halves of this economy on the same road home. The objection Ibn ʿAbbās records is answered in the order of these phrases. The trade permitted in the first phrases funds the journey the last phrases sanctify, and the pilgrim's gratitude is the seam between the two halves.

There is no blame on you for seeking the bounty of your Lord ˹during this journey˺. answers an objection the first generation raised in earnest: the merchants feared that trading during the pilgrimage diluted the worship. The verse's reply is a release from that scruple — the bounty sought lawfully is not a stain on the rites — and the release is addressed to the conscience that had begun to forbid what God allowed. The report of Ibn ʿAbbās places the objection concretely: a group stood against buying and selling in the Sacred Precinct, and the verse settled their scruple without mocking it. Because the objection was pious, the answer is gentle: no blame, no lecture, and the commerce restored. The worship of the journey includes the traveler's livelihood, and the two are not rivals in the account of the One who sent both. The hours of remembrance and the hours of commerce belong to one schedule (3:191 — **“˹They are˺ those who remember Allah while standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens”**)

**OBJECTING TO COMMERCE**

The scruple's logic deserves its answer stated slowly: if the House is holy, should the market stand outside it? The verse replies by refusing the partition — the sacred precinct is not a monastery, and the servant of Allah trades where he stands. The permission is placed beside the remembrance that follows it, so the day of the pilgrim contains both the coin and the prayer. Because the One who invites the pilgrim also feeds him, the transaction at the shrine is a transaction between the guest and the Host's other guests. The application is to bring the whole self to the rites and to keep the whole self honest: trade as one who will stand at ʿArafāt, and stand at ʿArafāt as one who must trade. The scruple is answered by the calendar and the coins in the same verse.

**DEPARTING AS ONE CROWD**

The verse's second movement is a scene of departure: When you return from ʿArafât, praise Allah near the sacred place. The standing at ʿArafāt is the rite's summit, and the descent from it is the pilgrim's re-entry into motion. The remembrance is commanded at the sacred monument, so the memory of the standing travels with the crowd. The reported practice of the Prophet at the descent — teaching the assembled pilgrims to take their rites from him — marks the monument as a classroom. Because the remembrance is attached to the geography, the departure is a liturgy and not an evacuation. The application is to mark the descent with the verse's own act: to praise and to remember the guidance that led the body to the plain. The crowd leaves the plain carrying one voice. The voice is the verse's final provision for the road home. Because the remembrance is commanded at the monument, the geography of the rites is stored with the words spoken over it, and the pilgrim can return to the plain by returning to the phrase. The application is to keep the phrase of the descent as a permanent possession of the year. The one who praises for the guidance keeps the guidance current.

**GUIDANCE RECALLED**

The close names the content of the praise: and praise Him for having guided you, for surely before this ˹guidance˺ you were astray. The pilgrim's gratitude is specific — he was lost before the guidance — and the specificity is the honesty of the rite. The remembrance of the misguidance is what makes the guidance weighty, and the weight is the fuel of the praise. Because the verse speaks in the past tense, the misguidance is over and the memory is a teacher. The application is to rehearse the before and after at the monument: to name the state one was in and the state the guidance has given. The one who praises for guidance without remembering the wandering praises a word rather than a rescue. The verse's two scenes — the marketplace and the plain — are therefore one economy of gratitude. The bounty that fills the sack and the guidance that fills the heart come from the same Lord, and the pilgrim thanks Him for both on the same road. The application is to hold the commerce and the standing in one schedule of gratitude, since the passage has placed them in one economy. The bounty sought on the road is repaid in the currency the Lord multiplies (2:245 — **“Who will lend to Allah a good loan which Allah will multiply many times over? It is Allah ˹alone˺”**)

---

## Verse 2:199

> Then go forth with the rest of the pilgrims. And seek Allah’s forgiveness. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**STANDING WITH EVERYONE**

The order of the phrases is itself the lesson of the pilgrim's last hour: ***“Then go forth with the rest of the pilgrims.”***, ***“And seek Allah’s forgiveness. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”***. The walk performs the pilgrim's last hour in order: the descent with the crowd and the speech of repentance together, and the order is the rite itself. The emptying plain is the deadline, and the verse keeps the clock visible to the crowd. The custom described by Ibn ʿAbbās is what the first phrases correct. The crowd's movement and the private speech of repentance are joined in the verse so tightly that neither can be performed without the other on that day. The joining is the pilgrim's last instruction.

Then go forth with the rest of the pilgrims. is a one-sentence correction of a tribal habit. The Quraysh used to stand at Muzdalifa and refuse to descend with the other people, and the verse commands the descent with the multitude as one body. The wording recorded by Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the direction clear: go forth from where the people go forth — the people of Yemen and the rest returning together. The command is about posture as well as geography: the pilgrim stands with the crowd rather than above it. Because the rite is designed for the assembled multitude, the exclusivity of the descent was a violation of the assembly's meaning. The verse restores the pilgrim to the human race at the very moment of the worship.

**A TRIBE'S DISTANCE**

The custom being corrected is a form of religious class — the tribe that stands apart at the rites — and the correction is a democratization of the worship. The descent ordered with the people is the rite's way of erasing the distance the tribal mind loves. Because the order is addressed to those who had made a custom of the distance, the verse treats custom as a candidate for correction. The application is to look for the modern versions of the Muzdalifa habit: the rites kept for the family's prestige, the charity kept inside the circle, the mosque kept for the clan. The one who descends with the crowd learns the humility the plain was designed to teach. The verse's road is the crowded one. The crowd is the point: the plain collects the proud and the humble in one garment. The descent with the multitude is therefore a rehearsal of the equality the rites exist to teach, and the rehearsal is performed with the feet. Because the order is given to the tribe that stood apart, the verse's sharpest edge is aimed at religious prestige. The application is to descend from one's own high ground with the same speed the Quraysh were ordered to descend from theirs.

**FORGIVENESS AS THE EXIT**

The second command of the verse is interior where the first was public: And seek Allah's forgiveness. The rite's conclusion is a prayer rather than a ceremony, and the prayer is aimed at the One who forgives the failure of the rites themselves. On Ibn ʿAbbās's reading, the forgiveness is commanded after the descent so that the pilgrim leaves the plain with a clean account. The pairing of the two acts — the descent with the people and the seeking of forgiveness — is the pilgrim's final posture. Because the forgiveness is sought at the exit, the journey's failures are settled before the traveler reaches home. The application is to end the rites where this verse ends them: among the people and in the speech of repentance.

**MERCY AT THE END OF RITES**

The closing names — Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful. — guarantee the answer to the verse's own command. The seeker of forgiveness is met by the names that promise the forgiveness he asks, and the passage closes like a completed circuit. The promise appears in the wider legislation of the return, where the same forgiveness and bounty are offered to the one who fears the stinginess the road tempts him toward (2:268 — **“while Allah promises you forgiveness and ˹great˺ bounties from Him. And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing”**). Because the names follow the command, the pilgrim's last word on the plain is answered before it is spoken. The application is to trust the answer: to descend, to ask, and to leave with the names in the ears. The rites end in mercy because mercy designed them. The verse's pairing of the public descent and the private prayer is worth carrying into every gathering the reader leaves. The crowd and the conscience are settled in one motion, and the motion is the pilgrim's last rite. Because the forgiveness is promised by name, the exit from the plain is an exit into mercy, and the traveler carries the names home as the journey's final provision.
